declaration, worked out once per type.

Package redact renders values, JSON documents, text and log attributes for
DISPLAY with their secrets replaced — a member whose name says it is one, a
struct field declared secret, the credentials of a URL — and within a byte
bound. It never mutates what it is given.

It is for showing data to a person: a developer console, a trace viewer, a
log panel, an error page. It is not an access control and it is not a
sanitiser for data that goes back into a system: a redacted document is a
different document, and a secret spelled in a way no rule recognises — a
password in a member called "p", a key pasted into free text — is shown.
What IS recognised is stated in each rule's own comment, so nobody has to
guess.

It implements the internal/core/security/redact port: the Redactor
interface, the values a caller compares results against — Placeholder,
Ellipsis, MinBytes, Unencodable, DocumentValue — and the domain's two codes
are declared there (ADR 0160). What is here is the engine and its
construction parameters (ADR 0074).

Package redact — hosts the compile-time interface assertion, keeping it out
of the production source so the runtime binary carries no diagnostic-only
declaration.

Package redact — text: the credentials of a URL, and a cut that respects
runes.

packages.name: secret
packages.doc:
Package secret — the read-only store over the process environment, with the
NAME_FILE convention Docker and Kubernetes secrets use.

Package secret — the file store: a directory the store owns, one record per
secret published atomically through vfs, writers serialised across
processes through the lock domain, and optional sealing at rest.

Package secret — the file store's construction parameters and the checks
that refuse a directory the store cannot keep secrets in.

Package secret — the file store's on-disk record: one JSON document per
secret, sealed when the store has a key.

Package secret — the file store's honest refusal where its mechanics do not
exist (ADR 0018 §(a): a uniform typed sentinel, never a silent downgrade and
never a build break).

The store rests on vfs.NewOS, which refuses the same platforms for reasons
its own osguard_other.go records: on Windows a directory cannot be flushed,
so a published name and the bytes it names can disagree after a crash, and
a permission mode is not an ACL, so 0600 would exclude nobody. A secret
store that reported success while doing neither is the one this domain
exists not to ship. The memory and environment stores work everywhere.

Package secret — the file store's platform gate, on the platforms that have
what it rests on: vfs's atomic publication with a flushed directory entry,
permission bits that exclude other accounts, and the lock domain's flock(2).

Package secret — the machine-local key file: one crypto.Key, created on
first use, the same key for every process that asks at once.

Package secret — the keyring: the versions of one secret seen as keys.

Package secret — a keyring read once: the root view a pass over many
wrapped keys uses.

Package secret — the in-process store.

Package secret — the rotator: a policy that mints new versions of one
secret on a schedule, keeping enough old ones that nothing sealed before a
rotation breaks because of it.

Package secret — the subject box: what SubjectKeys.Seal returns, and the
associated data it and a wrapped key are bound to.

Package secret — the bounded cache of opened subject keys, and the order it
keeps between filling an entry and destroying a key.

Package secret — subject keys: one data key per subject, wrapped by a root
keyring that rotates, and destroyed to erase everything it sealed (ADR 0142).

Package secret — the in-process subject-key store.

Package secret — what a rotation of the root costs the subject keys: one
re-wrap per subject, and a version kept while a key still needs it.

Package secret provides the concrete secret stores — in memory, the process
environment, a directory on disk — the Keyring that sees one secret's
versions as keys, and the Rotator that mints new versions on a schedule
(ADR 0096). Every store implements core/security/secret.Store.

This file holds the argument checks every store applies identically and the
version arithmetic they share, so that three backends cannot disagree about
what a valid Put or a correct prune is.

Package secret — the two ways this package turns a failure into a verdict:
storeFailure, around the error a caller's SubjectKeyStore returned, and
wrapAs, around one of the domain's sentinels. Every sentinel and code it
raises is declared in internal/core/security/secret (ADR 0160); this
package declares none.

No Public, Private or field built here carries a secret, a data key or a
sealed box. A secret's name, a version number, an environment variable's
NAME, a valid subject reference and an operation may travel as log-only
fields; a file path does not, because the directory a store owns is a
deployment detail an error has no reason to repeat.

packages.name: session
packages.doc:
Package session — the components ABOVE the store directory, which no flag on
an open can reach.

# What this closes

FileConfig.Dir is a path, and every component of it is a name somebody else
may have created. Measured against the store as it shipped, on darwin/arm64:
a symbolic link planted at a parent component inside a world-writable sticky
directory — the shape /tmp has — was followed by os.MkdirAll, the directory
check then judged the TARGET, and the store was built and filed every record
under the planter's tree:

	Dir demandé    = …/pub/app/sessions     (pub is 1777, app -> …/elsewhere)
	NewFileStore   : err=<nil>
	New            : err=<nil>
	record landed under the planted target = true

The owner-only rule on Dir could not see it, because the directory it judged
was a perfectly private 0700 one: the planter's, or one the store created
inside the planter's tree.

# The rule is the lock domain's, and so is the reason for it

internal/service/app/lock closed the same gap for its lock directory (ADR 0083),
on internal/kernel/fs/pathchain, and this is the same rule over the same walk:
an indirection is refused when the directory HOLDING it is world-writable —
when anybody could have planted it — and the sticky bit exempts nothing,
because planting a component CREATES an entry rather than unlinking one.

It is not "refuse a link". /tmp is a symbolic link on macOS, /var/run is one
on most Linux distributions, and every t.TempDir() on macOS resolves through
/var -> /private/var. What separates those from an attack is not the link,
it is the directory the link lives in: one only root can write was set up by
root.

# What it does not see, and what does

The audit runs once, at construction, BEFORE os.MkdirAll — auditing after it
would mean refusing the directory only after creating it inside the
planter's tree. A component replaced AFTER it returns is not seen by it; that
half is closed by a different mechanism: the store holds its directory as an
os.Root from construction on and resolves every name against that handle, so
a parent swapped later moves nothing (see file_store.go).

Package session — constant-time comparison of the values that name a session.

Package session — the in-memory store's construction parameters.

Package session — the at-rest framing of a record.

Package session — the file store's construction parameters.

Package session — one name in the store's held directory: what is there, and
an open that never reads or locks through an indirection planted at it.

# What this closes

Measured against the store as it shipped, on darwin/arm64:

	symbolic link at <digest>.session -> a copy kept outside the directory
	Load : err=<nil> where="outside"      (served from the link's target)

	symbolic link at .lock -> a path that does not exist yet
	NewFileStore : err=<nil>, and the link's target now exists

os.ReadFile and os.OpenFile follow a link at the final component, so the
first served a session from a file the planter chose and the second created
a file wherever the link pointed and took the store-wide lock on it. Writes
were never redirected — rename(2) replaces a link rather than following it —
which is why this file is about the two OPENS.

# Why not O_NOFOLLOW, which is what internal/service/app/lock uses

Because the store no longer opens anything by path. Every name resolves
against the os.Root held since construction (file_store.go), which is what
keeps a parent swapped after construction from moving the store — and
os.Root has no O_NOFOLLOW: it ORs the flag in itself and then resolves the
link on the caller's behalf, confined to the root (go1.27,
src/os/root_unix.go, rootOpenFileNolog). syscall.Openat, which would take
the flag relative to a held directory, exists in go1.27 for linux, aix and
wasip1 only (ADR 0083), so it cannot serve darwin or the BSDs.

So the refusal is spelled with what os.Root does offer, in two halves:

  - LOOK FIRST. Lstat through the held directory, which does not follow, and
    refuse a name that is a link — or anything but a regular file — before
    anything opens it. A dangling link is never followed into creating its
    target, and a FIFO is never opened, so it cannot park the reader while
    it holds the store-wide lock.
  - THEN PROVE THE HANDLE. A name swapped between the look and the open is
    followed by os.Root — inside the store directory only, since os.Root
    refuses a link that leaves it — and is caught by comparing the opened
    handle with what the name was: os.SameFile on the fstat of the handle.
    Nothing is read from, or locked on, a handle that fails it.

The two together are what O_NOFOLLOW gives on a path: the open never USES a
file the name did not lead to. They do not prevent the follow inside the
store directory during that race, and the only account that can race it
there is one that can already write a 0700 directory it does not own.

Package session — the file store's reading half, and the lock around it.

Package session — the small filesystem helpers behind atomic publication.

Package session — the on-disk store.

Package session — the file store's writing half.

Package session — the honest refusal on platforms without the mechanics the
file store requires (ADR 0018 §(a): a uniform typed sentinel where a
platform has no native mechanic, never a silent drop and never a build
break).

# Why Windows is refused rather than approximated

The file store's first guarantee is that a session record is unreadable by
any account but the one that wrote it. On Windows, Go's os.Chmod maps a
FileMode to the read-only attribute and nothing else: 0600 does not describe
an ACL, and a file created in a directory with an inheritable permissive DACL
is readable by whoever that DACL admits.

# The reason this file used to give is no longer the reason

It said the right DACL needs CreateFileW with a security descriptor "which
stdlib syscall does not expose". That stopped being the obstacle with ADR
0081 and ADR 0084: the kernel binds LockFileEx from kernel32
(internal/kernel/fs/flock) and GetNamedSecurityInfoW and GetAce from
advapi32 (internal/kernel/fs/winacl) through syscall.NewLazyDLL, with no new
dependency, and the same mechanism reaches every advapi32 export. What is
still missing is two things, and neither of them is a reuse of that code:

  - An owner-only DACL, BUILT and then VERIFIED. The kernel's reader
    (winacl.GrantsAnyone, ADR 0084/0086/0095) builds nothing, and the one
    question it answers — does an identifier meaning ANYBODY, Everyone,
    Authenticated Users or BUILTIN\Users, hold a right — is weaker than this
    store's rule: 0700 and 0600 exclude every other account, a named
    colleague included. A directory granting read to one named principal
    passes the reader and fails the Unix rule, so reusing it would ship a
    weaker guarantee under the same name. Applying a protected owner-only
    DACL at creation is new ABI (SetNamedSecurityInfoW, or a
    SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES on the create), with its own tests.
  - A directory flush. Every rename and unlink here is followed by an fsync
    of the directory, which is what makes Destroy a revocation a power cut
    cannot undo. Windows has no equivalent — FlushFileBuffers on a directory
    handle returns ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED (ADR 0056 D10) — which is why
    internal/service/data/vfs refuses Windows as well.

The lane that would hold a Windows store to ADR 0018's runtime bar is not
missing: e2e-cross's Windows job runs this package, where the store's suites
skip today because the store is refused — a green cross-compile alone would
not clear that bar.

The lock half is the one piece that exists: the kernel's LockFileEx (ADR
0081) could serialise this store's read-modify-write, and it is what
[fileStore.takeFlock] would call there. It is not enough on its own.

Approximating the rest — calling os.Chmod(0600), observing no error, skipping
the directory flush, and reporting success — would produce exactly the store
this domain refuses to be: one that makes a security claim it cannot keep,
on the platform where nobody would think to check. So the constructor
returns the typed proc.UnsupportedPlatform and the caller chooses a memory
store, an external store, or another host. Nothing past that refusal is
reachable here, the lock calls included.

Package session — the platform gate the file store reads, and the one
question a mode can answer here and cannot on Windows.

The file store rests on three guarantees, and only two of them are portable.
Atomic publication is rename(2), which POSIX requires to be atomic and which
Go's os.Rename also provides on Windows through MoveFileEx. Restrictive
permissions and advisory locking are not: they are the reason this file has a
build tag and a sibling that refuses. The lock itself is the kernel's
(internal/kernel/fs/flock, polled by [fileStore.takeFlock]); what stays here
is the gate that says both mechanics exist, and [plantable], which a mode
can answer here and cannot on Windows.

Package session — the in-process store.

Package session — the in-process store's writing half.

Package session — minting a session identifier from a random source.

Package session — the stored form of a session.

Package session — the AEAD sealer that renders an identifier as a cookie
value.

Package session implements the server-side session domain declared in
internal/core/security/session (ADR 0045): two concrete stores — one in memory, one on
disk — and the AEAD sealer that renders a session identifier as a cookie
value.

Both stores answer the same contract and differ only in where the record
lives and how long it survives. The memory store dies with the process; the
file store survives a restart, is confined to one host, and makes real
operating-system guarantees that this package refuses to fake where the
mechanism does not exist (see file_store.go and fsguard_unix.go).

Nothing here waits on the wall clock. Every deadline is read from an injected
kernel/clock.Clock, so an expiry test advances a ManualClock instead of
sleeping. The narrow half of the port is deliberate: a session store READS
time, it never waits on it, so it takes Clock rather than Timed.

Package session — the deadline policy shared by every store.

packages.name: token
packages.doc:
Package token — one JWK Set member, with its binding already derived.

Package token — the three numeric limits a verification policy resolves.

Package token — the claims <-> JSON conversion shared by both formats.

JWT and PASETO agree on the seven registered claim NAMES and disagree on
their value encodings: JWT writes NumericDate (RFC 7519 §2) and allows "aud"
to be a string or an array of strings; PASETO writes RFC 3339 timestamps and
allows exactly one audience. So the traversal is written once and the two
encodings are a [claimShape] each — rather than two claim decoders that
would drift apart on everything except the part that actually differs.

Package token — the one-pass, string-aware JSON nesting counter.

Package token — the Ed25519 signing binding.

Package token — the bounded wire primitives every format here goes through:
segment splitting, strict base64url, JSON depth and duplicate-member checks,
and PASETO's pre-authentication encoding.

Every function in this file runs on ATTACKER-CONTROLLED bytes before any key
is touched, so each one is O(len(input)) with a bound checked first and no
allocation proportional to a count the attacker chooses.

Package token — the ECDSA P-256 signing binding.

Package token — the HMAC-SHA-256 binding.

Package token — the JWT issuing policy.

Package token — the JWT/JOSE claim-value encoding.

Package token — JSON string rendering that cannot fail.

encoding/json's Marshal returns an error no string or []string can ever
produce, and discarding it at a dozen call sites is how a real failure
somewhere else eventually gets discarded too. Rendering the two shapes this
package actually emits by hand removes the error channel instead of ignoring
it — and removes a reflective encode from every mint.

Package token — verification against a JWK or a JWK Set.

This file holds the ONLY run-time algorithm selection in the package, and the
selector is the KEY, never the token. A relying party fetched the key set
from a publisher it trusts; the "kty"/"crv" members are that publisher's
statement about their own key, and deriving the algorithm from them is
exactly as trustworthy as the key itself. Deriving it from the token's "alg"
header would be trusting the attacker's statement about the relying party's
key — which is algorithm confusion, spelled out.

Package token — JWS Compact Serialization (RFC 7515): the header, and the
algorithm gate every verifier runs before a key reaches a primitive.

Package token — the JWS compact issuer.

Package token — the parsed, not-yet-authenticated shape of a compact token.

Package token — the single-key JWS compact verifier.

Package token — the JWT constructor set: one per algorithm, each accepting
only the Go key type its algorithm can use.

That is not documentation. NewHS256Verifier's parameter is a
core/crypto.Key — a struct with an unexported field — so the classic
confusion bug, handing it an EC or RSA public key so the attacker can sign
with the public half, is a call that does not compile.

Package token — the algorithm-bound key contracts and their constructors.

This file is where algorithm confusion is made unwritable. Each binding
holds ONE Go key type and reports ONE algorithm, and the bind* helpers below
are the only way to build one. There is no `bind(alg, []byte)`, because a
function that takes an algorithm name and a bag of bytes is a function whose
caller can be talked into passing a public key where a shared secret goes.

Package token — PASETO v4.public: the constructors and the scheme gate.

PASETO is the format that answers the question "what if the algorithm were
not negotiable". Its header is a version and a purpose — "v4.public." —
baked into the signed bytes through the pre-authentication encoding, so
there is no "alg" field to substitute and algorithm confusion has nothing to
grip. This implementation still binds the key type at construction, because
the property should hold for the same reason on both formats rather than by
accident on one of them.

Only v4.public ships. See the package CLAUDE.md §PASETO for v4.local.

Package token — the PASETO v4.public issuer.

Package token — the PASETO v4.public issuing policy.

Package token — the PASETO claim-value encoding.

Package token — the PASETO v4.public verifier.

Package token — the PASETO v4.public verification policy.

Package token — the validated, defaults-applied form of a verification
config, so the checks run once at construction rather than once per token.

Package token implements the two concrete security-token formats behind the
core/security/token ports: JWT over JWS Compact Serialization (RFC 7519 + RFC 7515)
and PASETO v4.public. It is stdlib-only and composes the SDK's own crypto
schemes — HMAC-SHA-256 from service/crypto/mac/hmacsha2, Ed25519 from
service/crypto/sign/ed25519sig — so it adds no dependency to internal/service.

# Algorithm confusion is prevented by the constructor set, not by a check

There is no NewVerifier(alg, key) here, and there is no verifier that reads
the token's "alg" header to decide what to do. There is one constructor per
algorithm, each accepting only the ONE Go type that algorithm can use:

	NewHS256Verifier(secret crypto.Key,     cfg VerifierConfig)
	NewES256Verifier(pub *ecdsa.PublicKey,  cfg VerifierConfig)
	NewEdDSAVerifier(pub ed25519.PublicKey, cfg VerifierConfig)

The textbook algorithm-confusion bug — an RSA/EC public key handed to
HMAC-SHA-256 as a shared secret, so that anybody holding the public key can
mint tokens — is a call that does not compile here: *ecdsa.PublicKey is not
a crypto.Key and never converts to one. Verification then compares the
header against the binding and refuses a mismatch with
coretoken.AlgorithmMismatch, before any key reaches any primitive.

[NewVerifierFromJWK] and [NewSetVerifier] are the only places an algorithm is
chosen at run time, and they choose it from the KEY's "kty"/"crv" — material
the relying party fetched from a trusted publisher — never from the token.

# What is refused, always

  - "alg":"none" in any capitalisation (RFC 7519 §6), with no option to
    enable it: the core Algorithm enum has no value that spells it.
  - a non-empty "crit" header (RFC 7515 §4.1.11).
  - a token past the configured size, or claims past the configured nesting
    depth, both checked before any decode.
  - a repeated JSON member in the header or the claims (RFC 8725 §2.6).
  - a token with no "exp", unless the profile opts out explicitly.

See the package CLAUDE.md for the RFC 8725 coverage table, including the
sections this package does NOT address.

Package token — hosts compile-time interface assertions
— keeping them out of the production
source so the runtime binary carries no diagnostic-only declarations.

Package token — the claim validation both formats share.

Everything here runs AFTER the signature has verified, and that ordering is a
security property, not an implementation detail: reporting "expired" for a
token whose signature was never checked tells an attacker what is inside a
forgery, and hands the application a claim set it may log.

Package token — the JWT verification policy.

symbols.name: Action
symbols.doc:
Action is what one command DOES. It receives the context [Executor.Execute]
was called with — a cancelled context is how a caller aborts a running
command — and the resolved [InvocationValue].

Returning a non-nil error is how a command fails. If it is an *errs.Error
the SDK's origin-wins rule (CLAUDE.md rule 6) preserves its Code and its
exit status all the way out of Execute, so a command's own exit status is
never overwritten by the framework that called it.

symbols.name: AmbiguousCommand

code.public: A command may declare an action or sub-commands, not both

symbols.doc:
AmbiguousCommand is returned by the constructor for a command carrying
both a Run and Commands.

The refusal is not fastidiousness. With both, `tool db migrate` means
"run db with the positional argument migrate" — until somebody adds a
child named migrate, at which point the identical command line means
something else, in a release that changed no line of db's own code. A
declaration whose meaning depends on which siblings exist today is the
same class of failure as prefix matching, and it is refused for the same
reason.

symbols.name: Binder
symbols.doc:
Binder declares one command's flags onto the set that will parse them.

It is handed the stdlib's *[flag.FlagSet] deliberately: every flag type the
stdlib ships, and every [flag.Value] a caller has already written, works
here with no adapter. The set is fresh, its name is the command path, and
its error handling is always [flag.ContinueOnError].

A Binder MUST only touch the set it is given, and MUST be safe to call more
than once: the engine runs it once at construction to validate the
declaration and to render help, and once per invocation to parse.

# What concurrency the SDK cannot give you

The engine keeps no per-invocation state, so two concurrent
[Executor.Execute] calls do not interfere. A Binder, however, usually writes
into a variable the CALLER closed over — fs.IntVar(&port, …) — and that
variable is the caller's, invisible to the SDK and written by every
concurrent invocation. Concurrent execution is therefore safe only when the
Binder allocates its destination per call (fs.Int, fs.String, …) and the
[Action] reads it back through [InvocationValue.Flags]. That is what those
sets are for. The alternative would be the SDK taking a lock around memory
it does not own, for a duration it cannot know.

symbols.name: CodeAmbiguousCommand
symbols.doc:
CodeAmbiguousCommand identifies a declaration refused for carrying BOTH a
Run and Commands, where the meaning of an existing command line would change
the day a child is added.

symbols.name: CodeCommandPanicked
symbols.doc:
CodeCommandPanicked identifies an Action whose goroutine panicked; the
engine recovered it, captured the originating stack, and turned it into this
command's failure so main still gets a typed exit status instead of the
runtime's 2.

symbols.name: CodeDuplicateCommand
symbols.doc:
CodeDuplicateCommand identifies a declaration refused because two children
of one group share a name, so the resolver could only ever reach one of
them.

symbols.name: CodeHelpWriteFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeHelpWriteFailed identifies a help request (-h) whose answer the
diagnostic stream did not take: a closed pipe, a full disk, a writer that
accepted only part of the page. Asking a question is not a failure, but an
answer nobody received is, so this is EX_IOERR and not the 0 a delivered
help earns.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidCommand
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidCommand identifies a declaration refused because the command
could never be reached or could never run: a blank name, a name carrying a
space or leading "-", a child with no summary, or neither a Run nor any
Commands.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidFlags
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidFlags identifies a flag vector package flag refused: an unknown
flag, a missing value, or a value its flag.Value could not parse. flag's own
text is preserved in Private, never in Public, because it quotes the
operator's value verbatim.

symbols.name: CodeMissingCommand
symbols.doc:
CodeMissingCommand identifies a group invoked with no sub-command at all. A
group has no action of its own, so this is an incomplete command line and
never a successful no-op.

symbols.name: CodeReservedFlag
symbols.doc:
CodeReservedFlag identifies a declaration refused because its Binder bound
"h" or "help", the two names the domain answers itself.

symbols.name: CodeUnknownCommand
symbols.doc:
CodeUnknownCommand identifies an argument vector naming a sub-command the
group does not declare. The group's help — which lists every name it DOES
declare — has been written to the diagnostic stream by the time this is
returned.

symbols.name: CommandPanicked

code.public: The command panicked and was recovered

symbols.doc:
CommandPanicked is the failure of an Action that panicked.

It is recovered rather than left to the runtime for one reason that is
not "hiding the bug": a panicking Go program exits with status 2, which
sysexits gives no meaning and which several supervisors read as a usage
error. Nothing is lost — the recovered value AND the stack of the
goroutine that actually failed both travel as fields — and what changes
is that main, rather than the runtime, decides what the process does
next. It keeps the default EX_SOFTWARE (70): the command line was fine.

symbols.name: CommandValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Name string; Summary string; Description string; Flags Binder; Run Action; Commands []CommandValue}
symbols.canonical: struct{Name string; Summary string; Description string; Flags github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/cli.Binder; Run github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/cli.Action; Commands []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/cli.CommandValue}

fields.name: Name
fields.doc:
Name is the single token an operator types to reach this command. It is
compared by exact byte equality — there is deliberately no abbreviation
matching and no case folding, because both make the meaning of an
existing command line depend on which siblings exist today.

It must be non-empty, must contain no space, and must not begin with
"-": a name beginning with "-" could never be typed, since the parent's
flag parse would consume it as a flag and stop before it.

fields.name: Summary
fields.doc:
Summary is the one-line description listed beside this command in its
parent's help. It is required for a child, because a command listed with
no summary is a name an operator has to guess at.

fields.name: Description
fields.doc:
Description is the optional long form shown in this command's OWN help,
under the usage line. It may span several lines; it is written verbatim.

fields.name: Flags
fields.doc:
Flags declares this command's flags. A nil Binder is a working
declaration and means "this command takes no flags" — unlike a nil Run,
which is a real absence, a command with no flags is an ordinary command.

fields.name: Run
fields.doc: Run is what a LEAF does. Exactly one of Run and Commands is set.

fields.name: Commands
fields.doc:
Commands are a GROUP's children, in the order the help lists them. Two
children may not share a Name.

symbols.doc:
CommandValue declares one command. The tree it forms is the whole
declaration: the engine walks it to resolve an argument vector, and the help
renderer walks the SAME tree to render the text, so a command that exists
and a command that is documented are one fact rather than two.

A command is a LEAF or a GROUP, never both:

  - a leaf has [CommandValue.Run] and no [CommandValue.Commands];
  - a group has [CommandValue.Commands] and no Run.

Both other combinations are refused at construction. Neither Run nor
Commands is an inert command — a name an operator can type that does
nothing, which is exactly the zero value ADR 0031 refuses. Both is worse: it
makes `tool db migrate` mean "run db with the argument migrate" until
somebody adds a child named migrate, at which point the same command line
silently means something else. A declaration whose meaning changes when a
SIBLING is added is not a declaration.

CommandValue is a published concrete shape (pkg/v1/app/cli.Command aliases it),
so ADR 0040 applies: it may still change while the module is v0, said out
loud, and not after v1.

symbols.name: IsGroup
symbols.doc:
IsGroup reports whether this command dispatches to children rather than
running an [Action]. It reads the declaration rather than a flag set at
construction, so it answers the same on a CommandValue the caller has just
written and on one the engine has already validated.

symbols.name: DuplicateCommand

code.public: Two sub-commands are declared under the same name

symbols.doc:
DuplicateCommand is returned by the constructor when two children of one
group share a name. The resolver stops at the first match, so the second
declaration would be unreachable code that looks reachable.

symbols.name: Executor
symbols.doc:
Executor resolves an argument vector against a command tree and runs the
command it names.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the concrete engine stays unexported behind its constructor in
internal/service/app/cli.

symbols.name: Execute
symbols.doc:
Execute resolves args against the tree and runs the command it names.
args is the vector WITHOUT the program name — os.Args[1:] at a call
site — because a library that reads os.Args itself cannot be tested and
cannot be embedded.

It returns nil when the command succeeded AND when help was requested,
because asking for help is not a failure. Every other outcome is an
*errs.Error whose exit status the caller reads with errs.ExitCodeOf.

symbols.name: HelpWriteFailed

code.public: The help could not be written

symbols.doc:
HelpWriteFailed is returned when -h asked for the help and the
diagnostic stream did not take it.

Only the -h path returns it. After a bad command line the usage error is
the verdict and the help is the actionable half of it, so a failed write
there does not replace the status the operator's mistake earned.

symbols.name: InvalidCommand

code.public: The command declaration is not runnable and was refused

symbols.doc:
InvalidCommand is returned by the constructor for a command that could
never be reached or could never run. The fields name the path and the
clause that failed.

"Neither Run nor Commands" is the case worth naming: it is the inert
declaration ADR 0031 refuses. A name an operator can type that does
nothing looks configured, reports success, and is discovered only by
somebody wondering why the tool did not do the thing.

symbols.name: InvalidFlags

code.public: The flags for this command could not be parsed

symbols.doc:
InvalidFlags is returned when package flag refuses the vector.

flag's own message quotes the operator's value ("invalid value \"abc\"
for flag -n"), so it lives in a field and in Private and never in
Public, which is the wire-safe half.

symbols.name: InvocationValue

fields.name: Path
fields.doc:
Path is the resolved command path, root first — {"tool", "db",
"migrate"}. It is what the help and every error message name the command
by, so a message and a shell prompt spell the same thing.

fields.name: Args
fields.doc:
Args are the positional arguments left after the LEAF's flags were
parsed: flag.FlagSet.Args of the last set in Flags.

It is nil when there were none, which is Go's ordinary spelling — len
and range answer identically for a nil and an empty slice, and manufacturing
an empty one would only hide that distinction from a caller who does not
need it.

fields.name: Flags
fields.doc:
Flags are the flag sets that parsed this invocation, root first, one per
element of Path; the leaf's own set is the last. A group's flags are
parsed by the group's set before its child's name is even read, which is
why they are separate sets and not one merged one.

The stdlib's set is handed over unchanged rather than wrapped, so
Lookup, Visit, VisitAll, NFlag and Arg all work exactly as their
documentation says. Calling Parse on one again is not defended against:
the engine has already parsed it, and re-parsing it is a caller's bug
the SDK cannot distinguish from a caller's intent.

fields.name: Output
fields.doc:
Output is the writer this command may print to. It is never nil.

It is NOT os.Stdout unless the caller said so: ADR 0030 makes stdout a
protocol channel that no SDK default may claim, so the zero
configuration resolves this to os.Stderr and a tool whose output IS a
protocol sets it explicitly, in main, on one visible line. An Action is
handed the writer precisely so it never has to reach for a stream
itself.

symbols.doc:
InvocationValue is one resolved command line: which command was reached,
what was left over after its flags were parsed, the sets that parsed them,
and the writer the command may print to.

InvocationValue is a published concrete shape (pkg/v1/app/cli.Invocation aliases
it), so ADR 0040 applies: it may still change while the module is v0, said
out loud, and not after v1.

symbols.name: Leaf
symbols.doc:
Leaf returns the flag set of the command that is actually running — the last
element of [InvocationValue.Flags] — or nil when the command declared no
flags anywhere on its path.

It exists so a caller reading its own flags does not index a slice whose
length is a property of how deep the command happens to sit in the tree.

symbols.name: MissingCommand

code.public: This command needs a sub-command

symbols.doc:
MissingCommand is returned when a group is invoked with nothing after
its flags.

It is a failure and not a quiet success on purpose: a group declares no
action, so `tool db` did nothing, and a script that read exit status 0
there would treat "I forgot the verb" as "the migration ran".

symbols.name: ReservedFlag

code.public: The flag names -h and -help are answered by the SDK

symbols.doc:
ReservedFlag is returned by the constructor when a Binder bound "h" or
"help".

The domain answers both names itself, and it must: package flag reports
an undefined -h as flag.ErrHelp rather than as a parse failure, and that
is the ONLY signal distinguishing "the operator asked for help" (exit 0)
from "the operator got it wrong" (exit 64). A command that binds -h
takes that signal away, and the engine would report a successful parse
where an operator expected a help page.

symbols.name: UnknownCommand

code.public: That sub-command does not exist

symbols.doc:
UnknownCommand is returned when a token does not name any child of the
group that was reached.

There is deliberately no "did you mean …?". The group's help has already
been written, and it lists every name that WOULD have worked — which is
the complete answer, cannot be wrong, and costs no edit-distance table
to keep correct. A suggestion is a second answer that can differ from
the first.

symbols.name: CodeConfigDecodeFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeConfigDecodeFailed identifies a merged-map → target-struct decode failure (type
mismatch, malformed value).

symbols.name: CodeConfigKeyMissing
symbols.doc:
CodeConfigKeyMissing identifies a load in which the schema declared a key
REQUIRED and no source supplied it. It is a load outcome, not a construction
one: the schema was well-formed, the deployment was not. Every missing key is
named in one error — an operator who restarts a service to discover the next
one is the failure a report prevents.

symbols.name: CodeConfigSchemaInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeConfigSchemaInvalid identifies a Schema refused AT CONSTRUCTION: a
malformed key, a key that names nothing in the target type, a duplicate key,
a default value that cannot travel through the loader's JSON round trip, or a
default that violates the very constraint the schema declares for its own key.
It is never a load outcome — no source was ever read.

symbols.name: CodeConfigSourceFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeConfigSourceFailed identifies a Source.Load that failed to read its backing
store (missing file, unreadable env, etc.).

symbols.name: CodeConfigUnknownKey
symbols.doc:
CodeConfigUnknownKey identifies a load in which a source supplied a key the
target type cannot address. The default is to REFUSE it, because the usual
cause is a typo in an environment variable and the usual symptom of ignoring
it is a production incident in which a setting silently never applied.

symbols.name: CodeConfigValidationFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeConfigValidationFailed identifies a decoded config whose Validate() returned an
error (the wrap cause is the validation error).

symbols.name: CodeConfigWatchFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeConfigWatchFailed identifies a Watcher that could not observe its source (stat
failure, unsupported target).

symbols.name: ConfigDecodeFailed

code.public: The configuration could not be decoded into the target

symbols.doc: ConfigDecodeFailed wraps a merged-map → struct decode failure.

symbols.name: ConfigKeyMissing

code.public: The configuration is missing required keys

symbols.doc:
ConfigKeyMissing is returned by a LOAD when the schema declares a key
required and no source supplied it. Its fields name every missing key —
all of them, in one error — and the count. It never names a value,
because a missing key has none and a neighbouring one may be a secret.

It is distinct from the validation domain's `required` rule on purpose,
and the difference is the one this domain exists to keep: this sentinel
answers "was the KEY supplied?", decided on the merged map while the key
is still a key; validation's `required` answers "is the VALUE non-zero?",
decided after the decode, where an absent key and an explicit zero are
the same bytes. `port = 0` satisfies this one and fails that one.

symbols.name: ConfigSchemaInvalid

code.public: The configuration schema cannot be built as declared

symbols.doc:
ConfigSchemaInvalid is returned by the Schema CONSTRUCTOR, never by a
load: the schema itself contradicts the type it declares, or contradicts
itself. Its fields name the key and the clause that failed and NEVER the
value, because a default may be a credential the author wrote in source.

It is the ADR 0031 half that must not be confused with the other: a
configuration with NO schema is legitimate and loads, while a schema that
declares a default outside the bounds it also declares would silently
produce an invalid configuration whenever the operator omitted the key —
a failure that appears only on the deployment where nobody set it.

symbols.name: ConfigSourceFailed

code.public: A configuration source could not be read

symbols.doc: ConfigSourceFailed wraps a Source.Load read failure.

symbols.name: ConfigUnknownKey

code.public: The configuration carries keys the target does not define

symbols.doc:
ConfigUnknownKey is returned by a LOAD when a source supplied a key the
target type cannot address, and the schema did not opt out of the check.

Refusing is the default because the alternative has a name: a typo in an
environment variable that passes silently. `APP_PORTT=9090` decodes into
nothing, the process starts on the old port, and the only evidence is the
absence of an effect. A schema is the statement "these are the keys I
read", so a key outside it is either a mistake or a deliberate one the
author opts into by name.

symbols.name: ConfigValidationFailed

code.public: The configuration failed validation

symbols.doc: ConfigValidationFailed wraps a decoded config's Validate() error.

symbols.name: ConfigWatchFailed

code.public: The configuration watcher could not observe its source

symbols.doc: ConfigWatchFailed wraps a Watcher observation failure.

symbols.name: DeclaredValue

fields.name: Key
fields.doc:
Key is the operator's key, in the dotted grammar
core/app/validation.JoinField produces — "database.max_conns", never
"MaxConns". A segment is one level of nesting in the merged map, so the
key an author declares here, the key an operator writes in a TOML table,
and the path a violation reports are the SAME string. That is the whole
reason the grammar is shared rather than reinvented: a message naming
something the operator never typed cannot be acted on.

A key with an empty segment, a leading or trailing separator, or no
counterpart in the target type is refused at construction — a default
nothing reads is worse than no default, because it looks configured.

fields.name: Value
fields.doc:
Value is the typed Go value the key takes when it is absent. It travels
the loader's ordinary path — marshalled to JSON with every other layer
and decoded by the same round trip — so a default cannot be typed by
rules a Source's value is not. A value the round trip cannot carry is
refused at construction rather than at the first load that needs it.

It is never echoed into an error: a default may be a placeholder
credential, and a refusal names the key and the clause instead.

symbols.doc:
DeclaredValue declares the value one configuration key takes when NO Source
supplied it. It is the domain's answer to the question every configuration
loader gets wrong: an absent key and a key explicitly set to the zero value
are different statements, and only one of them may be overridden.

A default is NOT a fallback applied to a zero value after decoding. It is a
LAYER, merged under every Source before the decode happens, so presence is
decided while the operator's key still exists as a key. `timeout = 0` in a
file therefore stays 0, and an omitted `timeout` becomes the default —
which a post-decode "if zero then default" can never distinguish.

The zero DeclaredValue declares nothing and is refused at construction: an
empty Key names no configuration.

A key that carries a default is never also REQUIRED. The two are mutually
exclusive and the contradiction is refused at construction, because a
required key the schema itself fills can never be missing — the requirement
would be a clause that cannot fire, and a rule that cannot fire is worse
than no rule: it is read as protection.

DeclaredValue is a published concrete shape (pkg/v1/app/config.Default aliases
it), so ADR 0040 applies: it may still change while the module is v0, said
out loud, and not after v1.

symbols.name: Describer
symbols.doc:
Describer is the optional sibling (ADR 0039) a [Source] implements to say
where its values come from. [Source] is frozen at one method, so the loader
discovers this capability by type assertion; a Source that does not
implement it is reported as [LayerSource] with its position.

Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use and MUST NOT return a value
in detail — a variable NAME, a file PATH, an endpoint, never what it holds.

symbols.name: Describe
symbols.doc:
Describe reports the kind of layer this source contributes and, for one
dotted key it supplied in its last Load, the detail an operator acts on.

symbols.name: LayerDefault
symbols.doc: LayerDefault is the schema's default layer, merged under every source.

symbols.name: LayerEnv
symbols.doc:
LayerEnv is the environment source; its detail is the VARIABLE that set
the key, such as "APP_DATA_DIR".

symbols.name: LayerFile
symbols.doc: LayerFile is a file source; its detail is the file's path.

symbols.name: LayerSource
symbols.doc:
LayerSource is a source that does not describe itself; its detail is
its position in the sources a load was given, counting from 0.

symbols.name: OriginValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Key string; Layer string; Detail string; Secret bool}
symbols.canonical: struct{Key string; Layer string; Detail string; Secret bool}

fields.name: Key
fields.doc: Key is the operator's key in the dotted grammar — "database.dsn".

fields.name: Layer
fields.doc:
Layer names the kind of layer that supplied the final value: one of the
Layer* constants, or the kind a [Describer] reports. It is EMPTY when the
key is absent from the merged layers — no layer supplied it, or a later
layer erased it by replacing one of its tables with a scalar or a null —
and the field then holds its Go zero value.

fields.name: Detail
fields.doc:
Detail is what an operator acts on: the variable that set the key, the
file that holds it. Empty when the layer has nothing more to say.

fields.name: Secret
fields.doc:
Secret reports that the key's field holds a core/security/secret.Value. The
origin never carries a value either way; Secret is what tells a
rendering that the value, if it shows one, must be masked.

symbols.doc:
OriginValue says which layer supplied the final value of one key of a load —
and says it WITHOUT the value, which is the point: an origin is written to a
start-up log, a --show-config table, a diagnostics page, and a
configuration value is routinely a password.

pkg/v1/app/config aliases it as Origin. It is a published shape the SDK RETURNS,
so ADR 0040 applies with its full cost after v1.

symbols.name: Source
symbols.doc:
Source yields a configuration layer as a flat map (later sources override
earlier ones in a Load). Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent Load.

symbols.name: Load
symbols.doc: Load reads the source and returns its key→value map (nil map = empty layer).

symbols.name: Validator
symbols.doc:
Validator is implemented by a decoded config struct that wants to self-check
after Load. A non-nil return aborts the Load with CONFIG_VALIDATION_FAILED.

symbols.name: Validate
symbols.doc: Validate reports whether the decoded configuration is internally consistent.

symbols.name: Watcher
symbols.doc:
Watcher observes a Source for change and invokes onChange (cross-OS poll in
the default implementation). Watch blocks until ctx is cancelled.

symbols.name: Watch
symbols.doc: Watch calls onChange whenever the underlying source changes, until ctx ends.

symbols.name: AdminPreconditionFailed

code.public: The administrative operation's precondition no longer holds

symbols.doc:
AdminPreconditionFailed is returned when a clearing or raising
operation names an alarm, version or contract that is not current.

symbols.name: AlarmID
symbols.doc:
AlarmID names an alarm by the index of the entry that raised it, so that a
clearing operation names the alarm it means to clear.

symbols.name: AuthenticatedPeerValue
symbols.spelled: struct{ID NodeID; Incarnation Incarnation; Slot string; SPKI [32]byte}

fields.name: ID
fields.doc: ID is the admitted member, 0 for a joiner.

fields.name: Incarnation
fields.doc: Incarnation is that member's incarnation.

fields.name: Slot
fields.doc: Slot is the slot the certificate's URI SAN names.

fields.name: SPKI
fields.doc: SPKI is the SHA-256 of the certificate's SubjectPublicKeyInfo.

symbols.doc:
AuthenticatedPeerValue is what the TLS handshake proved, never what a frame
claims. The certificate proves the slot and the key; the ID and the
incarnation are the member the transport admitted on that key. A peer that is
not yet a member, during a JOIN, has ID 0 and only Slot and SPKI set.

symbols.name: BatchingStateMachine
symbols.doc:
BatchingStateMachine is the sibling of a state machine that applies
committed commands in batches, one result slot per entry.

symbols.name: ApplyBatch
symbols.doc: ApplyBatch applies es in order and writes each result into results.

symbols.name: BootstrapRefused

code.public: The cluster cannot be bootstrapped

symbols.doc:
BootstrapRefused is returned when a listed peer already holds a history,
or the founding member lists differ.

symbols.name: ClusterID
symbols.doc:
ClusterID names one cluster: the founding, or a Recover or RestoreSnapshot
that started a new history. It is 16 bytes everywhere it is encoded, the URI
SAN included, where it is spelt in hex (see String).

symbols.name: IsZero
symbols.doc: IsZero reports whether the cluster id was never set.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc:
String renders the cluster id in lowercase hex, the form the certificate's
URI SAN carries.

symbols.name: ClusterMismatch

code.public: The peer belongs to another cluster

symbols.doc:
ClusterMismatch is returned when a peer's first frame names another
cluster or group.

symbols.name: CodeAdminPreconditionFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeAdminPreconditionFailed identifies an administrative operation that
named an alarm, version or contract that is not the current one.

symbols.name: CodeBootstrapRefused
symbols.doc: CodeBootstrapRefused identifies a bootstrap against a conflicting history.

symbols.name: CodeClusterMismatch
symbols.doc:
CodeClusterMismatch identifies a peer's first frame naming another cluster
or group.

symbols.name: CodeCompacted
symbols.doc: CodeCompacted identifies an index below the first retained one.

symbols.name: CodeConsensusMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeConsensusMisconfigured identifies a node refused at construction: a bound
missing or out of range, a timing rule broken, a lease without a drift.

symbols.name: CodeDataDirInUse
symbols.doc:
CodeDataDirInUse identifies an offline operation on a directory a live node
holds.

symbols.name: CodeDataDirLocked
symbols.doc: CodeDataDirLocked identifies a data directory another process holds.

symbols.name: CodeDataDirMismatch
symbols.doc:
CodeDataDirMismatch identifies a stamp naming another cluster, node or
incarnation.

symbols.name: CodeEntrySuperseded
symbols.doc:
CodeEntrySuperseded identifies a proposal whose position holds a COMMITTED
entry of another term: certainly not committed.

symbols.name: CodeEntryTooLarge
symbols.doc: CodeEntryTooLarge identifies a command above MaxEntryBytes.

symbols.name: CodeFrameInvalid
symbols.doc: CodeFrameInvalid identifies a frame that does not parse or is too large.

symbols.name: CodeHardStateCorrupt
symbols.doc: CodeHardStateCorrupt identifies an unreadable hard-state record.

symbols.name: CodeJoinRefused
symbols.doc: CodeJoinRefused identifies a pre-admission JOIN that was refused.

symbols.name: CodeLeadershipUnconfirmed
symbols.doc:
CodeLeadershipUnconfirmed identifies a barrier whose confirmation round did
not reach a majority in time.

symbols.name: CodeLineageMismatch
symbols.doc:
CodeLineageMismatch identifies a position, outbox identity or fence from
another LogIdentity lineage.

symbols.name: CodeLogCorrupt
symbols.doc: CodeLogCorrupt identifies damage to the log that is not a torn tail.

symbols.name: CodeLogQuarantined
symbols.doc: CodeLogQuarantined identifies a data directory carrying a quarantine marker.

symbols.name: CodeMembershipChangePending
symbols.doc:
CodeMembershipChangePending identifies a second membership change proposed
while one is still uncommitted.

symbols.name: CodeMembershipInvalid
symbols.doc: CodeMembershipInvalid identifies a membership change refused on its merits.

symbols.name: CodeNoSpace
symbols.doc: CodeNoSpace identifies a write refused while the no-space alarm is raised.

symbols.name: CodeNodeIDRetired
symbols.doc: CodeNodeIDRetired identifies a removed NodeID offered again.

symbols.name: CodeNodeStopped
symbols.doc: CodeNodeStopped identifies a call on a node that was closed or stopped itself.

symbols.name: CodeNotLeader
symbols.doc:
CodeNotLeader identifies a proposal that was certainly NOT appended, because
this node is not the leader and could not forward it.

symbols.name: CodeOutcomeUnknown
symbols.doc:
CodeOutcomeUnknown identifies a proposal that was appended, or possibly
delivered, and whose answer was lost. It may still commit.

symbols.name: CodeOverloaded
symbols.doc: CodeOverloaded identifies a proposal refused before append.

symbols.name: CodePayloadVersionRefused
symbols.doc:
CodePayloadVersionRefused identifies a proposal whose payload version is
above what some member announced.

symbols.name: CodePeerRejected
symbols.doc: CodePeerRejected identifies a peer whose certificate or key is not admitted.

symbols.name: CodeRecoverRefused
symbols.doc: CodeRecoverRefused identifies a Recover whose preconditions do not hold.

symbols.name: CodeRestoreRefused
symbols.doc:
CodeRestoreRefused identifies a RestoreSnapshot whose preconditions do not
hold.

symbols.name: CodeResultTypeMismatch
symbols.doc:
CodeResultTypeMismatch identifies an Apply result of another type than the
one ProposeAs asked for. The entry IS committed.

symbols.name: CodeSnapshotCorrupt
symbols.doc:
CodeSnapshotCorrupt identifies a snapshot whose digest or size does not match
its metadata.

symbols.name: CodeSnapshotTooLarge
symbols.doc: CodeSnapshotTooLarge identifies an announced snapshot above MaxSnapshotBytes.

symbols.name: CodeStateMachineFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeStateMachineFailed identifies a node whose Apply panicked or could not
complete. The entry IS committed.

symbols.name: CodeStopMarkerPresent
symbols.doc: CodeStopMarkerPresent identifies a node refused at start by a stop marker.

symbols.name: CodeStorageFailed
symbols.doc: CodeStorageFailed identifies a failed write, sync or read.

symbols.name: CodeTransferFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeTransferFailed identifies a leadership transfer whose target did not win
within one election timeout.

symbols.name: CodeTransportMisconfigured
symbols.doc: CodeTransportMisconfigured identifies a transport refused at construction.

symbols.name: CodeVersionUnsupported
symbols.doc:
CodeVersionUnsupported identifies an entry kind, record, frame or snapshot
version this node does not know.

symbols.name: Compacted

code.public: The requested log position has been compacted

symbols.doc:
Compacted is the answer for an index below the first retained one. It is
an expected outcome the engine acts on, never a failure.

symbols.name: ConsensusMisconfigured

code.public: The consensus node cannot be built from the given configuration

symbols.doc:
ConsensusMisconfigured is returned by a constructor whose configuration
it cannot honour: a bound out of range, a heartbeat not below a fifth of
the minimum election timeout, a lease without a stated clock drift, a
durability that disagrees with the state machine.

symbols.name: DataDirInUse

code.public: The data directory is in use by a running node

symbols.doc:
DataDirInUse is returned by an offline operation on a directory a live
node holds.

symbols.name: DataDirLocked

code.public: The data directory is held by another process

symbols.doc: DataDirLocked is returned when another process holds the data directory.

symbols.name: DataDirMismatch

code.public: The data directory belongs to another node or cluster

symbols.doc:
DataDirMismatch is returned when the stamp names another cluster, node
or incarnation, or an applied position cannot be trusted.

symbols.name: DurableStateMachine
symbols.doc:
DurableStateMachine is the sibling of a state machine that keeps its state
on disk: it persists the applied position atomically with the state that
entry produced, and the engine resumes after it.

symbols.name: AppliedPosition
symbols.doc:
AppliedPosition returns the log identity and the position of the last
entry whose effects are durable.

symbols.name: EntryClusterVersion
symbols.doc: EntryClusterVersion raises the protocol version every member must speak.

symbols.name: EntryCommand
symbols.doc: EntryCommand is a caller's command, handed to StateMachine.Apply.

symbols.name: EntryKind
symbols.doc:
EntryKind says what a log entry carries. Only [EntryCommand] reaches the
state machine; every other kind is the engine's own replicated state. A kind
a node does not know stops it with VERSION_UNSUPPORTED: it is never skipped.

symbols.name: Known
symbols.doc: Known reports whether the kind is one protocol version 1 defines.

symbols.name: EntryMembership
symbols.doc:
EntryMembership carries a whole new Membership and the change that
produced it. It takes effect when APPENDED.

symbols.name: EntryNoOp
symbols.doc:
EntryNoOp is the empty entry a new leader commits in its term before it
serves a read or accepts a membership change.

symbols.name: EntryNoSpaceClear
symbols.doc: EntryNoSpaceClear clears the no-space alarm it names.

symbols.name: EntryNoSpaceRaise
symbols.doc: EntryNoSpaceRaise raises the replicated no-space alarm.

symbols.name: EntrySuperseded

code.public: Another entry was committed at the proposal's position

symbols.doc:
EntrySuperseded is returned when a COMMITTED entry at the proposal's
index has another term: the proposal certainly did not commit.

symbols.name: EntryTimingContract
symbols.doc: EntryTimingContract carries a new committed timing contract.

symbols.name: EntryTooLarge

code.public: The proposed entry is too large

symbols.doc: EntryTooLarge is returned for a command above MaxEntryBytes.

symbols.name: EntryTransfer
symbols.doc: EntryTransfer records a leadership transfer and its operator.

symbols.name: EntryValue

symbols.canonical: struct{Position github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.PositionValue; Kind github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.EntryKind; Version uint32; BodySum uint32; ChainSum uint32; Data []byte; Token github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.TokenValue}

fields.name: Position
fields.doc: Position is the entry's term and index.

fields.name: Kind
fields.doc: Kind says what Data carries.

fields.name: Version
fields.doc:
Version is the payload version the proposer set; it selects the frozen
code path that applies the entry.

fields.name: BodySum
fields.doc: BodySum is the CRC-32C of Data, computed by the proposer.

fields.name: ChainSum
fields.doc:
ChainSum chains the previous entry's header: computed by the LEADER at
its serialized append point, verified at append and before Apply.

fields.name: Data
fields.doc:
Data is the payload: a command for EntryCommand, the engine's encoding
for the other kinds.

fields.name: Token
fields.doc:
Token is the entry's lineage-scoped command identity, set in memory by
the engine before Apply and never encoded in the log.

symbols.doc:
EntryValue is one record of the replicated log. Data is immutable once appended:
the store and the engine never write into it, and a caller that hands bytes
to Propose gives up their ownership.

symbols.name: FencedAttestationValue

fields.name: Voter
fields.doc: Voter is the old voter.

fields.name: Method
fields.doc: Method is how it was fenced: "stopped", "powered-off" or "cut".

fields.name: Receipts
fields.doc:
Receipts are Ed25519 signatures, one per witness key, over the old
cluster id, the new cluster id and the voter.

symbols.doc:
FencedAttestationValue is the operator's statement that an old voter was fenced
before a Recover: the voter, the method that fenced it, and one signed
receipt per witness (one per NAS).

symbols.name: FlagNeedSnapshot
symbols.doc:
FlagNeedSnapshot marks an append rejection from a node that holds no
usable snapshot and asks for one.

symbols.name: FlagNoLease
symbols.doc:
FlagNoLease marks a read the follower wants confirmed by a round, never
by a lease.

symbols.name: FlagProtocol2
symbols.doc:
FlagProtocol2 marks a frame from a node that speaks protocol version
2. It is the announcement D18 asks for: a node of protocol 1 tests
the bits it names only and ignores it, and a leader refuses to raise
the cluster version to 2 while a member's last frame of the term
lacks it.

symbols.name: FlagTransfer
symbols.doc:
FlagTransfer marks a vote request of a leadership transfer. It lifts the
live-leader refusal for ONE campaign, never the election restriction.

symbols.name: FlagTruncated
symbols.doc:
FlagTruncated marks an append rejection from a node that truncated
acknowledged entries through TruncateAndStaySilent: the leader lowers
its match to the node's log, the one exception to "match only grows".

symbols.name: FrameInvalid

code.public: A malformed frame was received

symbols.doc:
FrameInvalid is a frame that does not parse or exceeds MaxFrameBytes;
the connection closes.

symbols.name: FrameLane
symbols.doc:
FrameLane is the connection a frame belongs on: control, data or snapshot.
It is carried in the two high bits of the frame's type byte, so a transport
routes a frame of a type it does not parse.

symbols.name: GroupID
symbols.doc:
GroupID names a consensus group. v1 runs exactly one group, 1, and every
frame carries it so that a later version can multiplex groups without
changing the wire.

symbols.name: HardState
symbols.spelled: struct{Term uint64; Vote NodeID; Commit uint64}

fields.name: Term
fields.doc: Term is the node's current term.

fields.name: Vote
fields.doc: Vote is the candidate voted for in Term, 0 for none.

fields.name: Commit
fields.doc: Commit is the highest index known committed.

symbols.doc:
HardState is what a node must never forget: its term, its vote in that term
and the commit index it knows of. Term and vote are durable before any reply
depends on them; the commit index is written lazily, never above the last
synced index.

symbols.name: HardStateCorrupt

code.public: The consensus hard state is corrupt

symbols.doc:
HardStateCorrupt is an unreadable hard-state record or checkpoint; it is
never defaulted.

symbols.name: Incarnation
symbols.doc:
Incarnation is a random 128-bit value drawn when a data directory is first
stamped. A wiped machine that kept its certificate and its NodeID is still
a different incarnation, and is refused. It is an identifier, not a secret.

symbols.name: IsZero
symbols.doc: IsZero reports whether no incarnation was drawn.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String renders the incarnation in lowercase hex.

symbols.name: InstallAcceptValue
symbols.spelled: struct{SnapshotID string; Offset int64; Refused errs.Code; Held bool}
symbols.canonical: struct{SnapshotID string; Offset int64; Refused github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/errs.Code; Held bool}

fields.name: SnapshotID
fields.doc: SnapshotID is the snapshot answered.

fields.name: Offset
fields.doc:
Offset is the chunk-aligned ENCODED offset to resume from, 0 for a
fresh spool.

fields.name: Refused
fields.doc: Refused is zero, or why the offer is refused.

fields.name: Held
fields.doc:
Held reports that the receiver already holds the snapshot: an
idempotent success.

symbols.doc:
InstallAcceptValue is the receiver's answer to an offer. The RECEIVER chooses the
offset to resume from, from what it has durably spooled, so a resumed stream
never appends to bytes the receiver did not keep (D7, R8-21).

symbols.name: InstallOfferValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Term uint64; SnapshotID string; Meta SnapshotMetaValue}

fields.name: Term
fields.doc: Term is the sender's term.

fields.name: SnapshotID
fields.doc: SnapshotID equals Meta.ID.

fields.name: Meta
fields.doc: Meta describes the snapshot.

symbols.doc:
InstallOfferValue is what a leader sends before streaming a snapshot: the whole
metadata first, so the receiver refuses a snapshot too large, of another
version or already covered before a single byte of it is spooled (D7).

symbols.name: InstallParams
symbols.spelled: struct{Ctx context.Context; From AuthenticatedPeerValue; Offer InstallOfferValue; Offset int64; Body io.Reader}
symbols.canonical: struct{Ctx context.Context; From github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.AuthenticatedPeerValue; Offer github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.InstallOfferValue; Offset int64; Body io.Reader}

fields.name: Ctx
fields.doc: Ctx ends with the connection.

fields.name: From
fields.doc: From is the peer TLS authenticated.

fields.name: Offer
fields.doc: Offer is the accepted offer.

fields.name: Offset
fields.doc: Offset is the accepted offset.

fields.name: Body
fields.doc: Body is the encoded stream from Offset, ending with the connection.

symbols.doc:
InstallParams is what the transport hands the engine once bytes flow, after
the offer was accepted. Body ends with the connection: a stream cut short is a
short read, and the spool keeps its last whole chunk for the next offer.

symbols.name: JoinAuthorizer
symbols.doc:
JoinAuthorizer is the PRODUCT's port: a member calls it before it turns a
JOIN into an AddLearner. It decides whether the slot's previous member is
fenced, which only the product can know, and returns the Operator to record.

symbols.name: Authorize
symbols.doc: Authorize accepts or refuses the request.

symbols.name: JoinConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{Addresses []string; Stamp StampValue; Address string; Pins [][32]byte; MaxSnapshotBytes int64}
symbols.canonical: struct{Addresses []string; Stamp github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.StampValue; Address string; Pins [][32]byte; MaxSnapshotBytes int64}

fields.name: Addresses
fields.doc: Addresses are the members to try, in order.

fields.name: Stamp
fields.doc: Stamp is the joiner's stamp, from Init.

fields.name: Address
fields.doc: Address is where the joiner listens.

fields.name: Pins
fields.doc:
Pins are the SPKIs of the members the joiner trusts, from the
operator. An answer counts only from a peer presenting one of them,
and only when the membership it returns lists that peer under that
key; an empty list refuses the JOIN.

fields.name: MaxSnapshotBytes
fields.doc:
MaxSnapshotBytes is the joiner's own MaxSnapshotBytes, announced in
the JOIN so the members hold their cuts to it (R2-30); 0 announces
nothing, and the JOIN is the one a member that predates the
announcement reads.

symbols.doc:
JoinConfig is what a joining node needs to send its JOIN: where to reach the
members, and the stamp Init wrote, whose id and incarnation the member it
reaches proposes as a learner.

symbols.name: JoinReasonBinder
symbols.spelled: interface{BindJoinReason(group GroupID, join func(ctx context.Context, from AuthenticatedPeerValue, r JoinRequestValue) (PositionValue, errs.Code, string))}
symbols.canonical: interface{BindJoinReason(group github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.GroupID, join func(ctx context.Context, from github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.AuthenticatedPeerValue, r github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.JoinRequestValue) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.PositionValue, github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/errs.Code, string))}
symbols.doc:
JoinReasonBinder is the sibling of a transport that carries the reason of
a refused JOIN back to the joiner. A node that finds it binds this join
callback in place of Bind's: the reason is what the JoinAuthorizer chose
to say, sanitized and bounded, or the engine's own refusal, never more.

symbols.spelled: func(group GroupID, join func(ctx context.Context, from AuthenticatedPeerValue, r JoinRequestValue) (PositionValue, errs.Code, string))
symbols.canonical: func(group github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.GroupID, join func(ctx context.Context, from github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.AuthenticatedPeerValue, r github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.JoinRequestValue) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.PositionValue, github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/errs.Code, string))
symbols.doc:
BindJoinReason registers the group's JOIN callback that also returns
the refusal's reason, empty for none.

symbols.name: JoinRefused

code.public: The join request was refused

symbols.doc: JoinRefused is returned to a pre-admission JOIN that was refused.

fields.name: Cluster
fields.doc: Cluster is the cluster the joiner claims.

fields.name: ID
fields.doc: ID is the joiner's new NodeID.

fields.name: Incarnation
fields.doc: Incarnation is the joiner's incarnation.

fields.name: Slot
fields.doc: Slot is the slot its certificate names.

fields.name: SPKI
fields.doc: SPKI is its key, from the handshake.

fields.name: Address
fields.doc: Address is where it listens.

fields.name: MaxSnapshotBytes
fields.doc:
MaxSnapshotBytes is the largest snapshot the joiner accepts, as it
announced it; 0 when it announced none, as a joiner that predates
the announcement does.

symbols.doc:
JoinRequestValue is a pre-admission JOIN as a member received it: the slot and
the key from TLS, the new node's id and incarnation from its frame.

symbols.name: Joiner
symbols.doc: Joiner is the sibling a transport implements to carry a pre-admission JOIN.

symbols.name: Join
symbols.doc:
Join sends the JOIN and returns the position its AddLearner was
appended at.

symbols.name: LaneControl
symbols.doc: LaneControl carries votes, heartbeats, their replies and TimeoutNow.

symbols.name: LaneData
symbols.doc: LaneData carries entries, their acknowledgements and forwarded proposals.

symbols.name: LaneSnapshot
symbols.doc: LaneSnapshot carries snapshot streams.

symbols.name: LeadershipUnconfirmed

code.public: The leader could not confirm its leadership

symbols.doc:
LeadershipUnconfirmed is returned by Barrier when its round did not reach
a majority in time.

symbols.name: LeadershipWatcher
symbols.doc: LeadershipWatcher is the sibling of a node that notifies leadership changes.

symbols.name: Watch
symbols.doc:
Watch returns its OWN channel, of capacity one, holding the latest
status; it is unsubscribed and closed when ctx ends or the node closes.

symbols.name: LineageMismatch

code.public: The position belongs to another log lineage

symbols.doc:
LineageMismatch is returned for a position, outbox identity or fence
from another LogIdentity lineage.

symbols.name: LogCorrupt

code.public: The consensus log is corrupt

symbols.doc:
LogCorrupt is a CRC failure that is not a torn tail, or a gap in the
effective log. It is never repaired.

symbols.name: LogIdentityValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Cluster ClusterID; Epoch uint64; Predecessor ClusterID; PredecessorEpoch uint64; KeptIndex uint64; AdoptedFrom uint64}
symbols.canonical: struct{Cluster github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.ClusterID; Epoch uint64; Predecessor github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.ClusterID; PredecessorEpoch uint64; KeptIndex uint64; AdoptedFrom uint64}

fields.name: Cluster
fields.doc: Cluster is the cluster the log belongs to.

fields.name: Epoch
fields.doc: Epoch counts the histories of this cluster id: 1 at founding.

fields.name: Predecessor
fields.doc:
Predecessor is the cluster of the history this one was recovered from,
zero for a founding.

fields.name: PredecessorEpoch
fields.doc: PredecessorEpoch is the predecessor's epoch.

fields.name: KeptIndex
fields.doc:
KeptIndex is the last index Recover kept from the predecessor. An
applied position of the predecessor at or below it is still trusted
when its term is the one kept there: Recover adopts the verified
suffix past the commit the survivor persisted, which may hold
another term than the write the old cluster acknowledged.
Every node of the history applies the entries at or below it under the
predecessor's token: one admitted after the Recover learns it from the
snapshot it installs, never from an append.

fields.name: AdoptedFrom
fields.doc:
AdoptedFrom is the last index of the kept range the predecessor had
committed when Recover read it: the commit the survivor persisted,
or the snapshot a restore started from. An entry at or below it is
the one every node of the predecessor holds (Log Matching), so a
predecessor's token at or below it is trusted by its index once its
term can no longer be read; the adopted range above it, up to
KeptIndex, is not. 0 records nothing, and nothing is trusted that
way. It is recorded only in a cluster at protocol version 2, in the
stamp of the node Recover or RestoreSnapshot ran on: a snapshot does
not carry it, so a node that learns the lineage from one trusts
nothing that way (#509).

symbols.doc:
LogIdentityValue scopes positions: the ClusterID and a log epoch that Recover and
RestoreSnapshot bump, and the predecessor this history descends from with the
last index it kept. A position or a token from another identity is not
comparable with this log's.

symbols.name: Same
symbols.doc:
Same reports whether two identities name the same history (cluster and
epoch), whatever lineage they record.

symbols.name: LogQuarantined

code.public: The consensus log is quarantined

symbols.doc:
LogQuarantined is returned at start while the data directory carries a
quarantine marker; only ClearQuarantine lifts it.

symbols.name: LogReader
symbols.spelled: interface{Bounds() (first uint64, last uint64); Entries(lo uint64, hi uint64, maxBytes int, dst []EntryValue) ([]EntryValue, error); Term(index uint64) (uint64, error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Bounds() (first uint64, last uint64); Entries(lo uint64, hi uint64, maxBytes int, dst []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.EntryValue) ([]github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.EntryValue, error); Term(index uint64) (uint64, error)}
symbols.doc:
LogReader reads the log. Expected outcomes are answers, not failures: an
index below the first retained one is COMPACTED.

symbols.name: Bounds
symbols.doc: Bounds of an empty log after a snapshot at s are (s+1, s).

symbols.name: Entries
symbols.spelled: func(lo uint64, hi uint64, maxBytes int, dst []EntryValue) ([]EntryValue, error)
symbols.canonical: func(lo uint64, hi uint64, maxBytes int, dst []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.EntryValue) ([]github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.EntryValue, error)
symbols.doc:
Entries returns entries in [lo, hi), at most maxBytes, and always at
least one entry when lo < hi, even above maxBytes. lo below first is
COMPACTED.

symbols.name: Term
symbols.doc: Term answers for first-1 too, from the term kept at compaction.

symbols.name: LogStore
symbols.spelled: interface{Append(entries []EntryValue, hs *HardState) error; Close() error; CompactPrefix(through uint64) error; HardState() (HardState, error); Stamp() (StampValue, error); Sync() error; TruncateSuffix(from uint64) error; WriteStamp(StampValue) error; LogReader}
symbols.canonical: interface{Append(entries []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.EntryValue, hs *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.HardState) error; Close() error; CompactPrefix(through uint64) error; HardState() (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.HardState, error); Stamp() (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.StampValue, error); Sync() error; TruncateSuffix(from uint64) error; WriteStamp(github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.StampValue) error; github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/consensus.LogReader}
symbols.doc:
LogStore is the durable log. Term, vote and entries travel in one Append
and become durable under one Sync; readers see appended entries before they
are synced. One writer, many readers. When Sync and WriteStamp return nil,
what they cover survives a power loss: the safety of the whole domain rests
on it. FROZEN under ADR 0039.

symbols.name: Append
symbols.doc:
Append buffers entries and, when hs is not nil, a hard state, in ONE
record batch.

symbols.name: Close
symbols.doc: Close releases the store.

symbols.name: CompactPrefix
symbols.doc: CompactPrefix drops what a snapshot covers, through index through.

symbols.name: HardState
symbols.doc: HardState returns the last hard state appended.

symbols.name: Stamp
symbols.doc: Stamp returns the directory's stamp.

symbols.name: Sync
symbols.doc: Sync makes everything appended so far durable.

symbols.name: TruncateSuffix
symbols.doc:
TruncateSuffix writes ONE durable truncate record removing every entry
from index from on, and nothing else.

symbols.name: WriteStamp
symbols.doc: WriteStamp writes the stamp, durable on return.

fields.name: Incarnation
fields.doc: Incarnation is the node's data-directory incarnation.

fields.doc: Slot is the placement slot its certificate names.

MemberValue is one node of the membership: its identity, the key it is pinned
to, where it listens, and whether it votes.

symbols.name: MembershipChangePending

code.public: Another membership change is still pending

MembershipChangePending is returned while another membership change is
still uncommitted: one change at a time.

MembershipInvalid is returned for a change refused on its merits: an
unknown node, the last voter, a removal below MinVoters, a promotion
without durable progress, a change without a reachable majority.

fields.name: Index

fields.name: Members

fields.name: Retired

MembershipValue is the configuration at a position: its members and the set of
retired IDs, which is never reused.

symbols.name: Clone

Clone returns a deep copy, so that a membership handed out cannot be changed
under the engine.

symbols.name: IsRetired
symbols.doc: IsRetired reports whether the id was removed.

symbols.name: Member
symbols.doc: Member returns the member with that id.

symbols.name: Voters
symbols.doc: Voters returns the ids of the voters, in membership order.

symbols.name: MessageFlags
symbols.doc: MessageFlags are a message's boolean qualifiers.

symbols.name: MessageKind
symbols.doc:
MessageKind says what a Message is. The two high bits are its lane, so that
the frame header alone routes it (ADR 0152 D18).

symbols.name: Known
symbols.doc: Known reports whether protocol version 1 or 2 defines the kind.

symbols.name: Lane
symbols.doc: Lane returns the connection the kind belongs on.
