without a window keeps no such count, and reports zero.

fields.name: Failures
fields.doc:
Failures is, with a sliding window, how many of Calls failed; without
one, how many failures followed one another since the last success,
the count FailureThreshold is compared to.

fields.name: SlowCalls
fields.doc:
SlowCalls is how many of Calls lasted at least the window's
SlowAfter, failed or not. Zero without a window.

fields.name: Trips
fields.doc:
Trips counts the times the breaker opened on its own since it was
built — from Closed on its threshold, or from HalfOpen on a failed
trial. Isolate is not a trip.

fields.name: OpenUntil
fields.doc:
OpenUntil is when an Open breaker admits its next HalfOpen trial. It
is zero unless Phase is BreakerOpen, and zero for an isolated one,
which admits nothing until Reset.

symbols.doc:
BreakerStateValue is a circuit breaker's state as BreakerState.State
reports it: its phase and the counts that phase is decided on.

symbols.name: BulkheadFull

code.public: The call was rejected because the bulkhead is full

symbols.doc:
BulkheadFull is returned when every concurrency slot is occupied, and,
for a bulkhead that queues, when its queue is full or no slot freed
within its MaxWait.

symbols.name: CircuitOpen

code.public: The circuit breaker is open; the call was rejected

symbols.doc: CircuitOpen is returned when the breaker is Open and the call is rejected fast.

symbols.name: CodeBulkheadFull
symbols.doc:
CodeBulkheadFull identifies a call rejected because the bulkhead's concurrency
slots were all occupied — and, for a bulkhead that queues, its queue
was full or no slot freed within its MaxWait.

symbols.name: CodeCircuitOpen
symbols.doc:
CodeCircuitOpen identifies a call rejected fast because the circuit breaker is
in the Open state (the downstream is presumed unhealthy).

symbols.name: CodeFallbackFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeFallbackFailed identifies a fallback policy whose primary AND secondary
operations both failed on a live context (both errors travel as fields —
neither is dropped). A cancellation is reported as ctx.Err() instead.

symbols.name: CodePolicyMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodePolicyMisconfigured identifies a policy built with a configuration it
cannot honour, whose every call is refused without running the operation.

symbols.name: CodeRateLimited
symbols.doc:
CodeRateLimited identifies a call rejected because the rate limiter had
no token available, at once or within its MaxWait.

symbols.name: CodeRetryBudgetExceeded
symbols.doc:
CodeRetryBudgetExceeded identifies a retry policy that stopped before its
attempt budget because the shared retry budget refused the next attempt
(the last attempt's error is the wrap cause).

symbols.name: CodeRetryExhausted
symbols.doc:
CodeRetryExhausted identifies a retry policy that used its whole attempt
budget without a success (the last attempt's error is the wrap cause).

symbols.name: CodeThrottled
symbols.doc:
CodeThrottled identifies a call the adaptive throttle refused on the
client side, without sending it: the dependency had been refusing more
than its share of the calls recently sent to it.

symbols.name: CodeTimeoutExceeded
symbols.doc:
CodeTimeoutExceeded identifies an operation that did not complete within the
timeout policy's deadline.

symbols.name: FallbackFailed

code.public: The operation and its fallback both failed

symbols.doc:
FallbackFailed is returned when the primary operation AND the fallback
both failed. It is the policy's own outcome rather than either half's
error, so that neither can be dropped and neither can hijack the code:
both messages travel as the "primary" and "fallback" fields.

symbols.name: Operation
symbols.doc:
Operation is the unit of work a Runner guards. It MUST honour ctx
cancellation (return promptly when ctx.Done fires) so timeout/cancellation
propagate; a non-cancellable op caps a Timeout's precision at op granularity.

The port says nothing about idempotence, because most policies do not need
it: retry replays an Operation only after it has failed, and every other
policy runs it at most once. The hedging policy is the exception — it runs
copies CONCURRENTLY, so a non-idempotent Operation produces a double effect
(a double charge, a double insert) rather than a slow one. The SDK cannot
detect idempotence, so the hedging config makes the caller assert it in code
(HedgeConfig.Idempotent) instead of trusting a doc comment.

symbols.name: PolicyMisconfigured

code.public: The reliability policy was misconfigured and refused the call

symbols.doc:
PolicyMisconfigured is returned by every call to a policy that was built
with a configuration it cannot honour, in place of running the operation.
Unlike its siblings it is permanent, not transient (ADR 0031): the fix is
a code change at the construction site, never a retry.

symbols.name: RateLimited

code.public: The call was rejected by the rate limiter

symbols.doc:
RateLimited is returned when no token was available, at once or within
the limiter's MaxWait. A rejection by the SDK's limiters carries, as the field
retry_after_seconds, how long the bucket needs to earn the next token.

symbols.name: RetryBudget
symbols.doc:
RetryBudget bounds the extra attempts — retries and hedged duplicates —
that the policies sharing it may issue, so that during an outage every
call stops being multiplied by its attempt count. A call's FIRST attempt
never asks it: a budget throttles amplification, never traffic.

A sibling of Runner rather than a widening of it (ADR 0039): a budget is
not a policy that runs an Operation, it is a counter several policies
consult. NewRetryBudget is the SDK's implementation, the token bucket of
gRPC's retry throttling; a caller may supply their own.

Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use, and SHOULD not allocate:
AllowRetry and the two Record methods run on the retry's hot path.

symbols.name: AllowRetry
symbols.doc:
AllowRetry reports whether one more attempt beyond a call's first may
be issued now. It is a query: it spends nothing, and a policy that
asks it and then issues no attempt owes it nothing.

symbols.name: RecordFailure
symbols.doc:
RecordFailure records an attempt that failed in a way worth retrying,
which drains the budget. A deterministic failure, and a caller who left,
are not recorded.

symbols.name: RecordSuccess
symbols.doc: RecordSuccess records an attempt that succeeded, which replenishes the budget.

symbols.name: RetryBudgetExceeded

code.public: The operation failed and the retry budget refused another attempt

symbols.doc:
RetryBudgetExceeded wraps the last attempt's error when the shared retry
budget refused the next attempt: the dependency is failing for enough
callers that retrying would only multiply its load.

symbols.name: RetryExhausted

code.public: The operation failed after exhausting all retries

symbols.doc: RetryExhausted wraps the final attempt's error after the retry budget ran out.

symbols.name: Runner
symbols.doc:
Runner executes an Operation under a reliability policy and returns the
operation's error, a policy sentinel (RetryExhausted, RetryBudgetExceeded,
CircuitOpen, RateLimited, BulkheadFull, TimeoutExceeded, FallbackFailed,
Throttled), or ctx.Err().
Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use. Runners compose: a Runner
may itself invoke an inner Runner inside its Operation.

IFACE-PLUGIN: concrete policies (retry/breaker/...) implement this interface;
their concrete types stay unexported behind their constructors.

symbols.name: Throttled

code.public: The call was throttled on the client side

symbols.doc:
Throttled is returned when the adaptive throttle refused the call on
the client side, without sending it, because the dependency had been
refusing more than its share of the recent calls (Google SRE's
client-side throttling). It is transient: the probability of a refusal
falls as the dependency accepts again.

symbols.name: TimeoutExceeded

code.public: The operation exceeded its timeout

symbols.doc: TimeoutExceeded is returned when the operation outran the timeout deadline.

symbols.name: CodeDuplicateJob
symbols.doc:
CodeDuplicateJob identifies an Add refused because the entry's name is
already registered on this Scheduler.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidEntry
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidEntry identifies an Add refused because the entry could never
run: an empty name, a nil Job, or a nil Schedule.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidExpression
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidExpression identifies a cron expression this parser understands
the shape of but cannot accept: a malformed field, a value outside its
field's range, an inverted range, a non-positive step.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidInterval
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidInterval identifies a non-positive duration handed to Every,
which would be a schedule due infinitely often.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidLocation
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidLocation identifies a nil *time.Location handed to
ParseInLocation, which is what an unchecked time.LoadLocation looks like.

symbols.name: CodeJobPanicked
symbols.doc:
CodeJobPanicked identifies a Job that panicked; the scheduler recovered,
reported it as this entry's result, and kept running.

symbols.name: CodeSchedulerRunning
symbols.doc:
CodeSchedulerRunning identifies an Add or a second Run refused because the
Scheduler is already running.

symbols.name: CodeUnreachableSchedule
symbols.doc:
CodeUnreachableSchedule identifies a syntactically valid expression that
matches no instant on the calendar — "31 April", "30 February" — and is
therefore refused at construction rather than registered as a job that would
never run.

symbols.name: CodeUnsupportedSyntax
symbols.doc:
CodeUnsupportedSyntax identifies a cron construct that exists in some other
dialect and that this parser refuses BY NAME rather than by guessing: a
six-field (seconds) expression, @reboot, @every, and the Quartz L / W / # /
? operators.

symbols.name: DuplicateJob

code.public: A job is already registered under that name

symbols.doc: DuplicateJob is returned by Add when the entry's name is already taken.

symbols.name: EntryValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Name string; Schedule Schedule; Job Job; AllowOverlap bool; Overlap OverlapPolicy; StartingDeadline time.Duration}
symbols.canonical: struct{Name string; Schedule github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/scheduler.Schedule; Job github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/scheduler.Job; AllowOverlap bool; Overlap github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/scheduler.OverlapPolicy; StartingDeadline time.Duration}

fields.name: Name
fields.doc:
Name identifies the entry in results and errors. It must be non-empty
and unique within one Scheduler.

fields.name: Schedule
fields.doc: Schedule decides when the Job is due.

fields.name: Job
fields.doc: Job is the work to run.

fields.name: AllowOverlap
fields.doc:
AllowOverlap permits a fire while the previous run of THIS entry has not
returned. The zero value (false) skips that fire and reports it as
[ResultValue.Skipped] — the safe default, because the SDK cannot know
whether two concurrent copies of a Job are safe and the symptom of
getting it wrong is a duplicated side effect rather than an error.
Setting it is the caller's in-code assertion that concurrent copies are
safe, the same instrument resilience.HedgeConfig.Idempotent uses for the
same class of claim (ADR 0031). It is OverlapAllow written as a bool,
kept because it was there first; set with any Overlap but
OverlapSkip or OverlapAllow, Add refuses the entry.

fields.name: Overlap
fields.doc:
Overlap is what a fire does while the previous run of THIS entry has
not returned: OverlapSkip — the zero — skips it, OverlapAllow runs it
beside, OverlapReplace cancels the previous run and runs this one
once it has returned.

fields.name: StartingDeadline
fields.doc:
StartingDeadline bounds how late a fire may start. When the scheduler
wakes after a due instant — a machine that slept, a timer that
overran — it runs the latest instant missed, however late; with a
positive StartingDeadline, an instant more than StartingDeadline in
the past is not run but reported with [ResultValue].Expired, as
Kubernetes' startingDeadlineSeconds does. Zero, or less, is no
deadline, as before the field existed.

It is how a job whose run is worth something only near its instant
— a report for 02:00, a rotation tied to the hour — says so: a run
long after the fact is a surprise, not a catch-up.

symbols.doc:
EntryValue is one registered pairing of a [Schedule] with a [Job], under a
name that identifies it in every [ResultValue] and every error field.

The zero value is not runnable and is refused by Add ([InvalidEntry]) rather
than accepted and silently never fired.

symbols.name: InvalidEntry

code.public: The scheduler entry is not runnable and was refused

symbols.doc:
InvalidEntry is returned by Add for an entry that could never run, or
whose overlap is asked two contradictory ways (AllowOverlap with an
Overlap other than OverlapSkip or OverlapAllow), or an Overlap this
package does not define.

symbols.name: InvalidExpression

code.public: The cron expression is not valid

symbols.doc:
InvalidExpression is returned by Parse for a malformed or out-of-range
cron field.

symbols.name: InvalidInterval

code.public: The interval must be greater than zero

symbols.doc: InvalidInterval is returned by Every for a non-positive duration.

symbols.name: InvalidLocation

code.public: A time zone is required and none was given

symbols.doc: InvalidLocation is returned by ParseInLocation for a nil location.

symbols.name: Job
symbols.doc:
Job is the unit of work a [Scheduler] fires. It MUST honour ctx: the
scheduler passes the context Run was called with, so cancelling that context
is how a shutdown reaches a running job. A Job that ignores ctx delays Run's
return by its own duration — the scheduler waits for it rather than
abandoning it, because a job still running after the caller believes the
scheduler stopped is worse than a slow shutdown.

A Job's error is reported through [ResultValue] and is otherwise ignored: a
failing job never stops the scheduler and never affects another entry.

symbols.name: JobPanicked

code.public: The scheduled job panicked and was recovered

symbols.doc:
JobPanicked is the result Err for a Job that panicked. The scheduler
recovers it rather than letting it reach the runtime, because one job's
bug must not take the process — and every other job — down with it. The
recovered value travels as a field; it is never the wrap origin, so a
panicking job cannot hijack this code.

symbols.name: OverlapAllow
symbols.doc:
OverlapAllow runs the fire beside the previous run: the caller's in-code
assertion that concurrent copies are safe. [EntryValue].AllowOverlap
says the same.

symbols.name: OverlapPolicy
symbols.doc:
OverlapPolicy is what a fire does while the previous run of its entry has
not returned: [OverlapSkip] (the zero), [OverlapAllow] or
[OverlapReplace].

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc:
String renders the policy for a log line: "skip", "allow", "replace";
a value this package does not define renders "unknown".

symbols.name: OverlapReplace
symbols.doc:
OverlapReplace cancels the previous run's context and runs the fire once
that run has returned — never beside it. The cancelled run is reported
with [ResultValue].Replaced. A fire that comes due while its own
predecessor is still returning replaces the waiting one in turn, so at
most one run waits: the newest.

symbols.name: OverlapSkip
symbols.doc:
OverlapSkip does not run the fire and reports it as
[ResultValue].Skipped. It is the zero OverlapPolicy: the SDK cannot know
whether two copies of a Job are safe side by side.

symbols.name: ResultValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Name string; Scheduled time.Time; Started time.Time; Finished time.Time; Missed int; Skipped bool; Expired bool; Replaced bool; Err error}
symbols.canonical: struct{Name string; Scheduled time.Time; Started time.Time; Finished time.Time; Missed int; Skipped bool; Expired bool; Replaced bool; Err error}

fields.name: Name
fields.doc: Name is the entry's registered name.

fields.name: Scheduled
fields.doc:
Scheduled is the due instant this decision stands for. When fires were
missed it is the LATEST due instant at or before the wake-up, never the
oldest: the scheduler skips rather than catches up, so the run that
happens is the current one and the stale ones are what got dropped.

fields.name: Started
fields.doc: Started is when the Job was invoked. Zero when it was not.

fields.name: Finished
fields.doc: Finished is when the Job returned. Zero when it was not invoked.

fields.name: Missed
fields.doc:
Missed counts the due instants that were dropped because they had
already passed when the scheduler woke — a machine that slept, a
timer that overran, a job that held the slot. It never causes extra
runs; it exists so "skip" is not the same thing as "silently drop".

It counts only instants missed WITHIN one Run: the scheduler keeps no
state across restarts, so fires missed while the process was down are
not visible to it and are not counted here.

fields.name: Skipped
fields.doc:
Skipped reports that the fire was not run because the previous run of
this entry had not returned and its overlap policy is OverlapSkip.

fields.name: Expired
fields.doc:
Expired reports that the fire was not run because the scheduler came
to it more than the entry's StartingDeadline after its Scheduled
instant. Started and Finished are zero.

fields.name: Replaced
fields.doc:
Replaced reports a run whose context was cancelled because a newer
fire of the same OverlapReplace entry replaced it; Err is what the
Job returned. A run replaced before it started has zero Started and
Finished: it waited for its predecessor and never ran.

fields.name: Err
fields.doc:
Err is the Job's own error, verbatim and unwrapped, so errors.Is against
the caller's own sentinels keeps working. It is [JobPanicked] when the
Job panicked and the scheduler recovered.

symbols.doc:
ResultValue is what a [Scheduler] reports for every decision it takes about
an entry — a run that happened, and a fire that was deliberately not run.
Reporting the second is the point: a scheduler that only reports runs makes
a permanently-skipped entry indistinguishable from an entry that is doing
its job.

It is also the SDK's own test instrument. Because every decision emits one,
a test can WAIT for the decision it expects instead of sleeping to prove a
negative — which is what lets the scheduler suite assert cadences, missed
deadlines and overlap without a single time.Sleep.

This is a published concrete shape (pkg/v1/app/scheduler.Result is an alias), so
ADR 0040 applies: it may still gain or change a field while the module is
v0, loudly and in the commit message, and not after v1.

symbols.name: Schedule
symbols.doc:
Schedule reports the first instant STRICTLY after `after` at which a job is
due, and whether such an instant exists at all. A false second return means
the schedule will never fire again; the scheduler disarms that entry and
keeps running the others.

Implementations MUST be pure — the same `after` always yields the same
answer — and MUST be safe for concurrent use. The scheduler calls Next
repeatedly, including several times in one pass when fires were missed, and
a Schedule returning a value that is not strictly after its argument would
make that loop spin forever.

symbols.name: Scheduler
symbols.spelled: interface{Add(entry EntryValue) error; Run(ctx context.Context) error}
symbols.doc:
Scheduler owns a set of named [EntryValue] pairings and fires them.
Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the concrete engine stays unexported behind its constructor in
internal/service/app/scheduler.

symbols.name: Add
symbols.doc:
Add registers an entry. It is refused while Run is executing
([SchedulerRunning]), on a name already registered ([DuplicateJob]), and
on an entry that is not runnable — empty name, nil Job, nil Schedule
([InvalidEntry]).

symbols.name: Run
symbols.doc:
Run drives the registered entries until ctx is cancelled, then waits for
every in-flight job to return and reports nil. A Scheduler with no entry
is legitimate and simply waits for ctx: only an unrunnable ENTRY is
refused, never an empty entry set. Run is itself refused with
[SchedulerRunning] while already running; once it returns, the Scheduler
may be added to and run again.

symbols.name: SchedulerRunning

code.public: The scheduler is already running

symbols.doc:
SchedulerRunning is returned by Add, and by a second Run, while the
Scheduler is running. The entry set is fixed for the duration of a Run
so the loop needs no wake-up channel and no lock on its hot path; adding
between runs is allowed.

symbols.name: UnreachableSchedule

code.public: The cron expression matches no date on the calendar

symbols.doc:
UnreachableSchedule is returned by Parse for a valid expression that
matches no instant within the search horizon.

symbols.name: UnsupportedSyntax

code.public: That cron syntax is outside the accepted subset

symbols.doc:
UnsupportedSyntax is returned by Parse for a construct this subset
refuses by name instead of interpreting. Refusing loudly is the whole
point: a parser that silently ignores a Quartz "L" would run a job on
the wrong day and report success.

symbols.name: CodeDelayInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeDelayInvalid identifies a timer transition declared with a duration
that is not positive.

symbols.name: CodeEntityExists
symbols.doc:
CodeEntityExists identifies a Start whose entity's key the store already
holds.

symbols.name: CodeEntityMissing
symbols.doc:
CodeEntityMissing identifies a key the store holds no entity under — never
there, or deleted while a transition ran.

symbols.name: CodeEventInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeEventInvalid identifies a transition declared with an empty event name,
or with the name reserved for a creation.

symbols.name: CodeFunctionMissing
symbols.doc:
CodeFunctionMissing identifies a nil function where a definition needs one:
the state accessor, a guard, an instant function, a hook — or a nil
definition.

symbols.name: CodeFunctionPanicked
symbols.doc:
CodeFunctionPanicked identifies a guard or an instant function that panicked
while the loop asked it whether a transition was due.

symbols.name: CodeHookChangedKey
symbols.doc:
CodeHookChangedKey identifies an OnEnter hook that changed the key of the
entity it was entering.

symbols.name: CodeHookChangedState
symbols.doc:
CodeHookChangedState identifies an OnEnter hook that changed the state of
the entity it was entering.

symbols.name: CodeHookFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeHookFailed identifies a hook that returned an error: an OnEnter hook's
error fails its transition, an OnTransition hook's is reported.

symbols.name: CodeHookPanicked
symbols.doc: CodeHookPanicked identifies a hook that panicked, recovered as an error.

symbols.name: CodeInitialMissing
symbols.doc: CodeInitialMissing identifies a definition with no initial state.

symbols.name: CodeJournalFailed
symbols.doc: CodeJournalFailed identifies a Journal method that returned an error.

symbols.name: CodeKeyEmpty
symbols.doc: CodeKeyEmpty identifies an entity handed to Start whose key is empty.

symbols.name: CodeLoopPanicked
symbols.doc:
CodeLoopPanicked identifies a panic the loop recovered from the caller's own
code while looking at an entity: a store method, a journal, an observer.

symbols.name: CodeLoopRunning
symbols.doc: CodeLoopRunning identifies a Run or a Step asked for while another is going.

symbols.name: CodeReentrant
symbols.doc:
CodeReentrant identifies a transition asked for, through the context an
OnEnter hook was given, on the machine running that hook.

symbols.name: CodeStoreFailed
symbols.doc: CodeStoreFailed identifies a Store method that returned an error.

symbols.name: CodeStoreMissing
symbols.doc: CodeStoreMissing identifies a configuration with no store.

symbols.name: CodeTransitionDuplicate
symbols.doc:
CodeTransitionDuplicate identifies a second transition declared for one
event from one state.

symbols.name: CodeTransitionRefused
symbols.doc:
CodeTransitionRefused identifies an event no declared transition takes from
the entity's current state.

symbols.name: CodeTriggerUnknown
symbols.doc: CodeTriggerUnknown identifies a name ParseTrigger does not know.

symbols.name: CodeWaitAbandoned
symbols.doc:
CodeWaitAbandoned identifies a caller whose context ended while it waited
for another transition of the same entity to finish.

symbols.name: CreateEvent
symbols.doc:
CreateEvent is the event name of the step that brings a new entity into its
initial state. No declared transition may take it, so a history can always
tell a creation from an event.

symbols.name: DelayInvalid

code.public: A timer transition needs a positive duration

symbols.doc:
DelayInvalid refuses an After with a duration that is not positive: a
timer due the instant its state is entered is a guard that always
holds, and reads as a mistake.

symbols.name: EntityExists

code.public: An entity with that key already exists

symbols.doc:
EntityExists is returned by Start when the store already holds an
entity under the new one's key. Nothing was stored and no hook ran
after the refusal.

symbols.name: EntityMissing

code.public: No such entity

symbols.doc:
EntityMissing is returned when the store holds no entity under the key:
by Fire for a key never stored, and by any transition whose entity was
deleted while it ran — the store's Replace reported it gone, and the
transition stored nothing rather than bring it back.

symbols.name: EventInvalid

code.public: A transition needs a name, other than the reserved one

symbols.doc:
EventInvalid refuses a transition declared with an empty event name or
with the name a creation's history step takes.

symbols.name: FunctionMissing

code.public: The state machine was given no function where it needs one

symbols.doc:
FunctionMissing refuses a nil function a definition needs: the state
accessor, a guard, an instant function or a hook — and a nil
definition handed to NewStateMachine.

symbols.name: FunctionPanicked

code.public: A state-machine guard or deadline function panicked

symbols.doc:
FunctionPanicked is a guard or an instant function that panicked while
the loop asked whether a transition was due. The entity is retried
after a backoff; the value and the stack travel as log-only fields.

symbols.name: HookChangedKey

code.public: A state-machine hook changed the key of its entity

symbols.doc:
HookChangedKey refuses a transition whose OnEnter hook changed the
entity's key: storing it would replace, or create, another entity.

symbols.name: HookChangedState

code.public: A state-machine hook changed the state it was entering

symbols.doc:
HookChangedState refuses a transition whose OnEnter hook changed the
entity's state. A hook may change the entity, not where it is going:
the history would record one state and the store hold another.

symbols.name: HookFailed

code.public: A state-machine hook failed

symbols.doc:
HookFailed accompanies the error a hook returned, joined with it so
both errors.Is and errs.HasCode answer: an OnEnter hook's failure fails
its transition and is returned; an OnTransition hook's is reported
through Config.Report and the transition stands.

symbols.name: HookPanicked

code.public: A state-machine hook panicked

symbols.doc:
HookPanicked is a hook that panicked. The panic is recovered where the
hook ran, so an OnEnter hook fails its transition — and the entity's
lock is released on the way out, which is what kept a panicking hook
from leaving the machine locked for good. The recovered value and the
stack travel as log-only fields.

symbols.name: InitialMissing

code.public: The state machine has no initial state

symbols.doc:
InitialMissing refuses a definition that never called Initial: Start
would have no state to put a new entity in.

symbols.name: Journal
symbols.spelled: [S comparable] interface{Delete(ctx context.Context, keys ...string) error; Load(ctx context.Context) (records []RecordValue[S], err error); Save(ctx context.Context, records ...RecordValue[S]) error}
symbols.canonical: [S comparable] interface{Delete(ctx context.Context, keys ...string) error; Load(ctx context.Context) (records []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/statemachine.RecordValue[S], err error); Save(ctx context.Context, records ...github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/statemachine.RecordValue[S]) error}
symbols.doc:
Journal keeps, beside the store, what a machine knows about each entity and
the entity does not carry: the instant it entered its state and the
transitions that brought it there. Without one the machine keeps it in
memory, and after a restart every entity re-enters its state at the moment
the machine opens — which resets every After timer.

Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use. The engine calls them with
no lock of its bookkeeping held, one call at a time PER KEY: two writes of
one key arrive in the order the machine made them, and writes of different
keys may arrive at once — an implementation that rewrites one file orders
those itself. A journal may read the machine, its census or its records; it
must not tell it anything — Changed, Deleted, Start or Fire from inside a
journal call waits for itself.

Save and Delete take several records at once because a machine that opens
reconciles every entity in one pass; a journal that rewrites a whole file
then does it once rather than once per entity.

The method set is FROZEN at three (ADR 0039).

symbols.name: Delete
symbols.doc:
Delete forgets the records of keys; a key it does not hold is not an
error.

symbols.name: Load
symbols.doc:
Load returns every record the journal holds. The engine calls it once,
when a machine opens.

symbols.name: Save
symbols.doc: Save stores each record, replacing any record of the same key.

symbols.name: JournalFailed

code.public: The state machine's journal failed

symbols.doc:
JournalFailed wraps an error a Journal method returned. Load failing
fails the machine's opening; Save and Delete failing are reported and
the transition stands, since the store is the source of truth and a
lost record only costs a timer its origin after a restart.

symbols.name: KeyEmpty

code.public: The entity has no key

symbols.doc:
KeyEmpty is returned by Start for an entity whose key is empty. The
engine locks, records and schedules by key, so an empty one would make
every such entity the same entity.

symbols.name: LoopPanicked

code.public: The state machine's loop recovered a panic

symbols.doc:
LoopPanicked is a panic the loop recovered from the caller's own code —
a store method, a journal, an observer — while it looked at one
entity. When the panic interrupted the entity's pass, the entity is
retried after its backoff; when it came from the observer's end, the
transition was stored already and stands — call=observe-end says so.
Either way the loop goes on. Start and Fire, which run on the caller's
goroutine, let such a panic through, with the entity's lock released.
The value and the stack travel as log-only fields.

symbols.name: LoopRunning

code.public: The state machine's loop is already running

symbols.doc:
LoopRunning refuses a Run or a Step while another Run or Step of the
same machine is going: one loop at a time, so an entity takes at most
one automatic transition per run.

symbols.name: ParseTrigger
symbols.doc:
ParseTrigger reads a trigger's name, as String writes it. Anything else —
an empty name included — is refused with [TriggerUnknown], which does not
repeat the name.

symbols.name: RecordValue
symbols.spelled: [S comparable] struct{Key string "json:\"key\""; State S "json:\"state\""; Entered time.Time "json:\"entered\""; History []StepValue[S] "json:\"history,omitempty\""}
symbols.canonical: [S comparable] struct{Key string "json:\"key\""; State S "json:\"state\""; Entered time.Time "json:\"entered\""; History []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/statemachine.StepValue[S] "json:\"history,omitempty\""}

fields.name: Key
fields.doc: Key is the entity's key in the store.

fields.name: State
fields.doc: State is the state the entity is in.

fields.name: Entered
fields.doc: Entered is when the entity entered State.

fields.name: History
fields.doc: History holds the latest transitions, oldest first.

symbols.doc:
RecordValue is what a machine keeps about one entity beside the store: the
state it is in, since when, and the transitions that brought it there,
oldest first and bounded by the machine's history length.

State and Entered describe the entity as the machine last saw it. When an
entity's state changes behind the machine's back — a write that did not go
through a transition — the machine records the new state with Entered set
to the moment it learned of it, and adds no step: it knows the state, not a
transition.

symbols.name: Reentrant

code.public: A state-machine hook cannot fire its own machine

symbols.doc:
Reentrant refuses a Start or a Fire made, through the context an
OnEnter hook was given, on the machine running that hook. The hook runs
while the machine holds its entity's lock, so the call would wait for
itself; it is refused instead of deadlocking. Fire from an
OnTransition hook, which runs once the lock is released.

symbols.name: StepValue
symbols.spelled: [S comparable] struct{Event string "json:\"event\""; From S "json:\"from\""; To S "json:\"to\""; Trigger Trigger "json:\"trigger\""; Actor string "json:\"actor,omitempty\""; At time.Time "json:\"at\""}
symbols.canonical: [S comparable] struct{Event string "json:\"event\""; From S "json:\"from\""; To S "json:\"to\""; Trigger github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/statemachine.Trigger "json:\"trigger\""; Actor string "json:\"actor,omitempty\""; At time.Time "json:\"at\""}

fields.name: Event
fields.doc: Event is the transition's name; [CreateEvent] for a creation.

fields.name: From
fields.doc: From is the state left: the zero S for a creation.

fields.name: To
fields.doc: To is the state entered.

fields.name: Trigger
fields.doc: Trigger says what fired the transition.

fields.name: Actor
fields.doc:
Actor says who fired it when a caller did, as the machine's
configuration reads it from the caller's context; empty when the
machine's own loop fired it or nobody said.

fields.name: At
fields.doc: At is when the transition was stored.

symbols.doc:
StepValue is one transition in a record's history: which, from where to
where, what fired it, who asked, and when it was stored.

symbols.name: Store
symbols.spelled: [E any] interface{All(ctx context.Context) iter.Seq2[E, error]; Get(ctx context.Context, key string) (entity E, found bool, err error); Insert(ctx context.Context, entity E) (inserted bool, err error); Key(entity E) (key string); Replace(ctx context.Context, entity E) (replaced bool, err error)}
symbols.canonical: [E any] interface{All(ctx context.Context) iter.Seq2[E, error]; Get(ctx context.Context, key string) (entity E, found bool, err error); Insert(ctx context.Context, entity E) (inserted bool, err error); Key(entity E) (key string); Replace(ctx context.Context, entity E) (replaced bool, err error)}
symbols.doc:
Store is the port through which a machine reads and writes the entities
whose state it drives. The caller implements it over its own collection — a
document store, a table, a map — and hands it to the engine.

Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use: the engine calls them from
the goroutine firing a transition and from its own loop at once.

The method set is FROZEN at five (ADR 0039): pkg/v1/app/statemachine aliases this
interface, so a sixth method would break every downstream implementation at
compile time. A new capability arrives as a sibling interface reached by
type assertion.

symbols.name: All
symbols.doc:
All yields every entity, then stops; an error ends the sequence. The
engine ranges over it once, when a machine opens, to reconcile its
journal and build its agenda.

symbols.name: Get
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string) (entity E, found bool, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string) (entity E, found bool, err error)
symbols.doc:
Get returns the entity stored under key, and found == false — with a
nil error — when there is none.

symbols.name: Insert
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, entity E) (inserted bool, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, entity E) (inserted bool, err error)
symbols.doc:
Insert stores entity under a key no entity holds. When one does, it
stores nothing and reports inserted == false with a nil error.

symbols.name: Key
symbols.doc:
Key returns the key entity is stored under. It must be a pure function
of the entity: the engine locks, records and schedules by it, and a
transition never changes it.

symbols.name: Replace
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, entity E) (replaced bool, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, entity E) (replaced bool, err error)
symbols.doc:
Replace stores entity over the entity holding its key. When none does
— it was deleted while a transition ran — it stores nothing and reports
replaced == false with a nil error: a transition never brings back an
entity somebody deleted.

symbols.name: StoreFailed

code.public: The state machine's store failed

symbols.doc:
StoreFailed wraps an error a Store method returned. When the store's
error is itself an SDK error its code is kept and this one joins the
trail, so both errs.HasCode checks answer.

symbols.name: StoreMissing

code.public: The state machine has no store

symbols.doc:
StoreMissing refuses a configuration with no store: a machine's
entities have to live somewhere.

symbols.name: TransitionDuplicate

code.public: That event already leaves that state

symbols.doc:
TransitionDuplicate refuses a second transition for one event from one
state: Fire, and the loop's first-declared rule, would have two answers.

symbols.name: TransitionRefused

code.public: That transition is not possible from the current state

symbols.doc:
TransitionRefused is returned by Fire for an event no declared
transition takes from the entity's current state — including an event
that exists but leaves another state, and a timer or guard transition,
which only the machine's own loop fires. The entity is returned beside
it, so the caller can read the state that refused.

symbols.name: Trigger
symbols.doc:
Trigger says what fired a transition. The set is closed: every transition a
machine can take is declared one of these ways, and a history names which.

The values are STABLE — a journal may store them as numbers, and none is
ever renumbered — and the zero value is not a trigger, so a step read from
a journal that lost the field names no trigger rather than some default.
String and ParseTrigger give the text form.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc:
String returns the trigger's name — "start", "event", "delay", "deadline"
or "guard" — or "" for a value outside the set, which is how a caller tells
a trigger from one that is not.

symbols.name: TriggerDeadline
symbols.doc:
TriggerDeadline is a timer transition due at an instant the entity
itself carries — a due date, an expiry.

symbols.name: TriggerDelay
symbols.doc:
TriggerDelay is a timer transition due once an entity has spent a
declared duration in its state.

symbols.name: TriggerEvent
symbols.doc: TriggerEvent is an event transition, fired by a caller.

symbols.name: TriggerGuard
symbols.doc:
TriggerGuard is a transition due as soon as a condition on the entity
holds.

symbols.name: TriggerStart
symbols.doc:
TriggerStart is the creation of an entity: the step into its initial
state.

symbols.name: TriggerUnknown

code.public: That is not a state-machine trigger

symbols.doc:
TriggerUnknown refuses a name that is not one of the five triggers: a
journal written by something else, or damaged. The refused name is never
repeated — a journal is the caller's data.

symbols.name: WaitAbandoned

code.public: The request ended while the entity was busy

symbols.doc:
WaitAbandoned is returned when the caller's context ended while it
waited for another transition of the same entity to finish. Nothing was
read or stored.

symbols.name: CodeConstraintMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeConstraintMisconfigured identifies a constraint refused AT CONSTRUCTION
because its configuration cannot be honoured — an inverted numeric range, a
negative length bound, an empty allowed set, an uncompilable pattern. It is
never a validation outcome: the value was never reached.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidRule
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidRule identifies a struct tag refused at COMPILE time: an unknown
rule, a malformed argument, a rule applied to a kind it cannot check, or a
construct this dialect refuses by name. It is an error, never a violation —
the value was never reached.

symbols.name: CodeLengthOutOfRange
symbols.doc:
CodeLengthOutOfRange identifies a string, slice or array whose SIZE is
outside its allowed bounds. It is distinct from CodeOutOfRange because
"between 3 and 10" and "3 to 10 characters long" are different rules with
different fixes, and a caller routing on the code should not have to guess
which one fired.

symbols.name: CodeNotInSet
symbols.doc: CodeNotInSet identifies a value absent from the constraint's allowed set.

symbols.name: CodeOutOfRange
symbols.doc: CodeOutOfRange identifies an ordered value outside its allowed bounds.

symbols.name: CodePatternMismatch
symbols.doc: CodePatternMismatch identifies a string that did not match its pattern.

symbols.name: CodeRequired
symbols.doc:
CodeRequired identifies a value that is absent where presence was required.
It is a VIOLATION code — it travels on a ViolationValue, not on an error.

symbols.name: CodeUnsupportedTarget
symbols.doc:
CodeUnsupportedTarget identifies a Struct[T] whose T the tag engine cannot
walk — anything that is not a struct type.

symbols.name: CodeValidationFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeValidationFailed identifies the aggregate error a non-empty ReportValue
converts to. It is the code an error-typed contract sees; the individual
rules keep their own codes inside the report.

symbols.name: Constraint
symbols.spelled: [T any] func(path string, value T) ReportValue
symbols.doc:
Constraint reports what is wrong with value, at the path by which value was
reached. A value it accepts yields a nil [ReportValue] — the acceptance path
therefore allocates nothing, which matters because it is the path taken on
every field of every valid request.

path is the position of value inside the structure being validated, in the
grammar [JoinField] / [JoinIndex] define; [RootPath] means "the value itself".
A Constraint MUST propagate that path into every ViolationValue it reports,
and MUST NOT invent a different grammar — the path is the whole reason a
violation is actionable on a nested structure.

Implementations MUST be pure and safe for concurrent use: the same value at
the same path always yields the same report, and one compiled Constraint is
shared by every goroutine validating that type.

A Constraint MUST NOT copy the VALUE it rejected into the report. It names
the rule and the bound; the value may be a password, a token or a national
identifier, and a validation message is the one error message in a service
that is designed to reach the end user. See [ViolationValue].

symbols.name: ConstraintMisconfigured

code.public: The constraint cannot be built from the given configuration

symbols.doc:
ConstraintMisconfigured is returned by a constraint CONSTRUCTOR whose
arguments it cannot honour: a minimum above its maximum, a negative
length, an empty allowed set, an uncompilable pattern.

It is the ADR 0031 half that must not be confused with the other: a
validator with NO constraint is legitimate and passes, while a
constraint that could never be satisfied — or never be evaluated — is
refused before it can quietly reject, or quietly accept, everything.

symbols.name: InvalidRule

code.public: The validate struct tag could not be compiled

symbols.doc:
InvalidRule is returned by Struct when a validate tag cannot be
compiled. The fields name the field, the rule and the clause that
failed; the message never guesses at what was meant, it names what was
refused — an unsupported dialect construct is refused BY NAME so the fix
is one word, not an investigation.

symbols.name: JoinField
symbols.doc:
JoinField extends base with a struct member, producing the dotted form the
grammar defines:

	JoinField(RootPath, "user")        == "user"
	JoinField("user", "address")       == "user.address"
	JoinField("user.addresses[2]", "zip") == "user.addresses[2].zip"

name is whatever the calling front end names the member. The struct-tag
front end passes the json tag's name when the field has one, else the Go
field name (ADR 0046): the SDK's own config.Load decodes every format through
a JSON round trip, so the json name is the key the operator actually wrote.
The programmatic Field takes the name as an argument, so there the caller
decides.

The grammar does not quote. A member name that itself contains '.', '[' or
']' — json:"log.level" is legal — yields a path indistinguishable from a
nested or indexed one. The quoted segment that would disambiguate it is the
same one map descent needs, and ADR 0046 §Deferred defers both together
rather than growing the grammar for one of them.

symbols.name: JoinIndex
symbols.doc:
JoinIndex extends base with an element position, producing the bracketed
form the grammar defines:

	JoinIndex("addresses", 2) == "addresses[2]"

The bracket binds tighter than the dot: "a.b[0].c" is element 0 of a.b, and
there is never a dot before an opening bracket.

symbols.name: ReportValue
symbols.doc:
ReportValue is every violation one validation found, in the order the
constraints reported them. It is a SLICE rather than a struct so that the
zero value — nil — is a passing report: a validator with no constraint
passes, which is ADR 0046's first invariant and ADR 0031's "an empty
configuration is not the same thing as a broken one".

Composition is therefore plain append, and the accepting path allocates
nothing at all.

ReportValue is a published concrete shape (pkg/v1/app/validation.Report aliases
it), so ADR 0040 applies: it may still change while the module is v0, said
out loud, and not after v1.

symbols.name: Err
symbols.doc:
Err converts the report to the SDK error model, so a validation result can
satisfy an error-typed contract — principally core/app/config.Validator's
Validate() error, which is how a decoded config struct self-checks.

It returns a genuine nil interface when the report is OK. That is why
ReportValue does not implement error itself: a value type implementing error
and returned by value makes `if err != nil` true for a PASSING validation,
the typed-nil trap errs.Wrap has an explicit case for.

The error carries the violation COUNT and the list of paths, never the
messages and never the values: the full report is the report. A caller that
needs every message keeps the ReportValue; the error is the interop shape.

symbols.name: First
symbols.doc:
First returns the earliest violation and whether there was one. Constraints
report in the order they were composed, so "first" is the outermost rule on
the earliest field — the one a stop-at-first caller wants.

symbols.name: OK
symbols.doc:
OK reports whether the value satisfied every constraint. It is the question
to ask; comparing len(report) to zero says the same thing less clearly.

symbols.name: Paths
symbols.doc:
Paths returns the located path of every violation, in report order. It is
the shape an HTTP layer wants when it maps a report onto a form: the caller
already knows its own field names, and needs the SDK to say which ones.

symbols.name: RootPath
symbols.doc:
RootPath is the path of the value handed to a validator, before any descent.
A violation reported at RootPath is about the value as a whole — a
cross-field rule with no single culpable member.

symbols.name: UnsupportedTarget

code.public: Struct tag validation requires a struct type

symbols.doc:
UnsupportedTarget is returned by Struct when T is not a struct type.
The tag engine walks fields; there is nothing to walk on a scalar, a
slice or a pointer, and inventing a meaning for those would be a
different feature wearing this one's name.

symbols.name: ValidationFailed

code.public: One or more values did not satisfy their constraints

symbols.doc:
ValidationFailed is what ReportValue.Err returns for a non-empty report.
Its fields carry the violation count, the first rule, and the list of
paths — never a message and never a value. The full report stays the
ReportValue; this error is the shape an error-typed contract can hold.

symbols.name: ViolationValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Path string; Rule string; Message string; Code errs.Code}
symbols.canonical: struct{Path string; Rule string; Message string; Code github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/errs.Code}

fields.name: Path
fields.doc:
Path locates the offending value inside the structure that was
validated, in the grammar of [JoinField] / [JoinIndex] —
"user.addresses[2].zip". [RootPath] (the empty string) means the value
as a whole, which is what a cross-field rule reports when no single
field is at fault.

fields.name: Rule
fields.doc:
Rule names the constraint that refused, in lower case —
"required", "between", "length", "one_of", "pattern". It is the stable
identifier a caller switches on when the Code granularity is too coarse,
and the key an application uses to look up its own translated message.

fields.name: Message
fields.doc:
Message explains the rule in one wire-safe line: no newline, no private
data, and — the part that is a security property rather than a style
choice — NEVER the rejected value itself. A validation message is the
one error message in a service designed to reach the end user, so a
message that echoed the value would exfiltrate whatever the caller was
unwise enough to validate: a password, a token, a card number. It names
the rule and the bound instead ("must be between 8 and 64 characters").

fields.name: Code
fields.doc:
Code is the dotted-quad identity of the rule that refused, so a caller
routes on it with errs.HasCode / errs.NewPrefixMatcher instead of
string-matching Rule. The built-in constraints own 0.3.47.*; a
consumer-written Constraint SHOULD carry a Code in the third-party
Major range (ADR 0019, 0x40-0x7F).

symbols.doc:
ViolationValue is one located failure: WHERE it happened, WHICH rule it
broke, a wire-safe explanation, and a routable [errs.Code].

It is deliberately NOT an error. A validation normally produces several of
them, and errors.Join of five would render five bracket headers, lose the
ordering and bury the paths — while a single error would have to pick one
violation to be about. The aggregate that IS convertible to an error is
[ReportValue]; see its Err method.

The zero value is not meaningful; constraints build one per failure.

symbols.name: Available
symbols.doc:
Available returns every registered [Engine], sorted, so a caller can print
what its imports actually wired up. It is nil before any Register.

symbols.name: CodeDuplicateEngine
symbols.doc:
CodeDuplicateEngine identifies two distinct factories claiming one [Engine]
name. It panics for the same boot-time reason as [CodeEngineInvalid], and it
matters more here than in a codec registry: silently letting the second
registration win could swap the engine that escapes for one that does not.

symbols.name: CodeEngineInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeEngineInvalid identifies a boot-time [Register] of a nil Factory or one
claiming the empty [Engine] name. It panics: a broken registration is a
programming error that must be visible at import, not a value to thread
through a call chain nobody is executing yet.

symbols.name: CodeEngineUnknown
symbols.doc:
CodeEngineUnknown identifies an [Open] for an [Engine] no factory has
registered — usually a name resolved from configuration with a typo in it,
or an engine whose package was never imported.

symbols.name: CodeRenderFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeRenderFailed identifies a template that started executing and stopped —
a nil pointer in a field chain, a method that returned an error, a range over
the wrong type.

The engine's diagnostic for this is the single most leak-prone string in the
domain. html/template renders it as, verbatim,
`template: /srv/app/web/admin/page.html:1:7: executing "…" at <.User.Name>:
nil pointer evaluating interface {}.Name` — an absolute filesystem path, a
line and column, a fragment of the template's own source, and a Go type name.
All of it is reconnaissance, all of it is Private.

symbols.name: CodeRenderTooLarge
symbols.doc:
CodeRenderTooLarge identifies a render stopped at [Config.MaxBytes].

It is a denial-of-service guard, not a formatting complaint. A {{range}} over
a collection an attacker can grow has no recursion depth, so the stdlib's own
100000-frame limit never fires; the byte cap is the only thing between that
template and the machine's memory. The partial output is discarded, never
returned.

symbols.name: CodeTemplateNotFound
symbols.doc:
CodeTemplateNotFound identifies a Render for a name the engine does not hold.

It is a normal, expected verdict rather than a broken renderer: a Renderer
built over an empty tree is legitimate and refuses everything by name
(ADR 0031). The name asked for is a Field, never the Public — a template name
is part of the application's routing surface.

symbols.name: CodeTemplateParseFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeTemplateParseFailed identifies a template file html/template refused to
parse, or one it could not resolve a contextual escaping plan for.

Both are construction-time on purpose. html/template resolves escaping
lazily, at a template's first execution, so an {{if}} whose branches end in
different contexts or a {{template}} naming something absent would otherwise
surface as a 500 on whichever request first reached that page.

symbols.name: CodeTemplateSourceFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeTemplateSourceFailed identifies a template tree that could not be READ:
a walk that failed, a file that could not be opened.

It is kept distinct from a parse failure because the two have different
operators and different fixes. A source failure is usually a packaging bug —
an embed pattern that matched nothing, an os.DirFS pointed at a path that
does not exist in the container — and it is answered by looking at the
build, not at the template.

symbols.name: CodeUnsafeValue
symbols.doc:
CodeUnsafeValue identifies render data carrying one of the six html/template
trust types the domain refuses: CSS, HTMLAttr, JS, JSStr, URL or Srcset.

Each of them disables contextual escaping for the value it wraps, and each
has a working exploit that plain strings do not: measured,
template.URL("javascript:alert(1)") reaches the browser as
href="javascript:alert%281%29" and executes, while the same string
unconverted is rewritten to the inert "#ZgotmplZ".

symbols.name: CodeViewMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeViewMisconfigured identifies a Renderer refused AT CONSTRUCTION because
its [Config] cannot be honoured — most importantly a nil FS.

Every permanent fault a template tree can carry is discovered here, on
purpose: a tree that does not parse, or a template html/template cannot
contextually escape, will fail identically on every request forever, and a
deploy that refuses to come up is a cheaper way to learn that than a 500 on
the one page nobody smoke-tests.

symbols.name: Config

fields.name: FS
fields.doc:
FS is the tree the templates are read from. Required.

It is an fs.FS rather than a directory path so that embed.FS, os.DirFS
and fstest.MapFS are all first-class, and so that the domain never
touches the filesystem API. It also removes path traversal from the
problem statement: fs.ValidPath rejects "..", so no template name can
address a file outside the tree the caller handed over.

Every regular file under FS is parsed, and each template is named by its
SLASH PATH relative to the root — "admin/page.html", not "page.html".
See [Factory] for why that is not a cosmetic choice.

fields.name: Ext
fields.doc:
Ext optionally restricts which files are parsed, by extension including
the dot (".html", ".gohtml").

Empty means every regular file in FS, which is the honest default: the
caller already chose the tree, and second-guessing its contents is the
SDK inventing a naming convention. Set it when templates share a
directory with assets.

fields.name: MaxBytes
fields.doc:
MaxBytes caps a single render's output. Not positive clamps to
[DefaultMaxBytes]; there is deliberately no spelling for "unlimited".

The cap is the only bound that exists. text/template's Execute takes no
context, so a render cannot be cancelled, and the stdlib's own guard is a
recursion DEPTH limit (100000 frames) that says nothing about output
size: a {{range}} over an attacker-influenced collection has no depth at
all and will write until the machine stops. The same "no unbounded
setting" reasoning applies here as to the WebSocket ceilings in ADR 0047.

symbols.doc:
Config parameterises every [Factory]. It is deliberately small: this domain
ships an extension point, not a template language.

symbols.name: ContentTypeHTML
symbols.doc:
ContentTypeHTML is the value an HTML [Renderer] reports from ContentType.

The charset is not decoration. A response whose Content-Type carries no
charset is sniffed by the browser, and a document sniffed as UTF-7 or as a
legacy multi-byte encoding can smuggle markup past an escaper that judged
the bytes as UTF-8.

symbols.name: DefaultMaxBytes
symbols.doc:
DefaultMaxBytes is the ceiling [Config.MaxBytes] clamps to when it is not
positive: 8 MiB.

A rendered HTML document larger than this is a defect or an attack. The value
is generous by an order of magnitude for a page a browser is meant to parse,
and it is a CLAMP rather than a refusal because — unlike a lock's TTL, whose
two readings are opposites (ADR 0031, ADR 0052) — there is a defensible
universal answer here, and refusing view.Config{FS: templates} would make the
obvious spelling unusable for no safety gain.

symbols.name: DuplicateEngine

code.public: Two view engines claim the same name

symbols.doc:
DuplicateEngine is the boot-time panic for two distinct factories under
one [Engine] name.

Re-registering the SAME factory is idempotent and silent; two different
ones are a hard conflict, because last-write-wins in THIS registry can
mean the engine that escapes was replaced by one that does not, at import
time, with no call site to blame.

symbols.name: Engine
symbols.doc:
Engine names a registered template engine.

The zero value is the reserved invalid name: [Register] refuses it at boot,
so it can never reach [Lookup], [Open] or [Available].

symbols.name: EngineInvalid

code.public: The view engine registration is not usable

symbols.doc:
EngineInvalid is the boot-time panic for a nil Factory or an empty
[Engine] name.

symbols.name: EngineUnknown

code.public: No view engine is registered under that name

symbols.doc:
EngineUnknown is returned by [Open] for a name no factory claims.

It carries the registered names in a Field so the usual cause — an engine
package that was never imported, so its registration never ran — is
answerable from one log line.

symbols.name: Factory
symbols.doc:
Factory builds a [Renderer] of one engine from a [Config].

Two methods, and the registry hands instances back to callers so each engine
keeps its concrete type unexported — the stable contract is this interface.

# What an engine undertakes by registering

Registration is not merely a name binding; it is a promise the security model
rests on. An engine in this registry MUST:

  - Contextually escape every value it renders, for the media type its
    [Renderer.ContentType] reports. An engine that does not escape may not
    report an HTML content type.
  - Render into its own buffer and return complete bytes or none.
  - Honour [Config.MaxBytes], clamping a non-positive value to
    [DefaultMaxBytes].
  - Refuse at construction a [Config] it cannot honour, and refuse at render
    time — by name, with [TemplateNotFound] — a template it does not hold.
  - Name every template by its SLASH PATH within [Config.FS].

That last one looks cosmetic and is not. html/template's own ParseFS names
templates by filepath.Base, so a tree holding admin/page.html and
user/page.html ends up with ONE template called "page.html" — measured, the
second parse silently wins and every request for the admin page renders the
user page. Full-path naming is the SDK refusing to inherit that.

symbols.name: Engine
symbols.doc:
Engine returns the registry key this factory claims. It must be stable
and non-empty.

symbols.name: New
symbols.doc:
New builds a Renderer from cfg, parsing the whole template tree eagerly.

Eager parsing is the point: a template that cannot be parsed, or cannot
be contextually escaped, will fail identically forever, so the failure
belongs in the process's first second — a deploy that does not come up —
rather than in the first request that happens to reach that page.

symbols.name: HTML
symbols.doc:
HTML is the [Engine] name of the stdlib html/template implementation in
internal/service/app/view. It is the only engine the SDK ships.

symbols.name: Lookup
symbols.doc:
Lookup returns the [Factory] registered under name.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry hands plug-in Factory instances back to callers so
each engine keeps its concrete type unexported; the stable contract is the
Factory interface itself.

symbols.name: MaxPooledBytes
symbols.doc:
MaxPooledBytes is the largest scratch buffer the engine keeps for reuse.

A single 8 MiB render must not leave 8 MiB pinned in a pool for the life of
the process; anything above this is returned to the collector instead.

symbols.name: Open
symbols.spelled: func(name Engine, cfg Config) (renderer Renderer, err error)
symbols.doc:
Open resolves name and builds a [Renderer] from cfg.

It is the config-driven entry point, and it fails loudly on a name nobody
claims — [EngineUnknown] carrying the registered names — rather than falling
back to a default. A fallback here would mean a typo in a configuration file
silently choosing how every value in the program is escaped.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the engine's concrete Renderer stays unexported in
internal/service/app/view; the stable contract is the Renderer interface.

symbols.name: Register
symbols.doc:
Register inserts f under f.Engine() and returns it, so an engine package can
bind the singleton to a typed package-level variable:

	var Engine = view.Register(htmlFactory{})

It panics on a nil factory, on the empty [Engine] name, and when a DISTINCT
factory already claims the name. Re-registering the same factory is a no-op.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry hands plug-in Factory instances back to callers so
each engine keeps its concrete type unexported; the stable contract is the
Factory interface itself.

"Nil" here means UNUSABLE, not only an untyped nil: a typed nil pointer and a
plug-in whose type is not comparable both satisfy the port and neither can
serve one call (see internal/kernel/plugin).

symbols.name: RenderFailed

code.public: The page could not be rendered

symbols.doc:
RenderFailed is returned when execution started and could not finish.

Nothing is returned alongside it. The bytes produced before the failure
are discarded inside the engine, which is the whole reason Render returns
a slice instead of taking a writer: handed an http.ResponseWriter, the
same failure would have flushed the status line, the headers and a
plausible-looking prefix of the page before it was detectable — measured
at 17 bytes for a template that fails on its second action.

symbols.name: RenderTooLarge

code.public: The page could not be rendered

symbols.doc:
RenderTooLarge is returned when a render reached [Config.MaxBytes].

The engine stops at the ceiling rather than after it: the limit is
enforced by the writer html/template is executing into, so the bytes are
never accumulated in the first place and the process does not have to
survive the allocation in order to reject it.

symbols.name: Renderer
symbols.spelled: interface{ContentType() string; Render(ctx context.Context, name string, data any) ([]byte, error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{ContentType() string; Render(ctx context.Context, name string, data any) ([]byte, error)}
symbols.doc:
Renderer turns a named template and a data value into a complete document.

The method set is FROZEN at two. This interface is aliased by pkg/v1/app/view,
Go interfaces are structural, and a third method would break every
downstream implementation at compile time with no deprecation window
(ADR 0039). New capabilities arrive as SIBLING interfaces reached by type
assertion — the model is codec's Appender (ADR 0037).

symbols.name: ContentType
symbols.doc:
ContentType returns the media type the bytes from Render carry, ready to
be written as a Content-Type header — [ContentTypeHTML] for every engine
registered today.

It is a method rather than a package constant because it is the promise
an engine makes about the escaping it performs. An engine that does not
contextually escape HTML may not report an HTML content type, so a
framework that writes this header verbatim (with X-Content-Type-Options:
nosniff, which is the framework's job and not the SDK's) never labels
unescaped output as a document the browser will parse as HTML.

symbols.name: Render
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, name string, data any) ([]byte, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, name string, data any) ([]byte, error)
symbols.doc:
Render executes the template registered under name against data and
returns the complete document.

It returns ([]byte, error) rather than writing to an io.Writer so that a
failure mid-execution cannot leave a half-written response behind — see
the package documentation. On any error the returned slice is nil.

ctx is checked before the work starts and is otherwise not consulted:
text/template's Execute takes no context and cannot be interrupted, so a
runaway template is bounded by BYTES, not by time. That is the reason
Config.MaxBytes exists and the reason it has no "unlimited" spelling.

name is looked up exactly. A name the engine does not hold is
[TemplateNotFound] — a Renderer built over an empty template set is a
legitimate Renderer that refuses everything by name, which is a loud
behaviour rather than an inert one (ADR 0031).

symbols.name: TemplateNotFound

code.public: The requested view does not exist

symbols.doc:
TemplateNotFound is returned by Render for a name the engine does not
hold, including the empty name.

It is deliberately not a construction-time concern: a Renderer over an
empty tree is legitimate and refuses everything by name. That is ADR
0031's shape — the configuration nobody filled in produces a loud,
typed refusal on every call rather than an inert renderer that returns
empty pages.

symbols.name: TemplateParseFailed

code.public: A view template is not valid

symbols.doc:
TemplateParseFailed is returned by the constructor for a file
html/template refused to parse or could not build an escaping plan for.

symbols.name: TemplateSourceFailed

code.public: The view templates could not be read

symbols.doc:
TemplateSourceFailed is returned by the constructor when the template FS
could not be read.

symbols.name: TrustHTML
symbols.doc:
TrustHTML marks s as HTML that is already safe to write unescaped.

Every call is an assertion that s was produced by the server and sanitised —
a Markdown renderer's output, a fragment from a template the same program
authored. It is never correct to hand it a string that arrived from a
request, a database field a user controls, or a third-party API.

The function exists because the conversion it performs needs a NAME. A
reviewer scanning a diff for `template.HTML(` has to know that identifier
matters; a reviewer scanning for `TrustHTML` is reading the word "trust" in
the SDK's own vocabulary, at the call site where the decision was actually
made.

symbols.name: TrustedHTML
symbols.doc: TrustedHTML is an HTML fragment that the engine writes WITHOUT escaping. It is deliberately an ALIAS of html/template.HTML rather than a defined type of its own. That is not a convenience: html/template recognises its trust types by an exact type switch, so a `type TrustedHTML string` would be escaped like any other string — measured, it renders hi as <b>hi</b> — and a trust type that does not actually confer trust is worse than none, because callers stop looking for the reason their markup disappeared. The alias has a consequence that is stated rather than hidden: because TrustedHTML and html/template.HTML are the same type, the engine cannot tell a fragment marked through [TrustHTML] from one a caller converted directly. What the SDK buys is therefore precise, and it is worth naming exactly: - Six of html/template's seven trust types — CSS, HTMLAttr, JS, JSStr, URL and Srcset — are REFUSED outright when they appear in render data, with the path that carries them named in the error. Those six have no SDK spelling at all. - The seventh has one canonical, greppable spelling, [TrustHTML], so "where does this codebase decide to trust markup?" is one grep with one answer rather than a hunt through an import list. A build-time ban on the raw conversion in CONSUMER code belongs in tools/sdkguard (ADR 0033), which already reads consumer source for exactly this class of rule. It is not shipped here.

symbols.name: UnsafeValue

code.public: The page could not be rendered

symbols.doc:
UnsafeValue is returned when render data carries one of the six refused
html/template trust types.

It is a programming error surfaced as a runtime verdict, and it is
refused BEFORE the template runs so no partial page exists to reason
about. The field naming the location is a path — data.Items[3].Body,
built from GO field names because that is the vocabulary a template
author reads and a developer greps — because "an unsafe value is
somewhere in your model" is not something a developer can act on at
three in the morning.

symbols.name: ViewMisconfigured

code.public: The view renderer cannot be built from the given configuration

symbols.doc:
ViewMisconfigured is returned by a [Factory]'s New for a [Config] it
cannot honour: a nil FS, a template tree that does not parse, or a
template html/template cannot contextually escape.

The escaping half is the one worth naming. html/template resolves a
template's escaping context lazily, at its FIRST execution, and reports
three classes of failure there — a template that ends inside an
unterminated tag, an {{if}} whose branches end in different contexts, and
a {{template}} naming something that does not exist. Left alone, all
three are 500s on a live request. The engine therefore forces escaping at
construction and turns them into this.

symbols.name: AEAD
symbols.spelled: interface{Algorithm() Algorithm; ID() byte; Open(key Key, box []byte, aad []byte) (plaintext []byte, err error); Seal(key Key, plaintext []byte, aad []byte) (box []byte, err error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Algorithm() github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/crypto.Algorithm; ID() byte; Open(key github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/crypto.Key, box []byte, aad []byte) (plaintext []byte, err error); Seal(key github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/crypto.Key, plaintext []byte, aad []byte) (box []byte, err error)}
symbols.doc:
AEAD is an authenticated-encryption-with-associated-data scheme. Each
implementation owns its complete self-describing wire framing
([Version][id][nonce][ciphertext||tag]) so the registry can dispatch Open by
reading the 1-byte id, and so the nonce — generated from crypto/rand inside
Seal — never reaches a caller. Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent
use and MUST return the shared non-oracle DecryptionFailed for every Open
failure (bad tag, bad header, wrong key) so they cannot become an oracle.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry hands plug-in AEAD instances back to callers behind
this interface; concrete scheme types stay unexported in their own packages.

symbols.name: Algorithm
symbols.doc: Algorithm reports the canonical key under which this scheme registers.

symbols.name: ID
symbols.doc:
ID reports the 1-byte wire identifier embedded in the box header so Open
can resolve the scheme without the caller naming it.

symbols.name: Open
symbols.spelled: func(key Key, box []byte, aad []byte) (plaintext []byte, err error)
symbols.doc:
Open reverses Seal: it validates the framing, decrypts, and verifies aad,
returning the plaintext or the non-oracle DecryptionFailed.

symbols.name: Seal
symbols.spelled: func(key Key, plaintext []byte, aad []byte) (box []byte, err error)
symbols.doc:
Seal encrypts plaintext, binding aad, and returns the self-framed box
(Version + id + random nonce + ciphertext||tag).

symbols.name: Agreement
symbols.spelled: interface{Algorithm() Algorithm; GenerateKey() (pub []byte, priv []byte, err error); Shared(priv []byte, peerPub []byte) (secret []byte, err error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Algorithm() github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/crypto.Algorithm; GenerateKey() (pub []byte, priv []byte, err error); Shared(priv []byte, peerPub []byte) (secret []byte, err error)}
symbols.doc:
Agreement is a key-agreement scheme (Diffie-Hellman style): it produces an
ephemeral keypair and derives a shared secret from a local private key and a
peer public key. The raw Shared output is low-level key material and MUST be
run through a KDF (a Deriver) before use as a key — the pkg/v1 facade never
hands the raw secret back to generic callers. Implementations self-register
via RegisterAgreement.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry hands plug-in Agreement instances back behind this
interface; concrete scheme types stay unexported in their own packages.

symbols.name: Algorithm
symbols.doc: Algorithm reports the canonical key under which this scheme registers.

symbols.name: GenerateKey
symbols.doc:
GenerateKey draws a fresh public/private keypair from the scheme's
entropy source.

symbols.name: Shared
symbols.doc:
Shared derives the raw shared secret from priv and peerPub. The result
MUST be passed through a KDF before any use as a key.

symbols.name: AgreementFailed

code.public: Key agreement failed to derive a shared secret

symbols.doc:
AgreementFailed wraps an AgreementShared fault where the scheme rejected the
inputs (e.g. a low-order peer point); it never leaks key bytes.

symbols.name: AgreementShared
symbols.spelled: func(name Algorithm, priv []byte, peerPub []byte) (secret []byte, err error)
symbols.doc:
AgreementShared derives the raw shared secret with the Agreement scheme
registered as name. The result MUST be passed through a KDF before use as a
key. A name with no registered scheme returns UnknownAgreementAlgorithm; a
scheme Shared fault is wrapped into AgreementFailed, leaking no key bytes.

symbols.name: Algorithm
symbols.doc:
Algorithm is the typed key under which an AEAD registers (e.g.
"aes-256-gcm"). The zero value Algorithm("") is reserved invalid, mirroring
codec.Format.

symbols.name: Known
symbols.doc: Known reports whether a has been registered in the AEAD registry.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String implements fmt.Stringer and returns the raw identifier.

symbols.name: Available
symbols.doc:
Available returns the sorted list of registered Algorithms, or nil before
any Register.

symbols.name: AvailableAgreements
symbols.doc: AvailableAgreements returns the sorted list of registered agreement Algorithms.

symbols.name: AvailableDerivers
symbols.doc: AvailableDerivers returns the sorted list of registered KDF Algorithms.

symbols.name: AvailableHashers
symbols.doc: AvailableHashers returns the sorted list of registered hash Algorithms.

symbols.name: AvailableMACs
symbols.doc: AvailableMACs returns the sorted list of registered MAC Algorithms.

symbols.name: AvailablePasswordHashers
symbols.doc:
AvailablePasswordHashers returns the sorted list of registered password
Algorithms.

symbols.name: AvailableSigners
symbols.doc: AvailableSigners returns the sorted list of registered signature Algorithms.

symbols.name: AvailableStreamSealers
symbols.doc:
AvailableStreamSealers returns the sorted list of registered streaming-AEAD
Algorithms.

symbols.name: CodeAgreementFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeAgreementFailed identifies an AgreementShared call whose scheme rejected
the inputs (e.g. a low-order peer point) — wrapped, never leaking key bytes.

symbols.name: CodeDecryptionFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeDecryptionFailed identifies any Open failure — bad authentication tag,
malformed framing, unknown wire id, or wrong key. It is deliberately
undifferentiated so Open cannot become a padding/format oracle.

symbols.name: CodeDerivationFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeDerivationFailed identifies a Subkey call whose requested length exceeds
the scheme's maximum output — a caller data error, not a fault.

symbols.name: CodeDigestMismatch
symbols.doc:
CodeDigestMismatch identifies a VerifyingReader whose computed digest did not
match the expected hex at EOF. The digest is public, so the mismatch is
non-oracle — it surfaces only on the terminal read, never mid-stream.

symbols.name: CodeDuplicateRegistration
symbols.doc:
CodeDuplicateRegistration identifies an init-time collision on a scheme
registry; two distinct schemes tried to claim the same Algorithm or wire id.
Surfaced via panic at boot through the DuplicateRegistration sentinel.

symbols.name: CodeEntropyFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeEntropyFailed identifies a crypto/rand failure while generating a nonce in
Seal — a host entropy fault, not a caller error.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidKey
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidKey identifies a NewKey call whose input was not exactly KeyLen
bytes, or a cipher that rejected the key material.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidKeyEnvelope
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidKeyEnvelope identifies a structurally invalid key-envelope string
passed to UnwrapKey — a corrupt $kenv$ frame, NOT a wrong-passphrase oracle.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidPasswordHash
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidPasswordHash identifies a stored PHC string that cannot be parsed
during VerifyPassword — server-side data corruption, not a password mismatch.

symbols.name: CodeKeyGenerationFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeKeyGenerationFailed identifies a crypto/rand failure while generating a
signing keypair in GenerateKey — a host entropy fault, not a caller error.

symbols.name: CodePasswordHashFailed
symbols.doc:
CodePasswordHashFailed identifies a crypto/rand failure while generating a
password salt in HashPassword — a host entropy fault, not a caller error.

symbols.name: CodeSigningFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeSigningFailed identifies a Sign call whose private key was not well-formed
for the scheme (e.g. the wrong length) — a caller data error, not a fault.

symbols.name: CodeStreamTruncated
symbols.doc:
CodeStreamTruncated identifies a streaming Open that hit EOF before the
final-flag chunk — the stream was cut short, not legitimately ended.

symbols.name: CodeUnknownAgreementAlgorithm
symbols.doc:
CodeUnknownAgreementAlgorithm identifies a GenerateAgreementKey/AgreementShared
call naming a key-agreement Algorithm that no imported package has registered.

symbols.name: CodeUnknownAlgorithm
symbols.doc:
CodeUnknownAlgorithm identifies a Seal/SealAs call naming an Algorithm that no
imported package has registered.

symbols.name: CodeUnknownHashAlgorithm
symbols.doc:
CodeUnknownHashAlgorithm identifies a Sum/SumHex call naming a hash Algorithm
that no imported package has registered.

symbols.name: CodeUnknownKDFAlgorithm
symbols.doc:
CodeUnknownKDFAlgorithm identifies a Subkey call naming a key-derivation
