Algorithm that no imported package has registered.

symbols.name: CodeUnknownMACAlgorithm
symbols.doc:
CodeUnknownMACAlgorithm identifies a MACTag/MACVerify call naming a MAC
Algorithm that no imported package has registered.

symbols.name: CodeUnknownPasswordAlgorithm
symbols.doc:
CodeUnknownPasswordAlgorithm identifies a HashPassword/VerifyPassword call
whose Algorithm (or PHC id segment) no imported package has registered.

symbols.name: CodeUnknownSignatureAlgorithm
symbols.doc:
CodeUnknownSignatureAlgorithm identifies a Sign/Verify/GenerateKey call naming
an Algorithm that no imported signature package has registered.

symbols.name: DecryptionFailed

code.public: Decryption failed

symbols.doc:
DecryptionFailed is the single non-oracle error returned by Open for any
failure — bad tag, malformed framing, unknown wire id, or wrong key.

symbols.name: DerivationFailed

code.public: Requested derived-key length is too large

symbols.doc:
DerivationFailed is returned by Subkey when the requested length exceeds
the scheme's maximum output (e.g. HKDF's 255*HashLen ceiling).

symbols.name: Deriver
symbols.spelled: interface{Algorithm() Algorithm; Derive(secret []byte, salt []byte, info string, length int) (subkey []byte, err error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Algorithm() github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/crypto.Algorithm; Derive(secret []byte, salt []byte, info string, length int) (subkey []byte, err error)}
symbols.doc:
Deriver is a key-derivation function for KEY SEPARATION: it expands one
high-entropy secret into independent, purpose-bound subkeys. It is NOT a
password hash — the input must already be a strong key (an AEAD Key, an HKDF
PRK, a Diffie-Hellman shared secret), never a human password. Password
stretching (argon2id) is a separate, deliberately slow port.

salt is optional domain randomness (nil is allowed); info is a context label
that binds each subkey to its purpose ("aead-key", "mac-key", …) so two
derivations from the same secret never collide. Implementations MUST be safe
for concurrent use.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry hands plug-in Deriver instances back to callers
behind this interface; concrete scheme types stay unexported in their own
packages.

symbols.name: Algorithm
symbols.doc: Algorithm reports the canonical key under which this scheme registers.

symbols.name: Derive
symbols.spelled: func(secret []byte, salt []byte, info string, length int) (subkey []byte, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(secret []byte, salt []byte, info string, length int) (subkey []byte, err error)
symbols.doc:
Derive expands secret (with optional salt and the context label info) into
a length-byte subkey, or DerivationFailed when length exceeds the scheme's

so the comparison is non-oracle and surfaces only at the terminal read.

symbols.doc:

distinct scheme already holds the Algorithm — or, for an AEAD, the wire
id — a second one claims. The registrar panics with conflictText of it,
so the panic carries the dotted-quad header AND the key that collided.

symbols.doc:

it signals a host entropy fault rather than a caller error.

unchanged so callers see the original cause.

symbols.name: GenerateKey
symbols.doc:

with no registered signer returns UnknownSignatureAlgorithm (blank-import the

symbols.name: Hasher
symbols.doc:
Hasher is a fingerprint / content-addressing hash scheme producing a
non-keyed digest of arbitrary bytes (content IDs, cache keys, dedup keys).

It is explicitly NOT authentication: no Hasher is a MAC, none takes a key,
and a digest is public — never branch on a secret-dependent comparison of
one. Keyed/authenticated integrity belongs to the AEAD and (future) signature
ports. Implementations self-register via RegisterHasher.

interface; concrete scheme types stay unexported in their own packages.

symbols.name: InvalidKey

code.public: Encryption key has the wrong length

symbols.doc:

code.public: Key envelope is malformed

symbols.doc:

base64). It signals corruption only — a wrong passphrase surfaces the
non-oracle DecryptionFailed instead, so this is no key/password oracle.

symbols.doc:

symbols.name: Key
symbols.doc:
Key is an opaque, redacting 256-bit symmetric key. Every rendering — String,
GoString and Format, so %v, %s, %#v, %d and every other verb — writes
"<redacted>", so an accidental print never leaks the secret; Bytes hands a
fresh copy to the cipher and is the only way out. All copies of a Key share
one backing array, so Zeroize on any copy clears the secret everywhere —
call it when you are done with the key.

The bytes sit behind a pointer rather than in the struct: fmt cannot call
Format on a Key held in an UNEXPORTED field of another struct, so it prints
that field's own fields instead, and a pointer prints an address where a
slice would print the key as a list of byte values. A zero-size field of a
non-comparable type keeps == from compiling, so no pointer comparison can
pass for a key comparison.

symbols.name: Bytes
symbols.doc:
Bytes returns a fresh copy of the raw key material for handoff to a cipher.
Callers MUST NOT log the result; the redaction only covers the renderings.
A zero-value Key returns nil.

symbols.name: Format
symbols.doc:
Format implements fmt.Formatter, so EVERY verb writes "<redacted>" — %d
included, which bypasses String and would otherwise print the struct's
bytes. %q writes it quoted.

symbols.name: GoString
symbols.doc:
GoString implements fmt.GoStringer so %#v stays redacted too — fmt bypasses
String for Go-syntax formatting and would otherwise dump the raw slice.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc:
String implements fmt.Stringer and always redacts so the key never reaches a
log line through %v / %s.

symbols.name: Zeroize
symbols.doc:
Zeroize overwrites the key material with zeros. Because copies share one
backing array, this clears the secret for every copy of the Key.

code.public: Could not gather entropy for key generation

symbols.doc:

keypair; it signals a host entropy fault rather than a caller error.

symbols.doc:

AEADs — AES-256-GCM and XChaCha20-Poly1305 — take a 32-byte key, so a single
fixed length keeps the surface tiny and the validation total.

symbols.name: PasswordHasher
symbols.spelled: interface{Algorithm() Algorithm; Hash(password []byte) (phc string, err error); NeedsRehash(phc string) (stale bool); Verify(password []byte, phc string) (ok bool, err error)}

PHC-string hash for storage. UNLIKE the Deriver (key separation) and Hasher

crypto surface meant to consume a low-entropy human secret.

scheme id and its cost parameters, so Verify needs no side-channel: the stored
string fully describes how to check it. Implementations MUST compare digests
in constant time and MUST be safe for concurrent use.

callers behind this interface; concrete scheme types stay unexported.

the scheme's current cost parameters, or PasswordHashFailed on an entropy
fault.

constant time. A malformed phc returns InvalidPasswordHash; a genuine
mismatch is (false, nil) so Verify is not an oracle on WHY it failed.

symbols.doc:
VerifyPassword reports whether password matches the stored PHC hash. The
scheme is read from phc's id segment — no algorithm argument is needed. A
malformed phc or unregistered scheme returns an error; a genuine mismatch is
(false, nil).

symbols.name: Version
symbols.doc:
Version is the box wire-format version, the first byte of every sealed box
([Version][id][nonce][ciphertext||tag]). It is frozen post-v1.0.0; a future
framing change bumps it and Open rejects an unknown version as
DecryptionFailed. Concrete AEADs embed it via this constant.

symbols.name: AmbiguousKid

code.public: Several keys in the set carry that key id

symbols.doc:
AmbiguousKid is returned when a Set lookup matches more than one key.
Selecting one would depend on JSON member order; callers rotating keys
enumerate the candidates with AllByKid instead.

symbols.name: CodeJWKAmbiguousKid
symbols.doc:
CodeJWKAmbiguousKid identifies a Set lookup whose "kid" matches more than one
member. Picking one would depend on JSON member order; rotation callers use
AllByKid and decide explicitly (ADR 0031 — refuse rather than guess).

symbols.name: CodeJWKInvalidEncoding
symbols.doc:
CodeJWKInvalidEncoding identifies a member that is not unpadded base64url
(RFC 7515 §2), or whose decoded length is not the fixed size the declared
curve mandates (RFC 7518 §6.2.1.2 forbids stripping leading zero octets).

symbols.name: CodeJWKKeyMismatch
symbols.doc:
CodeJWKKeyMismatch identifies well-encoded material that does not describe a
key on the declared curve: an off-curve or identity point, a private scalar
outside [1, n-1], or a "d" whose derived public key differs from the declared
"x"/"y". It is the one check a naive JWK parser skips.

symbols.name: CodeJWKKeyNotFound
symbols.doc:
CodeJWKKeyNotFound identifies a Set lookup whose "kid" matches no member, or
a lookup with an empty "kid" (which would otherwise match every key that
carries none).

symbols.name: CodeJWKMalformed
symbols.doc:
CodeJWKMalformed identifies a document that is not the JSON shape RFC 7517
describes — invalid JSON, a non-object where a JWK was expected, or a JWK Set
whose "keys" member is not an array.

symbols.name: CodeJWKMissingMember
symbols.doc:
CodeJWKMissingMember identifies a JWK (or JWK Set) whose required member for
the declared key type is absent or empty — "kty", "crv", "x", "k", "keys".

symbols.name: CodeJWKNoPrivateMaterial
symbols.doc:
CodeJWKNoPrivateMaterial identifies a private-path call on a key that holds
only public members — MarshalPrivate, Ed25519Private, ECDSAPrivate, Secret.

symbols.name: CodeJWKNoPublicForm
symbols.doc:
CodeJWKNoPublicForm identifies the public-serialisation refusal: a symmetric
("oct") key has no public half, so emitting it on the public path would
publish the secret itself. See ADR 0030 — the default is never the dangerous
one.

symbols.name: CodeJWKTypeMismatch
symbols.doc:
CodeJWKTypeMismatch identifies a typed accessor called for the wrong "kty" —
Ed25519Public on an EC key, Secret on an OKP key.

symbols.name: CodeJWKUnsupportedCurve
symbols.doc:
CodeJWKUnsupportedCurve identifies a "crv" that is unknown, or known but
paired with the wrong "kty" (P-256 under OKP, Ed25519 under EC).

symbols.name: CodeJWKUnsupportedKeyType
symbols.doc:
CodeJWKUnsupportedKeyType identifies a "kty" this package does not model.
RSA lands here on purpose: the SDK ships no RSA signer, so representing an
RSA key would promise an interop the crypto domain cannot honour.

symbols.name: InvalidEncoding

code.public: JWK member is not valid unpadded base64url

symbols.doc:
InvalidEncoding is returned when a member is not unpadded base64url, or
its decoded length is not the fixed size the declared curve mandates.

symbols.name: KeyMismatch

code.public: JWK material does not match the declared curve

symbols.doc:
KeyMismatch is returned when well-encoded material does not describe a
key on the declared curve — off-curve point, out-of-range scalar, or a
private member whose derived public key differs from the declared one.

symbols.name: KeyNotFound

code.public: No key in the set carries that key id

symbols.doc:
KeyNotFound is returned when a Set lookup resolves no key, including the
empty-kid lookup that would otherwise match every key carrying none.

symbols.name: Malformed

code.public: JWK document is malformed

symbols.doc:
Malformed is returned when the document is not the JSON shape RFC 7517
describes — invalid JSON, a non-object JWK, or a non-array "keys".

symbols.name: MissingMember

code.public: JWK is missing a required member

symbols.doc:
MissingMember is returned when a member required for the declared key
type is absent or empty.

symbols.name: NoPrivateMaterial

code.public: JWK holds no private key material

symbols.doc:
NoPrivateMaterial is returned by a private-path call on a key that holds
only public members.

symbols.name: NoPublicForm

code.public: Symmetric keys have no public JWK form

symbols.doc:
NoPublicForm is the public-serialisation refusal: a symmetric key has no
public half, so the public path cannot represent it without publishing
the secret. Only MarshalPrivate may emit it.

symbols.name: TypeMismatch

code.public: JWK accessor does not match the key type

symbols.doc: TypeMismatch is returned by a typed accessor called for the wrong "kty".

symbols.name: UnsupportedCurve

code.public: JWK curve is not supported

symbols.doc:
UnsupportedCurve is returned for an unknown "crv", or a known curve
paired with the wrong "kty".

symbols.name: UnsupportedKeyType

code.public: JWK key type is not supported

symbols.doc:
UnsupportedKeyType is returned for a "kty" this package does not model.
RSA is deliberately here: the SDK ships no RSA signer.

symbols.name: CacheBackendFailed

code.public: The cache backend could not serve the operation

symbols.doc:
CacheBackendFailed is returned when the store itself could not serve the
operation. A miss is NOT this — a miss is (zero, false, nil).

symbols.name: CacheChainMisconfigured

code.public: The cache chain cannot be built from the given tiers

symbols.doc:
CacheChainMisconfigured is returned by NewChain for a tier set it cannot
honour.

The interesting refusal is the third one. Every tier must implement
[EntryFetcher] and [Tagger], and that is checked ONCE, at construction,
rather than per call. The reason is the whole point of tagging:
promoting a value into a nearer tier WITHOUT its tags produces a copy
that InvalidateTag can no longer reach, so the invalidation reports
success, the far tier forgets the entry, and the near tier keeps
serving it until its TTL runs out. A tag invalidation that silently
misses one copy is worse than one that was never offered — so the chain
refuses to be built rather than degrade at the moment nobody is looking.

symbols.name: CacheEntryRejected

code.public: The cache entry is not storable as given

symbols.doc:
CacheEntryRejected is returned by Set for an entry the store refuses:
an empty key, an empty tag, or a negative TTL other than NoExpiry.

Refusing is the point. An empty key is fetchable only by another empty
key, an empty tag names a set nobody can ask for, and a negative TTL
would be read by the underlying primitive as "no expiry" — so the three
silent outcomes of accepting them are an entry nobody meant to write, an
entry nobody can invalidate, and an entry that never goes away.

symbols.name: CacheFillFailed

code.public: The cache fill function failed and nothing was stored

symbols.doc:
CacheFillFailed is returned by Loader.Load when the caller's fill fails
and its error carries no SDK code of its own.

Nothing is stored. Caching a failure would turn one bad minute at the
origin into a full TTL of bad answers, served confidently, to every
caller — the failure mode a cache is least able to explain afterwards.

symbols.name: CacheMisconfigured

code.public: The cache cannot be built from the given configuration

symbols.doc:
CacheMisconfigured is returned by a store CONSTRUCTOR whose
configuration it cannot honour.

It is ADR 0031's refuse half. A capacity is the caller's intent and any
number the SDK picked would be arbitrary, so a non-positive one is
refused rather than clamped — and refusing at construction is what keeps
the other outcome off the table: a cache built with an unusable
configuration still answers every call correctly, it just never HOLDS
anything, and nothing downstream can tell the difference between that
and a genuinely cold workload.

symbols.name: CacheTierFailed

code.public: A tier of the cache chain could not serve the operation

symbols.doc:
CacheTierFailed is returned when a chained operation failed inside one
tier. Its fields name the tier's position and the operation, because a
chain's caller holds one Store and would otherwise have no way to tell
which of two backends broke.

symbols.name: CodeCacheBackendFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeCacheBackendFailed identifies a store that could not serve an operation
for a reason of its own — the transport, the medium, the process it depends
on. A plain MISS is not this: a cache that does not hold something has done
nothing wrong and reports (zero, false, nil).

symbols.name: CodeCacheChainMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeCacheChainMisconfigured identifies a NewChain refused AT CONSTRUCTION:
fewer than two tiers, a nil tier, or a tier that cannot answer the whole
contract a tier must answer (see the errors.go sentinel for why that is
checked once, up front, rather than discovered per call).

symbols.name: CodeCacheEntryRejected
symbols.doc:
CodeCacheEntryRejected identifies an entry a store refuses to store: an
empty key, an empty tag, or a negative TTL that is not cache.NoExpiry.

Each of the three is a value that has no meaning rather than an unusual one,
and storing it would produce an entry the caller can never deliberately
fetch, invalidate or replace.

symbols.name: CodeCacheFillFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeCacheFillFailed identifies a Loader.Load whose caller-supplied fill
returned an error. NOTHING was stored: a failed fill must not be cached, or
one bad minute at the origin becomes a TTL's worth of bad answers.

It applies only when the fill's error carries no SDK code of its own. One
that does propagates untouched, because relabelling it would discard the
origin's own diagnosis (ADR 0005 §origin wins).

symbols.name: CodeCacheMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeCacheMisconfigured identifies a store refused AT CONSTRUCTION because
its configuration cannot be honoured — a non-positive capacity, a negative
default TTL. It is never an operational outcome: no entry was ever stored.

symbols.name: CodeCacheTierFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeCacheTierFailed identifies a chained operation that failed inside one
specific tier.

It is distinct from CACHE_BACKEND_FAILED because a chain has more than one
backend, and "the cache is broken" and "the far tier is broken" are
different incidents with different responses: the first is an outage, the
second is a degradation the near tier is still absorbing.

symbols.name: EntryFetcher
symbols.spelled: [V any] interface{FetchEntry(ctx context.Context, key string) (EntryValue[V], bool, error)}
symbols.canonical: [V any] interface{FetchEntry(ctx context.Context, key string) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/cache.EntryValue[V], bool, error)}
symbols.doc:
EntryFetcher is the sibling that returns the whole entry rather than only
its value (ADR 0039). It exists because promotion between tiers has to carry
TTL and tags: a value promoted into a near tier without its tags is a value
that [Tagger.InvalidateTag] can no longer reach, and an invalidation that
silently misses one copy is worse than one that is not offered at all.

symbols.name: FetchEntry
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string) (EntryValue[V], bool, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/cache.EntryValue[V], bool, error)
symbols.doc:
FetchEntry is [Store.Fetch] returning the stored entry — value, remaining
TTL and tags. It mutates the store for the same reasons Fetch does.

The TTL it reports is the REMAINING time, not the one originally
supplied: promoting an entry with its original TTL would extend its life
every time it moved between tiers.

symbols.name: EntryValue
symbols.spelled: [V any] struct{Value V; TTL time.Duration; Tags []string}
symbols.canonical: [V any] struct{Value V; TTL time.Duration; Tags []string}

fields.name: Value
fields.doc: Value is the payload.

fields.name: TTL
fields.doc:
TTL is how long the entry stays fetchable.

  > 0        this exact lifetime
  0          the store's configured default
  [NoExpiry] no deadline at all

Any other negative value is a mistake, not a third meaning, and is
refused with [CacheEntryRejected] rather than reinterpreted.

fields.name: Tags
fields.doc:
Tags label the entry for bulk invalidation. Order is not significant and
duplicates are collapsed. An empty tag is refused: it names a set nobody
can ask for, so accepting it would index the entry under a key that can
only ever be reached by accident.

Tags cost memory in the store's reverse index — see
internal/service/data/cache/CLAUDE.md, which states the per-pair cost and
measures it.

symbols.doc:
EntryValue is what a caller stores: the value, how long it should live, and
the tags by which it can later be invalidated in bulk.

It is a VALUE — a store copies what it needs and never retains the slice the
caller passed, so a caller may reuse or mutate its Tags slice afterwards.

symbols.name: Fill
symbols.doc:
Fill computes the entry for a key that the cache does not hold. It is the
caller's code: a database query, an HTTP call, a derivation.

It is a FUNC port rather than a one-method interface, the shape
internal/core already admits for resilience.Operation, scheduler.Job and
validation.Constraint — and, per ADR 0039, a func type satisfies the
no-widening rule structurally, because it cannot grow a method at all.

symbols.name: Loader
symbols.spelled: [V any] interface{Load(ctx context.Context, key string, fill Fill[V]) (V, error)}
symbols.canonical: [V any] interface{Load(ctx context.Context, key string, fill github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/cache.Fill[V]) (V, error)}
symbols.doc:
Loader is the sibling for stores that can fill a miss while ensuring that
concurrent misses on ONE key run the fill ONCE (ADR 0039).

# What it protects against, and what it does not

A cache stampede is what happens when a hot key expires: every request that
was being served from it misses at the same instant and every one of them
calls the origin. The origin sees, in one moment, the traffic the cache was
hiding — which is the load the cache was bought to prevent, arriving when
the system is least able to absorb it.

[Loader.Load] collapses those calls into one WITHIN ONE PROCESS. It does
NOT coordinate across replicas: N instances of a service each running this
still produce N concurrent fills. Cross-process collapsing needs a shared
lease, which is a distributed system and not something a cache port can
promise. A reader who takes "stampede protection" to mean "my origin sees
one request" would be wrong by a factor of N, so the limit is stated here,
in the port, and again in every document that mentions the feature.

symbols.name: Load
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string, fill Fill[V]) (V, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string, fill github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/cache.Fill[V]) (V, error)
symbols.doc:
Load returns the value for key, calling fill exactly once across all
concurrent callers of this key in this process if the cache does not
hold it. A fill that fails stores nothing and returns
[CacheFillFailed] — unless the failure already carries an SDK code, in
which case it propagates untouched (ADR 0005 §origin wins).

fill does NOT receive ctx. It receives the shared call's context: the
first caller's values with every deadline removed, cancelled only once
every waiting caller has gone. A caller whose own ctx ends while it
waits gets its own ctx.Err() and leaves the fill running for the others.

symbols.name: NoExpiry
symbols.doc:
NoExpiry is the [EntryValue.TTL] that stores an entry with no deadline.

It is a distinct value from the zero TTL, which means "use the store's
default". A cache with a one-minute default holding one entry that must
never expire is a real combination, and reading both meanings out of 0 would
make it unspellable — the caller would have to know the default and restate
it, which stops being true the day the default changes.

symbols.name: Store
symbols.spelled: [V any] interface{Delete(ctx context.Context, key string) error; Fetch(ctx context.Context, key string) (V, bool, error); Set(ctx context.Context, key string, entry EntryValue[V]) error}
symbols.canonical: [V any] interface{Delete(ctx context.Context, key string) error; Fetch(ctx context.Context, key string) (V, bool, error); Set(ctx context.Context, key string, entry github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/cache.EntryValue[V]) error}
symbols.doc:
Store is the cache port. Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use.

The method set is deliberately three operations wide and is FROZEN: pkg/v1
aliases this interface, so under ADR 0039 a fourth method would break every
downstream implementer at compile time with no deprecation window. New
capabilities arrive as SIBLING interfaces discovered by type assertion —
[EntryFetcher], [Tagger] and [Loader] are the three that ship, and the model
is codec's Appender (ADR 0037).

IFACE-PLUGIN: the concrete stores stay unexported behind their constructors
in internal/service/data/cache.

symbols.name: Delete
symbols.doc:
Delete removes key. It is idempotent: deleting a key that names nothing
reports nil, because a caller who wanted it gone has got what they asked
for.

symbols.name: Fetch
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string) (V, bool, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string) (V, bool, error)
symbols.doc:
Fetch returns the value stored under key and whether it was present and
unexpired. It MUTATES the store — recency, counters, lazy expiry — which
is why it is not called Get. A miss is (zero, false, nil), never an
error: a cache that does not hold something has done nothing wrong.

symbols.name: Set
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string, entry EntryValue[V]) error
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string, entry github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/cache.EntryValue[V]) error
symbols.doc:
Set stores entry under key, replacing whatever was there. An empty key,
an empty tag, or a negative TTL that is not [NoExpiry] is refused with
[CacheEntryRejected] rather than stored.

symbols.name: Tagger
symbols.spelled: interface{InvalidateTag(ctx context.Context, tag string) (removed int, err error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{InvalidateTag(ctx context.Context, tag string) (removed int, err error)}
symbols.doc:
Tagger is the sibling for stores that index entries by tag (ADR 0039).

Tagging exists because the thing a caller wants to invalidate is usually not
a key. "Every entry derived from user 42" is a set whose members are known
to the writer and not to the invalidator, and without a tag the invalidator's
only options are to guess the key shape or to purge everything.

symbols.name: InvalidateTag
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, tag string) (removed int, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, tag string) (removed int, err error)
symbols.doc:
InvalidateTag removes every entry carrying tag and reports how many it
removed. A tag that names nothing removes zero and reports nil.

The cost is proportional to the number of entries carrying the tag, NOT
to the size of the store — see internal/service/data/cache/BENCH.md, which
measures it at two store sizes for exactly this claim.

symbols.name: Appender
symbols.spelled: interface{Append(dst []byte, v any) (out []byte, err error); Codec}
symbols.doc:
Appender is the optional extension implemented by codecs that can encode
directly into a caller-supplied byte slice instead of allocating their own.
Hot paths (logger record formatting, NDJSON streams, batch sinks) consume
this interface to avoid the buffer-copy cost imposed by Marshal.

Implementations MUST:
  - Append the encoded representation of v onto dst (typically via the
    standard append(dst, …) idiom).
  - Return the (possibly re-allocated) buffer back to the caller.
  - Be safe for concurrent use by multiple goroutines.

The returned buffer's length grows by the number of bytes written; the
underlying array MAY be a fresh allocation when dst's capacity is too
small. Callers retain ownership of dst and SHOULD reuse it across calls.

symbols.name: Append
symbols.doc:
Append encodes v and appends the bytes onto dst. The returned slice
MUST contain the prior contents of dst followed by the encoded form.

symbols.name: Available
symbols.doc:
Available returns the sorted list of registered Formats, or nil before any
Register.

symbols.name: CodeCodecNil
symbols.doc:
CodeCodecNil identifies a Register call made with a nil Codec — a
nil-argument programmer error distinct from a duplicate registration.
Surfaced via panic at boot (see registry.go), mirroring writer.CodeWriterNil.

symbols.name: CodeDuplicateRegistration
symbols.doc:
CodeDuplicateRegistration identifies an init-time collision on the codec
registry; two codecs tried to claim the same Name.

symbols.name: CodeEmptyInput
symbols.doc: CodeEmptyInput identifies Unmarshal being called with a zero-byte slice.

symbols.name: CodeKeyEmpty
symbols.doc:
CodeKeyEmpty identifies a Register call whose codec declares an empty
Name, MIME type or extension — one that is empty once normalised the way
its Lookup normalises it. Such a key is what a package variable read
before its initialiser ran holds, so refusing it names the codec at boot
instead of letting two of them collide on "". Surfaced via panic (see
registry.go), like CodeCodecNil.

symbols.name: CodeTargetInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeTargetInvalid identifies Unmarshal being called with a target that is
not a non-nil pointer to a storable value.

symbols.name: CodeValueInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeValueInvalid identifies Marshal being called on a value the codec
cannot serialise (channel, function, unsupported map key).

symbols.name: Codec
symbols.spelled: interface{Extensions() []string; MIMETypes() []string; Marshal(v any) (data []byte, err error); Name() string; Unmarshal(data []byte, v any) (err error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Extensions() []string; MIMETypes() []string; Marshal(v any) (data []byte, err error); Name() string; Unmarshal(data []byte, v any) (err error)}
symbols.doc:
Codec is the minimum contract every format codec satisfies. Instances MUST
be safe for concurrent use; format-specific options are supplied via the
codec's constructor, not via the Codec interface.

symbols.name: Decoder
symbols.doc: Decoder reads one or more values from the wrapped reader.

symbols.name: DuplicateRegistration

code.public: A codec is already registered under that name, MIME type or extension

symbols.doc:
DuplicateRegistration is the conflict Register refuses at boot: a distinct
codec already holds the Format name, MIME type or extension a second one
claims. It is never returned — Register panics with conflictText of it, so
the panic carries the dotted-quad header AND the key that collided.

symbols.name: Encoder
symbols.doc: Encoder writes one or more values to the wrapped writer.

symbols.name: Format
symbols.doc: Format is the typed string identifier of a codec.

symbols.name: Known
symbols.doc: Known reports whether f has been registered in the codec registry.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String implements fmt.Stringer and returns the raw identifier.

symbols.name: Lookup
symbols.doc:
Lookup returns the codec registered under f.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry stores plug-in codec instances behind the Codec
interface — concrete types are intentionally unexported per-format.

symbols.name: LookupExt
symbols.doc:
LookupExt returns the codec whose extension list contains ext.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry stores plug-in codec instances behind the Codec
interface — concrete types are intentionally unexported per-format.

symbols.name: LookupMIME
symbols.doc:
LookupMIME returns the codec whose MIME list matches. MIME parameters
(e.g. "; charset=utf-8") are stripped before the index lookup so that
"application/json; charset=utf-8" resolves like "application/json".

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry stores plug-in codec instances behind the Codec
interface — concrete types are intentionally unexported per-format.

symbols.name: Register
symbols.doc:
Register inserts c into the registry and returns it so callers can bind
the singleton to a typed package-level variable like
`var Codec codec.Codec = codec.Register(&jsonCodec{})`. Panics on nil
argument, on an empty Name / MIME / extension (KEY_EMPTY), or on a
duplicate Name / MIME / extension.

Register reads c.Name, c.MIMETypes and c.Extensions through the Codec
interface, so the initialiser of the calling package variable does NOT
depend, in the sense of the Go specification's package initialization
rules, on any package variable those methods read: a dependency is only
recorded for a method referenced through a non-interface type. A codec
whose methods read package variables must therefore make that dependency
visible in the initialiser itself — or, as the SDK's codecs do, return
fresh literals from the methods — otherwise those variables may still be
unset when Register runs (the gc compiler hides this by initialising
constant composite literals statically; garble -literals does not).

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry hands plug-in codec instances back to callers
so each domain can keep its concrete codec type unexported; the only
stable contract is the Codec interface itself.

"Nil" here means UNUSABLE, not only an untyped nil: a typed nil pointer and a
plug-in whose type is not comparable both satisfy the port and neither can
serve one call (see internal/kernel/plugin).

symbols.name: StreamingCodec
symbols.spelled: interface{NewDecoder(r io.Reader) Decoder; NewEncoder(w io.Writer) Encoder; Codec}
symbols.doc:
StreamingCodec is the optional extension for formats that support
incremental encode/decode over io.Writer / io.Reader. Codecs that CAN
stream SHOULD implement it; consumers detect support with a type assertion.

CodeBaseEncMarshalFailed identifies a JSON-encode failure that happens
before the base-N step in the universal "flatten to JSON, then base-N"
pipeline.

symbols.name: CodeBaseEncSizeExceeded

CodeBaseEncSizeExceeded identifies an Unmarshal input whose length
exceeds the 10 MiB hard cap (CWE-400 memory-exhaustion defence).

symbols.name: CodeBaseEncUnmarshalFailed

CodeBaseEncUnmarshalFailed identifies a JSON-decode failure that happens
after the base-N step in the universal "base-N decode, then JSON" pipeline.

symbols.name: CodeBSONDepthExceeded
CodeBSONMarshalFailed

CodeBSONMarshalFailed identifies a value Marshal or Append cannot encode: a
top level that is not a document, a type BSON has no representation for, a
string that is not UTF-8, a key holding a NUL, or an error a MarshalBSON
method returned.

symbols.name: CodeBSONSizeExceeded
symbols.doc:
CodeBSONSizeExceeded identifies an Unmarshal input whose length exceeds the
10 MiB hard cap (CWE-400 memory-exhaustion defence before any byte is read).

symbols.name: CodeBSONUnmarshalFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeBSONUnmarshalFailed identifies input Unmarshal refuses: bytes that are
not one well-formed BSON document, or a value the target cannot hold.

symbols.name: CodeBSONValueInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeBSONValueInvalid identifies a BSON value type that cannot be built from
what it was given: a malformed ObjectID hex string, a decimal128 string that
is not a number or not exactly representable, a JSON form of either that is
neither of the shapes accepted.

symbols.name: DepthExceeded

code.public: BSON nesting depth exceeds limit

symbols.doc:
DepthExceeded marks a document or value nested deeper than the codec
reads or writes.

symbols.name: MarshalFailed

code.public: BSON encoding failed

symbols.doc: MarshalFailed marks a value Marshal or Append cannot encode.

symbols.doc: SizeExceeded marks an Unmarshal input over the 10 MiB hard cap.

symbols.name: UnmarshalFailed

code.public: BSON decoding failed

symbols.doc: UnmarshalFailed marks input Unmarshal refuses.

symbols.name: ValueInvalid

code.public: BSON value is invalid

symbols.doc: ValueInvalid marks a BSON value type that cannot be built from its input.

symbols.name: CodeCBORMarshalFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeCBORMarshalFailed identifies an encoding failure: a value of a type
CBOR cannot carry, a string that is not UTF-8, a nesting deeper than the
decoder accepts, a failing writer, MarshalBinary or MarshalCBOR.

symbols.name: CodeCBORUnmarshalFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeCBORUnmarshalFailed identifies a decoding failure: input that is not
one well-formed, valid data item, a bound exceeded, or an item the target
cannot hold.

symbols.name: MarshalFailed

code.public: CBOR encoding failed

symbols.doc:
MarshalFailed is the sentinel every encoding failure matches: a value
CBOR cannot carry, a string that is not UTF-8, a nesting deeper than
the decoder accepts, a failing writer, MarshalBinary or MarshalCBOR.

symbols.name: UnmarshalFailed

code.public: CBOR decoding failed

symbols.doc:
UnmarshalFailed is the sentinel every decoding failure matches: input
that is not one well-formed, valid data item, a bound exceeded, or an
item the target cannot hold.

symbols.name: CodeCSVMarshalFailed

[]byte nor an implementation of BytesProvider.

symbols.doc:

than the package-level CWE-400 ceiling.

symbols.doc:

symbols.doc:

symbols.doc:
FlatbuffersTruncated fires when the buffer is shorter than the

or larger than the package-level CWE-400 ceiling.

symbols.name: CodeFormMultiValue

symbols.doc:
CodeFormValueInvalid identifies a Marshal / Append / Unmarshal call whose
argument is not one of the shapes the urlencoded wire format models
(url.Values, map[string][]string, map[string]string, or a pointer to one).

symbols.doc:
MultiValue fires when a repeated key is decoded into a map[string]string
target, which can hold exactly one value per key.

symbols.name: UnmarshalFailed

symbols.doc:
NotJSON refuses a document that is not exactly one JSON value. The fields

symbols.name: CodeMsgPackMarshalFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeMsgPackMarshalFailed identifies an encode failure: a value MessagePack

symbols.doc:
CodeMsgPackUnmarshalFailed identifies a decode failure: malformed or
truncated input, an input over the size or depth limit, trailing bytes, or a

symbols.doc: UnmarshalFailed is the sentinel of a decode failure.

symbols.name: BoundaryInvalid

code.public: multipart boundary is missing or invalid

symbols.doc: BoundaryInvalid fires when no usable RFC 2046 boundary is available.

symbols.name: CodeMultipartBoundaryInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeMultipartBoundaryInvalid identifies a boundary the codec cannot use:
caller-supplied but outside the RFC 2046 charset / length, or absent from a
body whose first delimiter line could not be recovered.

symbols.name: CodeMultipartLimitExceeded
symbols.doc:
CodeMultipartLimitExceeded identifies a payload that crossed one of the
configured bounds — per-part bytes, part count, or aggregate bytes.

symbols.name: CodeMultipartLimitsInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeMultipartLimitsInvalid identifies a Limits value the codec refuses to
interpret: a negative bound is neither a bound nor a documented default,
and guessing which one the caller meant is exactly what ADR 0031 forbids.

symbols.name: CodeMultipartMarshalFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeMultipartMarshalFailed identifies a failure while writing a
multipart/form-data body — a part header, a part body, or the JSON
intermediate produced for the JSON-mediated single-part shape.

symbols.name: CodeMultipartUnmarshalFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeMultipartUnmarshalFailed identifies a failure while parsing a
multipart/form-data body: a malformed part header, a part with no form-data
name, a missing closing delimiter, or a JSON-mediated part whose payload is
not valid JSON.

symbols.name: CodeMultipartValueInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeMultipartValueInvalid identifies a Marshal / Unmarshal / Encode call
whose argument shape the codec cannot honour — an Unmarshal target that is
not a non-nil pointer, a Part carrying no field name, or a Part whose Name,
FileName or ContentType carries a CR, LF or NUL (field "field" names which).

symbols.name: LimitExceeded

code.public: multipart payload exceeds a configured limit

symbols.doc: LimitExceeded fires when a payload crosses one of the configured bounds.

symbols.name: LimitsInvalid

code.public: multipart limits are not usable

symbols.doc: LimitsInvalid fires when a Limits value carries a negative bound.

symbols.name: MarshalFailed

code.public: multipart encoding failed

symbols.doc: MarshalFailed wraps a failure raised while writing a part.

symbols.name: UnmarshalFailed

code.public: multipart decoding failed

symbols.doc: UnmarshalFailed wraps a failure raised while parsing a body.

symbols.name: ValueInvalid

code.public: multipart codec rejected the value shape

symbols.doc: ValueInvalid fires when the caller's argument shape cannot be honoured.

CodeNDJSONUnmarshalFailed identifies a failure inside encoding/json.Unmarshal

code.public: NDJSON encoding failed

symbols.doc: MarshalFailed wraps a failure from encoding/json.Marshal on a single record.

CodePEMUnmarshalFailed identifies a failure inside encoding/pem.Decode

symbols.doc:
CodePEMValueInvalid identifies a Marshal call that did not receive a *pem.Block
or an Unmarshal call whose target is not a **pem.Block.

symbols.name: MarshalFailed

code.public: PEM encoding failed

symbols.doc: MarshalFailed wraps a failure from encoding/pem.Encode.

code.public: PEM decoding failed

symbols.doc: UnmarshalFailed fires when no PEM block could be decoded from the input.

symbols.doc: ValueInvalid fires when the caller does not pass a *pem.Block / **pem.Block.

symbols.name: AcquireBuffer
symbols.doc:
AcquireBuffer returns a clean, zero-length *bytes.Buffer from the shared
pool. The recycler reset the buffer on its previous Put, so callers append
directly without re-resetting. The caller owns it until ReleaseBuffer.

symbols.name: AcquireReader
symbols.doc:
AcquireReader returns a *bytes.Reader from the shared pool, reset to read
from src. The caller owns it until ReleaseReader; src must stay alive and
unmodified for as long as the reader is used.

symbols.name: DetachBuffer
symbols.doc:
DetachBuffer hands the caller the bytes encoded into buf and ends the
caller's ownership of buf, by the cheaper of two releases for its size. A
buffer within MaxRetainedBufBytes is cloned and repooled: the clone is small,
and the next encode reuses the buffer. An over-cap buffer would pay a full
copy of a large payload AND be dropped by the pool anyway, so it is orphaned
instead: the returned slice IS its storage, now the caller's, and buf is left
for the GC without a reset — a reset would not zero the bytes, but a later
write through buf would overwrite them. Either way, buf must not be used
after the call. A nil buf yields nil.

symbols.name: MaxRetainedBufBytes
symbols.doc:
MaxRetainedBufBytes is the project-wide cap-discard threshold for pooled
codec buffers. A buffer whose capacity exceeds this is dropped on release
rather than re-pooled, so a one-off oversized payload cannot pin a large
allocation for the lifetime of the pool's GC window. It bounds the shared
*bytes.Buffer pool below, and it is also the ceiling a codec passes to a
recycler.CappedPool of its own when it pools a buffer shape this package
does not offer — so the codec domain keeps one threshold, not one per codec.

symbols.name: ReleaseBuffer
symbols.doc:
ReleaseBuffer returns buf to the shared pool unless its capacity exceeds
MaxRetainedBufBytes, in which case the recycler orphans it for the GC.
Callers MUST NOT use buf — or any slice aliasing buf.Bytes() — after this
call; clone first if the encoded bytes must outlive the release.

symbols.name: ReleaseReader
symbols.doc:
ReleaseReader returns r to the shared pool. A bytes.Reader is fixed-size, so
there is no cap-discard. Callers MUST NOT use r after this call.

symbols.name: CodeDecodeMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeDecodeMisconfigured identifies a call the decoder refuses before
reading anything: a non-positive bound, or a target that is not a non-nil
pointer.

symbols.name: CodeDocumentEmpty
symbols.doc:
CodeDocumentEmpty identifies a JSON document of zero bytes: no value at all,
which a caller may read as "no body" rather than as a malformed one.

symbols.name: CodeDocumentMalformed
symbols.doc:
CodeDocumentMalformed identifies a document that is not exactly one
well-formed JSON value: a syntax error, a truncation, trailing data, a
duplicated member name, or invalid UTF-8.

symbols.name: CodeDocumentTooLarge
symbols.doc:
CodeDocumentTooLarge identifies a JSON document longer than the bound the
caller gave.

symbols.name: CodeDocumentUnreadable
symbols.doc:
CodeDocumentUnreadable identifies a reader that failed before the document
ended — a connection reset, a cancelled request.

symbols.name: CodeMediaTypeUnsupported
symbols.doc:
CodeMediaTypeUnsupported identifies a request body whose Content-Type is not
application/json or a +json structured-syntax type.

symbols.name: CodeMemberUnknown
symbols.doc:
CodeMemberUnknown identifies an object member the target type does not
declare.

symbols.name: CodeValueMismatched
symbols.doc:
CodeValueMismatched identifies a well-formed value the target cannot hold:
the wrong JSON kind, a number out of the field's range, a value a field's
own unmarshaler refused.

symbols.name: DecodeMisconfigured

code.public: The JSON decoder was called with an argument it cannot use

symbols.doc:
DecodeMisconfigured refuses a call the decoder can never honour: a
non-positive bound — whose two readings, "unbounded" and "nothing", are
opposites (ADR 0031) — or a target that is not a non-nil pointer.

symbols.name: DocumentEmpty

code.public: The JSON document is empty

symbols.doc:
DocumentEmpty reports a document of zero bytes. It is its own code so a
caller for whom a body is optional can tell "no body" from "a broken
one" without reading the input again.

symbols.name: DocumentMalformed

code.public: The JSON document is not well-formed

symbols.doc:
DocumentMalformed refuses a document that is not exactly one
well-formed JSON value.

symbols.name: DocumentTooLarge

code.public: The JSON document is larger than the limit

symbols.doc:
DocumentTooLarge refuses a document longer than the caller's bound,
whatever the bytes beyond it would have said.

symbols.name: DocumentUnreadable

code.public: The JSON document could not be read

symbols.doc:
DocumentUnreadable wraps a reader that failed before the document
ended. The reader's own error stays in the chain.

symbols.name: MediaTypeUnsupported

code.public: The request body must be application/json or a +json media type

symbols.doc:
MediaTypeUnsupported refuses a request body that does not declare itself
JSON.

symbols.name: MemberUnknown

code.public: The JSON document has a member the target does not accept

symbols.doc:
MemberUnknown refuses an object member the target does not declare,
including one that differs from a declared name only by case.

symbols.name: ValueMismatched

code.public: The JSON document has a value of the wrong type or out of range

symbols.doc: ValueMismatched refuses a well-formed value the target cannot hold.

symbols.name: CodeTLVMarshalFailed

symbols.name: CodeTLVUnmarshalFailed
symbols.doc:

symbols.doc:
CodeTLVUnsupportedType identifies a value whose reflect.Kind cannot be
TLV-encoded (chan, func, complex*, unsafe.Pointer).

symbols.name: DepthExceeded

code.public: TLV nesting depth exceeds limit

code.public: TLV input exceeds size limit

symbols.name: Truncated

symbols.doc: Truncated fires when a buffer ends mid-record.

CodeTOMLUnmarshalFailed identifies a document the decoder cannot read, or a

symbols.doc: AliasRefused marks an alias, refused by name.

symbols.doc: AnchorRefused marks an anchor, refused by name.

symbols.doc: CodeYAMLAliasRefused identifies an alias (*name): outside the subset.

symbols.doc: CodeYAMLAnchorRefused identifies an anchor (&name): outside the subset.

symbols.doc:
CodeYAMLComplexKeyRefused identifies a complex mapping key (the ? indicator,
or a collection used as a key): outside the subset.

symbols.name: CodeYAMLDirectiveRefused

CodeYAMLDirectiveRefused identifies a directive (%YAML, %TAG): outside the
subset.

symbols.name: CodeYAMLDuplicateKey
symbols.doc: CodeYAMLDuplicateKey identifies a mapping that holds the same key twice.

symbols.doc:

whose writer failed.

symbols.doc: CodeYAMLMergeKeyRefused identifies a merge key (<<): outside the subset.

symbols.name: CodeYAMLMultiDocRefused
symbols.doc:
CodeYAMLMultiDocRefused identifies a second document where one was
expected.

symbols.name: CodeYAMLTagRefused
symbols.doc:
CodeYAMLTagRefused identifies an explicit tag (!local, !!str, !<uri>):
outside the subset.

symbols.name: CodeYAMLUnmarshalFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeYAMLUnmarshalFailed identifies a document the decoder cannot read: a
syntax error, input past a bound, or a value its Go target cannot hold.
Every refusal below carries it in its trail, so errs.HasCode answers for
all of them.

symbols.name: ComplexKeyRefused

code.public: YAML complex keys (?) are outside the supported subset

symbols.doc: ComplexKeyRefused marks a complex mapping key, refused by name.

symbols.name: DirectiveRefused

code.public: YAML directives (%YAML, %TAG) are outside the supported subset

symbols.doc: DirectiveRefused marks a directive, refused by name.

symbols.name: DuplicateKey

code.public: YAML mapping holds the same key twice

symbols.doc: DuplicateKey marks a mapping that holds the same key twice.

code.public: YAML integer with a leading zero is octal in YAML 1.1 and decimal in 1.2

symbols.doc:
LeadingZeroRefused marks an integer whose leading zero changes its value
between YAML versions.

symbols.name: MarshalFailed

code.public: YAML encoding failed

symbols.doc: MarshalFailed marks a value the encoder cannot write as YAML.

symbols.name: MergeKeyRefused

code.public: YAML merge keys (<<) are outside the supported subset

symbols.doc: MergeKeyRefused marks a merge key, refused by name.

symbols.name: MultipleDocumentsRefused

code.public: YAML input holds more than one document

symbols.doc: MultipleDocumentsRefused marks a second document in a single-document read.

symbols.name: TagRefused

code.public: YAML tags (! and !!) are outside the supported subset

symbols.doc: TagRefused marks an explicit tag, refused by name.

symbols.name: UnmarshalFailed

code.public: YAML decoding failed

symbols.doc: UnmarshalFailed marks a document the decoder cannot read into its target.

symbols.name: Announcer
symbols.spelled: interface{OnDelete(fn func(key string)) (remove func()); OnWrite(fn func(key string)) (remove func())}
symbols.canonical: interface{OnDelete(fn func(key string)) (remove func()); OnWrite(fn func(key string)) (remove func())}
symbols.doc:
Announcer is the pair of hooks a document store answers: both engines
implement it exactly as it is. A registered function is told the key of
every document a write stored or a deletion removed once that write stands —
durable for the file engine, committed for the SQL engine, and never for a
write rolled back — on the writer's goroutine and outside every lock of the
store.

symbols.name: OnDelete
symbols.doc:
OnDelete registers fn to be told the key of every document Delete or
Trash removed, on the same terms as OnWrite.

symbols.name: OnWrite
symbols.doc:
OnWrite registers fn to be told the key of every document Put, Insert,
Replace, Update or Restore stored, and returns the function that removes
the registration. A nil fn registers nothing. A panic in fn reaches the
writer after its write stood.

symbols.name: CodeDocumentExists
symbols.doc:
CodeDocumentExists identifies an insertion under a key the store already
holds a document under.

symbols.name: CodeDocumentKeyChanged
symbols.doc:
CodeDocumentKeyChanged identifies an update whose function changed the key
of the document it was given.

symbols.name: CodeDocumentKeyEmpty
symbols.doc:
CodeDocumentKeyEmpty identifies a document whose key function returned the
empty string.

symbols.name: CodeDocumentNotFound
symbols.doc:
CodeDocumentNotFound identifies a read, an update, a replacement or a
deletion of a key the store holds no document under, and a unique-index
lookup that finds nobody.

symbols.name: CodeDocumentNotTrashed
symbols.doc:
CodeDocumentNotTrashed identifies a restoration or a purge of a key the
store holds no trashed document under.

symbols.name: CodeDocumentUndecodable
symbols.doc:
CodeDocumentUndecodable identifies a stored document that no longer decodes
into the store's type.

symbols.name: CodeDocumentUnencodable
symbols.doc: CodeDocumentUnencodable identifies a value encoding/json cannot encode.

symbols.name: CodeIndexBroken
symbols.doc:
CodeIndexBroken identifies stored documents that break a unique index, or
an index key function that panicked while the store was opening.

symbols.name: CodeIndexNotUnique
symbols.doc:
CodeIndexNotUnique identifies a single-document lookup in an index that may
file several documents under one key.

symbols.name: CodeIndexUnknown
symbols.doc: CodeIndexUnknown identifies a lookup in an index the store never declared.

symbols.name: CodeKeyTooLong
symbols.doc:
CodeKeyTooLong identifies a write whose store key, or one of whose index
keys, is longer than the SQL store's key columns hold.

symbols.name: CodeLoadFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeLoadFailed identifies a store whose files could not be read or are not
a store's files.

symbols.name: CodePersistFailed
symbols.doc: CodePersistFailed identifies a write the filesystem did not make durable.

symbols.name: CodeStatementFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeStatementFailed identifies a call the SQL store's database did not
complete: it could not be reached, or it refused a statement for a reason
that is not one of the store's own refusals. The driver's error travels
beside it, withheld from its text.

symbols.name: CodeStoreClosed
symbols.doc: CodeStoreClosed identifies a call on a store that has been closed.

symbols.name: CodeStoreMisconfigured
symbols.doc: CodeStoreMisconfigured identifies a configuration no store could honour.

symbols.name: CodeUniqueKeyTaken
symbols.doc:
CodeUniqueKeyTaken identifies a write a unique index refuses: another
document already holds one of its keys in that index.

indexes whose calls take no context — the port the file engine,
internal/service/data/docstore.Store, implements. Every read returns a
copy and every write stores one: a document is kept as its JSON encoding,
so what a caller holds never aliases what the store holds. No refusal
quotes a key.

The versions of a document are [Versioned], its sibling; the file engine's
Stats, Fold and Close are the engine's own, because a double of the port has
no files to fold.

DOCUMENT_NOT_FOUND. Its versions go with it.

every one when limit is not positive — each a copy the caller owns.

every document; an index is the way not to.

store-key order. It reads any index, unique or not, and no document is
an empty slice, not an error.

taken.

store never declared, INDEX_NOT_UNIQUE for one that may file several.

is never brought back.

the result, atomically with respect to every other write, and returns
it. An error from fn is returned as it is and changes nothing, and so
does a result whose key is not key (DOCUMENT_KEY_CHANGED). fn may read
the store and must not write to it.

would be a lie every Lookup tells.

file several documents under one key.

indexed, and a key listed twice is filed once.

unique, and the function that gives a document its keys in it. Build one
with [Unique] or [Index], and give it to an engine's constructor — Open or
OpenSQL in internal/service/data/docstore, which refuse the same
declarations alike. The file engine rebuilds its indexes when the store
opens; both keep them in step with every write.

symbols.doc: IndexUnknown refuses a lookup in an index the store never declared.

whose calls take no context: the sibling of [Collection] the file engine
implements beside it (ADR 0178). It reads no document, so what it costs
does not grow with what the documents weigh. A document the store no
longer holds — deleted, or in the trash ([Trashable]) — is not listed:
Keys lists what Get finds.

after — every key when after is empty — in key order, byte order as Go
compares strings, and no document. Stopping early is allowed, and
after is where a later call resumes. A failure is yielded once, with
an empty key, and ends the listing; a closed store yields
STORE_CLOSED.

whose index keys, is longer than its key columns hold. It is refused
before any statement, because MySQL outside strict mode would truncate
the key rather than refuse it — and a truncated key is another key.

command — and read back with it. The store copies it and never reads
it.

the current version keeps its number, its instant and its Meta, and
holds the new document. A framework stamps so a workflow's transition,
which its journal already records. A creation is version 1 all the
same.

Stamped writes. Its zero value is what Put, Insert, Replace and Update say:
nothing, and a new version.

symbols.doc:
StatementFailed reports a call the SQL store's database did not
complete: it could not be reached, its context ended, or it refused a
statement for a reason that is none of the store's own refusals. What
the call was writing did not take effect.

The driver's error travels beside it under errors.Join, reachable by
errors.Is and errors.As — a context's deadline included — and WITHHELD
from its text: a driver quotes the row a constraint refused, and that
row holds a key (ADR 0139).

key function, an index without a name, a function or a unique one, a
filesystem without a path, a negative Versions, a Held without
Versions; for the SQL store, a transactor that cannot join or defer, an
unknown dialect, a table name that is not one.

clock and kept to the nanosecond, as a version's instant is.

TombstoneValue is a document in the trash, as [Trashable].Tombstones
lists it: its key and when it was trashed. The document and its versions
are read through [Versioned].Versions.

Trashable is a document's trash, on a store whose calls take no context:
the sibling of [Collection] and [Versioned] the file engine implements
beside them (ADR 0143, amended for ADR 0178). Only a store that keeps
versions has a trash; one that keeps none answers every call with
VERSIONS_NOT_KEPT.

A document in the trash is gone from every read — Get, List, Lookup,
Find — and its unique keys are free, as a former version's are; its
versions stay, readable through Versioned, and its number is kept: a
creation under its key is a write over the trashed document, which takes
it out of the trash and continues its versions. Delete never reaches the
trash, and a trashed document is not Delete's to find: Delete takes a
document and its versions at once, which is what an erasure needs. How
long a document stays in the trash is the caller's to decide, through
Tombstones and Purge.

symbols.name: Purge
symbols.doc:
Purge empties the trash of the document trashed under key: the
trashed document and every version it kept go, and a document written
later under the key starts again at version 1. It calls no hook — the
document already left every read — and asks no hold, as Delete does
not. DOCUMENT_NOT_TRASHED when no document is trashed under key.

symbols.name: Restore
symbols.doc:
Restore brings the document trashed under key back, exactly as it was
— the same JSON, the same current version — and files it again. It
calls OnWrite. DOCUMENT_NOT_TRASHED when no document is trashed under
key, UNIQUE_KEY_TAKEN when another document took one of its unique
keys meanwhile, which then stays in the trash.

symbols.name: Tombstones
symbols.doc:

and when it was trashed, for a caller that empties the trash after a
while.

symbols.name: Trash
symbols.doc:
Trash moves the document stored under key to the trash: it is gone from
every read and its index keys are freed, while its versions are kept
and the trash records the instant. It calls OnDelete.
DOCUMENT_NOT_FOUND when no document is stored under key.

store's clock and kept to the nanosecond — by the file engine for the
years 0 to 9999, which RFC 3339 writes, and by the SQL engine for any
instant. It is zero for the first version of a document the store held
before it kept versions: when that one was written is not known.

fields.doc:

command — as its [StampValue] gave it; nil when it said nothing. The
store keeps it and never reads it.

fields.name: JSON
fields.doc:
JSON is the document as the version holds it, compact, a copy the
caller owns. The newest version's is the document itself.

fields.name: Number
fields.doc:
Number counts a document's versions from 1. No number is given twice
while the document exists or is in the trash, pruning included; a
document deleted, or purged from the trash, and written again is a new
document, and starts again at 1.

made it ran, what that write's caller said about it, and the document as the
version holds it.

reads no document: the file engine keeps the weight as a counter every
write moves, so asking costs the same whatever the store holds. Only a
store that keeps versions has it; one that keeps none answers
VERSIONS_NOT_KEPT.

many former versions, how many documents in the trash, and the bytes
of the JSON they hold. A closed store answers STORE_CLOSED.

[VersionWeigher].VersionWeight reports it: what the store keeps beyond
the documents it holds. A document's current version is the document
itself, and counts in none of its fields. Both engines count the same

symbols.doc:
VersionWriter writes a document with its versions as they are given, on a
store whose calls take no context: the sibling of [Collection],
[Versioned] and [Trashable] the file engine implements beside them (ADR
0178). It exists for a copy — a store moved from one engine to another —
that must keep each version's number, instant and metadata, and the
trash's instant: no other write can, since a write numbers the version it
makes after the current one and stamps it with the store's clock. Only a
store that keeps versions has it; one that keeps none answers
VERSIONS_NOT_KEPT.

itself — then the former ones, each kept as given, its number, its
instant (zero for a version 1 made before its store kept versions),
its metadata and its JSON, compacted and HTML-escaped as json.Marshal
writes a document. With trashedAt zero the document is stored and
filed in every index, and OnWrite is told; with trashedAt set, the
document is put in the trash at that instant, filed nowhere, and no
hook is told. Read back, Versions and Tombstones answer what was
given.

DOCUMENT_EXISTS otherwise. VERSIONS_INVALID, its "problem" field
naming which, refuses no version, a number 0, numbers that do not
strictly decrease, an unknown instant on a version other than 1, a
version that is not JSON, and a current document whose own key is not
key; DOCUMENT_UNDECODABLE one the store's type does not decode, and
UNIQUE_KEY_TAKEN a stored document whose unique key another holds. It
asks Held nothing and prunes nothing: the versions are written as
given, and the next write prunes as every write does. A refusal
writes nothing.

— a savepoint of the one ctx carries for the store's database — so the
document, its index rows and its versions exist if and only if that
transaction commits; OnWrite is told once it has.

symbols.name: VersionsInvalid

symbols.doc:
VersionsInvalid refuses a document PutDocument cannot write with its
versions as they are given: no version, a number 0, numbers that do
not strictly decrease from the newest, an unknown instant on a version
other than 1, a version that is not JSON, or a current document whose
own key is another. The "problem" field names which. Nothing changed.

It refuses rather than corrects: a copy that renumbered, re-stamped or
re-keyed what it copied would no longer be a copy.

symbols.name: VersionsNotKept

code.public: This store keeps no versions

symbols.doc:
VersionsNotKept refuses a call on a document's versions — Versions,
Version, RewriteVersions — to a store whose configuration keeps none.
Answering the current document as its only version would tell the
caller a history exists and is empty, which is not what happened.

symbols.name: VersionsRewriteRefused

VersionsRewriteRefused refuses what a rewrite's function returned: a
rewrite may drop a former version and change what one holds and what
its writer said, never add one, reorder them or change when one was
made. Nothing changed.

symbols.name: WriteUnconfirmed

code.public: The document was stored, but its durability could not be confirmed

symbols.doc:
WriteUnconfirmed reports a write the filesystem published but could
not confirm durable — vfs's DirectorySyncFailed: the rename happened,
the flush of the directory that records it did not. It is not
PersistFailed, because the write TOOK EFFECT: the file shows it, so the
store applies it too rather than disagree with its own files. What is
in doubt is only whether it survives a power loss.

symbols.name: Broker
symbols.spelled: interface{Ack(ctx context.Context, receipt ReceiptValue) error; Nack(ctx context.Context, receipt ReceiptValue, cause error) (NackValue, error); Publish(ctx context.Context, payload []byte) (MessageValue, error); Receive(ctx context.Context, max int) ([]DeliveryValue, error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Ack(ctx context.Context, receipt github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.ReceiptValue) error; Nack(ctx context.Context, receipt github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.ReceiptValue, cause error) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.NackValue, error); Publish(ctx context.Context, payload []byte) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.MessageValue, error); Receive(ctx context.Context, max int) ([]github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.DeliveryValue, error)}
symbols.doc:
Broker is one named queue: producers publish into it, consumers lease from
it, and it — not the consumer — owns the delivery count and the decision to
dead-letter. Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use by multiple
goroutines AND, where the implementation is durable, by multiple processes.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the concrete brokers stay unexported behind their
constructors in internal/service/data/queue.

The interface is FROZEN at these four methods. pkg/v1/data/queue aliases it, Go
interfaces are structural, and a fifth method would break every downstream
implementation at compile time with no deprecation window (ADR 0039). A new
capability arrives as a sibling interface reached by type assertion —
[DeadLetterReader], [LeaseExtender], [Waker], [Rejecter], [Releaser],
[DelayedNacker], [DelayedPublisher], [OncePublisher],
[DeadLetterManager], [DeadLetterWriter], [MessageReader] and
[MessageWriter] are the ones that ship.

# Why the BROKER owns the delivery count

Because the consumer is the thing that dies. A count held by the consumer
engine is lost by exactly the event the count exists to survive, so a
process that crashes on every third message would retry forever and never
dead-letter. The count travels with the message, in whatever the
implementation's durable representation is, and the broker compares it
against [PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries] on every [Broker.Nack] and on every
lapsed lease.

symbols.name: Ack
symbols.doc:
Ack removes the leased message permanently. It is the only call that
does.

A receipt whose lease has already lapsed is [LeaseExpired] and removes
NOTHING: the message is back in the queue, or in the dead-letter
store, and another consumer may already hold it. Reporting that is the
same decision core/app/lock makes for a lapsed lease — a holder that lost
its claim must not be able to end somebody else's turn, and must find
out that it lost it.

A receipt this broker never issued, or one it cannot parse, is
[UnknownReceipt].

symbols.name: Nack
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, receipt ReceiptValue, cause error) (NackValue, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, receipt github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.ReceiptValue, cause error) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.NackValue, error)
symbols.doc:
Nack reports that processing failed and hands the message back.

The broker decides what happens next and reports it: the message
becomes visible again after [PolicyValue.RetryDelay] — grown by
[PolicyValue.MaxRetryDelay] when the policy asks for it — or, when it
has now been delivered [PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries] times, it is moved to
the dead-letter store together with cause. See [NackValue]. A failure
no retry can fix is not nacked but rejected ([Rejecter]).

cause is recorded. What is kept of it is the implementation's to
document, and the rule this domain follows is CLAUDE.md rule 4: the
wire-safe Public half and the dotted-quad code travel with the dead
letter, the Private half stays in the failing process's log, and the
message identifier is the join key between them. A nil cause is
accepted and recorded as an unexplained failure, because a consumer
that knows only "this did not work" must still be able to say so.

A lapsed or unknown receipt is refused exactly as [Broker.Ack] refuses
it.

symbols.name: Publish
symbols.doc:
Publish appends payload to the queue and returns the message the
broker minted for it.

It takes BYTES and not a [MessageValue] on purpose: the identifier and
the enqueue instant are the broker's to assign, and a struct with
fields the caller must leave blank is a struct that will eventually be
filled in.

When it returns nil, a durable implementation has flushed the message
to its device: a crash one instruction later does not lose it. That
flush is most of what the call costs — see the domain's BENCH.md. An
implementation that joins the transaction ctx carries (ADR 0151) has
instead made the message part of that transaction: it is durable, and
receivable, once the transaction commits, and it never existed if the
transaction rolls back.

A payload larger than [PolicyValue.MaxMessageBytes] is
[MessageTooLarge]; an empty payload is legitimate, because a message
whose whole meaning is its arrival is a normal thing to send.

symbols.name: Receive
symbols.doc:
Receive leases up to max messages and returns them. It does NOT block
waiting for work: an empty queue yields an empty slice and a nil
error, and polling is the caller's (see internal/service/data/queue.Consume,
which does it for you).

Each returned message is invisible to every other consumer until its
[DeliveryValue.Lease] expires. A consumer that finishes acknowledges
with [Broker.Ack]; a consumer that fails reports it with [Broker.Nack];
a consumer that DIES does neither, and the lapsed lease is what makes
the message reappear.

max must be positive: [InvalidBatchSize] otherwise, rather than an
empty slice forever from a consumer loop that spins and processes
nothing.

symbols.name: CodeConsumerMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeConsumerMisconfigured identifies a ConsumerConfig the engine refuses:
no Handler, or a Handler whose author has not asserted that it is
idempotent under at-least-once delivery.

symbols.name: CodeDeadLetterNotFound
symbols.doc:
CodeDeadLetterNotFound identifies a replay or a deletion naming a dead
letter the store does not hold.

symbols.name: CodeHandlerPanicked
symbols.doc:
CodeHandlerPanicked identifies a handler whose call panicked; the engine
recovered it, nacked the message, and kept consuming.

There is deliberately no companion CodeHandlerFailed. A handler that merely
returns an error hands that error to Nack UNMODIFIED — see Consume's guard
— because the destination is a dead-letter record whose structured fields
already say "a handler failed", and an engine verdict wrapped around the
cause would displace the reason an investigator needs.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidBatchSize
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidBatchSize identifies a Receive, DeadLetters or Messages asked
for a non-positive number of messages.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidDeadLetter
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidDeadLetter identifies a dead letter a broker refuses to write:
one naming an identifier, a delivery count below one, an instant a
durable broker cannot record, or a reason or cause no store keeps as
written (ADR 0178).

symbols.name: CodeInvalidMessage
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidMessage identifies a live message a broker refuses to write:
one naming an identifier, marked leased, with a delivery count below zero
or above what a durable broker records, or an instant a durable broker
cannot record (ADR 0178).

symbols.name: CodeLeaseExpired
symbols.doc:
CodeLeaseExpired identifies an Ack, Nack or Extend on a lease that has
lapsed. The call changed nothing and the message is elsewhere.

symbols.name: CodeMessageTooLarge
symbols.doc:
CodeMessageTooLarge identifies a Publish whose payload exceeds
PolicyValue.MaxMessageBytes.

symbols.name: CodeNotRetryable
symbols.doc:
CodeNotRetryable identifies a handler's failure no retry can fix. DoNotRetry
adds it to the wrap trail of the handler's own cause, so errs.HasCode finds
it while the cause stays the origin a dead letter records (ADR 0151).

symbols.name: CodeQueueBackendFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeQueueBackendFailed identifies an operation a durable broker depends on
that its storage refused: a filesystem call the operating system refused,
or a statement the SQL broker's database did not complete.

symbols.name: CodeQueueDirectoryUnusable
symbols.doc:
CodeQueueDirectoryUnusable identifies a queue directory that cannot be
prepared, is not a directory, or is writable by accounts that must not be
able to inject or remove messages.

symbols.name: CodeQueueMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeQueueMisconfigured identifies a PolicyValue field a broker cannot
honour, refused at construction rather than at first use.

symbols.name: CodeRetryRequested
symbols.doc:
CodeRetryRequested identifies a handler's failure it wants retried no
sooner than a delay of its own choosing. RetryAfter adds it to the wrap
trail of the handler's own cause, as DoNotRetry adds CodeNotRetryable
(ADR 0183).

symbols.name: CodeSQLQueueMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeSQLQueueMisconfigured identifies an SQLConfig the SQL broker refuses at
construction: no transactor, one it cannot join a transaction of, a dialect
it cannot spell, or a table name it cannot interpolate safely (ADR 0151).

symbols.name: CodeUnknownReceipt
symbols.doc:
CodeUnknownReceipt identifies an Ack, Nack or Extend naming a lease this
broker never issued, or a receipt it cannot parse.

symbols.name: ConsumerMisconfigured

code.public: The consumer configuration is not runnable and was refused

symbols.doc:
ConsumerMisconfigured refuses a ConsumerConfig the engine cannot run.

It is the sentinel behind the domain's one mandatory assertion. This
queue delivers AT LEAST ONCE, so a handler will be called twice for
one message — after a crash, after a lease expiry, after a slow
downstream. The SDK cannot detect whether that is safe, so it makes
the caller say so in code: ConsumerConfig.HandlerIsIdempotent, whose
zero value is false and is refused. That is exactly
resilience.HedgeConfig.Idempotent's instrument, for exactly its reason
— a precondition the SDK cannot check becomes a required, greppable
assertion instead of a comment nobody reads.

symbols.name: DeadLetterManager
symbols.spelled: interface{DeleteDeadLetter(ctx context.Context, id string) error; ReplayDeadLetter(ctx context.Context, id string) error}
symbols.canonical: interface{DeleteDeadLetter(ctx context.Context, id string) error; ReplayDeadLetter(ctx context.Context, id string) error}
symbols.doc:
DeadLetterManager puts a dead letter back into its queue, or deletes it.

Reading the store ([DeadLetterReader]) is evidence and never changes it;
these two calls are the decisions an operator takes after reading it — the
failure was fixed downstream, so the message is replayed; the message is
obsolete, so it is deleted. They take the dead letter's [MessageValue].ID,
the identifier DeadLetters returned and the failing consumer logged.

A sibling of [Broker] for the reason [DeadLetterReader] is. The three
brokers in internal/service/data/queue implement it.

	if manager, ok := broker.(queue.DeadLetterManager); ok {
		err := manager.ReplayDeadLetter(ctx, dead.Message.ID)
	}

symbols.name: DeleteDeadLetter
symbols.doc:
DeleteDeadLetter removes the dead letter id for good, payload, cause
and all. It is the only call in the domain that destroys a message
without its consumer's acknowledgement, and it is never made by the
SDK itself. An id the store does not hold is [DeadLetterNotFound].

symbols.name: ReplayDeadLetter
symbols.doc:
ReplayDeadLetter moves the dead letter id back into the queue, visible
at once, with its delivery count reset: its next delivery counts 1 and
it gets [PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries] attempts again. It keeps its ID, its
payload and its EnqueuedAt, so the log lines of both its lives join on
one identifier; the dead-letter record, its cause included, is gone once
the message is queued again — log it first if it matters.

An id the store does not hold is [DeadLetterNotFound], and nothing is
queued. Two replays of one dead letter racing each other may both
queue it on a broker that cannot tell them apart, which is a duplicate
the at-least-once guarantee already permits; the brokers say which
they are.

symbols.name: DeadLetterNotFound

code.public: No dead letter has that identifier

symbols.doc:
DeadLetterNotFound refuses a replay or a deletion naming a dead letter
the store does not hold: one that never died, or was already replayed
or deleted — by this caller or, concurrently, by another. Nothing moved.

symbols.name: DeadLetterReader
symbols.doc:
DeadLetterReader reads the messages a broker gave up on.

It is a SIBLING of [Broker] reached by type assertion, never a fifth method
on it, because reading the dead letters back is a capability and not every
broker has one: a connector onto a third-party system usually dead-letters
into a second queue that is read with the same [Broker] interface, and one
that dead-letters into an operator's console cannot return anything at all.
The three brokers in internal/service/data/queue implement it.

	if reader, ok := broker.(queue.DeadLetterReader); ok {
		dead, err := reader.DeadLetters(ctx, 100)
	}

symbols.name: DeadLetters
symbols.doc:
DeadLetters returns up to max dead letters, oldest first. It does NOT
remove them: a dead letter is evidence, and a read that consumed it
would make the second investigator's job impossible. Removing one is a
decision, and [DeadLetterManager] is where it is made.

max must be positive ([InvalidBatchSize]).

symbols.name: DeadLetterValue
symbols.spelled: struct{FailedAt time.Time; Reason string; Cause string; Message MessageValue; Trail []uint32; Code uint32; Deliveries int}
symbols.canonical: struct{FailedAt time.Time; Reason string; Cause string; Message github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.MessageValue; Trail []uint32; Code uint32; Deliveries int}

fields.name: FailedAt
fields.doc: FailedAt is when the last attempt failed and the message was moved.

fields.name: Reason
fields.doc:
Reason is the SCREAMING_SNAKE identifier of the failure — the
errs.Error Reason of the cause, NOT_RETRYABLE for a handler's
[DoNotRetry] around an error that carried none, or LEASE_EXPIRED when
the message died by exhausting its deliveries without any consumer ever
reporting anything.

fields.name: Cause
fields.doc:
Cause is the wire-safe Public half of the last failure, or an empty
string when the consumer reported no cause at all. It never carries
the message payload, which is a security property this domain shares
with the rest of the SDK: a queue moves bytes a consumer must not
leak, and an error message is the classic place they leak from.

fields.name: Message
fields.doc:
Message is the work, unmodified, with the identifier it was published
under.

fields.name: Trail
fields.doc:
Trail is the dotted-quad codes the last failure gathered as it was
wrapped, oldest first — errs.TrailOf of the cause, whose origin is
Code and not repeated here —, at most sixteen, the newest kept when
there were more. It is what tells a failure apart once its process
