is gone: a mail spool's SEND_REFUSED is a rejected mail when the
spool added MAIL_REJECTED to its trail, and a dead letter keeps that
code where its Reason and Cause keep only the origin's. Nil when the
cause gathered none, for a dead letter written before the field
existed, and on an SQL broker whose SQLConfig.Trail is not set.
Like Code, each entry is a uint32: errs.Code(dl.Trail[i]) converts.

fields.name: Code
fields.doc:
Code is the dotted-quad errs.Code of the last failure, or 0 when the
cause carried none. It is a uint32 rather than an errs.Code so that
this package's values stay free of the kernel's error type in a shape
a consumer may serialise; errs.Code(dl.Code) converts.

fields.name: Deliveries
fields.doc:
Deliveries is how many times the message was delivered before it was
abandoned. It equals [PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries] for every dead letter
this SDK's brokers produce by running out of attempts, and is the count
the message had for one a handler rejected ([Rejecter]).

symbols.doc:
DeadLetterValue is one message the broker gave up on, together with why.

A dead letter without its cause is an investigation nobody can run, so the
cause is part of the record rather than a line in whatever log has since
rotated away. What is kept of the cause is CLAUDE.md rule 4's split, and
the split is deliberate: the wire-safe Public half and the dotted-quad code
go to the store, the Private half stays in the log of the process that
failed, and [MessageValue.ID] joins the two. A dead-letter store is read by
whoever is investigating — frequently not the process, the host or the
trust domain that produced the failure — so it is the wrong place for the
half of an error the SDK defines as log-only.

symbols.name: DeadLetterWriter
symbols.doc:
DeadLetterWriter writes a dead letter into the dead-letter store as it is
given, without the message ever being delivered there.

It exists for a copy: a queue moved from one broker to another — a file
queue into a table of the database (ADR 0178) — must carry its dead letters
with what they recorded, and no other verb can. [Rejecter] buries a message
this broker leased, at the count it reached here and with a cause that is
an SDK error, so a death by an expired lease, with no code, could only be
re-enacted; [DeadLetterManager] replays or deletes, it never inserts.

A sibling of [Broker] for the reason [DeadLetterReader] is. The three
brokers in internal/service/data/queue implement it.

	if writer, ok := target.(queue.DeadLetterWriter); ok {
		dead.Message.ID = "" // the target mints its own
		id, err := writer.PutDeadLetter(ctx, dead)
	}

symbols.name: PutDeadLetter
symbols.doc:
PutDeadLetter writes dead into the dead-letter store and returns the
identifier the broker minted for it. Everything else is kept as given:
the payload, the enqueue instant, the failure instant, the delivery
count, the reason, the cause, the code — 0 included, the code of a
failure that carried none — and the trail, which an SQL broker
without SQLConfig.Trail does not keep. What
[DeadLetterReader.DeadLetters] then returns of it equals dead but for
the identifier — an empty trail read back nil —, and
[DeadLetterManager] acts on it as on any other dead letter.

dead.Message.ID must be empty: the identifier is the broker's to mint,
as [Broker.Publish] mints it, and one a caller set would not be kept.
dead is refused with [InvalidDeadLetter] — the "field" field naming
which — when its Deliveries is below one or above 2147483647, when an
instant lies outside what a durable broker records (1970 to 2262),
when its Reason or Cause is longer than 120 runes or holds a line
break, or when its Trail holds more than sixteen codes; a payload
above [PolicyValue.MaxMessageBytes] is [MessageTooLarge]. A refused
dead letter writes nothing.

It is never delivered and wakes no consumer. A broker that joins the
transaction ctx carries (ADR 0151) writes it in that transaction, so
it exists if and only if the transaction commits.

symbols.name: DefaultMaxMessageBytes
symbols.doc:
DefaultMaxMessageBytes bounds a payload when [PolicyValue.MaxMessageBytes]
is left at zero. One mebibyte is the value the industry converged on —
NATS's default, Kafka's default `message.max.bytes`, four times SQS's
maximum — and the reason it is a CLAMP rather than a refusal is that its
zero has exactly one sensible reading and the wrong answer is survivable:
too small is a refused publish at the call site that made the mistake, and
the alternative to any bound at all is one producer filling a disk.

symbols.name: DelayedNacker
symbols.spelled: interface{NackAfter(ctx context.Context, receipt ReceiptValue, cause error, delay time.Duration) (NackValue, error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{NackAfter(ctx context.Context, receipt github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.ReceiptValue, cause error, delay time.Duration) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.NackValue, error)}
symbols.doc:
DelayedNacker hands a leased message back as [Broker.Nack] does, but after
a delay its caller names instead of the policy's retry delay (ADR 0183).

It is the broker's half of a handler saying "try again, but not before
then" — [RetryAfter] is the handler's — and
internal/service/data/queue.Consume joins the two. It is JetStream's
delayed negative acknowledgement and SQS's ChangeMessageVisibility on a
message that failed.

It is a sibling of [Broker] for the reason [DeadLetterReader] is: a
connector onto a system whose redelivery delay is fixed cannot implement
it, and the engine falls back to Nack for such a broker — the message then
comes back after the policy's retry delay, so the delay asked for is lost
and never the message. The three brokers in internal/service/data/queue
implement it.

symbols.name: NackAfter
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, receipt ReceiptValue, cause error, delay time.Duration) (NackValue, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, receipt github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.ReceiptValue, cause error, delay time.Duration) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.NackValue, error)
symbols.doc:
NackAfter reports that processing failed and hands the message back,
receivable again delay after now on the broker's clock — whatever
[PolicyValue.RetryDelay] and [PolicyValue.MaxRetryDelay] would have
made it wait. Everything else is [Broker.Nack]'s: the delivery is
counted, and a message delivered [PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries] times is
moved to the dead-letter store with cause instead, the delay unused.
See [NackValue].

A zero delay makes the message receivable at once, and a negative one
is read as zero: both have the one reading "now". A delay whose instant
a durable broker cannot record (past 2262, Unix nanoseconds) is
[QueueMisconfigured], refused before anything moves, and the lease the
caller holds stays valid. A lapsed or unknown receipt is refused
exactly as [Broker.Ack] refuses it.

symbols.name: DelayedPublisher
symbols.spelled: interface{PublishAt(ctx context.Context, payload []byte, at time.Time) (MessageValue, error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{PublishAt(ctx context.Context, payload []byte, at time.Time) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.MessageValue, error)}
symbols.doc:
DelayedPublisher publishes a message no consumer receives before an
instant its producer names: one deadline, kept as durably as the message
itself (ADR 0183).

It is what a producer needs for work that falls due once — a reminder at
nine, a trial that ends in fourteen days, an order cancelled if it is
still unpaid in an hour — and that must survive the process that decided
it. It is NOT a scheduler: the message is delivered at or after its
instant, once as any message is, and nothing recurs. Work that repeats on
a calendar is internal/core/app/scheduler's (ADR 0041), which owns the
recurrence and keeps no state a restart would need; the two meet where a
scheduled job publishes into a queue.

It is SQS's DelaySeconds without its fifteen-minute ceiling and River's
ScheduledAt. A sibling of [Broker] for the reason [DeadLetterReader] is: a
connector onto a system with no delayed delivery cannot implement it. The
three brokers in internal/service/data/queue implement it.

symbols.name: PublishAt
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, payload []byte, at time.Time) (MessageValue, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, payload []byte, at time.Time) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.MessageValue, error)
symbols.doc:
PublishAt appends payload to the queue as [Broker.Publish] does, and
hands it to no consumer before at. Its EnqueuedAt is the broker's now,
as every publication's is; at is when it becomes visible, which
[MessageReader.Messages] reports as its VisibleAt.

An at already past — the zero time.Time included — means now: the
message is receivable at once, as a published one is. An at a durable
broker cannot record (past 2262, Unix nanoseconds) is
[QueueMisconfigured], and nothing is published.

Everything else is Publish's: durable when it returns nil, part of the
transaction ctx carries on a broker that joins one (ADR 0151), a
payload above [PolicyValue.MaxMessageBytes] refused with
[MessageTooLarge]. Idle consumers are woken, and from then on wait
until at rather than polling for it. A queue delivers by visibility,
so a deferred message comes behind every message visible before it.

symbols.name: DeliveryValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Lease LeaseValue; Message MessageValue; Deliveries int}

fields.name: Lease
fields.doc: Lease is the claim this delivery grants and the receipt that ends it.

fields.name: Message
fields.doc: Message is the work.

fields.name: Deliveries
fields.doc:
Deliveries counts how many times this message has been handed to a
consumer, INCLUDING this one. It is 1 on the first delivery.

It is a field of the port rather than a note in the documentation
because it is the at-least-once guarantee made unignorable: a consumer
cannot read a delivery without reading the number that says this may
not be the first time. A value above 1 means a previous consumer
failed, timed out, or died — the three are indistinguishable from
here, deliberately, since none of them changes what the handler must
do.

It is also the number [PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries] is compared against:
a delivery whose count already equals the maximum is the last one this
message gets before the dead-letter store.

symbols.doc:
DeliveryValue is one message handed to one consumer, with everything the
consumer needs to decide what to do about it.

symbols.name: DoNotRetry
symbols.doc:
DoNotRetry marks cause as a failure no retry can fix, so the consumer engine
dead-letters the message at once instead of handing it back for another
attempt (ADR 0151).

	var order Order
	if err := json.Unmarshal(d.Message.Payload, &order); err != nil {
		return queue.DoNotRetry(err) // the same bytes will never decode
	}

It is for a failure that belongs to the MESSAGE — a payload that does not
decode, a reference to something since deleted, a request the handler will
refuse however often it is asked — and never to the moment: a downstream
that is down, a lock that is held, a deadline that passed are what retries
are for. Retrying the first kind spends [PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries] leases
and retry delays on an outcome already known, and keeps the dead letter an
operator needs to see out of the store for as long.

The mark is an errs.Wrap onto cause, so what a dead letter records of the
failure is unchanged: an SDK error keeps its own Reason, Code and Public —
origin wins, and [CodeNotRetryable] joins only its wrap trail — while a
cause that is not an SDK error, or no cause at all, records [NotRetryable]
itself, whose Public says what happened. Recognise the mark with
errs.HasCode(err, CodeNotRetryable); errors.Is(err, NotRetryable) answers
only where NotRetryable is the origin.

The engine reaches the broker's [Rejecter] for it. A broker without that
sibling is nacked as before, so the message is retried until
MaxDeliveries and dead-lettered with the same cause: the shortcut is lost,
never the message. A panic is never read as the mark — the recovered value
travels as a field of the engine's own verdict, not as its origin.

symbols.name: Handler
symbols.doc:
Handler processes one delivery. It is the port a consumer implements, and
it is a FUNCTION type rather than an interface — the shape
internal/core/CLAUDE.md already admits for resilience.Operation,
scheduler.Job, lifecycle.Start and events.Listener. ADR 0039's rule is that
a published port must not grow a method; a func type satisfies it
structurally, because it cannot grow one at all.

It receives the whole [DeliveryValue] and not just the payload, so that
[DeliveryValue.Deliveries] is in front of whoever writes the handler. A
handler WILL be called more than once for the same message — that is the
guarantee, not a malfunction — and the count is the only thing that lets it
say so in a log.

Returning nil acknowledges. Returning an error nacks: the message is
retried, or dead-lettered once it has exhausted
[PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries]. Returning [DoNotRetry](err) says no retry can
fix it, and the message is dead-lettered at once, with err, through a
broker's [Rejecter]; returning [RetryAfter](err, delay) says when to try
again, and the message is nacked with that delay through a broker's
[DelayedNacker]. ctx is the consumer's and IS honoured: unlike
events.Listener, a handler that outlives its context is holding a lease it
is about to lose, so abandoning the work is the correct response and the
message will simply be redelivered. internal/service/data/queue.Consume
ends it a margin before the lease does, with [LeaseExpired] as its
context.Cause, and when the consumer stops.

symbols.name: HandlerPanicked

code.public: The queue handler panicked and was recovered

symbols.doc:
HandlerPanicked is the failure of a handler whose call panicked.

The engine recovers it rather than letting it reach the runtime: a
panic escaping one handler would kill the consumer PROCESS, abandoning
every other in-flight lease — which then has to time out, one
visibility timeout at a time, before anything moves again. Recovered,
it becomes an ordinary nack: this message is retried and eventually
dead-lettered, and its siblings are untouched.

The recovered value and the panicking goroutine's stack travel as
FIELDS, never as the wrap origin, so a panic carrying an *errs.Error
cannot hijack this code.
A handler that merely RETURNS an error gets no sentinel of its own:
Consume hands that error to Broker.Nack unmodified. service/app/events
joins its ListenerFailed verdict beside the listener's cause because
Publish returns the aggregate to a caller who must be able to ask "did
anything fail?"; here the aggregate's destination is a dead-letter
record, which already says that by existing and has structured fields
for the rest. A verdict around the cause would displace the reason an
investigator needs, and TestAFailingHandlerIsRetriedAndThenDeadLettered
pins that it does not.

symbols.name: InvalidBatchSize

code.public: A batch size must be positive

symbols.doc:
InvalidBatchSize refuses a Receive, DeadLetters or Messages asked for a
non-positive count.

Returning an empty slice instead would be ADR 0031's inert policy: a
consumer loop asking for zero messages spins forever, processes
nothing, reports no error, and looks exactly like an idle queue.

symbols.name: InvalidDeadLetter

code.public: The dead letter cannot be written as it was given

symbols.doc:
InvalidDeadLetter refuses a dead letter [DeadLetterWriter.PutDeadLetter]
cannot write as it was given: an identifier set by the caller, which the
broker mints; a delivery count below one or above what a durable broker
records; an enqueue or failure instant outside 1970 to 2262; a reason or
cause longer than 120 runes or holding a line break, which every store
would otherwise cut; a trail of more than sixteen codes. The "field"
field names which value. Nothing was written.

It refuses rather than corrects, because a copy that silently changed
what it copies is the one outcome a copy must never have.

symbols.name: InvalidMessage

code.public: The message cannot be written as it was given

symbols.doc:
InvalidMessage refuses a live message [MessageWriter.PutMessage] cannot
write as it was given: an identifier set by the caller, which the broker
mints; a message marked leased, whose lease is another broker's; a
delivery count below zero or above what a durable broker records; an
enqueue or visibility instant outside 1970 to 2262. The "field" field
names which value. Nothing was written.

It refuses rather than corrects, as [InvalidDeadLetter] does.

symbols.name: LeaseExpired

code.public: The lease on that message has expired and the acknowledgement was ignored

symbols.doc:
LeaseExpired reports an Ack, Nack or Extend whose lease had already
lapsed. NOTHING happened: the message is back in the queue or in the
dead-letter store, and another consumer may already hold it.

Reporting it beats returning nil, for the reason core/app/lock gives about
releasing a lock one no longer holds: a holder that lost its claim must
not be able to end somebody else's turn, and must find out that it lost
it. A consumer that gets this has produced a duplicate — which the
at-least-once guarantee permits — and the one thing it must not do is
believe the work is finished.

symbols.name: LeaseExtender
symbols.spelled: interface{Extend(ctx context.Context, receipt ReceiptValue, by time.Duration) (LeaseValue, error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Extend(ctx context.Context, receipt github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.ReceiptValue, by time.Duration) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.LeaseValue, error)}
symbols.doc:
LeaseExtender renews a lease a handler is still working under.

It is the honest answer to the one question [PolicyValue.VisibilityTimeout]
cannot settle: the timeout must be longer than the slowest handler, and the
slowest handler is not known in advance. Rather than inviting a caller to
set an hour-long visibility timeout — which turns every consumer crash into
an hour of silence — a handler that legitimately needs longer says so.

It is a sibling for the same reason [DeadLetterReader] is: a broker over a
transport with no renewal verb cannot implement it, and the assertion is
how a caller finds that out. The three brokers in internal/service/data/queue
implement it.

Under internal/service/data/queue.Consume, a handler that calls it on its
own delivery's receipt is renewing a lease the engine no longer tracks:
the engine still stops it a margin before the lease it handed over, so it
renews to park its message and returns. To keep working past a lease,
the handler asks the engine to renew (ConsumerConfig.AutoExtend).

symbols.name: Extend
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, receipt ReceiptValue, by time.Duration) (LeaseValue, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, receipt github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.ReceiptValue, by time.Duration) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.LeaseValue, error)
symbols.doc:
Extend renews the lease named by receipt for a further by, measured
from now, and returns the lease that replaces it.

It returns a NEW [LeaseValue] — a new receipt included — and the old
receipt is void from that moment. That is not ceremony: an
implementation whose lease deadline lives in a durable name can only
change it by replacing the name, and a receipt that silently kept
meaning something after the thing it named had moved would be the one
bug this whole domain is built to avoid.

A lapsed lease is [LeaseExpired] and is NOT renewed, even when no
other consumer has taken the message yet: expiry is a deadline, not
"until somebody else wants it". The handler that asks and is refused
has learnt that its work is now a duplicate, which is exactly when it
needed to know.

A non-positive by is [QueueMisconfigured]: the two readings of zero —
"lapse now" and "never lapse" — are opposites and both harmful. So is a
by whose deadline reaches past what a durable implementation can record
(2262, Unix nanoseconds): it is refused before anything moves, and the
lease the caller holds stays valid. Validate never sees this duration,
so [MaxDeadlineOffset] cannot bound it; the instant itself is checked.

symbols.name: LeaseValue

fields.name: ExpiresAt
fields.doc:
ExpiresAt is when the claim lapses and the message becomes eligible for
redelivery. It is the broker's clock.

It is a promise about VISIBILITY and not about mutual exclusion: after
this instant another consumer may hold the same message while this one
is still running. A handler that is still working past it is producing
a duplicate, which the at-least-once guarantee already permits — see
[LeaseExtender] for the way to avoid producing one on purpose.

fields.name: Receipt
fields.doc: Receipt names this lease to [Broker.Ack] and [Broker.Nack].

symbols.doc:
LeaseValue is a consumer's exclusive claim on one message: the receipt that
proves it and the instant it lapses.

The two travel together because neither is usable alone. A receipt without
a deadline cannot tell a long-running handler whether it still owns the
work; a deadline without a receipt cannot acknowledge anything.

symbols.name: LiveMessageValue
symbols.spelled: struct{VisibleAt time.Time; Message MessageValue; Deliveries int; Leased bool}
symbols.canonical: struct{VisibleAt time.Time; Message github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.MessageValue; Deliveries int; Leased bool}

fields.name: VisibleAt
fields.doc:
VisibleAt is when the message may next be delivered: its visibility
for a waiting one — now, or later after a retry delay —, the deadline
of its lease for a leased one. An instant already past means
receivable now.

fields.name: Message
fields.doc: Message is the work, with the identifier it was published under.

fields.name: Deliveries
fields.doc:
Deliveries is how many times the message has been delivered: 0 for
one never leased, the count a retry or a lapsed lease left.

fields.name: Leased
fields.doc:
Leased reports that a consumer holds the message's lease. Such a
message is still alive: it comes back at VisibleAt unless it is
acknowledged.

symbols.doc:
LiveMessageValue is one message a broker holds alive, as it records it:
what [MessageReader.Messages] lists and [MessageWriter.PutMessage]
writes.

symbols.name: MaxDeadlineOffset
symbols.doc:
MaxDeadlineOffset is the furthest ahead of now a deadline built from a
policy may lie: the ceiling on [PolicyValue.VisibilityTimeout] and
[PolicyValue.RetryDelay], REFUSED above it rather than clamped.

It is not a judgement about how long a lease should last — ADR 0054 argues
against even an hour. It is the representable range, with a margin. Every
deadline is now plus one of these durations, and a durable broker records it
as Unix nanoseconds in an int64 — that is the form a filename carries, and
time.Time.UnixNano's own range — which ends on 2262-04-11. Past that instant
the number wraps negative, and a name carrying it cannot be read back: the
message it names is never reclaimed and never delivered, and its receipt
reads [UnknownReceipt]. math.MaxInt64, the value somebody reaches for to
mean "never", is 292 years, so it wraps a deadline set today.

A century keeps every deadline representable for any clock reading before
2162, and no lease or retry delay has a reading anywhere near it. Validate
has no clock, so a fixed ceiling is the only bound it can check; an
implementation that computes a deadline from its own clock at runtime — a
lease extension, whose duration Validate never sees — checks the instant
itself.

symbols.name: MessageReader
symbols.spelled: interface{Messages(ctx context.Context, after string, max int) ([]LiveMessageValue, error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Messages(ctx context.Context, after string, max int) ([]github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.LiveMessageValue, error)}
symbols.doc:
MessageReader lists the messages a broker holds alive — waiting, and leased
— without leasing one or changing what it records of any.

It exists for a copy: a queue moved from one broker to another (ADR 0178)
must carry each live message with what the broker records of it, and
[Broker.Receive] cannot read one without leasing it and counting a
delivery, nor read one another consumer leases. The dead ones are
[DeadLetterReader]'s. A sibling of [Broker] for the reason
[DeadLetterReader] is. The three brokers in internal/service/data/queue
implement it.

	if reader, ok := source.(queue.MessageReader); ok {
		live, err := reader.Messages(ctx, "", 100)
	}

symbols.name: Messages
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, after string, max int) ([]LiveMessageValue, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, after string, max int) ([]github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.LiveMessageValue, error)
symbols.doc:
Messages returns up to max live messages whose identifier sorts after
after — from the first when after is empty —, in the byte order of
their identifiers, each with its payload, its enqueue instant, its
delivery count, whether a consumer leases it and when it may next be
delivered. It leases nothing, counts no delivery and reclaims no lapsed
lease: what it reads is what the broker records, and the last
identifier it returns is where a later call resumes. A message
published, acknowledged or dead-lettered meanwhile may be listed or
not.

max must be positive ([InvalidBatchSize]).

symbols.name: MessageTooLarge

code.public: The message payload exceeds the queue's configured maximum size

symbols.doc:
MessageTooLarge refuses a Publish whose payload exceeds the policy's
bound. It is refused at the producer, because that is the only place
the payload can still be made smaller — a consumer discovering it
cannot do anything about it, and a broker accepting it lets one
producer fill a device every other producer shares.

Its fields carry the two SIZES and never the payload.

symbols.name: MessageValue

fields.name: EnqueuedAt
fields.doc:
EnqueuedAt is when the broker accepted the message. It is the ordering
key a FIFO implementation sorts on, and it is the broker's clock, not
the producer's.

fields.name: ID
fields.doc:
ID identifies the message for the life of the queue and beyond it: a
dead letter carries the same value, so the log line the failing
consumer wrote and the record left on disk can be joined without either
one carrying the other's half of the story (CLAUDE.md rule 4).

It is opaque. Its shape is the implementation's, it is unique within
one queue, and nothing outside the broker that minted it may parse it.

fields.name: Payload
fields.doc:
Payload is the caller's bytes, unmodified and uninterpreted. This
domain does not encode: pick a codec, marshal, publish the bytes.

The slice belongs to the receiver — a durable broker read it from a
device, and an in-memory one copies before handing it over, so a
handler may keep it, mutate it, or hold it past the acknowledgement
without corrupting a redelivery.

symbols.doc:
MessageValue is one unit of work as the broker minted it. Every field is
assigned by [Broker.Publish]; a caller never fills one in, which is why
Publish takes a payload rather than one of these.

symbols.name: MessageWriter
symbols.doc:
MessageWriter writes a live message into a queue as it is given, without
the message ever being published there.

It is [DeadLetterWriter]'s sibling for a message that has not died, and
exists for the same copy: [Broker.Publish] counts no delivery and stamps
its own enqueue instant, so a message a copy moves would come back as if
it had never been tried. A sibling of [Broker] for the reason
[DeadLetterReader] is. The three brokers in internal/service/data/queue
implement it.

	if writer, ok := target.(queue.MessageWriter); ok {
		live.Message.ID, live.Leased = "", false // the target mints its own; a lease stays the source's
		id, err := writer.PutMessage(ctx, live)
	}

symbols.name: PutMessage
symbols.doc:
PutMessage writes live into the queue as a waiting message and returns
the identifier the broker minted for it. Everything else is kept as
given: the payload, the enqueue instant, the delivery count — 0
included — and the instant it becomes visible, before which it is
never delivered. What [MessageReader.Messages] then returns of it
equals live but for the identifier, and its next delivery counts one
more than live.Deliveries.

live.Message.ID must be empty: the identifier is the broker's to mint,
as [Broker.Publish] mints it. live.Leased must be false: a lease is
the broker's that granted it, and a written message is waiting. live is
refused with [InvalidMessage] — the "field" field naming which — for
either, for a delivery count below 0 or above 2147483647, and for an
instant outside what a durable broker records (1970 to 2262); a
payload above [PolicyValue.MaxMessageBytes] is [MessageTooLarge]. A
refused message writes nothing.

A broker that joins the transaction ctx carries (ADR 0151) writes it in
that transaction, so it exists if and only if the transaction commits,
and wakes its consumers after the commit, as a publication does.

symbols.name: NackValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Deliveries int; VisibleAt time.Time; DeadLettered bool}
symbols.canonical: struct{Deliveries int; VisibleAt time.Time; DeadLettered bool}

fields.name: Deliveries
fields.doc:
Deliveries is how many times the message had been delivered when it
failed, counting from 1.

fields.name: VisibleAt
fields.doc:
VisibleAt is when the message becomes available again. It is the zero
Time when DeadLettered is true.

fields.name: DeadLettered
fields.doc:
DeadLettered reports that the message exhausted
[PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries] and was moved to the dead-letter store
with its cause. It will not be delivered again, unless somebody replays
it ([DeadLetterManager]).

symbols.doc:
NackValue is what [Broker.Nack] decided.

It exists because "I reported the failure" and "that message is now dead"
are different facts, and a consumer that cannot tell them apart cannot log
the one that matters. Every field is a scalar: a nack is on the failure
path, but it is on the failure path of a queue that is expected to retry,
so it is not rare enough to allocate on.

symbols.name: NotRetryable

code.public: The message cannot be processed and was dead-lettered without a retry

symbols.doc:
NotRetryable is the failure a handler reports when no retry can fix it:
returned as it is, or — the usual form — added by DoNotRetry to the
handler's own cause. The consumer engine recognises its code with
errs.HasCode and dead-letters the message at once through a broker's
Rejecter, instead of spending MaxDeliveries leases on an outcome
already known.

Returned bare, it is the cause the dead letter records. Added by
DoNotRetry to an SDK error it is only a mark in the wrap trail, and the
error's own Reason, Code and Public are what the dead letter keeps:
origin wins (CLAUDE.md rule 6), which is the reason an investigator
needs.

symbols.name: OncePublisher
symbols.spelled: interface{PublishOnce(ctx context.Context, key string, payload []byte, window time.Duration) (message MessageValue, published bool, err error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{PublishOnce(ctx context.Context, key string, payload []byte, window time.Duration) (message github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.MessageValue, published bool, err error)}
symbols.doc:
OncePublisher publishes a message at most once per key over a window: a
second publication under a key the window still holds publishes nothing
(ADR 0183).

It is the producer's half of the duplicates at-least-once delivery leaves.
A producer that retries a publication whose answer it never got — a
timeout, a crash between the call and its log line — would otherwise
enqueue the same work twice; under a key derived from the work, the retry
inside the window is recognised and dropped. It is JetStream's
Nats-Msg-Id, two minutes by default, SQS FIFO's deduplication ID, five
minutes, and River's unique jobs. It narrows duplicates at the producer
and does not remove them: the queue still delivers at least once, and a
handler still asserts it is idempotent.

A sibling of [Broker] for the reason [DeadLetterReader] is. The three
brokers in internal/service/data/queue implement it.

symbols.name: PublishOnce
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string, payload []byte, window time.Duration) (message MessageValue, published bool, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string, payload []byte, window time.Duration) (message github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.MessageValue, published bool, err error)
symbols.doc:
PublishOnce publishes payload as [Broker.Publish] does and reserves key
for window from now — unless key is still reserved, and then it
publishes nothing. It reports which: true with the message it minted,
or false with the zero [MessageValue] when an earlier publication's
window still holds key.

A duplicate is an answer and not an error, on purpose: it is the
expected outcome of the retry this call exists for, and a caller
asking "did it go out?" must not have to tell a sentinel from a
failure. The message the earlier publication minted is not returned:
the key is what the caller holds.

The window runs on the broker's clock from the publication that
reserved key, and ends there: a publication after it publishes again
and reserves the key anew. A reservation past its window is removed
lazily, by a later publication through this sibling. Keys are compared
byte for byte; the durable brokers keep only their SHA-256.

An empty key is refused, and so is a non-positive window — "never
deduplicate" and "forever" are opposite readings of zero, and either
would be a publication that reads as deduplicated and is not — or one
whose end a durable broker cannot record (2262): [QueueMisconfigured],
naming the argument, and nothing is published. A payload above
[PolicyValue.MaxMessageBytes] is [MessageTooLarge].

A broker that joins the transaction ctx carries (ADR 0151) reserves key
in that transaction: the reservation and the message exist if and only
if it commits. What a crash between the two costs is the broker's to
say, and it is at most a duplicate, never a lost message.

symbols.name: PolicyValue
symbols.spelled: struct{VisibilityTimeout time.Duration; RetryDelay time.Duration; MaxRetryDelay time.Duration; MaxDeliveries int; MaxMessageBytes int}
symbols.canonical: struct{VisibilityTimeout time.Duration; RetryDelay time.Duration; MaxRetryDelay time.Duration; MaxDeliveries int; MaxMessageBytes int}

fields.name: VisibilityTimeout
fields.doc:
VisibilityTimeout is how long a [Broker.Receive] hides a message from
every other consumer. It is the deadline the consumer is racing, and
it must be longer than the slowest run of the handler — or the handler
must renew it through [LeaseExtender].

It is the single knob that sets how quickly a dead consumer's work is
picked up: a message held by a process that has been SIGKILLed
reappears exactly this long after it was leased, and not before.

A non-positive value is refused ([QueueMisconfigured]), and so is one
above [MaxDeadlineOffset].

fields.name: RetryDelay
fields.doc:
RetryDelay is how long a NACKED message stays invisible before it
becomes eligible again, measured from the nack.

It does NOT apply to a lease that simply lapsed: that message has
already been invisible for a whole visibility timeout, and charging it
a second wait would punish a crashed consumer more than a failing one.

Zero is a working value and means "eligible as soon as the nack
returns". Negative is read as zero. Above [MaxDeadlineOffset] it is
refused ([QueueMisconfigured]).

It is the same wait after every failure unless [PolicyValue]
.MaxRetryDelay makes it grow.

fields.name: MaxRetryDelay
fields.doc:
MaxRetryDelay makes the retry delay GROW, and is where the growth
stops. When it is positive, a message nacked on its n-th delivery waits
RetryDelay × 2^(n−1), held at MaxRetryDelay — the SDK's one backoff
curve (kernel/backoff, ADR 0103), keyed on the delivery that failed,
so a downstream that is down is asked less and less often instead of at
a fixed cadence it is already failing to keep up with (ADR 0151).

Zero keeps RetryDelay constant, which is what every policy did before
this field existed: a policy that does not name it behaves exactly as
it did. That is the zero's one reading — a ceiling nobody set is not a
request for unbounded growth, which could not be recorded anyway.

A negative value is refused, because it is not a ceiling and the caller
who wrote it meant something; so is one above [MaxDeadlineOffset],
whose deadline a durable broker could not record; so is a ceiling with
no RetryDelay to grow from, which would leave every retry at zero while
reading like a backoff; and so is a ceiling below RetryDelay, which
would silently shorten every wait the caller asked for
([QueueMisconfigured], naming the field).

fields.name: MaxDeliveries
fields.doc:
MaxDeliveries is how many times one message may be handed to a
consumer before the broker gives up and dead-letters it. It is
compared against [DeliveryValue.Deliveries], which counts from 1, so a
value of 1 means "one attempt, then the dead-letter store" and is a
legitimate configuration rather than an off-by-one.

A non-positive value is refused ([QueueMisconfigured]).

fields.name: MaxMessageBytes
fields.doc:
MaxMessageBytes bounds one payload. A larger payload is refused at
[Broker.Publish] with [MessageTooLarge], at the call site that built
it, rather than accepted and discovered by a consumer that cannot read
it back.

Zero means [DefaultMaxMessageBytes]. Negative is refused, because it
is not a bound at all and the caller who wrote it meant something.

symbols.doc:
PolicyValue is the delivery discipline a broker enforces: how long a lease
lasts, how many attempts a message gets, how long a failure waits, and how
large a payload may be.

# Its zero value is REFUSED, and that is the decision

ADR 0031 gives two branches — clamp where a working default needs no
explanation, refuse where any value the SDK invented would be arbitrary —
and this one struct uses both, which is why they are worth reading side by
side.

  - [PolicyValue.VisibilityTimeout] and [PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries] are
    REFUSED at zero. Each has two natural readings that are OPPOSITES, and
    in each case one of them silently destroys the guarantee: a zero
    visibility timeout is either "redeliver immediately", which is a
    delivery storm, or "never redeliver", which is a lost message; zero
    deliveries is either "unlimited", which lets one poison message loop
    forever and the dead-letter store stay empty, or "none", which is a
    queue that delivers nothing. This is core/app/lock's argument for refusing
    a zero TTL, and it is the same argument because it is the same class of
    value: a lifetime belongs to the work being protected, and only the
    caller knows what that is.
  - [PolicyValue.RetryDelay] and [PolicyValue.MaxMessageBytes] are CLAMPED.
    A zero retry delay means "as soon as the lease lapses", which is one
    reading, is harmless, and is what a caller who has not thought about
    backoff wants. A zero size bound means [DefaultMaxMessageBytes].
  - [PolicyValue.MaxRetryDelay] is neither: its zero is the behaviour the
    struct had before the field existed — a retry delay that does not grow —
    which is one reading and the only backward-compatible one.

Both branches in one struct is the point. A domain in which every zero is
refused teaches a reader nothing except that the author was nervous.

The three durations are bounded from ABOVE as well, by [MaxDeadlineOffset],
and that refusal is about arithmetic rather than about readings: a deadline
further out than that cannot be recorded by a durable broker at all.

symbols.name: Normalized
symbols.doc:
Normalized returns the policy with its clamped fields resolved, so that
every implementation reads the same numbers rather than each remembering to
apply the same default.

It does NOT validate: call [PolicyValue.Validate] first, at construction,
where the refusal reaches the caller who wrote the mistake.

symbols.name: Validate
symbols.doc:
Validate reports whether the policy is one a broker can honour, and refuses
it BY FIELD when it is not.

It lives in core so that the memory, file and SQL brokers refuse identical
inputs identically — the property that makes the first usable as a test
double for the other two. It is the same instrument core/data/vfs's ValidatePath
and ValidatePerm are, for the same reason.

symbols.name: QueueBackendFailed

code.public: The queue's storage refused an operation

symbols.doc:
QueueBackendFailed reports a refusal from a durable broker's storage:
for the file broker the operating system's — an open, a rename, an
unlink, a directory read or a flush — and for the SQL broker a
statement its database did not complete.

The cause stays in the chain, so a caller may still ask
errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist), reach the *fs.PathError, or reach a
driver's own error with errors.As. Its fields name the operation and,
where it is not the payload, the path or the table — never the message
bytes; and the SQL broker WITHHOLDS the driver's text from every
rendering, because a driver quotes the row a statement touched.

symbols.name: QueueDirectoryUnusable

code.public: The queue directory cannot be used safely

symbols.doc:
QueueDirectoryUnusable refuses a queue directory at CONSTRUCTION.

A durable queue whose directory any account may write is a queue any
account may inject work into or silently drain, and the failure is
invisible: messages simply stop arriving. It is the same refusal
service/app/lock makes about its lock directory, and it is made at wiring
time for the same reason — at first use it would be a mystery, at
construction it names the directory.

symbols.name: QueueMisconfigured

code.public: The queue policy is not one this broker can honour

symbols.doc:
QueueMisconfigured refuses a PolicyValue a broker cannot honour — a
zero with opposite readings, or a duration past MaxDeadlineOffset — and
an argument a call cannot honour: an Extend duration that is
non-positive, a PublishOnce key that is empty or window that is not
positive, and a NackAfter delay, a PublishAt instant, an Extend or a
window that reaches past what a durable broker can record. The "field"
field names which value.

It is a refusal and not a clamp for the fields whose zero has two
opposite readings — see PolicyValue's documentation, which also names
the two fields this sentinel deliberately does NOT guard.

symbols.name: ReceiptValue
symbols.doc:
ReceiptValue is the handle to ONE lease: the only thing [Broker.Ack],
[Broker.Nack] and [LeaseExtender.Extend] accept, and the only proof that
this consumer is the one currently holding the message.

It is opaque and it is NOT the message identifier. Two deliveries of the
same message carry the same [MessageValue.ID] and different receipts, which
is what lets a broker refuse an acknowledgement from a consumer whose lease
has already lapsed and been taken by somebody else. Do not parse it, do not
construct one, and do not store one past the lease it names.

It is a defined string rather than a struct with an unexported field
because a receipt has to survive being handed to a goroutine, put in a map
and printed in a log, and because it is not a secret: it names a lease on a
queue the holder can already read. What it must not be is FORGEABLE into
somebody else's lease, and that is a property of how the implementation
mints it, not of the type.

symbols.name: Rejecter
symbols.spelled: interface{Reject(ctx context.Context, receipt ReceiptValue, cause error) error}
symbols.canonical: interface{Reject(ctx context.Context, receipt github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.ReceiptValue, cause error) error}
symbols.doc:
Rejecter dead-letters a leased message at once, with the cause that
condemned it, whatever its delivery count.

It is the broker's half of a handler saying "do not retry" — [DoNotRetry]
is the handler's — and internal/service/data/queue.Consume joins the two: a
handler whose failure carries [CodeNotRetryable] is rejected rather than
nacked, so a payload that will never decode reaches the dead-letter store
on its first failure instead of its MaxDeliveries-th, and an operator sees
it one lease and no retry delay later.

It is a sibling of [Broker] for the reason [DeadLetterReader] is: a
connector onto a system with no in-band dead-letter move cannot implement
it, and the engine falls back to Nack for such a broker — the message is
then retried until MaxDeliveries and dead-lettered with the same cause, so
the shortcut is lost and never the message. The three brokers in
internal/service/data/queue implement it.

symbols.name: Reject
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, receipt ReceiptValue, cause error) error
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, receipt github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.ReceiptValue, cause error) error
symbols.doc:
Reject moves the leased message named by receipt to the dead-letter
store with cause, recorded as [Broker.Nack] records the cause of a
message that ran out of attempts: its Reason, its dotted-quad Code and
its wire-safe Public half, never the Private one. The dead letter's
Deliveries is the count the message had, which may be below
[PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries].

A lapsed receipt is [LeaseExpired] and one this broker cannot read is
[UnknownReceipt], exactly as [Broker.Ack] refuses them; neither moves
anything.

symbols.name: Releaser
symbols.doc:
Releaser hands a leased message back at once, without counting the
delivery it was leased under.

It is the broker's half of a consumer saying "I never started this" — a
worker stopped in the middle of its batch, or a message whose lease ran
out before its turn came — and internal/service/data/queue.Consume uses it
for exactly those: a message the handler never ran is not a failure, so it
must not wait out a retry delay, nor move one delivery closer to the
dead-letter store, as a [Broker.Nack] would make it (kitsunium/sdk#474).
It is what SQS's ChangeMessageVisibility to zero does.

It is a sibling of [Broker] for the reason [DeadLetterReader] is: a
connector onto a system whose delivery count cannot be given back cannot
implement it, and the engine falls back to Nack for such a broker — the
message then comes back after its retry delay with the delivery counted,
so the courtesy is lost and never the message. The three brokers in
internal/service/data/queue implement it.

symbols.name: Release
symbols.doc:
Release makes the leased message named by receipt receivable again
now, by any consumer, with its delivery count put back to what it was
before this lease: its next delivery carries the [DeliveryValue]
.Deliveries this one did. It is never dead-lettered, whatever that
count, and no retry delay applies. It wakes an idle consumer, as a
Nack that hands a message back does.

A lapsed receipt is [LeaseExpired] and one this broker cannot read is
[UnknownReceipt], exactly as [Broker.Ack] refuses them; neither moves
anything. The receipt is void once Release returns nil.

symbols.name: RetryAfter
symbols.doc:
RetryAfter marks cause as a failure to retry no sooner than delay from now,
so the consumer engine hands the message back through the broker's
[DelayedNacker] with that delay instead of the policy's retry delay
(ADR 0183).

	if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
		return queue.RetryAfter(errThrottled, retryAfter(resp)) // what the server asked for
	}

It is for a failure whose moment is known — a downstream that answered
with a Retry-After, a mail server that greylisted the sender, a resource
that frees up at a known instant. The delivery is counted as a nack counts
it, so a message that has used its [PolicyValue.MaxDeliveries] is
dead-lettered with cause, the delay unused. A negative delay is read as
zero — retry at once — and one above [MaxDeadlineOffset] is held there.

The mark is an errs.Wrap onto cause, as [DoNotRetry]'s is: an SDK cause
keeps its own Reason, Code and Public, [CodeRetryRequested] joins its wrap
trail and the delay rides as a field; any other cause, or none, records
[RetryRequested] itself. [RetryAfterOf] reads the delay back. A failure
marked both ways is not retried: [DoNotRetry] wins.

A broker without the sibling is nacked as before: the message comes back
after the policy's retry delay, so the delay asked for is lost, never the
message.

symbols.name: RetryAfterOf
symbols.doc:
RetryAfterOf returns the delay [RetryAfter] put on err, and whether it put
one: err carries [CodeRetryRequested] in its chain and the delay it was
marked with. When err was marked more than once, the outermost mark's
delay is the one returned.

symbols.name: RetryRequested

code.public: The message was handed back to be retried after a delay

symbols.doc:
RetryRequested is the failure a handler reports when the message must be
retried no sooner than a delay of the handler's choosing: added by
RetryAfter to the handler's own cause — the usual form — or, around a
cause that is not an SDK error or around none, the origin a dead letter
records. The consumer engine recognises its code with errs.HasCode and
hands the message back through a broker's DelayedNacker (ADR 0183).

symbols.name: SQLQueueMisconfigured

code.public: The SQL queue's configuration cannot be used

symbols.doc:
SQLQueueMisconfigured refuses, at construction, an SQLConfig no SQL
broker could run: a nil Transactor, one that is not a core/data/sql Joiner
and Deferrer — without which a publication could neither join the
caller's transaction nor wake a consumer after its commit — a dialect
the SDK does not speak, or a table name that is not a lower-case SQL
identifier the broker can interpolate safely. The "setting" and
"problem" fields name which (ADR 0151).

symbols.name: UnknownReceipt

code.public: The receipt does not name a lease this queue issued

symbols.doc:
UnknownReceipt refuses an acknowledgement naming a lease this broker
never issued, or one whose encoding it cannot read.

It is distinct from LeaseExpired on purpose. "This was yours and you
were too slow" and "this was never yours" are different bugs: the
first is a visibility timeout too short for the handler, the second is
a receipt built by hand, kept across a restart of an in-memory broker,
or handed to the wrong queue. Collapsing them would send every reader
looking for the wrong one half the time.

symbols.name: WakeValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Signal <-chan struct{}; In time.Duration; Scheduled bool}
symbols.canonical: struct{Signal <-chan struct{}; In time.Duration; Scheduled bool}

fields.name: Signal
fields.doc:
Signal is closed by the next event that may make a message receivable
through this broker in this process: a Publish, or a Nack that hands a
message back. It is never nil, and it is never closed by a publication
made in another process.

fields.name: In
fields.doc:
In is how long, measured on the broker's own clock at the moment Wake
was called, until a message the broker already holds becomes
receivable with no further event: a retry delay ending, or a lease
lapsing because its consumer died. It is meaningful only when
Scheduled is true; zero or less means now.

It is a duration and not an instant so that a consumer whose clock is
not the broker's still waits the right length of time rather than
comparing two clocks that disagree.

fields.name: Scheduled
fields.doc:
Scheduled reports that In names such a moment. It is false when the
broker holds nothing that will become receivable on its own.

symbols.doc:
WakeValue is what an idle consumer waits on: an event, or an instant the
broker already knows about.

symbols.name: Waker
symbols.doc:
Waker tells an idle consumer when to look at a broker again, so it can
sleep until there may be work instead of polling on a fixed cadence.

It is a SIBLING of [Broker] for the reason [DeadLetterReader] is: waking is
a capability, and a broker over a transport that cannot see its own
publications — or one whose state lives in another process — has no honest
answer to give. The consumer engine asks by type assertion and polls when
the answer is no, so an implementation that omits it loses latency, never
correctness.

A wake is a HINT, in both directions. A signal may arrive with nothing to
receive — another consumer took it — and work may appear with no signal at
all: a durable broker cannot see a publication made by another process. So
a consumer that uses it still polls, at whatever cadence bounds the second
case, and treats the first as a cheap empty Receive.

symbols.name: Wake
symbols.doc:
Wake returns what an idle consumer should wait on. Call it BEFORE the
Receive that may come back empty: a publication landing between that
Receive and the wait closes the channel already handed out, so it is
not missed.

symbols.name: Aborter
symbols.spelled: interface{OnAbort(ctx context.Context, fn func(ctx context.Context)) (held bool)}
symbols.canonical: interface{OnAbort(ctx context.Context, fn func(ctx context.Context)) (held bool)}
symbols.doc:
Aborter is an ADR 0039 sibling of [Transactor], and the complement of
[Deferrer]: a transactor that holds a function until the work a context
carries is undone. Discover it by type assertion; the SDK's own transactor
implements it.

It is how a callee that announced something BEFORE the commit — a
registration a later delivery waits on, a resource reserved for the
commit — takes it back when the commit never comes, since a function held
with Defer is then dropped without a word (ADR 0139, amended 2026-10-14).

symbols.name: OnAbort
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, fn func(ctx context.Context)) (held bool)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, fn func(ctx context.Context)) (held bool)
symbols.doc:
OnAbort holds fn until the work of the scope ctx carries for this
transactor is undone, and reports true.

The work is undone when the scope's savepoint rolls back, or when any
scope around it does, the root included: the root's unit of work
returned an error or panicked, its commit was refused — a poisoned
transaction — or the COMMIT itself failed, which [CommitFailed] reports
as a unit of work that had no effect. A savepoint that is released
hands what it held to the scope around it, which decides in turn; a
commit that stands drops every function still held, unrun.

The held functions run once, newest first, on the goroutine that ends
the scope, after its ROLLBACK or ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT and before that
scope's Transact returns — or before its panic continues. Each is
handed ctx without its cancellation or deadline: a function that
cleans up after a rollback must not die of the cancellation that
caused it. It must not panic, and it must not open a transaction on
ctx, which is over.

For a function held with OnAbort and another with Defer under the same
scope, exactly one of the two runs, unless a function held with Defer
before it panics.

OnAbort reports false and holds nothing when ctx carries no open
transaction of this transactor. There is nothing to undo, so fn is the
caller's again. A nil fn holds nothing and gets the same answer.

symbols.name: BeginFailed

code.public: The database refused to open a transaction

symbols.doc:
BeginFailed is joined with the driver's error when a transaction could
not be opened. Nothing ran.

symbols.name: Checker
symbols.doc:
Checker reports whether the database is reachable. Implementations MUST be
safe for concurrent use.

symbols.name: Check
symbols.doc:
Check probes the database under a bounded budget and returns nil when
it answered. A non-nil error is always typed and never carries the
connection string.

symbols.name: CodeBeginFailed
symbols.doc: CodeBeginFailed identifies a transaction the driver would not open.

symbols.name: CodeCommitFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeCommitFailed identifies a transaction whose COMMIT was rejected. The
unit of work did NOT take effect.

symbols.name: CodeConfigInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeConfigInvalid identifies a constructor refused because the Config could
never produce a working port: a nil *sql.DB or an unusable Dialect.

symbols.name: CodeDialectRefused
symbols.doc:
CodeDialectRefused identifies a dialect this SDK RECOGNISES and declines,
because its savepoint grammar is a different algorithm rather than a
different string. The reason travels in a field.

symbols.name: CodeDuplicateMigration
symbols.doc:
CodeDuplicateMigration identifies two migrations declaring the same
version.

symbols.name: CodeHealthCheckFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeHealthCheckFailed identifies a liveness probe the database answered
with an error.

symbols.name: CodeHealthCheckTimeout
symbols.doc:
CodeHealthCheckTimeout identifies a liveness probe that did not answer
within its budget.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidMigration
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidMigration identifies a migration that could never run: version
zero, an empty name, a nil Up, or a nil Down.

symbols.name: CodeMigrationFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeMigrationFailed identifies a migration step, or its version-table
bookkeeping, that failed. The transaction was rolled back.

symbols.name: CodeMigrationIrreversible
symbols.doc:
CodeMigrationIrreversible identifies a Down refused because the caller
declared the migration irreversible with the Irreversible step.

symbols.name: CodeMigrationLockTimeout
symbols.doc:
CodeMigrationLockTimeout identifies a migration run abandoned because
another holder kept the lock for the whole budget.

symbols.name: CodeMigrationLockUnsupported
symbols.doc:
CodeMigrationLockUnsupported identifies a Migrator refused at construction
because the dialect offers no lock that dies with its holder. No dialect the
SDK speaks answers it since ADR 0140.

symbols.name: CodeMigrationOutOfOrder
symbols.doc:
CodeMigrationOutOfOrder identifies a pending migration whose version is
lower than one already applied — the two-branches-merged hazard.

symbols.name: CodeMigrationUnknownVersion
symbols.doc:
CodeMigrationUnknownVersion identifies a version recorded in the database
that this binary carries no migration for — so it cannot be reversed.

symbols.name: CodeNestedIsolation
symbols.doc:
CodeNestedIsolation identifies a nested Transact that asked for an
isolation level or read-only-ness a savepoint cannot provide.

symbols.name: CodePoolMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodePoolMisconfigured identifies a pool policy the SDK refuses to apply
because the value database/sql would read is not the one the caller meant.

symbols.name: CodeRollbackFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeRollbackFailed identifies a ROLLBACK the driver refused. It travels
alongside the error that triggered the rollback, never instead of it.

symbols.name: CodeSavepointFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeSavepointFailed identifies a SAVEPOINT, RELEASE SAVEPOINT or ROLLBACK
TO SAVEPOINT statement the engine rejected.

symbols.name: CodeTxClosed
symbols.doc:
CodeTxClosed identifies an Executor used after the scope that lent it
returned.

symbols.name: CodeTxPoisoned
symbols.doc:
CodeTxPoisoned identifies an operation refused because the transaction can
no longer be trusted: its savepoint rollback failed, so the engine's state
is unknown and nothing more may be committed on it.

symbols.name: CodeUnknownDialect
symbols.doc: CodeUnknownDialect identifies a dialect name this SDK has never heard of.

symbols.name: CodeVersionTableInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeVersionTableInvalid identifies a version-table name that cannot be
interpolated into SQL safely. Identifiers cannot be bound as parameters.

symbols.name: CommitFailed

code.public: The transaction could not be committed and had no effect

symbols.doc:
CommitFailed is joined with the driver's error when COMMIT was
rejected. It says the unit of work did NOT take effect, which is the
one fact a caller must not have to infer.

symbols.name: ConfigInvalid

code.public: The SQL configuration is incomplete and was refused

symbols.doc:
ConfigInvalid is returned by every constructor in
internal/service/data/sql for a Config that could never produce a
working port.

symbols.name: Deferrer
symbols.doc:
Deferrer is an ADR 0039 sibling of [Transactor]: a transactor that holds a
function until the transaction a context carries has committed. Discover it
by type assertion; the SDK's own transactor implements it.

It is how an effect that must not happen for work that is rolled back — a
store's write hooks, a message, a mail — waits for the commit (ADR 0139).

symbols.name: Defer
symbols.doc:
Defer holds fn until the transaction ctx carries for this transactor
commits, and reports true.

The held functions run once, in the order they were held, on the
goroutine that commits, after the commit and before the outermost
Transact returns. A rollback drops them, and so does the rollback of
the savepoint they were held in; a savepoint that is released hands
them to the scope around it. A panic in one reaches the caller of the
outermost Transact after the commit stood, and the functions held after
it do not run.

Defer reports false and holds nothing when ctx carries no open
transaction of this transactor. There is no commit to wait for, so fn
is the caller's again, usually to run at once. A nil fn holds nothing
and gets the same answer.

symbols.name: Dialect
symbols.doc:
Dialect names a SQL engine whose savepoint grammar, placeholder syntax,
identifier quoting, row-lock clauses and advisory-lock mechanism this SDK
knows exactly.

The set is CLOSED and small on purpose. Every feature this domain adds — a
savepoint, a `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, an advisory lock — is spelled
differently by each engine, and there is no portable subset that covers all
three. So the domain refuses a dialect it cannot spell AT CONSTRUCTION,
by name, rather than generating SQL that will fail at the first savepoint of
the first nested transaction on a production database (ADR 0055 §D4).

The zero value is [DialectUnknown] and is not usable: it is what an unset
configuration field looks like, and reading it as "probably Postgres" is how
a MySQL deployment discovers the difference in production (ADR 0031).

symbols.name: ForUpdate
symbols.doc:
ForUpdate renders the clause that ends a read by locking the rows it returns
until the transaction ends, leading space included: " FOR UPDATE" on
PostgreSQL and MySQL. On MySQL it is also a locking read, which reads the
latest committed rows rather than a REPEATABLE READ transaction's snapshot.

SQLite has no row lock and no such clause, and renders the empty string: a
SQLite transaction excludes every other writer with the database's one write
lock, which it takes at its first WRITE, so a transaction that must read
under exclusion writes first (ADR 0140). A dialect that is not
[Dialect.Valid] renders the clause: an engine without one refuses the
statement, which is louder than a lock dropped in silence.

symbols.name: ForUpdateSkipLocked
symbols.doc:
ForUpdateSkipLocked renders the clause that ends a read by locking the rows
it returns and SKIPPING those another transaction holds, leading space
included: " FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED" on PostgreSQL and MySQL. Two readers
then never wait on each other's rows and never take the same one.

It needs PostgreSQL 9.5, MySQL 8.0.1 or MariaDB 10.6 — later than the
floors [DialectPostgres] and [DialectMySQL] name — and an older server
refuses the statement. SQLite renders the empty string and a dialect that is
not [Dialect.Valid] the clause, for the reasons [Dialect.ForUpdate] gives: a
SQLite transaction that has written holds the database's only write lock,
so no row it reads is held by anybody else.

symbols.name: Placeholder
symbols.doc:
Placeholder renders the bind marker of a statement's n-th argument, counted
from 1.

This is the divergence that makes a "portable" hand-written query a fiction:
PostgreSQL numbers its markers — $1, $2 — while MySQL and SQLite share the
positional ?, whose position is the argument's order. Every statement the SDK
binds an argument to takes its markers from here, so a fourth engine is
spelled in one place or not at all.

A dialect that is not [Dialect.Valid] — an unset field — has no marker and
renders the empty string, so a statement built from it parses on no engine
rather than on whichever one a guess favoured (ADR 0031).

symbols.name: QuoteIdent
symbols.doc:
QuoteIdent renders name as an identifier of the dialect: delimited, so a
table called "order" or "user" is a name rather than a keyword, and with the
delimiter doubled wherever the name holds it, which is how every engine
spells a delimiter inside a delimited identifier. MySQL delimits with
backticks, whatever its ANSI_QUOTES mode says; PostgreSQL and SQLite with
the standard's double quotes.

It validates nothing. An identifier cannot be a bound argument, so the SDK
interpolates only names it validated at construction, and that check is the
whole defence: what a name may hold, and how long it may be — PostgreSQL
TRUNCATES a longer one, into what may be another table's name — is the
caller's to refuse before quoting it. A dialect that is not [Dialect.Valid]
renders the empty string, for the reason [Dialect.Placeholder] gives.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String returns the dialect's canonical lowercase name.

symbols.name: SupportsAdvisoryLock
symbols.doc:
SupportsAdvisoryLock reports whether the engine offers a SESSION-SCOPED
advisory lock — one the server releases when the connection holding it
drops.

SQLite does not: it has no advisory-lock function, only the file lock that
serialises writers. That distinction decides HOW [Migrator] promises mutual
exclusion across processes, so it is a property of the dialect and not a
runtime discovery (ADR 0055 §D7). On SQLite the runner holds the database
file's write lock for the whole run instead, which the operating system
releases when its holder dies, as a server releases an advisory lock
(ADR 0140).

symbols.name: Valid
symbols.doc: Valid reports whether d is a dialect this domain can actually spell.

symbols.name: DialectMySQL
symbols.doc: DialectMySQL is MySQL 5.7+ / MariaDB 10.x with InnoDB.

symbols.name: DialectPostgres
symbols.doc:
DialectPostgres is PostgreSQL 9.1+ (and wire-compatible engines that
implement pg_advisory_lock, e.g. CockroachDB advertises the function
but the caller must verify it is a real lock before claiming this).

symbols.name: DialectRefused

code.public: That SQL engine is recognised and deliberately not supported

symbols.doc:
DialectRefused is returned by ParseDialect for an engine this SDK
recognises and declines. It is a DIFFERENT answer from UnknownDialect:
a caller debugging a refusal needs to know whether their engine is
unheard-of or known-and-declined, because only the second one comes
with a reason they can evaluate.

symbols.name: DialectSQLite
symbols.doc: DialectSQLite is SQLite 3.6.8+.

symbols.name: DialectUnknown
symbols.doc: DialectUnknown is the unusable zero value.

symbols.name: DuplicateMigration

code.public: Two migrations declare the same version

symbols.doc:
DuplicateMigration refuses two migrations declaring the same version.
The version IS the identity, so a duplicate makes "has this been
applied?" unanswerable.

symbols.name: Executor
symbols.spelled: interface{ExecContext(ctx context.Context, query string, args ...any) (stdsql.Result, error); QueryContext(ctx context.Context, query string, args ...any) (*stdsql.Rows, error); QueryRowContext(ctx context.Context, query string, args ...any) *stdsql.Row}
symbols.canonical: interface{ExecContext(ctx context.Context, query string, args ...any) (database/sql.Result, error); QueryContext(ctx context.Context, query string, args ...any) (*database/sql.Rows, error); QueryRowContext(ctx context.Context, query string, args ...any) *database/sql.Row}
symbols.doc:
Executor is the surface a statement runs against: a pool, a connection, or
a transaction. Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use, with the
documented exception of a transaction-scoped executor, which is confined to
its scope (see internal/service/data/sql).

The method set is a strict SUBSET of what *sql.DB, *sql.Tx and *sql.Conn
already expose, so all three satisfy this port with no adapter. That is the
point: the SDK is not wrapping database/sql, it is naming the part of it a
caller should be allowed to reach.

It is FROZEN at three methods. pkg/v1/data/sql aliases it, so under ADR 0039 a
fourth method would break every downstream double at compile time with no
deprecation window. New capabilities arrive as SIBLING interfaces the
implementation is type-asserted for — [Preparer] is the first.

# What is deliberately absent

There is no Commit, no Rollback and no Begin. A function that receives an
Executor therefore CANNOT end the transaction it was handed: the method does
not exist, so the mistake does not compile. Ownership of a transaction stays
with the [Transactor] that opened it (ADR 0055 §D3).

symbols.name: ExecContext
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, query string, args ...any) (stdsql.Result, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, query string, args ...any) (database/sql.Result, error)
symbols.doc: ExecContext runs a statement that returns no rows.

symbols.name: QueryContext
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, query string, args ...any) (*stdsql.Rows, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, query string, args ...any) (*database/sql.Rows, error)
symbols.doc: QueryContext runs a statement that returns rows. The caller closes them.

symbols.name: QueryRowContext
symbols.doc: QueryRowContext runs a statement expected to return at most one row.

symbols.name: HealthCheckFailed

code.public: The database is not reachable

symbols.doc:
HealthCheckFailed is joined with the driver's error when the probe was
answered with a failure.

symbols.name: HealthCheckTimeout

code.public: The database did not answer the health check in time

symbols.doc:
HealthCheckTimeout is returned when the probe did not answer inside its
budget. It is a separate code from HealthCheckFailed because a database
that refuses is a different operational fact from one that hangs, and a
readiness endpoint routes on the difference.

symbols.name: InvalidMigration

code.public: The migration is not runnable and was refused

symbols.doc:
InvalidMigration is returned for a migration that could never run. The
"missing" field names which half is absent.

symbols.name: Irreversible
symbols.doc:
Irreversible is the [Step] a caller assigns to [MigrationValue.Down] to
declare that the migration cannot be reversed. It always fails, with a typed
error naming the version.

It is a value rather than a nil convention so the claim appears in the diff
and in the version-table review, and so `Down` reports a refusal the caller
wrote rather than a nil dereference the SDK discovered.

symbols.name: Joiner
symbols.doc:
Joiner is an ADR 0039 sibling of [Transactor]: a transactor that says where
a statement issued under a context runs. Discover it by type assertion; the
SDK's own transactor implements it.

It is what lets a callee JOIN the transaction its caller opened instead of
opening a second one. A second transaction takes a second connection, does
not see the caller's uncommitted writes, and under a pool of one waits
forever for the connection its own caller holds (ADR 0139).

symbols.name: Join
symbols.doc:
Join returns the executor a statement issued under ctx runs on.

When ctx carries a transaction THIS transactor opened, that is the
executor of the innermost scope ctx names, and inTx is true. It is
valid only while that scope runs and refuses afterwards: a context
that outlived its transaction must not fall back to the pool, where
its statements would run outside the transaction they were written
for.

When ctx carries none — no transaction, or only another transactor's —
it is the pool, outside any transaction, and inTx is false.

symbols.name: MigrationFailed

code.public: A migration did not apply and was rolled back

symbols.doc:
MigrationFailed is joined with the step's own error when a migration or
its bookkeeping row fails. The transaction was rolled back, so neither
the schema change nor the version row took effect — except on engines
with non-transactional DDL, which is stated in the package doc rather
than papered over.

symbols.name: MigrationIrreversible

code.public: That migration was declared irreversible and cannot be rolled back

symbols.doc:
MigrationIrreversible is what the Irreversible step returns. It is the
caller's own declaration coming back at them, not a defect the SDK
found — which is why it reads as a statement about the migration rather
than about the runner.

symbols.name: MigrationLockTimeout

code.public: Another process is running migrations and did not finish in time

symbols.doc:
MigrationLockTimeout is returned when another holder kept the migration
lock for the whole budget. Nothing was applied.

symbols.name: MigrationLockUnsupported

code.public: That dialect has no advisory lock, so migrations cannot be serialised

symbols.doc:
MigrationLockUnsupported is the refusal of a Migrator over a dialect
that offers no lock dying with its holder — never a run without one: a
runner that silently drops mutual exclusion is at its most dangerous
exactly when two instances start together, which is the case it exists
for.

No dialect the SDK speaks answers it since ADR 0140: PostgreSQL and
MySQL serialise on the session's advisory lock, SQLite on the database
file's write lock. It stays defined because it is published, and a
caller matching it would otherwise stop compiling.

symbols.name: MigrationOutOfOrder

code.public: A pending migration is older than one already applied

symbols.doc:
MigrationOutOfOrder refuses a pending migration whose version is lower
than one already applied. It is the two-branches-merged hazard: both
branches numbered from the same base, one shipped first, and the other
would now apply UNDER it — producing a schema that matches neither
branch's expectation and a version table that cannot express what
happened.

symbols.name: MigrationUnknownVersion

code.public: The database records a migration this build does not carry

symbols.doc:
MigrationUnknownVersion refuses a Down over a version the running
binary has no migration for. The database is ahead of the code, and
reversing a change whose Down is not present would be guessing.

symbols.name: MigrationValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Version uint64; Name string; Up Step; Down Step}
symbols.canonical: struct{Version uint64; Name string; Up github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.Step; Down github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.Step}

fields.name: Version
fields.doc:
Version orders the migration. It must be non-zero and unique within one
set: zero is reserved as "before every migration", the value Down takes
to reverse everything.

Any strictly-increasing scheme works; a UTC timestamp (20260910143000)
is the conventional one because two branches developed in parallel then
merge without colliding.

fields.name: Name
fields.doc:
Name is the human label recorded in the version table. It must be
non-empty: a schema history whose rows say only "42" is a schema
history nobody can read during an incident.

fields.name: Up
fields.doc: Up applies the change. Required.

fields.name: Down
fields.doc:
Down reverses it. Required — and [Irreversible] is how a caller says
"this one cannot be reversed" OUT LOUD.

A nil Down is refused rather than accepted as "irreversible", because
"I forgot the reversal" and "there is no reversal" are the same nil and
only one of them is a defect. The same rule core/app/lifecycle applies to a
nil Stop, for the same reason.

symbols.doc:
MigrationValue is one versioned schema change and its reversal.

The SDK does NOT own a migration FILE FORMAT, a directory layout, or a
naming convention, and it ships no example directory. A migration is a value
the consumer constructs, because the moment the SDK reads a directory it has
invented a convention every consumer must adopt and no consumer asked for
(ADR 0055 §D8). Where the statements come from — a Go literal, an embed.FS,
a generator — is the caller's decision and none of the SDK's business.

The zero value is not runnable and is refused at construction.

symbols.name: Validate
symbols.doc:
Validate reports why the migration could never run, or nil.

It is a method on the value rather than a check inside the runner so a
caller can validate a set at start-up — before any connection exists —
which is where a wiring fault should be found.

symbols.name: Migrator
symbols.spelled: interface{Down(ctx context.Context, target uint64) error; Plan(ctx context.Context) ([]MigrationValue, error); Up(ctx context.Context) error}
symbols.canonical: interface{Down(ctx context.Context, target uint64) error; Plan(ctx context.Context) ([]github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.MigrationValue, error); Up(ctx context.Context) error}
symbols.doc:
Migrator applies an ordered, versioned set of [MigrationValue] to a schema,
under mutual exclusion. Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use, and
MUST be safe against a SECOND PROCESS running the same migrations at the
same instant.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the concrete runner stays unexported behind its constructor in
internal/service/data/sql.

symbols.name: Down
symbols.doc:
Down reverses every applied migration whose version is STRICTLY GREATER
than target, in descending order, each in its own transaction, under the
migration lock. Down(ctx, 0) reverses everything.

symbols.name: Plan
symbols.doc:
Plan reports what Up would apply, in the order it would apply it,
WITHOUT applying anything and without taking the migration lock. It is
the dry run: a read of the version table and a set difference.

symbols.name: Up
symbols.doc:
Up applies every pending migration in ascending version order, each in
its own transaction, under the migration lock.

symbols.name: NestedIsolation

code.public: A nested transaction cannot change isolation or read-only mode

symbols.doc:
NestedIsolation is returned when a nested Transact asks for non-zero
options. A nested scope is a SAVEPOINT inside an already-open
transaction, and a savepoint changes neither the isolation level nor
the read-only-ness of that transaction. Honouring the request is
impossible; ignoring it would hand the caller a weaker transaction than
the one they asked for, under a nil error.

symbols.name: ParseDialect
symbols.doc:
ParseDialect resolves a dialect name. It never guesses.

A name in the accepted set resolves. A name in the refused set returns
[DialectRefused] carrying WHY, so the caller learns their engine is known
and declined rather than unrecognised. Anything else returns
[UnknownDialect].

symbols.name: PoolMisconfigured

code.public: The connection-pool policy is not one this SDK will apply

symbols.doc:
PoolMisconfigured is returned when a pool field's zero value would be
read by database/sql as a policy nobody chose. MaxOpen is the case that
matters: database/sql reads 0 as UNLIMITED, and "as many connections as
the application happens to want" is a decision made by forgetting a
line, not by taking one (ADR 0031's refusal side).

symbols.name: Preparer
symbols.doc:
Preparer is the first ADR 0039 sibling of [Executor]: an executor that can
also prepare a statement for repeated execution. Discover it by type
assertion rather than by widening Executor.

*sql.DB, *sql.Tx and *sql.Conn all satisfy it; a transaction-scoped executor
does too, and the prepared statement it returns is bound to that
transaction and dies with it.
