symbols.name: PrepareContext
symbols.doc: PrepareContext compiles a statement. The caller closes it.

symbols.name: RollbackFailed

code.public: Rolling the transaction back did not complete cleanly

symbols.doc:
RollbackFailed travels ALONGSIDE the error that triggered the rollback,
never instead of it. A teardown that also breaks is a second defect,
and reporting only it would hide the first — the rule ADR 0050 wrote
for UnwindFailed, applied to the same shape one layer down.

symbols.name: SavepointFailed

code.public: A savepoint statement was rejected by the database

symbols.doc:
SavepointFailed is returned when SAVEPOINT, RELEASE SAVEPOINT or
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT is rejected. The "statement" field names which of
the three, because the consequences differ: a failed SAVEPOINT means
the nested scope never started, while a failed ROLLBACK TO means the
engine's state is unknown and the transaction is poisoned.

symbols.name: Step
symbols.doc:
Step is one direction of a migration: the statements that move the schema.

A FUNCTION port, for the same reason [TxFunc] is: one behaviour, so a named
func IS the contract, and a func type cannot grow a method (ADR 0039).

It receives the SAME [Executor] the surrounding transaction runs on, which
is what makes a migration and its version-table row commit together.

symbols.name: Transactor
symbols.spelled: interface{Transact(ctx context.Context, opts TxOptionsValue, fn TxFunc) error}
symbols.doc:
Transactor owns transactions. Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent
use.

It is FROZEN at one method, and the options travel in a struct rather than
as a second method, precisely so the port never needs a sibling for
"Transact, but read-only" (ADR 0039).

IFACE-PLUGIN: the concrete manager stays unexported behind its constructor
in internal/service/data/sql.

symbols.name: Transact
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, opts TxOptionsValue, fn TxFunc) error
symbols.doc:
Transact runs fn inside a transaction and commits when fn returns nil.

If ctx already carries a transaction opened by THIS Transactor, fn runs
inside a SAVEPOINT of that transaction instead of a new one, and opts
must be the zero value — a savepoint cannot change isolation or
read-only-ness, so asking for either is refused with [NestedIsolation]
rather than silently ignored (ADR 0055 §D5).

A panic inside fn is NOT recovered: the deferred rollback still runs,
and the panic reaches the caller with its original stack.

symbols.name: TxClosed

code.public: That transaction handle is no longer valid

symbols.doc:
TxClosed is returned when an Executor is used after the scope that lent
it returned. database/sql would answer ErrTxDone for a finished
transaction and would EXECUTE for a nested scope whose outer
transaction is still open — the second case is the one worth catching.

symbols.name: TxFunc
symbols.doc:
TxFunc is the unit of work a [Transactor] runs inside a transaction.

It is a FUNCTION port, the shape internal/core/CLAUDE.md already admits for
resilience.Operation, scheduler.Job and lifecycle.Start: one behaviour, so a
named func IS the contract. ADR 0039 is satisfied structurally — a func type
cannot grow a method at all.

ctx is the transaction-scoped context. Passing it on is what lets a callee
join THIS transaction rather than open a second one, and what lets a nested
[Transactor.Transact] become a savepoint instead of a deadlock against the
transaction its own caller is holding.

Returning nil commits (or releases the savepoint). Returning an error rolls
back (or rolls back to the savepoint) and the error is returned to the
caller VERBATIM, so errors.Is keeps working across the boundary.

ex is valid ONLY for the duration of the call. Using it afterwards is
refused with a typed error rather than left to database/sql's ErrTxDone.

symbols.name: TxOptionsValue

fields.name: Isolation
fields.doc:
Isolation is the transaction isolation level. The zero value
(sql.LevelDefault) defers to the driver.

fields.name: ReadOnly
fields.doc:
ReadOnly asks the engine to refuse writes. Not every driver enforces
it; those that do not report an error at Begin rather than accepting
writes silently, which is why this is passed through rather than
emulated.

symbols.doc:
TxOptionsValue parameterises ONE transaction. It is a value, not a manager
setting, because isolation is a property of the unit of work and not of the
pool it runs on.

The zero value is a working configuration: the driver's default isolation
level, read-write. That is the only non-arbitrary default available — every
engine defines its own default level and picking one here would silently
change the semantics of an existing application on migration (ADR 0031's
clamp side, where the default needs no explanation because it is the
database's own).

It is deliberately a struct rather than two extra method parameters so
[Transactor] stays frozen at one method: a new option is a new FIELD, which
breaks nobody, where a new method breaks every downstream double (ADR 0039).

symbols.name: IsZero
symbols.doc:
IsZero reports whether the options ask for nothing beyond the driver's
defaults.

It exists because a NESTED scope is a savepoint, and a savepoint can change
neither the isolation level nor the read-only-ness of the transaction it
sits inside. Non-zero options on a nested call are therefore refused with
[NestedIsolation] rather than ignored — silently downgrading a caller's
explicit `Serializable` to whatever the outer transaction happened to use is
the kind of "helpful" behaviour that produces a data race nobody can find
(ADR 0055 §D5).

symbols.name: StdOptions
symbols.doc:
StdOptions renders the value as the stdlib's own option struct, ready for
(*sql.DB).BeginTx.

symbols.name: TxPoisoned

code.public: The transaction is no longer usable and will not be committed

symbols.doc:
TxPoisoned refuses every further operation on a transaction whose
savepoint rollback failed.

This is the answer to "does a failed sub-transaction condemn the outer
one?". Normally NO: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT is precisely the statement
that clears PostgreSQL's aborted state, so a caught inner failure
leaves a usable transaction. But when that statement ITSELF fails, the
engine's state is no longer known, and continuing would commit a
transaction containing work the SDK believes it undid.

symbols.name: UnknownDialect

code.public: The SQL dialect is not one this SDK supports

symbols.doc:
UnknownDialect is returned by ParseDialect for a name that is in
neither the accepted nor the refused set.

symbols.name: VersionTableInvalid

code.public: The version-table name is not a plain SQL identifier

symbols.doc:
VersionTableInvalid refuses a version-table name that is not a bare SQL
identifier. A table name cannot be a bound parameter, so it is
interpolated — which makes validating it the only thing between a
configuration string and an injection.

symbols.name: Algorithm
symbols.doc:
Algorithm is the typed key under which a Compressor registers (e.g. "gzip",
"flate", "zlib"). The zero value Algorithm("") is reserved invalid, mirroring
codec.Format and crypto.Algorithm. Note that "flate" is the raw DEFLATE
stream of RFC 1951 and "zlib" is the RFC 1950 envelope HTTP misnames
"deflate" — distinct Algorithms, not aliases.

symbols.name: Known
symbols.doc: Known reports whether a has been registered in the Compressor registry.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String implements fmt.Stringer and returns the raw identifier.

symbols.name: Available
symbols.doc:
Available returns the sorted list of registered Algorithms, or nil before
any Register.

symbols.name: BoundedDecompressor
symbols.spelled: interface{DecompressBounded(dst []byte, src []byte, max int64) (out []byte, err error); Compressor}
symbols.canonical: interface{DecompressBounded(dst []byte, src []byte, max int64) (out []byte, err error); github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/transform.Compressor}
symbols.doc:
BoundedDecompressor is the optional extension for schemes that can be told
how much plaintext they are allowed to materialise. Consumers detect support
with a type assertion, exactly as they do for the codec layer's Appender.

It exists because a caller that enforces a TIGHTER ceiling than the scheme's
own backstop otherwise has no way to say so, and must instead let the scheme
materialise everything and then judge the result. Judging afterwards is a
correct verdict reached by doing the attacker's work first: a frame layer
capping output at 64 MiB but calling plain Decompress still lets a few
hundred kilobytes of crafted input drive the scheme's full 256 MiB backstop
before the answer is known.

max is a ceiling, never a promise: a scheme MAY refuse a stream below it for
its own reasons, and MUST NOT return more than max bytes. A ceiling of zero
is a real ceiling — it admits an empty stream and nothing else — and a
negative one is clamped to zero rather than given a third meaning, so the
bound is monotone in max. A stream that would exceed max fails with
DecompressedTooLarge rather than being silently truncated: a short read that
looked like success would turn a bomb into a parsing bug further up.

DecompressedTooLarge and NOT the scheme's own sentinel, because the two
answer different questions, and because the implementation cannot honestly
give the scheme's: it stops reading at the ceiling, short of the trailer the
scheme would need to pronounce on the stream at all.

symbols.name: DecompressBounded
symbols.spelled: func(dst []byte, src []byte, max int64) (out []byte, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(dst []byte, src []byte, max int64) (out []byte, err error)

symbols.name: CodeCompressedFrameInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeCompressedFrameInvalid identifies a malformed compressed frame OR a
tripped decompression-bomb guard (max output size / max expansion ratio). It
is owned by the pkg/v1/data/codec frame layer (a later commit); declared here so
the 0.2.5.* block is allocated in one place per ADR 0014.

symbols.name: CodeCompressionFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeCompressionFailed identifies a Compress call whose underlying compressor
returned an error — typically a writer fault while flushing the stream.

symbols.name: CodeDecompressedTooLarge
symbols.doc:
CodeDecompressedTooLarge identifies a stream whose plaintext exceeded the
ceiling the CALLER supplied to BoundedDecompressor.DecompressBounded. It is
distinct from the scheme sentinels (GZIP_FAILED and friends) on purpose: a
corrupt body and a body that is merely too big are different facts, and a
caller that imposed the ceiling is the only one able to say which of the two
its own limit produced. Collapsing them would force that caller to report a
malformed stream for one whose only established fault is its size.

symbols.name: CodeDecompressionFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeDecompressionFailed identifies a Decompress call whose underlying
decompressor returned an error — malformed input or a truncated stream.

symbols.name: CodeDuplicateRegistration
symbols.doc:
CodeDuplicateRegistration identifies a boot-time collision on the Compressor
registry: a nil scheme, or a distinct scheme claiming an already-registered
Algorithm. It is surfaced via panic at boot (see registry.go). Its reason is
DUPLICATE_REGISTRATION so the bracket header "[<code> <REASON>]" stays a valid
(code,reason) pairing per ADR 0005 §Semantics — mirroring the codec registry's
CodeDuplicateRegistration (0.2.2.1).

symbols.name: CodeFlateFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeFlateFailed identifies a failure inside compress/flate during either a
Compress (writer) or Decompress (reader) operation.

symbols.name: CodeGzipFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeGzipFailed identifies a failure inside compress/gzip during either a
Compress (writer) or Decompress (reader) operation; the wrap trail and the
COMPRESSION_FAILED / DECOMPRESSION_FAILED sentinels distinguish the
direction.

symbols.name: CodeUnknownCompressor
symbols.doc:
CodeUnknownCompressor identifies a Lookup/Decompress call naming an Algorithm
that no imported package has registered. It is also surfaced via panic at
boot on a duplicate registration (see registry.go), not only as a sentinel.

symbols.name: CodeZlibFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeZlibFailed identifies a failure inside compress/zlib during either a
Compress (writer) or Decompress (reader) operation. It is distinct from
CodeFlateFailed because the zlib envelope (RFC 1950) is a distinct wire format
from the raw DEFLATE stream (RFC 1951): a stream rejected under one scheme is
routinely valid under the other, so the two must be told apart at the code.

symbols.name: CompressedFrameInvalid

code.public: Compressed frame is malformed or exceeds the safety bound

symbols.doc:
CompressedFrameInvalid is returned for a malformed compressed frame or a
tripped decompression-bomb guard. The pkg/v1/data/codec frame layer (a later
commit) is its emitter; defined here so the 0.2.5.* block lands in one place.

symbols.name: CompressionFailed

code.public: Compression failed

symbols.doc:
CompressionFailed wraps a failure from a compressor's underlying writer
(e.g. compress/gzip or compress/flate) while encoding the payload.

symbols.name: Compressor
symbols.spelled: interface{Algorithm() Algorithm; Compress(dst []byte, src []byte) (out []byte, err error); Decompress(dst []byte, src []byte) (out []byte, err error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Algorithm() github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/transform.Algorithm; Compress(dst []byte, src []byte) (out []byte, err error); Decompress(dst []byte, src []byte) (out []byte, err error)}
symbols.doc:
Compressor is the contract every byte-transform scheme satisfies. Instances
MUST be safe for concurrent use; scheme-specific options are supplied via the
scheme's constructor, not via the Compressor interface. Compress and
Decompress follow the append-to-dst convention of the stdlib (dst may be nil)
so callers can reuse buffers on the hot path.

src must not overlap dst's spare capacity, dst[len(dst):cap(dst)]: every
scheme writes its output there while it is still reading src, so an aliased
src is overwritten mid-read and the output is corrupt. Reusing one buffer
means passing buf[:0] as dst and a DIFFERENT buffer as src — the same rule
as copy-free encoders across the stdlib, stated here because no scheme can
check it cheaply.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry stores plug-in scheme instances behind this
interface — concrete scheme types stay unexported per package.

symbols.name: DecompressedTooLarge

code.public: Decompressed payload exceeds the caller's ceiling

symbols.doc:
DecompressedTooLarge reports that a stream's plaintext exceeded the
ceiling its caller passed to DecompressBounded. It establishes exactly
that and nothing more: more than max plaintext bytes were produced. It
does NOT report a well-formed stream — the decode stops at the ceiling,
so the trailer is never reached and the bytes past it are never read.
Claiming well-formedness here would be claiming the result of work this
error exists to avoid doing.

symbols.name: DecompressionFailed

code.public: Decompression failed

symbols.doc:
DecompressionFailed wraps a failure from a decompressor's underlying
reader while decoding the payload — malformed or truncated input.

symbols.name: DuplicateRegistration

code.public: A compressor is already registered under that algorithm

symbols.doc:
DuplicateRegistration is the boot-time panic sentinel for the Compressor
registry: a nil scheme or a distinct scheme claiming a taken Algorithm. Its
reason matches the bracket-header word so code 0.2.5.5 resolves to
DUPLICATE_REGISTRATION — never the unrelated UNKNOWN_COMPRESSOR (0.2.5.1).

symbols.name: FlateFailed

code.public: flate transform failed

symbols.doc: FlateFailed wraps a failure from compress/flate (Compress or Decompress).

symbols.name: GzipFailed

code.public: gzip transform failed

symbols.doc: GzipFailed wraps a failure from compress/gzip (Compress or Decompress).

symbols.name: Lookup
symbols.doc:
Lookup returns the Compressor registered under name.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry stores plug-in scheme instances behind the
Compressor interface — concrete types are intentionally unexported per scheme.

symbols.name: Register
symbols.doc:
Register inserts c into the registry under c.Algorithm() and returns it so
callers can bind the singleton to a typed package-level variable like
`var GzipCompressor = transform.Register(gzipCompressor{})`. Panics on a nil
scheme or when a distinct scheme already claims the same Algorithm.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the registry hands plug-in Compressor instances back to callers
so each scheme keeps its concrete type unexported; the stable contract is the
Compressor interface itself.

"Nil" here means UNUSABLE, not only an untyped nil: a typed nil pointer and a
plug-in whose type is not comparable both satisfy the port and neither can
serve one call (see internal/kernel/plugin).

symbols.name: UnknownCompressor

code.public: No compressor is registered under that algorithm

symbols.doc:
UnknownCompressor is returned when no Compressor is registered under the
requested Algorithm — typically a missing blank-import of the scheme.

symbols.name: ZlibFailed

code.public: zlib transform failed

symbols.doc:
ZlibFailed wraps a failure from compress/zlib (Compress or Decompress),
including a failed Adler-32 check the raw-DEFLATE scheme cannot detect.

symbols.name: AtomicWriter
symbols.spelled: interface{WriteAtomic(name string, data []byte, perm fs.FileMode) error}
symbols.canonical: interface{WriteAtomic(name string, data []byte, perm io/fs.FileMode) error}
symbols.doc:
AtomicWriter publishes a whole file in one indivisible step. It is the ADR
0039 sibling of [WritableFS]: reached by type assertion, never by widening
the port, because it is a CAPABILITY and not every filesystem has one — an
object store with no rename, a read-through overlay, a tar archive.

	if publisher, ok := filesystem.(vfs.AtomicWriter); ok {
		err = publisher.WriteAtomic("index.html", page, 0o644)
	}

Both filesystems in internal/service/data/vfs implement it.

symbols.name: WriteAtomic
symbols.spelled: func(name string, data []byte, perm fs.FileMode) error
symbols.canonical: func(name string, data []byte, perm io/fs.FileMode) error
symbols.doc:
WriteAtomic publishes data at name so that a concurrent reader sees
either the previous content or the new content, and never a partial
file, a truncated one, or a name that resolves to nothing.

The contract on FAILURE is why this method exists, and it is what
[PublishFailed] asserts: when WriteAtomic returns an error, the bytes
previously at name are unchanged, and no temporary file survives
anywhere the caller can see. An implementation that cannot promise
both must not implement this interface.

Durability beyond the process is the implementation's to describe: the
operating-system filesystem flushes the file AND the directory entry,
while an in-memory one has no device to flush and says so.

symbols.name: CodeDirectoryNotEmpty
symbols.doc:
CodeDirectoryNotEmpty identifies a Remove aimed at a directory that still
has entries. RemoveAll is the call that was wanted.

symbols.name: CodeDirectorySyncFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeDirectorySyncFailed identifies the ONE failure that arrives after a
successful rename: the directory entry could not be flushed to the device.

It is a separate code from PublishFailed because it means the opposite
thing. PublishFailed says nothing changed; this says the new content IS
visible and may not survive a power loss.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidPath
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidPath identifies a name that is not a valid filesystem path for
this domain: rooted, empty, backslash-separated, or carrying a "." or ".."
element. It is the LEXICAL half of the confinement guarantee.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidPermission
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidPermission identifies a file mode that cannot be honoured as
written: zero — which the SDK refuses to read as "pick a default" — or bits
outside fs.ModePerm, which would make a typo able to mint a setuid file.

symbols.name: CodeNotRegularFile
symbols.doc:
CodeNotRegularFile identifies a name that exists and is not a regular file,
where writing it would replace a directory, a device or a socket.

symbols.name: CodePathEscaped
symbols.doc:
CodePathEscaped identifies a lexically valid name that resolved OUTSIDE the
filesystem's root — a symbolic link pointing away from the tree, or a
traversal the operating system refused. It is the half fs.ValidPath cannot
see.

symbols.name: CodePublishFailed
symbols.doc:
CodePublishFailed identifies an atomic publication that did not complete.
Its contract is the interesting part: the previous content is intact and no
temporary file survives.

symbols.name: CodeReadFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeReadFailed identifies an open, stat or directory listing the filesystem
refused. The cause is wrapped rather than replaced, so errors.Is against
fs.ErrNotExist and fs.ErrPermission keeps answering.

symbols.name: CodeRootUnavailable
symbols.doc:
CodeRootUnavailable identifies a root directory that could not be opened, or
that is not a directory at all. It is reported by the constructor, so the
refusal arrives where the program is wired rather than at the first write.

symbols.name: CodeWriteFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeWriteFailed identifies a create, write, mkdir or remove the filesystem
refused. As with CodeReadFailed the cause stays in the chain.

symbols.name: DirectoryNotEmpty

code.public: That directory still has entries in it

symbols.doc:
DirectoryNotEmpty is returned by Remove for a directory that still has
entries — POSIX ENOTEMPTY, made typed and made identical in both
implementations so a memory filesystem is a faithful double.

symbols.name: DirectorySyncFailed

code.public: The file was published but the directory entry was not flushed

symbols.doc:
DirectorySyncFailed is returned when the rename succeeded and the
parent directory could not be flushed afterwards.

It deliberately does NOT roll back. The rename has already happened, so
the new content is what every reader sees; undoing it would mean a
second non-atomic write to repair a durability problem, which is how a
good file gets replaced by a worse one. The caller is told exactly what
is true — published, not proven durable — and decides whether that is
acceptable for its data.

symbols.name: FS
symbols.doc:
FS is the read half of a filesystem, and it is io/fs.FS unchanged.

It is an ALIAS rather than a fresh interface, so a vfs.FS and an fs.FS are
the same type to the compiler and no conversion, adapter or assertion sits
between an SDK filesystem and the standard library's walkers. The name
exists to say, in one place, that the SDK's answer for reading is the
stdlib's answer for reading.

symbols.name: FullFS
symbols.doc:
FullFS is the union of [WritableFS] and [AtomicWriter], and it is what the
SDK's own constructors return.

It is the shape core/observe/metrics already uses for FullMeter, and it exists for
the same reason: the port stays frozen and the capability stays assertable
for a THIRD-PARTY filesystem that cannot publish atomically, while a caller
wiring one of the SDK's own does not have to type-assert for the headline
feature. A parameter should still ask for the narrowest thing it uses —
WritableFS when it only writes, AtomicWriter when it only publishes.

symbols.name: InvalidPath

code.public: That path is not usable on this filesystem

symbols.doc:
InvalidPath is returned for a name outside the fs.ValidPath grammar,
and by [ValidateWritePath] for the root itself.

It is a REFUSAL rather than a cleanup. Normalising "../../etc/passwd"
into something safe is the single most reliable way to ship a
traversal bug: every normaliser is a small parser, every small parser
has a case its author did not think of, and the caller never learns
that the path it asked for is not the path it got.

symbols.name: InvalidPermission

code.public: A file mode is required and must be a plain permission mode

symbols.doc:
InvalidPermission is returned for a zero file mode, or one carrying
bits outside fs.ModePerm.

ADR 0031's refusing half: any mode the SDK invented here would be
arbitrary. 0644 and 0600 differ by who may read the bytes, and the
caller is the only party that knows what the bytes are — so a zero is
read as "the field was never filled in", which it almost always is.

symbols.name: NotRegularFile

code.public: That path already holds something other than a file

symbols.doc:
NotRegularFile is returned when a name exists and is not a regular
file. Writing it would replace a directory, a device or a socket, and
no caller has ever meant that by WriteFile.

symbols.name: PathEscaped

code.public: That path leaves the filesystem it was resolved against

symbols.doc:
PathEscaped is returned when a lexically valid name resolved outside
the filesystem's root.

fs.ValidPath cannot see this: every element of "link/secret" is legal,
and whether it leaves the tree depends on what "link" points at, which
is a runtime property of the filesystem and not of the string.

symbols.name: PublishFailed

code.public: The filesystem could not publish that file

symbols.doc:
PublishFailed is returned when an atomic publication did not complete.

Its guarantee is the whole point of the domain and is asserted by a
test, not by this comment: on this error the bytes previously at the
name are unchanged and no temporary file survives. It is therefore
safe to retry, and safe to give up.

symbols.name: ReadFailed

code.public: The filesystem could not read that path

symbols.doc:
ReadFailed is returned when an open, stat or directory listing was
refused. The cause stays in the error chain, so a caller may still ask
errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist) and get the answer io/fs would give.

symbols.name: RootUnavailable

code.public: The filesystem root could not be opened

symbols.doc:
RootUnavailable is returned by NewOS when the root cannot be opened.

It is a CONSTRUCTION-time refusal on purpose: a filesystem whose root
does not exist will fail every call it is ever given, and the useful
place to learn that is where the program is assembled, not on the first
request that happens to write something.

symbols.name: ValidatePath
symbols.doc:
ValidatePath reports whether name is a path this domain will resolve, and
returns [InvalidPath] when it is not.

The rule is fs.ValidPath and nothing else, on purpose. io/fs already imposes
it on every reader, so a second, subtly different grammar for writers would
mean a name that can be written and not read back — and the SDK would have
invented that discrepancy itself. Concretely it rejects the empty string, a
leading or trailing slash, a doubled slash, a Windows-style backslash path,
and any "." or ".." element.

This is a LEXICAL guarantee. It closes "../../etc/passwd" and it does not
close a symbolic link that leaves the tree — see [PathEscaped], which is the
implementation's half of the same promise.

One result is worth stating because it surprises people: the separator here
is "/" and nothing else, so `..\..\etc\passwd` is ACCEPTED — it is one legal,
if peculiar, POSIX filename, and a file written under it lands inside the
root rather than above it. Rejecting backslashes would make a legal filename
unwritable to buy a confinement the grammar already provides.

symbols.name: ValidatePerm
symbols.doc:
ValidatePerm reports whether perm is a mode this domain will apply, and
returns [InvalidPermission] when it is not.

Two refusals, and ADR 0031 is the reason for both.

A ZERO mode is refused rather than defaulted. ADR 0031 admits clamping where
a working default needs no explanation and demands a refusal where any
SDK-chosen value would be arbitrary — and a file mode is the second case,
unambiguously: 0644 and 0600 differ by who may read the bytes, the SDK does
not know what the bytes are, and a mode of 0 is what an unfilled struct
field looks like. Silently choosing would make the SDK the author of a
security decision it has no information about.

Bits OUTSIDE fs.ModePerm are refused by name. setuid, setgid, the sticky bit
and the type bits are each a deliberate act; none of them should be
reachable by mistyping a permission literal, and a mode argument that also
carries them makes "0o4755 instead of 0o755" a one-character privilege
escalation. A caller who genuinely wants one of those wants a call that says
so, which this domain does not offer.

symbols.name: ValidateWritePath
symbols.doc:
ValidateWritePath is [ValidatePath] plus the one refusal a writer needs: the
root itself is not a target.

fs.ValidPath accepts "." because a reader legitimately opens the tree to list
it. A writer that accepts it accepts `RemoveAll(".")`, which is a call that
empties the entire filesystem and reads, in a diff, exactly like a
no-op — and accepts `WriteFile(".")`, which cannot mean anything at all.

symbols.name: WritableFS
symbols.spelled: interface{MkdirAll(name string, perm fs.FileMode) error; Remove(name string) error; RemoveAll(name string) error; WriteFile(name string, data []byte, perm fs.FileMode) error; FS}
symbols.canonical: interface{MkdirAll(name string, perm io/fs.FileMode) error; Remove(name string) error; RemoveAll(name string) error; WriteFile(name string, data []byte, perm io/fs.FileMode) error; github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/vfs.FS}
symbols.doc:
WritableFS is the write half, and it is FROZEN at four methods on top of the
embedded [FS]. A new capability arrives as a sibling interface reached by
type assertion — never by widening this one (ADR 0039): pkg/v1/data/vfs aliases
it, Go interfaces are structural, and a fifth method would break every
downstream implementation at compile time with no deprecation window.

Every method validates its name through [ValidateWritePath], and every
method taking a mode validates it through [ValidatePerm], so the two
implementations refuse identical inputs identically. That is what makes an
in-memory filesystem usable as a test double for a real one.

Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the concrete filesystems stay unexported behind their
constructors in internal/service/data/vfs.

symbols.name: MkdirAll
symbols.doc:
MkdirAll creates name and every missing parent, applying perm to each
directory it creates. An existing directory is success; an existing
non-directory is [NotRegularFile].

symbols.name: Remove
symbols.doc:
Remove removes one file or one EMPTY directory. A non-empty directory
is [DirectoryNotEmpty] rather than a recursive delete, because the two
are different decisions and only one of them is reversible by accident.

symbols.name: RemoveAll
symbols.doc:
RemoveAll removes name and everything beneath it. A name that does not
exist is success — the caller asked for it to be gone, and it is.

symbols.name: WriteFile
symbols.spelled: func(name string, data []byte, perm fs.FileMode) error
symbols.canonical: func(name string, data []byte, perm io/fs.FileMode) error
symbols.doc:
WriteFile writes data to name, creating the file if it is absent and
truncating it if it is not, with perm applied on creation. Missing
parent directories are NOT created: a typo in a path is a far more
common event than a genuinely absent directory, and inventing the
tree silently is how a file ends up somewhere nobody looks. It is not
atomic — [AtomicWriter] is the call that is.

symbols.name: WriteFailed

code.public: The filesystem could not write that path

symbols.doc:
WriteFailed is returned when a create, write, mkdir or remove was
refused. Like [ReadFailed] it keeps the cause reachable.

symbols.name: AddressValue

fields.name: Network
fields.doc:
Network is the socket family: tcp, tcp4, tcp6, udp, udp4, udp6, unix,
unixgram or unixpacket.

fields.name: Addr
fields.doc:
Addr is the bind target: "host:port" for the IP families, a filesystem
path for the unix families.

symbols.doc:
AddressValue names one socket to bind. It is a value type so a group's listen
set is comparable and copyable, and so a configuration file can express it
directly.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String renders the address as "network://addr" for logs and error fields.

symbols.name: AlreadyStarted

code.public: The server is already started

symbols.doc: AlreadyStarted is returned by Start on a server that is already serving.

symbols.name: CallFailed

code.public: The outbound call failed

symbols.doc: CallFailed is returned when an outbound call produced no response.

symbols.name: CallHook
symbols.doc:
CallHook receives one CallValue per completed outbound call. It is a function
port rather than an interface because it is a single-method contract with no
state, and a func keeps the domain free of a dependency on the logger or the
metrics package: the consumer wires it to whichever it uses.

A CallHook MUST be safe for concurrent use and MUST NOT block — it runs on the
calling goroutine, so a slow hook slows every request.

symbols.name: CallValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Method string; Host string; Path string; Status int; Bytes int64; Duration time.Duration; Err error}
symbols.canonical: struct{Method string; Host string; Path string; Status int; Bytes int64; Duration time.Duration; Err error}

fields.name: Method
fields.doc: Method is the uppercase HTTP method.

fields.name: Host
fields.doc: Host is the authority the call was sent to.

fields.name: Path
fields.doc: Path is the request path.

fields.name: Status
fields.doc: Status is the HTTP status code, or zero when the call produced no response.

fields.name: Bytes
fields.doc: Bytes is the number of response body bytes read.

fields.name: Duration
fields.doc:
Duration is the wall-clock time from request start to response headers.
It deliberately excludes the body: the record is emitted once the body is
done with, but this field measures the upstream's time to first answer,
which is the one a slow upstream and a large payload do not share.

fields.name: Err
fields.doc:
Err is what ended the call: a policy refusal, a transport failure, the
response ceiling, or a failed close. Nil when the body was read in full.

symbols.doc:
CallValue records one completed outbound call for observation, so a caller
can log, meter or trace every egress without wrapping each call site by hand.

It is handed to a CallHook once the response body is FINISHED WITH — read to
the end, failed, or closed — not when the headers arrive. A body's size is
only known after it has been read, and an over-sized body or a failed close
happens later still, so a record emitted at the headers could carry neither:
it reported every call as a clean success of zero bytes. A refused request
and an unreachable upstream are still reported immediately, because in
neither case is there a body to wait for.

symbols.name: Chain
symbols.doc:
Chain applies middlewares to a handler, outermost first.

Chain(h, a, b, c) yields a(b(c(h))): the first middleware listed is the first
to see a connection. That ordering matches how the list reads on the page,
which is the only ordering a reader will guess correctly.

symbols.name: ClientConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{BaseURL string "json:\"base_url\""; DialTimeout DurationValue "json:\"dial_timeout\""; HandshakeTimeout DurationValue "json:\"handshake_timeout\""; ResponseTimeout DurationValue "json:\"response_timeout\""; TotalTimeout DurationValue "json:\"total_timeout\""; MaxResponseSize int64 "json:\"max_response_size\""; MaxRedirects int "json:\"max_redirects\""; RedirectOrigins []string "json:\"redirect_origins\""; DefaultHeaders map[string]string "json:\"default_headers\""}
symbols.canonical: struct{BaseURL string "json:\"base_url\""; DialTimeout github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.DurationValue "json:\"dial_timeout\""; HandshakeTimeout github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.DurationValue "json:\"handshake_timeout\""; ResponseTimeout github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.DurationValue "json:\"response_timeout\""; TotalTimeout github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.DurationValue "json:\"total_timeout\""; MaxResponseSize int64 "json:\"max_response_size\""; MaxRedirects int "json:\"max_redirects\""; RedirectOrigins []string "json:\"redirect_origins\""; DefaultHeaders map[string]string "json:\"default_headers\""}

fields.name: BaseURL
fields.doc: BaseURL is the origin every relative path resolves against.

fields.name: DialTimeout
fields.doc: DialTimeout bounds establishing the TCP connection.

fields.name: HandshakeTimeout
fields.doc: HandshakeTimeout bounds the TLS handshake.

fields.name: ResponseTimeout
fields.doc:
ResponseTimeout bounds the wait for response headers after the request
has been written. It is separate from TotalTimeout so a slow upstream is
distinguishable from a large body.

fields.name: TotalTimeout
fields.doc: TotalTimeout bounds the whole call, body included.

fields.name: MaxResponseSize
fields.doc:
MaxResponseSize caps the response body in bytes. A body of exactly this
size is admitted; only one past it fails the call, and the body is never
truncated.

fields.name: MaxRedirects
fields.doc:
MaxRedirects caps the redirect chain. Every hop is re-authorised by the
policy, and a hop to another origin is refused unless RedirectOrigins
names it, so a redirect cannot walk out of the allowed surface.

fields.name: RedirectOrigins
fields.doc:
RedirectOrigins names the origins, each written scheme://host[:port], a
redirect may lead to besides the origin of the request that started the
chain. Empty — the default — refuses with RequestDenied every redirect
that changes the scheme, the host or the port, https to http included:
the built-in policies judge the method and the path, so a hop that keeps
the path and swaps the origin would otherwise pass them. A listed origin
is followed, and receives none of the DefaultHeaders. An entry that is
not a bare http or https origin fails New with InvalidAddress.

fields.name: DefaultHeaders
fields.doc:
DefaultHeaders are added to every request that does not already set them
and is sent to the origin of BaseURL — or, with no BaseURL, to whatever
origin the request names. They are never sent to another origin: a
request built for one does not receive them, and a redirect that leaves
the origin of the request that started the chain is sent without them.

symbols.doc:
ClientConfig describes an outbound client. Durations use DurationValue so a
configuration file can say "5s" rather than a nanosecond count.

It sits in core beside LimitsValue and TimeoutsValue, which carry the same
kind of knobs for the inbound half. Keeping both faces' configuration in one
layer is what lets a consumer decode a whole network stanza against the
contract package alone, without importing an implementation to name the type
of a field it is setting.

symbols.name: CodeAlreadyStarted
symbols.doc: CodeAlreadyStarted identifies a Start call on a server that is already serving.

symbols.name: CodeCallFailed
symbols.doc: CodeCallFailed identifies an outbound call that did not produce a response.

symbols.name: CodeConnLimitReached
symbols.doc:
CodeConnLimitReached identifies a connection rejected because the group's
concurrency ceiling was saturated.

symbols.name: CodeDrainTimeout
symbols.doc:
CodeDrainTimeout identifies a shutdown whose drain budget expired with
connections still in flight; the remainder is closed hard.

symbols.name: CodeGroupDuplicate
symbols.doc:
CodeGroupDuplicate identifies a second declaration of an already-declared
listener group name.

symbols.name: CodeGroupUnknown
symbols.doc: CodeGroupUnknown identifies a lookup for a listener group that was never declared.

symbols.name: CodeHandlerAlreadySet
symbols.doc:
CodeHandlerAlreadySet identifies a second handler declaration on one stream
group — Handle, HandleFunc, HandleHTTP or HandleLoop, in any order — which
does not replace the first (ADR 0186 §D1).

symbols.name: CodeHandlerMissing
symbols.doc: CodeHandlerMissing identifies a listener group that was bound without a handler.

symbols.name: CodeHandlerPanic
symbols.doc:
CodeHandlerPanic identifies a panic recovered inside a handler; the connection
is closed but the process survives.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidAddress
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidAddress identifies a listen or dial address that is syntactically
unusable (empty host and port, malformed socket path, negative port).

symbols.name: CodeInvalidDuration
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidDuration identifies a configuration duration that is neither a Go
duration literal nor an integer nanosecond count.

symbols.name: CodeListenFailed
symbols.doc: CodeListenFailed identifies a listener that could not be bound to its address.

symbols.name: CodeLoopBackendUnavailable
symbols.doc:
CodeLoopBackendUnavailable identifies an explicit loop backend the running
kernel's probe refused, on a platform that has the mechanic (ADR 0186 §D5).

symbols.name: CodeLoopNoDescriptors
symbols.doc:
CodeLoopNoDescriptors identifies a loop group refused at Start because the
effective RLIMIT_NOFILE is zero or unreadable, which leaves no descriptor
for a ring's table or a connection (ADR 0186 §D5).

symbols.name: CodeLoopOptionUnsupported
symbols.doc:
CodeLoopOptionUnsupported identifies an option a group cannot honour on its
engine: Loop on a group not served by a loop handler, or, on a loop group,
Use or an option neither the engine nor the handler honours (ADR 0186 §D1).

symbols.name: CodeLoopOutputFull
symbols.doc:
CodeLoopOutputFull identifies a write refused because the connection's
output, or the loop's global output budget, is at its ceiling.

symbols.name: CodeLoopPostQueueFull
symbols.doc:
CodeLoopPostQueueFull identifies a Post refused because the loop's
preallocated queue of posted operations is full.

symbols.name: CodeLoopSpillFull
symbols.doc:
CodeLoopSpillFull identifies an unconsumed tail that does not fit the
connection's spill, or the loop's global spill budget.

symbols.name: CodeLoopStaleRef
symbols.doc:
CodeLoopStaleRef identifies an operation on a connection reference whose
generation has ended: the connection closed, and its slot may already
serve another one.

symbols.name: CodeLoopTLSUnsupported
symbols.doc:
CodeLoopTLSUnsupported identifies a loop group given a TLS identity: the
loop engine speaks plaintext only, and the SDK owns no TLS stack it could
drive without a blocking net.Conn (ADR 0186 §D2).

symbols.name: CodeLoopWrongThread
symbols.doc:
CodeLoopWrongThread identifies a loop operation called from a thread other
than the loop's own, detected under the loopdebug build tag.

symbols.name: CodeNotStarted
symbols.doc:
CodeNotStarted identifies an operation that requires a running server on one
that has not been started.

symbols.name: CodePacketTooLarge
symbols.doc: CodePacketTooLarge identifies a datagram longer than the group's accepted size.

symbols.name: CodeRequestDenied
symbols.doc:
CodeRequestDenied identifies an outbound request refused by the transport
policy before it left the process.

symbols.name: CodeResponseTooLarge
symbols.doc:
CodeResponseTooLarge identifies a response body that exceeded the configured
read ceiling.

symbols.name: CodeSSEFieldInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeSSEFieldInvalid identifies a Server-Sent Events frame the wire format
cannot carry: a line terminator inside an id, an event name or a comment
(the format has no escape — a newline SPLITS a value, so an id carrying one
would silently become a different id plus a stray field), a negative retry,
a retry under one millisecond (the wire field is an integer millisecond
count, and truncating to zero would say "reconnect immediately"), or a frame
with no field set at all.

symbols.name: CodeSSEFlushUnsupported
symbols.doc:
CodeSSEFlushUnsupported identifies a ResponseWriter that cannot be flushed.
Server-Sent Events is a streaming format: without a flush every event sits in
the transport buffer until the handler returns, which for an endless stream
means the client receives nothing, ever.

symbols.name: CodeSSEStreamClosed
symbols.doc:
CodeSSEStreamClosed identifies a send on a stream that has already ended —
the client disconnected, the server began draining, or the handler closed it.

symbols.name: CodeSSEStreamMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeSSEStreamMisconfigured identifies a stream option the domain refuses to
interpret rather than guess at: a negative keep-alive interval or a negative
per-write budget (ADR 0031).

symbols.name: CodeServerClosed
symbols.doc:
CodeServerClosed identifies work refused because the server already stopped
accepting; it is the expected terminal outcome of a graceful shutdown.

symbols.name: CodeSocketAdoptFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeSocketAdoptFailed identifies an inherited socket that could not be adopted
from the supervisor.

symbols.name: CodeStaticMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeStaticMisconfigured identifies a static file handler refused at
construction: no file tree to serve, a security header value the handler
will not send, or a Referrer-Policy token no browser recognises (ADR 0130).

symbols.name: CodeTLSHandshakeFailed
symbols.doc: CodeTLSHandshakeFailed identifies a TLS or mTLS handshake that did not complete.

symbols.name: CodeTLSMaterialInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeTLSMaterialInvalid identifies TLS material that is absent, malformed, or
yields no usable certificate; it is never downgraded to an empty trust store.

symbols.name: CodeTooManyRedirects
symbols.doc: CodeTooManyRedirects identifies an outbound call that exceeded its redirect budget.

symbols.name: CodeUnsafePath
symbols.doc:
CodeUnsafePath identifies an outbound path carrying a dot segment, literal or
percent-encoded. Such a path is refused before any allowlist pattern is tried,
because an anchored pattern like ^/v1/supi/[^/]+$ happily matches "/v1/supi/.."
which the upstream then normalises to a different resource.

symbols.name: CodeUnsupportedNetwork
symbols.doc:
CodeUnsupportedNetwork identifies a network name the domain does not serve
(anything outside tcp, tcp4, tcp6, udp, udp4, udp6, unix, unixgram, unixpacket).

symbols.name: CodeWSConnClosed
symbols.doc:
CodeWSConnClosed identifies an operation on a connection that has ended — the
peer sent Close, the server began draining, the handler closed it, or the
socket died. It is the terminal outcome a receive loop runs until.

symbols.name: CodeWSConnMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeWSConnMisconfigured identifies a connection option the domain refuses to
interpret rather than guess at: a negative ping interval or write budget, or
a non-positive size ceiling (ADR 0031).

symbols.name: CodeWSHandshakeFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeWSHandshakeFailed identifies an HTTP request that is not a valid RFC 6455
opening handshake: wrong method, absent or non-"websocket" Upgrade token, a
Connection header without "Upgrade", a Sec-WebSocket-Key that does not decode
to sixteen bytes, a Sec-WebSocket-Version other than 13, or an Origin the
server's policy refuses. The response is written before this is returned, so
the handler has nothing left to answer.

symbols.name: CodeWSInvalidPayload
symbols.doc:
CodeWSInvalidPayload identifies a payload the protocol cannot carry: a text
message or close reason that is not valid UTF-8 (§8.1), a close code that
must never appear on the wire (1004, 1005, 1006, 1015 and the unallocated
ranges — §7.4.2), or a close reason past the control-frame ceiling.

symbols.name: CodeWSMessageTooLarge
symbols.doc:
CodeWSMessageTooLarge identifies a frame or an accumulated message beyond the
connection's configured ceiling. The frame's announced length is checked
BEFORE any buffer is sized from it, because a 64-bit length field a peer
chooses is an out-of-memory condition one allocation away.

symbols.name: CodeWSProtocolViolation
symbols.doc:
CodeWSProtocolViolation identifies a frame RFC 6455 forbids: an unmasked
client frame (§5.1), a set reserved bit or reserved opcode (§5.2), a
fragmented or oversized control frame (§5.5), a non-minimal length encoding
(§5.2), a continuation with no message in progress or a new data frame
interrupting one (§5.4), or a malformed close payload (§5.5.1). Each fails
the connection.

symbols.name: CodeWSUpgradeUnsupported
symbols.doc:
CodeWSUpgradeUnsupported identifies a ResponseWriter whose connection cannot
be taken over — an HTTP/2 request, or a middleware wrapper that hides
http.Hijacker. WebSocket is not a response format: it replaces HTTP on the
socket, so without the hijack there is nothing to upgrade.

symbols.name: Conn
symbols.spelled: interface{Buffer() []byte; Group() string; ID() uint64; stdnet.Conn}
symbols.canonical: interface{Buffer() []byte; Group() string; ID() uint64; net.Conn}
symbols.doc:
Conn is one accepted stream connection.

It embeds stdlib net.Conn, so a handler reads and writes it exactly as it
would any socket and every io helper keeps working — io.Copy, bufio, encoding
wrappers, crypto/tls. Everything the domain adds is additive, which is what
keeps "plug a handler in" a four-line exercise.

A Conn is pooled and recycled once ServeConn returns. A handler MUST NOT
retain it, nor the slice returned by Buffer, past that point — the same
contract the logger's builder already carries.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the concrete type stays unexported in internal/service/net/server.

symbols.name: Buffer
symbols.doc:
Buffer returns a connection-scoped scratch buffer sized by the group's
read-buffer limit. It is recycled with the connection, which is what lets
a handler read without allocating per connection.

symbols.name: Group
symbols.doc:
Group returns the name of the listener group that accepted this
connection, so one handler serving several groups can tell them apart.

symbols.name: ID
symbols.doc:
ID returns the monotonic identifier assigned at accept time, for
correlating log lines belonging to one connection.

symbols.name: ConnHandler
symbols.doc:
ConnHandler serves one accepted stream connection.

Returning an error does not kill the server: the connection is closed and the
error is logged and metered. That is deliberate — one malformed peer must
never be able to take down the process.

Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use: the server runs one
goroutine per connection and they all share the handler.

symbols.name: ConnHandlerFunc
symbols.doc: ConnHandlerFunc adapts a plain function to ConnHandler.

symbols.name: ServeConn
symbols.doc: ServeConn implements ConnHandler by calling f.

symbols.name: ConnLimitReached

code.public: The server is at its connection limit

symbols.doc: ConnLimitReached is returned when the group's connection ceiling is full.

symbols.name: DrainSignal
symbols.doc:
DrainSignal returns the drain channel carried by ctx, or nil when the server
serving this request publishes none.

A nil channel is the right absence: receiving from it blocks forever, so a
select that watches it alongside other cases simply never fires that case.
A caller therefore needs no nil check.

symbols.name: DrainTimeout

code.public: The server did not drain before its deadline

symbols.doc: DrainTimeout is returned when the shutdown drain budget expired.

symbols.name: DurationValue
symbols.doc:
DurationValue is a time.Duration that round-trips through JSON as either a Go
duration string ("30s", "1m30s") or a raw nanosecond count. The SDK's config
loader (ADR 0028) decodes through a JSON round-trip, and encoding/json renders
a bare time.Duration as nanoseconds — which would force an operator to write
30000000000 in a YAML file to mean thirty seconds. This type accepts both and
always emits the readable form.

The mixed receivers are required by encoding/json and are not a style slip:
MarshalJSON must take a value so a non-pointer struct field marshals, and
UnmarshalJSON must take a pointer so it can assign. The standard library's
time.Time carries the same asymmetry for the same reason.

PROMOTION CANDIDATE: this type is domain-neutral and stdlib-only, so it
belongs in internal/kernel or internal/core/app/config the moment a second domain
needs it. It is declared here because the repo's bar for a shared primitive is
two real consumers arising from an actual duplication, and today there is one.

symbols.name: Duration
symbols.doc: Duration returns the value as a plain time.Duration.

symbols.name: MarshalJSON
symbols.doc:
MarshalJSON emits the readable duration string so a written-back configuration
file stays legible.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String renders the canonical Go duration form, e.g. "1m30s".

symbols.name: UnmarshalJSON
symbols.doc:
UnmarshalJSON accepts a quoted Go duration string ("30s") or a bare number of
nanoseconds, so both a hand-written config file and a machine-generated one
decode.

symbols.name: GroupDuplicate

code.public: The listener group is already declared

symbols.doc: GroupDuplicate is returned for a second declaration of one group name.

symbols.name: GroupUnknown

code.public: The listener group is not declared

symbols.doc: GroupUnknown is returned for a lookup of an undeclared group.

symbols.name: HandlerAlreadySet

code.public: The listener group already has a handler

symbols.doc:
HandlerAlreadySet is returned by Start for a stream group whose handler was
declared twice — by Handle, HandleFunc, HandleHTTP or HandleLoop, in any
order. The second declaration does not replace the first; the "group" field
names the group.

symbols.name: HandlerMissing

code.public: The listener group has no handler

symbols.doc: HandlerMissing is returned when a group was bound without a handler.

symbols.name: HandlerPanic

code.public: The connection handler failed unexpectedly

symbols.doc: HandlerPanic wraps a panic recovered inside a handler.

symbols.name: IdentityFileParams
symbols.spelled: struct{CertFile string "json:\"cert_file\""; KeyFile string "json:\"key_file\""; RootsFile string "json:\"roots_file\""; ClientCAFile string "json:\"client_ca_file\""; ServerName string "json:\"server_name\""; MinVersion uint16 "json:\"min_version\""; NextProtos []string "json:\"next_protos\""; RequireClientCert bool "json:\"require_client_cert\""}
symbols.canonical: struct{CertFile string "json:\"cert_file\""; KeyFile string "json:\"key_file\""; RootsFile string "json:\"roots_file\""; ClientCAFile string "json:\"client_ca_file\""; ServerName string "json:\"server_name\""; MinVersion uint16 "json:\"min_version\""; NextProtos []string "json:\"next_protos\""; RequireClientCert bool "json:\"require_client_cert\""}

fields.name: CertFile
fields.doc:
CertFile is the PEM leaf certificate followed by any intermediates.
Supplying it without KeyFile is always a configuration slip, never an
intention, and is refused: an mTLS client that silently degrades to plain
TLS is a security hole that reports nothing.

fields.name: KeyFile
fields.doc: KeyFile is the PEM private key matching CertFile.

fields.name: RootsFile
fields.doc:
RootsFile is the PEM CA bundle used to verify the peer. Leaving it empty
selects the platform trust store, which is right for a public endpoint and
wrong for a private PKI.

fields.name: ClientCAFile
fields.doc:
ClientCAFile is the PEM CA bundle a server accepts client certificates
from. Required whenever RequireClientCert is set.

fields.name: ServerName
fields.doc:
ServerName overrides the name verified against the peer certificate.

This is far more often required than its "optional" typing suggests. Any
deployment reached through a port forward or a tunnel connects to
127.0.0.1 while the peer certificate names the real service, and the
handshake then fails every single time until ServerName is set. Treat it
as mandatory whenever the dial address is not the certificate's name.

fields.name: MinVersion
fields.doc:
MinVersion is the lowest accepted TLS version. Zero selects TLS 1.3;
anything below TLS 1.2 is refused.

fields.name: NextProtos
fields.doc: NextProtos is the ALPN protocol list, e.g. {"h2", "http/1.1"}.

fields.name: RequireClientCert
fields.doc: RequireClientCert turns a server identity into mutual TLS.

symbols.doc:
IdentityFileParams names TLS material to read from the filesystem. Every path
is optional on its own; the combination is validated once the bytes are in
hand, by the same core constructor that validates in-memory material.

It is the disk-sourced twin of IdentityParams and lives beside it on purpose:
the two describe one domain concept — the material an identity is built from
— and splitting them across layers would let the rules that govern them drift
apart, which is exactly what this domain refuses for TLS.

symbols.name: IdentityParams
symbols.spelled: struct{CertPEM []byte; KeyPEM []byte; RootsPEM []byte; ClientCAPEM []byte; ServerName string; MinVersion uint16; NextProtos []string; RequireClientCert bool}
symbols.canonical: struct{CertPEM []byte; KeyPEM []byte; RootsPEM []byte; ClientCAPEM []byte; ServerName string; MinVersion uint16; NextProtos []string; RequireClientCert bool}

fields.name: CertPEM
fields.doc:
CertPEM is the PEM-encoded leaf certificate followed by any intermediates.
Paired with KeyPEM; supplying one without the other is an error.

fields.name: KeyPEM
fields.doc: KeyPEM is the PEM-encoded private key matching CertPEM.

fields.name: RootsPEM
fields.doc:
RootsPEM is the PEM-encoded CA bundle used to verify the peer. When empty
the platform trust store is used, which is the right default for a public
endpoint and the wrong one for a private PKI.

fields.name: ClientCAPEM
fields.doc:
ClientCAPEM is the PEM-encoded CA bundle a server accepts client
certificates from. It is meaningless on a client identity.

fields.name: ServerName
fields.doc:
ServerName overrides the name verified against the peer certificate. It is
required when connecting to a host by IP whose certificate names a DNS name.

fields.name: MinVersion
fields.doc:
MinVersion is the lowest accepted TLS version. Zero selects TLS 1.3;
anything below TLS 1.2 is refused outright.

fields.name: NextProtos
fields.doc: NextProtos is the ALPN protocol list, e.g. {"h2", "http/1.1"}.

fields.name: RequireClientCert
fields.doc:
RequireClientCert turns a server identity into mutual TLS: the peer must
present a certificate that chains to ClientCAPEM.

symbols.doc:
IdentityParams carries in-memory TLS material. Every field is optional on its
own; the combination is what is validated by NewIdentity. Sourcing material
from memory rather than from disk is what lets a consumer pull certificates
out of a secret manager without ever writing them to a filesystem.

symbols.name: IdentityValue
symbols.doc:
IdentityValue is an opaque TLS identity: a certificate chain, the trust
anchors used to verify the peer, and the negotiated-version policy. Its String
and GoString output is always "<redacted>" so an accidental %v, %s or %#v can
never spill key material into a log line. The only way out is ClientConfig or
ServerConfig, which mint a fresh *tls.Config per call.

The zero value is valid and means "no identity" — IsZero reports it.

symbols.name: ClientConfig
symbols.doc:
ClientConfig returns a fresh *tls.Config for dialling a peer. Each call yields
a new value so a caller mutating the result cannot affect any other user of
the same identity.

"Fresh" covers the slices and the trust pool, not only the outer struct. A
new *tls.Config whose Certificates and RootCAs still point at the identity's
own would leave cfg.Certificates[0] = other and cfg.RootCAs.AddCert(evil)
reaching every other configuration the identity has ever minted, including
ones already in use — which is the opposite of what an opaque, immutable
identity is for. Who pays that cost, and how often, is the CALLER's choice
and not a property of this method: net/client calls it once inside New and
net/server once per listener, but service/app/mail calls it per connection —
which for SMTP is per message — deliberately, because StartTLS takes the
config and a transport that reused one would hand every send a *tls.Config
another send could still be mutating. Three slice clones are nothing beside
an SMTP round trip; the sentence that used to sit here said "never per
request", which was true of the two net callers and false of the third.

symbols.name: GoString
symbols.doc:
GoString implements fmt.GoStringer so %#v stays redacted too — fmt bypasses
String for Go-syntax formatting and would otherwise dump the unexported fields.

symbols.name: IsZero
symbols.doc:
IsZero reports whether the identity carries no material at all, which is the
zero value a caller gets when no TLS was configured.

symbols.name: ServerConfig
symbols.doc:
ServerConfig returns a fresh *tls.Config for accepting connections, switching
to mutual TLS when the identity requires a client certificate.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc:
String implements fmt.Stringer and always redacts so key material never
reaches a log line through %v or %s.

symbols.name: InvalidAddress

code.public: The network address is not valid

symbols.doc: InvalidAddress is returned for a syntactically unusable address.

symbols.name: InvalidDuration

code.public: The duration value is not valid

symbols.doc:
InvalidDuration is returned for a configuration duration that parses as
neither a Go duration literal nor an integer nanosecond count.

symbols.name: LimitsValue
symbols.spelled: struct{MaxConns int "json:\"max_conns\""; ReadBufferSize int "json:\"read_buffer_size\""; MaxPacketSize int "json:\"max_packet_size\""; Backlog int "json:\"backlog\""; Shards int "json:\"shards\""; BatchSize int "json:\"batch_size\""}
symbols.canonical: struct{MaxConns int "json:\"max_conns\""; ReadBufferSize int "json:\"read_buffer_size\""; MaxPacketSize int "json:\"max_packet_size\""; Backlog int "json:\"backlog\""; Shards int "json:\"shards\""; BatchSize int "json:\"batch_size\""}

fields.name: MaxConns
fields.doc:
MaxConns caps concurrent connections in the group. Beyond it, a new
connection is accepted and immediately closed with ConnLimitReached, which
is kinder than letting the accept queue silently overflow.

fields.name: ReadBufferSize
fields.doc:
ReadBufferSize sizes the per-connection scratch buffer returned by
Conn.Buffer.

fields.name: MaxPacketSize
fields.doc:
MaxPacketSize is the largest datagram accepted. A larger one is DROPPED
and counted in StateValue.OversizedPackets, never delivered truncated:
the kernel discards the tail, so the prefix that survives reads exactly
like a complete message and the handler cannot tell the difference.

fields.name: Backlog
fields.doc: Backlog is the listen backlog depth where the platform honours it.

fields.name: Shards
fields.doc:
Shards is the number of independent listeners to open on one address with
SO_REUSEPORT, each with its own accept loop, to remove accept contention.
Zero selects the platform default.

fields.name: BatchSize
fields.doc:
BatchSize is how many datagrams to read per syscall. Zero selects the
default; one disables batching.

symbols.doc:
LimitsValue bounds what one listener group may consume. Every field is
optional; zero means "use the domain default", never "unbounded" — an unset
ceiling must not be the dangerous one.

symbols.name: ListenFailed

code.public: The server could not bind its listening address

symbols.doc: ListenFailed is returned when a listener could not be bound.

symbols.name: ListenerStateValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Group string "json:\"group\""; Address string "json:\"address\""; Network string "json:\"network\""; Shards int "json:\"shards\""; Degraded bool "json:\"degraded\""; DegradedReason string "json:\"degraded_reason,omitempty\""; Adopted bool "json:\"adopted\""}
symbols.canonical: struct{Group string "json:\"group\""; Address string "json:\"address\""; Network string "json:\"network\""; Shards int "json:\"shards\""; Degraded bool "json:\"degraded\""; DegradedReason string "json:\"degraded_reason,omitempty\""; Adopted bool "json:\"adopted\""}

fields.name: Group
fields.doc: Group is the listener group's name.

fields.name: Address
fields.doc:
Address is the address actually bound, which for a port of zero is the
one the kernel chose rather than the one requested.

fields.name: Network
fields.doc: Network is the socket family.

fields.name: Shards
fields.doc: Shards is how many listeners were actually opened on this address.

fields.name: Degraded
fields.doc:
Degraded reports that a requested optimisation was unavailable and the
server fell back. It is surfaced rather than logged once at startup,
because a silent fallback is indistinguishable from a working one and
nobody re-reads yesterday's logs to find out.

fields.name: DegradedReason
fields.doc: DegradedReason names the fallback in plain words when Degraded is set.

fields.name: Adopted
fields.doc:
Adopted reports a listener inherited from a supervisor rather than bound
by this process.

symbols.doc:
ListenerStateValue reports one bound listener.

It carries the address actually bound rather than the one requested, and it
reports any fallback explicitly, so a caller never has to infer either.

symbols.name: LoopBackend
symbols.doc:
LoopBackend names the mechanic a loop group runs on (ADR 0186 §D5). The zero
value is LoopBackendAuto.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String renders the backend as State and the start line spell it.

symbols.name: LoopBackendAuto
symbols.doc:
LoopBackendAuto takes the best backend the platform's probe reaches:
io_uring, then epoll on Linux, the portable backend elsewhere.

symbols.name: LoopBackendEpoll
symbols.doc: LoopBackendEpoll is epoll, on every Linux architecture.

symbols.name: LoopBackendIOURing
symbols.doc:
LoopBackendIOURing is io_uring, on linux/amd64, arm64, riscv64 and loong64,
after the kernel's staged probe.

symbols.name: LoopBackendPortable
symbols.doc:
LoopBackendPortable is the default engine's accept path and goroutines,
serialised onto one handler goroutine, on every platform.

symbols.name: LoopBackendUnavailable

code.public: The requested loop backend is not available on this kernel

symbols.doc:
LoopBackendUnavailable is returned by Start for an explicit loop backend the
running kernel's probe refused. The "stage" and "reason" fields name the probe
step that failed. A GOOS that has no such mechanic at all returns the shared
UnsupportedPlatform instead (ADR 0018 §(a)).

symbols.name: LoopConnRef
symbols.spelled: struct{Ring uint32; Slot uint32; Gen uint32}
symbols.canonical: struct{Ring uint32; Slot uint32; Gen uint32}

fields.name: Ring
fields.doc: Ring is the ring, inside its loop, that holds the connection.

fields.name: Slot
fields.doc: Slot is the connection's index in the ring's table.

fields.name: Gen
fields.doc:
Gen is the slot's generation. It is never zero for a live connection, so
the zero LoopConnRef is stale on every loop.

symbols.doc:
LoopConnRef names one connection of a loop: the ring it lives on, its slot
in that ring's table and the generation of that slot. It is a comparable value
with no behaviour, so a handler can key a map with it and hold it without
holding anything of the engine.

A slot is reused only once every operation of its previous generation has
completed, and the generation then moves on, so an operation on a reference
whose connection closed does nothing and returns LoopStaleRef — it can never
reach the connection that took the slot since. The zero value names no
connection.

symbols.name: LoopHandler
symbols.spelled: interface{OnBatchEnd(io LoopIO); OnClose(io LoopIO, ref LoopConnRef, err error); OnData(io LoopIO, ref LoopConnRef, buf []byte) int; OnOpen(io LoopIO, ref LoopConnRef); OnTimeout(io LoopIO, ref LoopConnRef); OnWritable(io LoopIO, ref LoopConnRef)}
symbols.canonical: interface{OnBatchEnd(io github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopIO); OnClose(io github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopIO, ref github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopConnRef, err error); OnData(io github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopIO, ref github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopConnRef, buf []byte) int; OnOpen(io github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopIO, ref github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopConnRef); OnTimeout(io github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopIO, ref github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopConnRef); OnWritable(io github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopIO, ref github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopConnRef)}
symbols.doc:
LoopHandler is the port a consumer implements to be served by a loop group
(ADR 0186 §D4).

One thread calls it: every callback of one loop runs on that loop's thread,
one at a time, so a handler needs no lock for state it keeps per loop. It
MUST NOT block: a blocking callback stalls every connection of its loop. A
callback receives the LoopIO of the loop that calls it and the reference of
the connection concerned; neither is valid past the loop's life, and a
reference past its connection's OnClose is stale.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the engines live in internal/service/net/loop and
internal/service/net/server; this port is what a consumer writes.

symbols.name: OnBatchEnd
symbols.doc:
OnBatchEnd is called once per loop iteration, after the OnData calls of
every ring of the loop, and before any buffer handed to them returns to the
kernel. It is where a handler flushes work it batched — one database
commit for every request of the batch, say — before writing the answers.

symbols.name: OnClose
symbols.spelled: func(io LoopIO, ref LoopConnRef, err error)
symbols.doc:
OnClose is called once per connection, last. err is nil when the peer
closed cleanly or the handler called Close, and otherwise names why the
loop closed it — LoopSpillFull, an idle timeout, the drain, a socket
error. ref is stale once OnClose returns.

symbols.name: OnData
symbols.spelled: func(io LoopIO, ref LoopConnRef, buf []byte) int
symbols.doc:
OnData hands the handler the bytes received on ref and returns how many of
them it consumed, from 0 to len(buf). buf stays valid until the next
OnBatchEnd returns, never later, and the handler must not write to it.
The unconsumed tail is kept in the connection's spill and handed back
first, followed by the next bytes, on the next OnData; a tail past the
spill ceiling closes the connection with LoopSpillFull. A value outside
0 to len(buf) is treated as len(buf).

symbols.name: OnOpen
symbols.doc:
OnOpen is called once per accepted connection, before any OnData for it.
Pressure(ref) already answers for this connection.

symbols.name: OnTimeout
symbols.doc:
OnTimeout is called when the deadline set by SetDeadline on ref expires.
The connection stays open: closing it is the handler's choice.

symbols.name: OnWritable
symbols.doc:
OnWritable is called when ref's pending output falls below the loop's
low-water mark after a Write was refused with LoopOutputFull or left output
pending past the mark, so a producer that paused can resume.

symbols.name: LoopIO
symbols.spelled: interface{Close(ref LoopConnRef) error; Post(op PostFunc, arg uintptr) error; Pressure(ref LoopConnRef) bool; SetDeadline(ref LoopConnRef, d time.Duration) error; Write(ref LoopConnRef, p []byte) error}
symbols.canonical: interface{Close(ref github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopConnRef) error; Post(op github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.PostFunc, arg uintptr) error; Pressure(ref github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopConnRef) bool; SetDeadline(ref github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopConnRef, d time.Duration) error; Write(ref github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.LoopConnRef, p []byte) error}
symbols.doc:
LoopIO is what a loop offers its handler: the operations on its connections
(ADR 0186 §D4). Each loop implements it with a pointer of its own, handed to
every callback.

Write, Close and SetDeadline belong to the loop's thread: they are called from
a callback, never from another goroutine, which is what lets them take no
lock. Under the loopdebug build tag a call from another thread is refused with
LoopWrongThread. Post is the one operation another goroutine may call. Every
error is a preallocated sentinel; none of the calls allocates when p belongs
to the caller's heap or mapping.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the concrete loops stay unexported in
internal/service/net/loop and internal/service/net/server.

symbols.name: Close
symbols.doc:
Close closes ref's connection once the output already written has left,
and calls OnClose. A second Close, or a Close on a stale reference, returns
LoopStaleRef and does nothing.

symbols.name: Post
symbols.doc:
Post queues op to run once on the loop's thread with arg, and wakes the
loop. It is the one operation any goroutine may call. The queue is
preallocated and holds no closure: op is a plain function and arg an
integer the caller gives meaning to. Each posted operation runs exactly
once, in the order posted; a full queue refuses with LoopPostQueueFull, and
a loop that has stopped with ServerClosed.

symbols.name: Pressure
symbols.doc:
Pressure reports whether ref's connection was accepted, or has since come,
under the loop's soft pressure: the group serves more connections than its
soft bound. It is a primitive; what a protocol makes of it — HTTP/1.1
answers Connection: close — is the protocol adapter's. A stale reference
reports false.

symbols.name: SetDeadline
symbols.doc:
SetDeadline arms ref's timer to fire OnTimeout after d, on the loop's
coarse timer wheel: it fires no earlier than d and at most one wheel tick
late. A d of zero or less disarms it. Arming again replaces the previous
deadline.

symbols.name: Write
symbols.doc:
Write copies p into ref's output and returns. Writes on one reference leave
in the order they were made, and p may be reused once Write returns. It is
refused with LoopOutputFull, copying nothing, when p would pass the
connection's output ceiling or the loop's global output budget, and with
LoopStaleRef when ref's connection has closed.

symbols.name: LoopNoDescriptors

code.public: The process has no file descriptor available for the loop

symbols.doc:
LoopNoDescriptors is returned by Start for a loop group when the effective
RLIMIT_NOFILE soft limit is zero or cannot be read: no ring table and no
connection could hold a descriptor. It is checked before the ring count is
derived, so it is never a division by zero.

symbols.name: LoopOptionHonourer
symbols.doc:
LoopOptionHonourer is the optional capability of a LoopHandler that honours
group options the loop engine does not: a protocol adapter that applies a
header deadline, say. At Start, server refuses with LoopOptionUnsupported
every option set on a loop group that neither the engine nor the handler
honours (ADR 0186 §D1). A handler without it honours nothing of its own.

symbols.name: Honours
symbols.doc: Honours reports whether the handler applies the option of kind k itself.

symbols.name: LoopOptionUnsupported

code.public: The group option is not supported by its engine

symbols.doc:
LoopOptionUnsupported is returned by Start for an option a group cannot honour
on its engine: Loop on a group served by Handle, HandleFunc or HandleHTTP, or
on one with no handler; Use on a loop group; or an option neither the loop
engine nor its handler honours. The "option" field names it. It is judged at
Start, once the handler is known, whatever order the declarations came in.

symbols.name: LoopOutputFull

code.public: The connection cannot take more output now

symbols.doc:
LoopOutputFull is returned by Write when the bytes would pass the connection's
output ceiling or the loop's global output budget. Nothing is copied; the
caller waits for OnWritable or closes.

symbols.name: LoopPostQueueFull

code.public: The loop cannot take more posted work now

symbols.doc:
LoopPostQueueFull is returned by Post when the loop's preallocated queue is
full. The operation is not queued and will not run.

fields.name: Loop
fields.doc: Loop is the loop's index in its group.

fields.name: Ring
fields.doc: Ring is the ring's index in its loop.

fields.name: Conns
fields.doc: Conns is the number of connections the ring holds now.

fields.name: Accepted
fields.doc: Accepted is the number of connections the ring accepted.

fields.name: Closed
fields.doc: Closed is the number of connections the ring closed.

fields.name: Batches
fields.doc: Batches is the number of loop iterations that reaped this ring.

fields.name: Completions
fields.doc: Completions is the number of completions or events the ring reaped.

fields.name: BufferStarved
fields.doc:
BufferStarved is the number of receives that found no provided buffer
(ENOBUFS) and waited for one to come back.

fields.name: EnterRetries
fields.doc:
EnterRetries is the number of times submitting to the kernel was retried
after it was busy — the completion queue full, typically.

fields.name: AcceptPauses
fields.doc:
AcceptPauses is the number of times the ring stopped accepting: the
descriptor reserve reached, or the process out of descriptors.

fields.name: Evicted
fields.doc: Evicted is the number of idle connections closed to admit others.

fields.name: WatchdogFires
fields.doc:
WatchdogFires is the number of times the liveness watchdog saw a stall it
could observe and acted on it.

fields.name: Draining
fields.doc:
Draining reports a ring the watchdog judged sick: it accepts nothing new
and closes its connections as they fall idle.

symbols.doc:
LoopRingStateValue reports one ring of one loop: counters the loop refreshes
at the end of each batch, read without stopping it (ADR 0186 §D8).

symbols.name: LoopSpillFull

code.public: The connection sent more than it may hold unread

symbols.doc:
LoopSpillFull is the error OnClose receives for a connection whose unconsumed
input passed its spill ceiling or the loop's global spill budget. The loop
closes it rather than read further.

symbols.name: LoopStaleRef

code.public: The connection is closed

symbols.doc:
LoopStaleRef is returned by a loop operation on a reference whose connection
has closed. The operation does nothing: the slot may already name another
connection, and the generation is what tells the two apart.

symbols.name: LoopStateValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Group string "json:\"group\""; Backend LoopBackend "json:\"backend\""; ProbeStage string "json:\"probe_stage\""; Degraded bool "json:\"degraded\""; DegradedReason string "json:\"degraded_reason,omitempty\""; Loops int "json:\"loops\""; Rings int "json:\"rings\""; RingsSource string "json:\"rings_source\""; RLimitNoFile uint64 "json:\"rlimit_nofile\""; GOMAXPROCS int "json:\"gomaxprocs\""; BatchP99 DurationValue "json:\"batch_p99\""; RingStates []LoopRingStateValue "json:\"ring_states\""}
