fields.name: Err
fields.doc:
Err is the failed attempt's error, for EventRetrying and
EventDeadLettered. A dead letter's carries CodeMailRejected or
CodeMailExpired when that is why it was given up — errs.HasCode
reads either —, and the transport's own error, an SMTP reply
included, stays reachable through errors.As.

fields.name: Meta
fields.doc: Meta is what Config.Annotate returned when the mail was sent.

fields.name: At
fields.doc:
At is when it happened; QueuedAt when the mail was queued; Next when
the next attempt is due, for EventRetrying.

fields.name: QueuedAt
fields.doc:
At is when it happened; QueuedAt when the mail was queued; Next when
the next attempt is due, for EventRetrying.

fields.name: Next
fields.doc:
At is when it happened; QueuedAt when the mail was queued; Next when
the next attempt is due, for EventRetrying.

fields.name: ID
fields.doc: ID is the spool's identifier for the mail.

fields.name: Message
fields.doc:
Message is the mail, as it was stamped at Send: sender, date and
Message-ID filled in.

fields.name: Attempt
fields.doc: Attempt numbers the delivery attempt, from 1; zero for EventQueued.

fields.name: Kind
fields.doc: Kind says what happened.

symbols.doc:
EventValue is one thing that happened to one mail. The mail, its metadata
and its queue time travel with every event, because a spool may deliver a
mail an earlier process queued, and an observer building a mailbox has
seen no Send for it.

symbols.name: MaxIDBytes
symbols.doc:
MaxIDBytes bounds a mail's identifier, whoever minted it. It is well above
every identifier the SDK mints — a UUID, a ULID, a TypeID under the longest
prefix TypeID allows — and low enough that "Message-ID: <id@domain>" keeps
within RFC 5322's line limit beside the longest domain an address may carry.

symbols.name: New
symbols.doc:
New builds a spool from cfg over cfg.Broker, else a durable queue in
cfg.Dir, else an in-memory one. It starts nothing: Run delivers.

symbols.name: Spool
symbols.doc:
Spool is a durable outbox for mail. Build one with [New]; Send and
SendWithID queue, Run delivers. It is safe for concurrent use.

symbols.name: Close
symbols.doc:
Close refuses every later Send and closes the queue the spool built, once
the publications in flight have landed; a Config.Broker stays its
caller's, to close after. Closing twice is closing once. Stop Run
first — cancel its context and wait for it to return — or a delivery may be
cut off mid-attempt; the mail it held comes back when its lease lapses.

symbols.name: DeadLetters
symbols.doc:
DeadLetters returns up to max mails the spool gave up on, oldest first,
with the last failure of each. It removes nothing: a dead letter is
evidence.

symbols.name: Run
symbols.doc:
Run delivers the spool until ctx ends, on the calling goroutine: it returns
nil when ctx ends, and the queue's error when the spool's storage fails —
a spool whose directory stopped answering is not something to retry in a
loop, and a supervisor restarting Run is. A delivery's failure is never
returned: it is retried, and then dead-lettered.

symbols.name: Send
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, msg coremail.MessageValue) (id string, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, msg github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/mail.MessageValue) (id string, err error)
symbols.doc:
Send validates msg, stamps what a retry must not change, and queues it
under an identifier Config.NewID mints. It returns that identifier once the
mail is in the spool — on disk, with a Dir; in the caller's transaction,
with a Broker that joins it, and in the spool once that commits. A mail
without a sender gets
Config.From; without a Date, the spool's clock; without a Message-ID, one
made of its identifier at the sender's domain, which every attempt keeps.

A refusal is the mail domain's own typed verdict (HeaderInjection,
InvalidAddress, NoRecipients, EmptyBody…), the queue's (MessageTooLarge),
SpoolMisconfigured for an identifier from Config.NewID that breaks the rule
SendWithID states, or SpoolClosed; nothing is queued. A Send racing Close
either lands before the queue closes or is SpoolClosed.

symbols.name: SendWithID
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, id string, msg coremail.MessageValue) error
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, id string, msg github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/mail.MessageValue) error
symbols.doc:
SendWithID is Send under an identifier its caller minted, for a caller that
must know the identifier before the spool has the mail: a framework that
holds a mail until its transaction commits returns the identifier at the
call and queues the mail after the commit. SendWithID stamps what Send
stamps, the Message-ID it makes is id at the sender's domain, and the
events, the attempts and the dead letter carry id.

The identifier must be non-empty, at most MaxIDBytes, and an RFC 5322
dot-atom — the grammar of a Message-ID's left half: printable ASCII, no
special, no empty label — even when the mail brings its own Message-ID,
because the rule belongs to the identifier and not to one mail. Anything
else is InvalidMailID, which names the rule it broke and never the
identifier; nothing is queued. Identifiers are compared byte for byte.

The identifier is the caller's promise that the mail is new, as one from
Config.NewID is. The spool does not look for it among the mails it holds;
a repeated identifier meets the ledger every redelivery meets. A mail under
an identifier this process delivered — among the last DeliveredMemory — is
dropped at delivery with EventDuplicate, after its own EventQueued, instead
of being sent. So SendWithID repeated after a failure that hid a landed
publication sends the mail once, while the process remembers it. An
identifier whose mail was dead-lettered was never delivered, and carries a
new attempt. After a restart the ledger is empty, and a repeat is sent
again — under the same Message-ID, when that was made of id.

Every other refusal is Send's, and a SendWithID racing Close lands or is
SpoolClosed.

symbols.name: AdaptiveThrottleConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{K float64; Window time.Duration; Buckets int; Rejected func(error) bool; Clock clock.Clock; Random func() float64}
symbols.canonical: struct{K float64; Window time.Duration; Buckets int; Rejected func(error) bool; Clock github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/clock.Clock; Random func() float64}

fields.name: K
fields.doc:
K is how many requests per accept the throttle lets through before
it starts refusing: a call is refused with probability
max(0, (requests − K × accepts) / (requests + 1)). Zero is 2, the
SRE book's value. A lower K refuses sooner and wastes less of the
dependency's capacity on calls it will refuse; a higher one refuses
later and keeps more traffic flowing. A K below 1 would refuse calls
to a dependency accepting every one of them, and is refused, as is
one that is not a finite number.

fields.name: Window
fields.doc:
Window is how far back the requests and accepts are counted. Zero
is two minutes, the SRE book's history. A negative Window is
refused.

fields.name: Buckets
fields.doc:
Buckets is how many slots the window is kept in: a slot leaves the
window whole, so it reaches back between Window − Window/Buckets
and Window. Zero is 10; more than 1000 is refused, as is a Window
too short to give each slot a nanosecond.

fields.name: Rejected
fields.doc:
Rejected classifies a non-nil error of the operation: true is a
refusal by the dependency — overload, quota, unavailability —,
false an answer it gave, which counts as an accept however
unwelcome. Nil counts every error as a refusal. It is not
consulted for a context.Canceled returned once the caller's
context is closed: that call counts as an accept.

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc: Clock is what the window is kept on. Nil means clock.System.

fields.name: Random
fields.doc:
Random returns a number in [0, 1) each time a call might be
refused; the call is refused when it is below the probability.
Nil is math/rand/v2's Float64. A test hands it a sequence to
decide each refusal.

symbols.doc:
AdaptiveThrottleConfig parameterises NewAdaptiveThrottle, in the terms
of Google's SRE book: the multiplier K, the window the requests and
accepts are counted over, and what counts as a refusal. Every field
has a default; a value out of range is refused with
PolicyMisconfigured, naming the field (ADR 0031).

symbols.name: BackoffValue
symbols.doc:
BackoffValue is an exponential backoff: the wait after the n-th consecutive
failure is BaseDelay × Multiplier^(n−1), held at MaxDelay when one is set and
widened by Jitter when one is asked for. Delay(attempt) never returns a
negative duration, however large attempt is (ADR 0103).

It is the policy NewRetry has always applied between attempts, published so
a loop that retries on its own terms — a supervised goroutine, an outbox, a
state machine's failed transition — computes the same curve instead of
writing a fourth copy of it. RetryConfig keeps its four fields of the same
names; NewRetry builds its waits from the same two halves.

It is an alias of kernel/backoff.Value, the layer that OWNS the curve (ADR
0074): the curve names no policy and no domain, so the domains that only
need the curve import the kernel directly instead of this package.

symbols.name: BreakerConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{FailureThreshold int; OpenDuration time.Duration; Clock clock.Clock; Retryable func(error) bool; Window *BreakerWindowValue; OnStateChange func(from coreres.BreakerPhase, to coreres.BreakerPhase); OpenBackoff *BackoffValue; HalfOpenTrials int}
symbols.canonical: struct{FailureThreshold int; OpenDuration time.Duration; Clock github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/clock.Clock; Retryable func(error) bool; Window *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/service/app/resilience.BreakerWindowValue; OnStateChange func(from github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/resilience.BreakerPhase, to github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/resilience.BreakerPhase); OpenBackoff *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/service/app/resilience.BackoffValue; HalfOpenTrials int}

fields.name: FailureThreshold
fields.doc:
FailureThreshold is how many consecutive failures open a breaker
without a Window. A non-positive value defaults to 5. It is not read
when Window is set.

fields.name: OpenDuration
fields.doc:
OpenDuration is how long an Open breaker rejects calls before admitting
one HalfOpen trial. A non-positive value clamps to 30s: a zero cooldown
would let the very next call through, which is a breaker that never
rejects anything and so protects nothing while the caller believes it
does (ADR 0031).

fields.name: Retryable
fields.doc:
Retryable classifies a non-nil operation error as a dependency failure
worth counting against the breaker's health. false means the error is
deterministic — the caller's own fault, not the dependency's — so it is
returned verbatim and folded into neither the failure count nor the
success path: a stream of HTTP 400s can no longer trip the breaker, and
one of them cannot close a HalfOpen breaker either. A nil predicate
counts every error as a failure, which is the pre-classifier behaviour.
It is not consulted for a context.Canceled returned once the caller's
context is closed: that call is neutral whatever the predicate says.
Shares its shape with RetryConfig.Retryable so one classifier serves a
nested Retry(Breaker(op)) stack.

fields.name: Window
fields.doc:
Window, when set, opens the breaker on a RATE rather than a streak:
of failures, or of slow calls, among the calls a sliding time window
holds. Nil — the zero value — is the consecutive-failure breaker,
exactly as it was before the field existed.

A streak misses a dependency that fails every other call: S, F, S,
F never reaches a threshold of five, and neither does a dependency
that answers every call, eventually, a minute late. A rate over a
window sees both. The window's fields have defaults of their own,
taken from Polly and resilience4j — see BreakerWindowValue.

fields.name: OnStateChange
fields.doc:
OnStateChange, when set, is called on every change of phase, with the
phase left and the phase entered: Closed to Open on a trip, Open to
HalfOpen when a call is admitted as the trial, HalfOpen to Closed or
Open on its outcome, and whatever Isolate and Reset change.

It is called outside the breaker's lock, one call at a time and in
the order the changes happened, on the goroutine of the call that
made the change — or of one already delivering an earlier change,
which then delivers this one too. It may call State, Isolate or
Reset. It must not block: a call that changed the phase waits for
it. Nil hears nothing.

fields.name: OpenBackoff
fields.doc:
OpenBackoff, when set, makes each opening last longer than the one
before while the dependency keeps failing its trials: the n-th
opening since the breaker last closed lasts OpenBackoff.Delay(n),
in place of OpenDuration. The count starts over when a trial closes
the breaker, and on Reset.

Its BaseDelay and its MaxDelay are both required — a zero base is
a cooldown of nothing, and a zero ceiling one that may grow to
centuries — and are refused when not positive, with
PolicyMisconfigured naming the field. Its Multiplier, Jitter and
JitterMode read as BackoffValue reads them. Nil keeps every opening
at OpenDuration.

fields.name: HalfOpenTrials
fields.doc:
HalfOpenTrials is how many trials in a row must succeed before a
HalfOpen breaker closes. The trials still run one at a time, and
any one that fails opens the breaker again. Zero, or less, is one:
the first successful trial closes it, as before the field existed.

One success is thin evidence that a dependency has recovered — the
trial may have reached the one healthy replica, or a cache — and a
breaker that closes on it and trips again at once doubles the load
it meant to spare. A few trials in a row cost a few more cooldowns'
worth of latency to the first callers after recovery, which is what
resilience4j's permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState buys too.

symbols.doc:
BreakerConfig parameterises NewCircuitBreaker. A non-positive FailureThreshold
defaults to 5; a non-positive OpenDuration defaults to 30s; a nil Clock
defaults to clock.System; a nil Retryable counts every error as a failure;
a nil Window opens on consecutive failures; a nil OnStateChange hears
nothing; a nil OpenBackoff keeps every opening at OpenDuration; a
non-positive HalfOpenTrials closes on one successful trial.

symbols.name: BreakerWindowValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Size time.Duration; Buckets int; MinCalls int; FailureRatio float64; SlowAfter time.Duration; SlowRatio float64}
symbols.canonical: struct{Size time.Duration; Buckets int; MinCalls int; FailureRatio float64; SlowAfter time.Duration; SlowRatio float64}

fields.name: Size
fields.doc: Size is how far back the window reaches. Zero is 30 seconds.

fields.name: Buckets
fields.doc:
Buckets is how many slots the window is kept in: a slot leaves the
window whole, so the window reaches back between Size − Size/Buckets
and Size. Zero is 10; more than 1000 is refused, the memory of a
breaker being one slot each.

fields.name: MinCalls
fields.doc:
MinCalls is how many calls the window must hold before a ratio is
read at all: below it, a single failure would be a rate of 100%.
Zero is 100.

fields.name: FailureRatio
fields.doc:
FailureRatio is the share of failed calls, in (0, 1], at or above
which the breaker opens. Zero is 0.1.

fields.name: SlowAfter
fields.doc:
SlowAfter is the duration, measured on the breaker's clock from
admission to return, at or above which a call is slow, whether it
succeeded or failed. Zero is 60 seconds.

fields.name: SlowRatio
fields.doc:
SlowRatio is the share of slow calls, in (0, 1], at or above which
the breaker opens. Zero is 1: only a window where every call was
slow opens it.

symbols.doc:
BreakerWindowValue is a circuit breaker's sliding window: the calls of the
last Size, kept in Buckets slots of Size/Buckets each on the breaker's
clock, the oldest slot dropped as time moves past it. The breaker opens
when the window holds at least MinCalls calls and either FailureRatio of
them failed or SlowRatio of them lasted SlowAfter or longer.

A zero field takes its default, each one a published library's own:
Size 30s, Buckets 10, MinCalls 100 and FailureRatio 0.1 are Polly v8's
SamplingDuration, its ten sampling windows, MinimumThroughput and
FailureRatio; SlowAfter 60s and SlowRatio 1 are resilience4j's
slowCallDurationThreshold and slowCallRateThreshold. A negative value,
a ratio above 1 or not a number, more than 1000 Buckets, or a Size too
short to split into Buckets, is refused: every call returns
PolicyMisconfigured, naming the field.

A call is counted when it ends, in the slot of its end, if the breaker
is still Closed and it was not admitted before the breaker last opened. A
deterministic error and a caller who left are not counted at all. The
window is emptied each time the breaker changes phase.

symbols.name: BulkheadWaitConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{Max int; Queue int; MaxWait time.Duration; Clock clock.Timed}
symbols.canonical: struct{Max int; Queue int; MaxWait time.Duration; Clock github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/clock.Timed}

fields.name: Max
fields.doc:
Max is how many operations run at once. A non-positive Max is 1,
as NewBulkhead's limit is.

fields.name: Queue
fields.doc:
Queue is how many calls may wait for a slot beyond the Max
running; a call that finds the queue full is rejected at once with
BulkheadFull. Zero, or less, is no queue. It bounds the memory
and the goroutines a saturated dependency can pin, which an
unbounded queue would not.

fields.name: MaxWait
fields.doc:
MaxWait is how long a queued call waits for a slot before it is
rejected with BulkheadFull. Zero, or less, is no wait. Size it
below the caller's own deadline: a wait the caller cannot afford
only moves the timeout from this policy to the caller.

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock is what MaxWait is measured on. Nil means clock.System; a
ManualClock lets a test run the wait out without sleeping.

symbols.doc:
BulkheadWaitConfig parameterises NewBulkheadWait: how many calls run at
once, how many more may wait for a slot, for how long, and on which
clock. Its zero value is NewBulkhead(1) — one slot and no waiting —:
each field's zero is the reject-at-once bulkhead the SDK has always
had, never a queue nobody sized (ADR 0031).

symbols.name: FallbackConfig

fields.name: Fallback
fields.doc:
Fallback is the secondary Operation run when the primary one fails. It
has no default: a nil Fallback makes NewFallback return a policy that
refuses every call with PolicyMisconfigured (ADR 0031). The two values
the SDK could invent are both worse than a refusal — running the primary
and passing its error through is a policy that silently does nothing
while the caller believes their plan B is wired up, and a no-op fallback
that returns nil would report success for work that never happened.

It is an Operation, not a func(ctx, primaryErr) error, so that the whole
policy vocabulary composes on the fallback side too: the plan B can
itself be a Runner stack (NewRetry(...).Run, a second region's client
behind its own breaker) with no adapter. What the fallback would have
learned from the primary error is decided ahead of it, by Retryable.

The port carries no result value, so a "fallback VALUE" is expressed as
a closure assigning the default into the caller's own variable:

	var page []byte
	cfg := FallbackConfig{Fallback: func(context.Context) error {
		page = cachedPage
		return nil
	}}

fields.name: Retryable
fields.doc:
Retryable classifies a non-nil PRIMARY error as one worth falling back
on. false returns that error verbatim without running the fallback: a
deterministic failure — a malformed request, an authorisation refusal,
a policy misconfiguration — is the caller's own, and serving a cached
answer for it hides a bug behind a stale success. A nil predicate falls
back on every failure. It shares its shape with RetryConfig.Retryable
and BreakerConfig.Retryable, so one classifier serves a nested
Fallback(Retry(Breaker(op))) stack.

symbols.doc:
FallbackConfig parameterises NewFallback. A nil Fallback is refused (there is
no defensible SDK-side substitute for the caller's own plan B); a nil
Retryable falls back on every primary failure.

symbols.name: HedgeConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{Idempotent bool; Delay time.Duration; MaxHedges int; MaxInFlight int; Clock clock.Timed; Budget coreres.RetryBudget}
symbols.canonical: struct{Idempotent bool; Delay time.Duration; MaxHedges int; MaxInFlight int; Clock github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/clock.Timed; Budget github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/resilience.RetryBudget}

fields.name: Idempotent
fields.doc:
Idempotent asserts that the guarded Operation is safe to run more than
once, concurrently, with at most one of the copies being observed. It
has no default: false — the zero value — makes NewHedge return a policy
that refuses every call with PolicyMisconfigured.

This is the one precondition in the package that is a property of the
CALLER'S CODE rather than of a number, and the SDK has no way to detect
it: a hedged non-idempotent Operation does not fail, it succeeds twice —
a double charge, a double insert, a duplicate outbound message — and
nothing in the policy or its errors will ever mention it. A doc comment
is the wrong instrument for a hazard whose symptom is silent success, so
the claim is made in code, at the construction site, where review sees
it and `grep -r 'Idempotent:'` enumerates every hedged call path in a
codebase. Requiring it (rather than defaulting it to true) also means a
caller cannot arrive at hedging by copying a config and deleting the
field.

fields.name: Delay
fields.doc:
Delay is how long the policy waits for an outstanding attempt before
issuing a duplicate. It has no default: a non-positive Delay makes
NewHedge return a policy that refuses every call with
PolicyMisconfigured.

Zero is the value that matters, because it is what forgetting the field
yields, and a zero-delay hedge duplicates EVERY call the instant it
starts — a load amplifier wearing a resilience policy's name, doing the
exact opposite of its job on the dependency it is supposed to protect.
It is refused rather than clamped for the same reason as
RateLimiterConfig.Rate: the useful value is the caller's own latency
distribution (a p95/p99 they measured), and an SDK-chosen one would
either hedge constantly or never.

fields.name: MaxHedges
fields.doc:
MaxHedges is how many DUPLICATE attempts a single call may issue beyond
the first, one per Delay elapsed. It clamps to 1: a hedging policy that
may issue no duplicate is inert — it would run the primary attempt and
nothing else while claiming a tail-latency protection it does not
provide — and "issue at least one duplicate" is exactly the kind of
obvious floor that ADR 0031 clamps rather than refuses (cf. Burst,
NewBulkhead's limit).

There is no ceiling, because none is needed: the budget bounds how many
duplicates a call may issue and nothing else — no per-call allocation
grows with it. math.MaxInt therefore means "as many as the Delay and
MaxInFlight allow".

fields.name: MaxInFlight
fields.doc:
MaxInFlight bounds how many duplicate attempts this Runner may have
running at once, across all concurrent calls. It has no default: a
non-positive MaxInFlight makes NewHedge return a policy that refuses
every call with PolicyMisconfigured.

It is the answer to hedging's second hazard: a dependency that has gone
slow makes every in-flight call hedge at the same moment, so the policy
adds load precisely when the dependency has least to spare and deepens
the outage it was meant to hide. The cap counts duplicates only — the
first attempt of every call always runs, so reaching the cap degrades
the policy to no-hedging rather than rejecting the call. A caller who
wants rejection under saturation composes NewBulkhead, whose job that
is.

It is refused rather than defaulted because both directions of a guess
are harmful in this specific knob, which is the rarer case where neither
clamping nor defaulting has a safe side: a conservative SDK default
silently stops hedging under exactly the load the caller bought hedging
for (inert, ADR 0031's own failure mode), and a generous one hands back
the amplifier. The number is a capacity decision about the caller's
downstream, and only they hold it.

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock is what Delay is measured on. Nil means clock.System.

It exists so a test drives the race with a ManualClock — advancing past
Delay to issue the duplicate instead of sleeping through it, and
asserting that no duplicate is issued a nanosecond earlier. The retry,
the breaker and the rate limiters already take one; the hedge, the other
policy that measures a wait, did not.

fields.name: Budget
fields.doc:
Budget, when set, is asked before each duplicate: a refusal issues
none, and the call proceeds on the attempts already running, as when
MaxInFlight is reached. Each call's outcome is recorded in it — a
success, or a failure on a live context — so a hedge and a retry
sharing one budget stop amplifying a failing dependency together, as
gRPC's retry throttling covers hedging. Nil is the hedge without a
budget.

symbols.doc:
HedgeConfig parameterises NewHedge. Three of its four knobs have no default:
Idempotent, Delay and MaxInFlight are refused when unset, because every value
the SDK could pick for them is either a guess at the caller's requirement or
a licence to duplicate load the caller never agreed to (ADR 0031). MaxHedges
is the one with an obvious floor and clamps to 1. A nil Clock measures the
delay on the wall clock, and a nil Budget never refuses a duplicate.

symbols.name: KeyedRateLimiterConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{Key func(ctx context.Context) string; Clock clock.Clock; Rate float64; Burst int; MaxKeys int; IdleTimeout time.Duration}
symbols.canonical: struct{Key func(ctx context.Context) string; Clock github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/clock.Clock; Rate float64; Burst int; MaxKeys int; IdleTimeout time.Duration}

fields.name: Key
fields.doc:
Key names who a call is charged to — the authenticated user, the
client's address, a tenant. Calls whose keys differ never share a
bucket, which is the whole point: one client emptying its bucket is
refused while the others are not, so a single client cannot lock
everybody out of a sign-in endpoint the way one shared bucket lets it.

It is called once per Run, with the Run's context. It is required: a
limiter with nothing to key on is NewRateLimiter.

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock reads time for every bucket and for idleness. Nil means
clock.System.

fields.name: Rate
fields.doc:
Rate is each key's sustained admission rate, in tokens per second. It
has no default, exactly as RateLimiterConfig.Rate has none.

fields.name: Burst
fields.doc: Burst is each key's bucket capacity, clamped to at least 1.

fields.name: MaxKeys
fields.doc:
MaxKeys bounds how many keys are tracked at once; beyond it the least
recently used key is forgotten. It is required: its zero reads either
as "unbounded", which lets a stream of distinct keys grow the process
without limit, or as "none", which admits nothing. Size it above the
number of clients active within IdleTimeout — a key pushed out by
capacity comes back with a FULL bucket, so a flood of new keys buys
every evicted client a fresh burst.

fields.name: IdleTimeout
fields.doc:
IdleTimeout is how long a key may go without a call before it is
forgotten; its next call starts over with a full bucket. It slides: a
key in use is never forgotten for idleness. It is required: its zero
reads either as "forget at once", which gives every call a full bucket
and so limits nothing, or as "never".

Forgetting a key is observable only when IdleTimeout is shorter than the
time the bucket takes to refill (Burst / Rate): below that, a key that
comes back is admitted a burst it would not yet have earned.

symbols.doc:
KeyedRateLimiterConfig parameterises NewKeyedRateLimiter: a token bucket per
key, at most MaxKeys of them, each forgotten after IdleTimeout without a
call.

Four fields have no default and a zero in any of them is refused with
PolicyMisconfigured on every call (ADR 0031): Rate for the reason
RateLimiterConfig.Rate gives, and the three below because each of their
zeros has two readings and one of them silently disarms the limiter.

symbols.name: NewAdaptiveThrottle
symbols.doc:
NewAdaptiveThrottle returns a Runner that refuses calls on the client
side, before sending them, when the dependency has been refusing more
than its share: the adaptive throttling of Google's SRE book ("Handling
Overload"). Over the last cfg.Window it counts requests — every call
Run was asked to make, the ones it refused included — and accepts —
the calls the dependency answered without refusing them — and refuses
each new call with probability

	max(0, (requests − K × accepts) / (requests + 1))

returning Throttled without running the operation. While the
dependency accepts at least one call in K, nothing is refused; past
that, the refusals grow with the excess. A dependency that refuses
everything still receives a trickle of calls — the traffic that tells
it, and us, when it has recovered — and the refusals fade as its
accepts come back into the window.

A call's error is a refusal when cfg.Rejected says so — every error
when it is nil —; a nil error is an accept, and so is a call that
ended in context.Canceled once the caller's own context was closed: a
caller who left says nothing about the dependency. The refusal is drawn
from cfg.Random, so a test decides it.

A K below 1 or not a number, a negative Window, more than 1000
Buckets, or a Window too short to split into its Buckets, is refused:
every call returns PolicyMisconfigured, naming the field. A call that
is not refused costs one lock and no allocation.

symbols.name: NewBulkhead
symbols.doc:
NewBulkhead returns a Runner that admits at most maxConcurrent simultaneous
operations (clamped to >= 1). Excess calls return BulkheadFull immediately
(reject mode — no queuing).

symbols.name: NewBulkheadWait
symbols.doc:
NewBulkheadWait returns a Runner that admits at most cfg.Max simultaneous
operations (clamped to >= 1) and lets up to cfg.Queue more calls wait, each
at most cfg.MaxWait on cfg.Clock, for a slot to free — Polly's
ConcurrencyLimiter(permitLimit, queueLimit), failsafe-go's bulkhead
WithMaxWaitTime. A call that finds the queue full, or whose wait runs out,
returns BulkheadFull; one whose context ends while it waits returns
ctx.Err() and frees its place in the queue.

A non-positive Queue or MaxWait is no waiting at all: the call is
rejected at once, as NewBulkhead rejects it, so the zero
BulkheadWaitConfig is NewBulkhead(1). Waiters take the freed slots in
the order they started waiting, as far as the Go runtime's channel
queues keep it.

A call that finds a slot free pays what NewBulkhead's does and
allocates nothing; a call that waits arms one timer on cfg.Clock.

symbols.name: NewCircuitBreaker
symbols.doc:
NewCircuitBreaker returns a Runner guarding op with a Closed→Open→HalfOpen
breaker. Open calls return CircuitOpen until OpenDuration elapses; a
non-positive OpenDuration clamps to defaultOpenDuration, because a breaker
whose cooldown is zero admits the next call immediately and therefore
protects nothing (ADR 0031). An error rejected by cfg.Retryable is returned
verbatim and left out of the state machine entirely, so deterministic
failures cannot trip the breaker. Once the cooldown elapses ONE HalfOpen
trial runs at a time and every other call returns CircuitOpen until it
settles; cfg.HalfOpenTrials successful trials in a row close the
breaker, and any failed one opens it again. The outcome of a call
admitted before the breaker last opened is ignored: its success cannot
close the breaker and its failure cannot restart the cooldown.

A call that ends in context.Canceled once the caller's own context is
closed is neutral — neither a success nor a failure — because the caller
left, not the dependency: a wave of client disconnects cannot open the
breaker on a healthy dependency, and a HalfOpen trial abandoned that way
frees the slot for the next call. context.DeadlineExceeded stays a
failure: a dependency too slow for the caller's deadline is a slow
dependency.

With a nil cfg.Window the breaker opens on FailureThreshold consecutive
failures. With one, it opens on the rate of failures, or of slow calls,
among the calls of a sliding time window on cfg.Clock, once that window
holds at least MinCalls of them; a HalfOpen trial that lasts SlowAfter
or longer counts as failed. A Window or an OpenBackoff with a value it
cannot honour is refused: every call returns PolicyMisconfigured,
naming the field, and the Runner returned is not a BreakerState.

The Runner returned otherwise implements BreakerState: State reports
the phase and its counts, Isolate opens the breaker until Reset, and
Reset closes it. cfg.OnStateChange hears every change of phase.

symbols.name: NewFallback
symbols.doc:
NewFallback returns a Runner that runs cfg.Fallback when the Operation passed
to Run fails, and returns nil when the fallback succeeds — that masking IS
the policy. When both fail the result is FallbackFailed, carrying both
messages as fields so neither failure is lost.

A cancelled context is reported as itself, never as FallbackFailed: when it
is already dead after the primary the fallback does not run at all, and when
it dies WHILE the fallback runs, a failed fallback returns ctx.Err(). A
fallback that succeeds despite a late cancellation still returns nil — the
work was done.

A nil cfg.Fallback is refused: every call returns PolicyMisconfigured without
running the operation (ADR 0031). A fallback policy with no fallback would
run the primary and pass its error through unchanged — indistinguishable
from no policy at all, while the caller believes their plan B is in place.

The primary error is NOT surfaced when the fallback succeeds; that is what a
fallback is for. A caller who needs to know how often plan B fires
instruments the fallback Operation itself, which is an ordinary closure.

symbols.name: NewHedge
symbols.doc:
NewHedge returns a Runner that guards tail latency by DUPLICATING a slow
Operation: when the first attempt has been outstanding for cfg.Delay, a
second copy starts, and so on every cfg.Delay up to cfg.MaxHedges extra
copies. The first attempt to succeed wins and Run returns nil; the losers'
context is cancelled on the way out and their results are discarded.

# The Operation MUST be idempotent

Every other policy here runs the Operation at most once at a time; this one
runs copies CONCURRENTLY, so a non-idempotent Operation is not made slow by
hedging, it is made WRONG — two charges, two inserts, two outbound messages,
with the policy reporting one clean success. The SDK cannot detect
idempotence, so cfg.Idempotent is a mandatory in-code assertion rather than a
warning in prose: its zero value refuses the policy (ADR 0031).

# Hedging acts on latency, never on failure

An attempt that FAILS before cfg.Delay elapses ends the call with that error,
verbatim; no duplicate is issued. Reacting to a failure by launching another
attempt is retrying, and this package already has NewRetry — compose
NewRetry(NewHedge(op)) to get both. Keeping them separate is also what keeps
the duplication bounded by latency rather than by failure: a dependency that
is failing fast gets no extra traffic from this policy, only a slow one does.

# Load

cfg.MaxInFlight caps the duplicates in flight across all calls, so a
dependency that has gone slow cannot make every caller hedge at once. When
the cap is reached the duplicate is simply not issued and the call proceeds
on its first attempt alone — degrading to no-hedging, never to a rejection.

# A panic reaches the caller, with its original value

This is the one policy that runs the Operation on goroutines of its own, and
a panic that reaches the top of any goroutine ends the process — where under
every other policy the same panic reaches the caller's goroutine and is
contained by net/http or by the caller's own recover. So a copy's panic is
recovered on that copy's goroutine and re-raised from Run, on the caller's
goroutine, with the Operation's ORIGINAL value: the caller's recover compares
equal to exactly what was panicked with, and http.ErrAbortHandler still
aborts a handler silently instead of being logged as a crash.

What does NOT survive is the stack. The re-raised panic's stack is the
re-raise site inside Run, not the Operation's frame: a value re-raised on
another goroutine cannot carry the panicking goroutine's stack without being
wrapped, and wrapping it would break both http.ErrAbortHandler and value
equality. A copy that panics after Run has returned — a loser, once a winner
was found or the caller went away — is recovered and dropped; it never
reaches the caller and never ends the process.

The delay is measured on cfg.Clock — the wall clock when nil — so a test
issues a duplicate by advancing a clock.ManualClock past cfg.Delay.

Run costs one goroutine per attempt (including the first, so the delay stays
observable) and one ticker per call: this is the one policy in the package
that is not allocation-trivial, which is the price of racing. Neither cost
grows with cfg.MaxHedges, which bounds how many duplicates a call may issue
and nothing else.

A false cfg.Idempotent, a non-positive cfg.Delay, or a non-positive
cfg.MaxInFlight is refused: every call returns PolicyMisconfigured without
running the operation (ADR 0031). A cfg.MaxHedges below one clamps to one.

With a cfg.Budget, a duplicate the budget refuses is not issued — the
call proceeds on the attempts already running, as when MaxInFlight is
reached — and each call's outcome is recorded in it: a success, or a
failure on a live context. A cfg.Budget NewRetryBudget refused makes
every call return PolicyMisconfigured.

symbols.name: NewKeyedRateLimiter
symbols.doc:
NewKeyedRateLimiter returns a Runner admitting at most cfg.Rate calls per
second, with a cfg.Burst allowance, PER KEY — the key being whatever cfg.Key
names for the call's context. A call whose bucket is empty is rejected with
RateLimited; the others are not.

At most cfg.MaxKeys keys are held: a new key beyond that forgets the least
recently used one. A key unused for cfg.IdleTimeout is forgotten too. A
forgotten key's next call starts over with a full bucket.

A Rate that is not a finite positive number, a nil Key, and a non-positive
MaxKeys or IdleTimeout are each refused: every call returns
PolicyMisconfigured, naming the field, without running the operation.

symbols.name: NewRateLimiter
symbols.doc:
NewRateLimiter returns a Runner that admits at most Rate calls/sec (with a
Burst allowance), rejecting excess calls with RateLimited. A Rate that is not
a finite positive number — zero, negative, NaN or infinite — is refused
rather than defaulted: every call returns PolicyMisconfigured without running
the operation (ADR 0031).

With a positive cfg.MaxWait, a call whose token is due within MaxWait
reserves it and waits for it on cfg.Clock instead of being rejected; a
call whose context ends while it waits returns ctx.Err() and hands its
token back. A cfg.Clock that cannot wait — a clock.Clock that is not a
clock.Timed — is refused when MaxWait is positive, naming Clock.

symbols.name: NewRetry
symbols.doc:
NewRetry returns a Runner that retries op up to cfg.MaxAttempts times,
sleeping an exponentially-growing (capped) delay between attempts and aborting
early on ctx cancellation. The final attempt's error wraps as RetryExhausted.
An error rejected by cfg.Retryable ends the loop at once and is returned
verbatim, so a deterministic failure neither spends the budget nor hides
behind RetryExhausted. When cfg.Delay reads a wait from the failure — a
Retry-After, a RateLimited rejection — that wait replaces the backoff,
held at cfg.MaxDelay. cfg.JitterMode chooses how the backoff is
randomised: added Jitter (the zero), full, or decorrelated from the
previous wait of the same call.

With a cfg.Budget, every success and every retryable failure is recorded
in it, and a retry it refuses ends the loop with RetryBudgetExceeded
wrapping the last error. cfg.OnRetry hears each retry before its wait. A
cfg.Budget NewRetryBudget refused makes every call return
PolicyMisconfigured.

symbols.name: NewRetryBudget
symbols.doc:
NewRetryBudget returns the token-bucket RetryBudget of gRPC's retry
throttling (gRFC A6), to share between the NewRetry and NewHedge policies
that call one dependency. It starts full, at cfg.MaxTokens tokens; each
recorded failure costs one token, each recorded success returns
cfg.TokenRatio of one, never past cfg.MaxTokens; and AllowRetry is true
only while more than half of cfg.MaxTokens remain. The first attempt of a
call is never refused, so a dependency that recovers is seen to recover:
its successes refill the bucket.

The bucket drains while recorded failures exceed TokenRatio times the
recorded successes — with 0.1, more than one failure per ten successes —
and retries stop once it has lost half its tokens; it refills, and
retries resume, when failures fall back below that ratio. 0.1 is the
order of the per-client retry budget Google's SRE book recommends (10%)
and of the AWS SDKs' retry quota.

A non-positive cfg.MaxTokens, and a cfg.TokenRatio that is not a finite
number of at least one thousandth, are refused (ADR 0031): the budget
returned allows no retry, and NewRetry or NewHedge given it refuses
every call with PolicyMisconfigured, naming the field. The counts are
kept in thousandths of a token, as gRPC does, without a lock and without
allocating.

symbols.name: NewTimeout
symbols.doc:
NewTimeout returns a Runner that fails an Operation with TimeoutExceeded if it
does not finish within d. The Operation MUST honour ctx for the deadline to
fire promptly (a ctx-ignoring op caps precision at op granularity).

A non-positive d is refused: every call returns PolicyMisconfigured without
running the operation (ADR 0031). context.WithTimeout(ctx, 0) yields an
already-expired context, so the previous behaviour failed even an
instantaneous operation with TimeoutExceeded — a policy that could never
admit anything, reporting it with the error it uses when it is working.

Only this policy's own deadline is reported as TimeoutExceeded. When the
caller's context is already finished — cancelled, or past a deadline of
its own — the call returns that context's error instead: the caller
left or ran out of time, and the policy did not time anything out.

The deadline runs on the wall clock; NewTimeoutWith takes a clock.

symbols.name: NewTimeoutWith
symbols.doc:
NewTimeoutWith is NewTimeout with the deadline measured on cfg.Clock, so
a test expires it by advancing a clock.ManualClock past cfg.Duration
instead of sleeping through it (ADR 0090). A nil cfg.Clock, or
clock.System, is NewTimeout(cfg.Duration) exactly.

Under any other clock the Operation's context reports
context.DeadlineExceeded once the clock passes the deadline, and its
Deadline method reports the caller's deadline, not this one: a deadline
on a clock that is not the wall clock is not a time a socket can be
given. A non-positive cfg.Duration is refused like NewTimeout's.

symbols.name: RateLimiterConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{Rate float64; Burst int; Clock clock.Clock; MaxWait time.Duration}
symbols.canonical: struct{Rate float64; Burst int; Clock github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/clock.Clock; MaxWait time.Duration}

fields.name: Rate
fields.doc:
Rate is the sustained admission rate in tokens per second. It has no
default: a Rate that is not a finite positive number — zero, negative,
NaN or infinite — makes NewRateLimiter return a policy that refuses
every call with PolicyMisconfigured. Any rate the SDK picked on
the caller's behalf would be a guess at their requirement, and a caller
who silently received one would believe they were limited at the rate
they intended (ADR 0031). Contrast Burst, which does have an obvious
floor — admit at least one call — and is therefore clamped.

fields.name: MaxWait
fields.doc:
MaxWait is how long a call may wait for its token instead of being
rejected: a call whose token is due within MaxWait reserves it at
once — later calls queue behind the reservation — and waits for
it on Clock. Zero, or less, rejects at once with RateLimited, as
the limiter always has. A call whose token is due later than
MaxWait is rejected at once, saying when it would have been due.

Waiting needs a clock that can wait: with a positive MaxWait, a
Clock that is not a clock.Timed is refused with
PolicyMisconfigured, naming Clock. A nil Clock waits on the wall
clock.

symbols.doc:
RateLimiterConfig parameterises NewRateLimiter. Burst is the bucket capacity
(clamped to >= 1); a nil Clock defaults to System; a zero MaxWait
rejects at once a call that finds no token.

symbols.name: RetryAfter
symbols.doc:
RetryAfter reports the delay err says to wait before the next attempt,
and whether it says one. It reads the retry_after_seconds field of the
outermost *errs.Error in err's chain — a number of seconds, whole or
fractional — and reports false when there is none, or when it is not a
finite positive number.

Three producers in the SDK set it: the OTLP/HTTP exporters on a
retryable answer whose Retry-After header holds delta-seconds, the
guarded HTTP client (net/client) on a 429 or a 503 whose Retry-After
does the same, and RateLimited from NewRateLimiter and
NewKeyedRateLimiter, with the time the bucket needs to earn its next
token. An HTTP-date Retry-After is not read: converting it compares the
peer's clock to ours. Any other error sets the same field with
errs.Int or errs.Float to take part.

Its shape is RetryConfig.Delay's, so honouring the delay is one line:

	Delay: func(_ int, err error) (time.Duration, bool) { return RetryAfter(err) }

A delay too long for a time.Duration reports the longest one.

symbols.name: RetryBudgetConfig

fields.name: MaxTokens
fields.doc:
MaxTokens is the bucket's size and its starting content. Retries are
allowed while more than MaxTokens/2 remain, so the budget absorbs
about MaxTokens/2 more failures than its successes repay before it
starts refusing. A non-positive MaxTokens is refused; values above
2^40 are held there.

fields.name: TokenRatio
fields.doc:
TokenRatio is what a recorded success puts back, in tokens, a
failure costing one. It is read to a thousandth, as gRPC reads it: a
value that is not finite, or that rounds below 0.001, is refused —
its zero would be a budget that, once drained, never refills.

symbols.doc:
RetryBudgetConfig parameterises NewRetryBudget, in the terms of gRPC's
retryThrottling: the bucket's size and what a success puts back. Neither
has a default; both are refused when unusable (ADR 0031).

symbols.name: RetryConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{MaxAttempts int; BaseDelay time.Duration; MaxDelay time.Duration; Multiplier float64; Retryable func(error) bool; Jitter float64; JitterMode kbackoff.JitterMode; Clock clock.Timed; Delay func(attempt int, err error) (time.Duration, bool); Budget coreres.RetryBudget; OnRetry func(attempt int, err error, delay time.Duration)}
symbols.canonical: struct{MaxAttempts int; BaseDelay time.Duration; MaxDelay time.Duration; Multiplier float64; Retryable func(error) bool; Jitter float64; JitterMode github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/backoff.JitterMode; Clock github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/clock.Timed; Delay func(attempt int, err error) (time.Duration, bool); Budget github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/resilience.RetryBudget; OnRetry func(attempt int, err error, delay time.Duration)}

fields.name: Retryable
fields.doc:
Retryable classifies a non-nil operation error as replayable. It is
consulted once per failed attempt: false returns that error verbatim —
no backoff, no further attempt, no RetryExhausted relabel — so a
deterministic failure (policy refusal, HTTP 400, invalid input) surfaces
as itself at the first attempt instead of costing the whole budget. A
nil predicate replays every error, which is the pre-classifier
behaviour. BreakerConfig accepts the same shape, so one classifier
serves a nested Retry(Breaker(op)) stack.

fields.name: Jitter
fields.doc:
Jitter widens each backoff by a random fraction of itself, drawn
uniformly from [0, Jitter) and ADDED to the computed delay. 0 — the zero
value — is the deterministic backoff this policy has always had, so an
existing caller's timing is unchanged. 0.5 is the common choice: it
desynchronises callers that failed together without letting the average
wait stop growing monotonically. Values outside [0, 1] clamp into it.

It exists because deterministic backoff SYNCHRONISES the very callers it
is meant to spread. N clients that fail against one dependency at the
same instant retry at the same instant, N times over, and every retry
round lands as one burst on a dependency that is already struggling.
Jitter is what turns those bursts back into a distribution.

It applies AFTER the MaxDelay cap, deliberately: the cap bounds the
growth, and jitter spreads callers around the bound rather than being
squeezed flat against it. The consequence is worth stating — WHEN a cap is
configured, the effective ceiling on one wait becomes MaxDelay * (1 +
Jitter), not MaxDelay. A zero MaxDelay is no cap at all, so there is no
ceiling to raise: the backoff grows geometrically and the jitter widens
whatever it reaches, bounded only by what a time.Duration can represent.

It is read only under the zero JitterMode.

fields.name: JitterMode
fields.doc:
JitterMode is how the backoff is randomised. The zero,
JitterAdditive, adds Jitter as above. JitterFull waits a uniform
draw from [0, the capped curve]; JitterDecorrelated draws each wait
from [BaseDelay, 3 × the previous wait of this call], held at
MaxDelay. Both are the AWS Builders' Library's variants and ignore
Jitter; a wait the failure imposed through Delay is not randomised
and is not the previous wait a decorrelated draw starts from.

Full jitter spreads callers that failed together the most, at the
cost of sometimes retrying almost at once; decorrelated jitter
keeps the waits growing while drifting each caller off the others'
curve. With a zero MaxDelay a decorrelated wait is bounded only by
what a time.Duration can represent.

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock is what the backoff waits on. Nil means clock.System.

It exists so a test drives the whole retry loop with a ManualClock —
advancing past each backoff instead of sleeping through it, and asserting
the exact wait rather than a wall-clock tolerance. The breaker and the
rate limiter have taken a clock since they shipped; the retry, which is
the one policy here that actually WAITS, did not.

fields.name: Delay
fields.doc:
Delay decides the wait before a retry when the failure itself says how
long to wait. It is called once per retry, with the retry's number —
1 before the second attempt — and the error of the attempt that just
failed; a true second result makes its duration the wait, in place of
the backoff curve and without Jitter. A false one, and a nil Delay,
wait the curve, which is the behaviour before the field existed.

The wait it returns is held at MaxDelay when one is set, and a
negative one is no wait. A server's hint longer than the caller is
prepared to wait is therefore cut to MaxDelay, never followed past
it; a caller who would rather give up classifies that error as not
retryable instead.

RetryAfter has its shape, so honouring a Retry-After, an OTLP
collector's throttling or a RateLimited rejection is one line:

	Delay: func(_ int, err error) (time.Duration, bool) { return resilience.RetryAfter(err) }

fields.name: Budget
fields.doc:
Budget, when set, bounds the retries of every policy sharing it: each
success and each retryable failure is recorded in it, and before
every retry it is asked whether one may run. A refusal ends the loop
with RetryBudgetExceeded wrapping the last error, without waiting. A
deterministic error and a cancelled context record nothing.

Nil — the zero value — is the policy without a budget, as it was
before the field existed. Share one budget per dependency, between
its retry and its hedge: that is what stops a failing dependency from
receiving every call times MaxAttempts. A Retry(Hedge(op)) whose two
policies share a budget records a failed call at both levels, which
drains and refills it twice as fast and leaves its threshold where it
was.

fields.name: OnRetry
fields.type: func(attempt int, err error, delay time.Duration)
fields.doc:
OnRetry, when set, is called before each retry's wait, on the
calling goroutine, with the retry's number — 1 before the second
attempt —, the error that caused it and the wait about to start. It
is how a caller counts retries in their own metrics without this
package depending on one. It is not called for the first attempt,
nor for a retry the budget refused. It must not block: the retry
waits for it.

symbols.doc:
RetryConfig parameterises NewRetry. A non-positive MaxAttempts clamps to 1; a
Multiplier of 1 or below (or NaN) defaults to 2; a zero MaxDelay means no
cap; a nil Retryable replays every error; a zero Jitter backs off
deterministically, and a zero JitterMode is that additive Jitter; a nil
Clock waits on the wall clock; a nil Delay
always waits the backoff curve; a nil Budget never refuses a retry; a nil
OnRetry hears nothing.

BaseDelay, MaxDelay, Multiplier, Jitter and JitterMode are the five
fields of BackoffValue, under the same names and with the same meaning:
NewRetry builds its curve from them, so a loop that retries on its own
terms and a Retry policy configured alike wait alike — save that a
decorrelated retry draws each wait from the one it actually waited
before, which the memoryless BackoffValue.Delay cannot know.

symbols.name: TimeoutConfig

fields.name: Duration
fields.doc:
Duration is how long the Operation may run. A non-positive Duration
makes NewTimeoutWith return a policy that refuses every call with
PolicyMisconfigured, exactly as NewTimeout refuses a non-positive d.

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock is what Duration is measured on. Nil means clock.System, under
which the policy is NewTimeout's: a context.WithTimeout whose
deadline the Operation can read.

symbols.doc:
TimeoutConfig parameterises NewTimeoutWith: the deadline and the clock it
is measured on. Duration has no default and is refused when not positive
(ADR 0031); a nil Clock is the wall clock.

symbols.name: Config

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock is the time source the engine reads AND waits on. A nil Clock
falls back to clock.System.

It is clock.Timed rather than clock.Clock because this engine does both
halves: it stamps results and it waits for deadlines. Depending on
package time directly instead would make every cadence assertion in the
test suite a sleep, which is the claim ADR 0039 exists to make true.

fields.name: OnResult
fields.doc:
OnResult observes every decision the scheduler takes — each run, with
the job's own error, and each fire skipped for overlap.

Calls are SERIALISED: the hook need not be safe for concurrent use, and
in exchange a hook that blocks blocks the scheduler. Keep it short; hand
off to a logger or a channel rather than doing work in it.

A nil hook is a working configuration, not a refusal: a caller whose
jobs log their own failures has nothing to observe here. It does mean
the job's error goes NOWHERE — the SDK will not write it to stderr on
the caller's behalf (ADR 0030) — so a caller who wants to know their
jobs are failing must wire this.

symbols.doc:
Config parameterises [New]. Both fields are optional and the zero value
builds a working scheduler — one that runs on the wall clock and reports
nothing.

symbols.name: Every
symbols.doc:
Every returns a [coresched.Schedule] due one period after each previous due
instant. It exists because @every is refused by the cron parser: an interval
is not a calendar expression, and pretending it is confuses two different
ideas — "every 30 seconds" has no month, no weekday and no DST question,
while "0 2 * * *" has all three.

The period is measured from the previous DUE instant, not from the previous
completion, so a slow job does not shift the cadence. When a run overruns
its period the next fire is already late; the scheduler then applies the
domain's missed-deadline rule (skip and count) rather than queueing.

A non-positive period is refused ([coresched.InvalidInterval]) rather than clamped: a
schedule due infinitely often is not a slow schedule, it is a busy loop, and
no substitute value would be anything but a guess at the caller's intent
(ADR 0031). Sub-minute periods are accepted here — unlike cron, which stops
at the minute — but the timing guarantee is the domain's: not early, and
late by however much the platform's timers and the machine's load impose.

symbols.name: New
symbols.doc:
New returns a Scheduler built from cfg. It cannot fail: a nil Clock falls
back to clock.System and a nil OnResult to no observation, both of which are
working configurations rather than inert ones (ADR 0031). What CAN fail —
an unrunnable entry, an unparseable expression — fails at Add and at Parse,
where the caller made the mistake.

symbols.name: Parse
symbols.doc:
Parse compiles a five-field POSIX cron expression, evaluated in UTC.

UTC is the default rather than time.Local because time.Local depends on TZ
and on the host: the same expression would mean different instants on two
machines in one fleet, and the difference would surface as a job that ran an
hour early on one node. A caller who wants local time says so, with
ParseInLocation(expr, time.Local).

Accepted: five space-separated fields — minute (0-59), hour (0-23),
day-of-month (1-31), month (1-12 or JAN-DEC), day-of-week (0-6 or SUN-SAT,
Sunday = 0) — each of which may be "*", a value, an "a-b" range, a
comma-separated list, or a "*/n" / "a-b/n" step. Names are
case-insensitive. The macros @yearly, @annually, @monthly, @weekly, @daily,
@midnight and @hourly expand to the expressions above.

Refused, by name rather than by guessing: six- and seven-field expressions
(seconds / year), @reboot, @every, the Quartz operators L, W, # and ?, a
step written over a single value, an inverted range, 7 for Sunday, and a
valid expression that matches no date on the calendar.

When both day fields are restricted, POSIX makes them an OR: "0 0 13 * FRI"
fires on every 13th AND on every Friday, not only on Friday the 13th.

symbols.name: ParseInLocation
symbols.spelled: func(expr string, loc *time.Location) (parsed coresched.Schedule, err error)
symbols.doc:
ParseInLocation compiles a cron expression evaluated in loc.

A nil loc is REFUSED, not read as UTC: nil is what an unchecked
time.LoadLocation returns on failure, so accepting it would turn a missing
tzdata into a schedule that silently runs on a different clock. Parse is the
way to ask for UTC.

Around a DST transition in loc the semantics are exact and are not
negotiable per caller:

  - Spring forward. A wall-clock time that does not exist that day does not
    fire. "0 2 * * *" in a zone that skips 02:00-03:00 skips that day
    entirely; it is not shifted to 01:00 or 03:00, because both of those are
    instants the expression does not name.
  - Fall back. A wall-clock time that happens twice fires ONCE, at the first
    occurrence. The schedule is strictly increasing by contract, and the
    second occurrence is behind the instant already returned.

fields.doc: Entity is the entity as stored after the transition.

fields.name: At

fields.name: Key
fields.doc: Key is the entity's key in the store.

fields.name: Event
fields.doc:
Event is the transition's name; core/app/statemachine.CreateEvent for a
creation.

fields.name: Actor
fields.doc:
Actor is who fired it, as Config.Actor read it from the caller's
context; empty when the machine's loop fired it.

fields.name: From
fields.doc: From is the state left: the zero S for a creation.

fields.name: To
fields.doc: To is the state entered.

fields.name: Trigger
fields.doc: Trigger says what fired it.

symbols.doc:
ChangeValue describes one stored transition, as an OnTransition hook
receives it.

fields.name: Store
fields.doc: Store holds the entities. Required.

fields.name: Journal
fields.doc:
Journal keeps each entity's record beside the store. Nil keeps the
records in memory: after a restart every entity re-enters its state
when the machine opens, which restarts every After timer.

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock is what the machine stamps and waits on. Nil is clock.System; a
clock.ManualClock drives every timer of a test.

fields.name: Actor
fields.doc:
Actor reads, from the context a caller hands Start or Fire, who fired
the transition; the result lands in the record's history and in the
change hooks receive. Never called for a transition the loop fires.
Nil records nobody.

fields.name: Observe
fields.type: func(ctx context.Context, firing FiringValue[S]) (context.Context, func(err error))
fields.doc:
Observe brackets every transition the machine's OWN loop fires — the
ones no caller can wrap: it is called before the transition with the
loop's context, returns the context the transition's hooks and store
calls run under — a tracer puts its span there — and a function the
engine calls with the outcome once the OnTransition hooks have run and
the loop has recorded it: a panic there is reported as LoopPanicked and
changes nothing, the transition stands. A caller wraps its own Start and
Fire itself. It is called while the loop holds the entity, so it must
not fire that entity. Nil observes nothing.

fields.name: Report
fields.doc:
Report receives every error no caller's return value carries: an
OnTransition hook's failure, a Journal write that failed, and each
transition the loop could not fire. It is called with no lock of the
machine held, so it may read the machine — its census, a record — or
fire it. Nil drops them — the SDK does not write to stderr on the
caller's behalf (ADR 0030) — so wire it.

fields.name: OnLoop
fields.doc:
OnLoop is told what Run does: a run starting, a run ending with what
it fired and when the loop wakes next, and the loop re-arming earlier
because a write arrived. Called on the loop's goroutine; keep it short.
Nil observes nothing.

fields.name: MinGap
fields.doc:
MinGap is the least time between the end of one run of the loop and
the start of the next. Not positive means DefaultMinGap.

fields.name: Backoff
fields.doc:
Backoff is how long an entity whose automatic transition failed waits
before it is tried again, by consecutive failures. A zero BaseDelay
means 1s doubling to a minute.

fields.name: MaxHistory
fields.doc:
MaxHistory is how many transitions each record keeps. Not positive
means DefaultMaxHistory.

symbols.doc:
Config parameterises NewStateMachine. Only Store is required; every other zero
field resolves to a working default.

symbols.name: DefaultMaxHistory
symbols.doc:
DefaultMaxHistory is how many transitions a record keeps when
Config.MaxHistory is not positive.

symbols.name: DefaultMinGap
symbols.doc:
DefaultMinGap is the least time between the end of one run of a machine's
loop and the start of the next, when Config.MinGap is not positive: a burst
of writes is one run, and a transition chain advances one step per run.

symbols.name: FiringValue
symbols.spelled: [S comparable] struct{Key string; Event string; From S; To S; Trigger corestm.Trigger}
symbols.canonical: [S comparable] struct{Key string; Event string; From S; To S; Trigger github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/app/statemachine.Trigger}

fields.name: Key
fields.doc: Key is the entity's key.

fields.name: Event
fields.doc: Event is the transition's name.

fields.name: From
fields.doc: From is the state the entity is in.

fields.name: To
fields.doc: To is the state it is about to enter.

fields.name: Trigger
fields.doc: Trigger is a delay, a deadline or a guard: the loop fires nothing else.

symbols.doc:
FiringValue is a transition the machine's own loop is about to fire, as
Config.Observe is told it.

fields.name: Err
fields.doc: Err joins what failed in the run; nil when nothing did.

fields.name: Started
fields.doc: Started is when the run started.

fields.name: Ended
fields.doc: Ended is when the run ended.

fields.name: Next
fields.doc:
Next is when the loop wakes by itself next — never sooner than
Config.MinGap after the run ended; zero when only a write will wake it.

fields.name: Fired
fields.doc: Fired counts the transitions the run stored.

fields.name: Failed
fields.doc: Failed counts the transitions the run could not fire.

fields.name: Kind
fields.doc: Kind says what is reported.

fields.name: Wake
fields.doc: Wake says why the run started.

symbols.doc:
LoopEvent is what Config.OnLoop is told about [StateMachine.Run]. Which fields
are set depends on Kind.

symbols.name: LoopEventKind
symbols.doc: LoopEventKind says what a [LoopEvent] reports.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String returns "run-started", "run-ended" or "waiting"; "" outside the set.

symbols.name: LoopRunEnded
symbols.doc: LoopRunEnded reports a run ending: every field is set.

symbols.name: LoopRunStarted
symbols.doc: LoopRunStarted reports a run starting: Wake and Started are set.

symbols.name: LoopWaiting
symbols.doc:
LoopWaiting reports the loop re-armed to wake earlier, at Next, because
a write arrived while it slept.

symbols.name: MachineSpec
symbols.doc:
MachineSpec declares a state machine over entities of type E whose state is
an S: the state a new entity enters, the transitions between states and how
each is fired, and the hooks that run on the way.

A MachineSpec is DATA. Every transition is declared before a machine runs,
which is what lets a caller draw the machine exactly — [MachineSpec.States]
and [MachineSpec.Transitions] read it back — and what lets the engine know,
for any state, which timers and guards can move an entity out of it.

Four kinds of transitions:

  - On: an event, fired by a caller with [StateMachine.Fire];
  - After: a duration spent in a state, fired by the machine's loop;
  - At: an instant the entity carries — a due date, a deadline — fired by
    the loop once it has come;
  - When: a guard on the entity, fired by the loop as soon as it holds. A
    guard sees the entity only and is asked again each time the entity is
    written; a condition on the time is an instant, declared with At.

When several automatic transitions leave a state and more than one is due,
the one declared FIRST fires.

A mistake — a duplicate, an empty event name, a nil function, a duration
that is not positive — is recorded rather than panicked on, read back with
[MachineSpec.Problems], and refused by NewStateMachine. Build a MachineSpec on one
goroutine; once a machine is built from it, the machine keeps its own copy
and later declarations do not reach it.

symbols.name: After
symbols.spelled: func(event string, delay time.Duration, from S, to S) *MachineSpec[E, S]
symbols.canonical: func(event string, delay time.Duration, from S, to S) *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/service/app/statemachine.MachineSpec[E, S]
symbols.doc:
After declares a timer transition: an entity that has spent delay in state
from moves to state to, fired by the machine's loop. The time is counted
from when the entity entered the state, which the machine's journal keeps
across restarts.

symbols.doc:
At declares a timer transition at an instant the entity carries: an entity
in state from moves to state to once the instant instant returns has come;
false means no instant for now. The engine asks again each time the entity
is written, and its loop sleeps until the earliest instant.

symbols.name: Can
symbols.doc:
Can reports whether [StateMachine.Fire] with event would move entity: an event
transition by that name leaves its current state. It is a function of the
declaration alone and needs no running machine.

symbols.name: Initial
symbols.doc:
Initial sets the state a new entity enters with [StateMachine.Start]. A second
call replaces the first.

symbols.name: InitialState
symbols.doc:
InitialState returns the state a new entity enters, and whether Initial
was called.

symbols.name: On
symbols.spelled: func(event string, from S, to S) *MachineSpec[E, S]
symbols.canonical: func(event string, from S, to S) *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/service/app/statemachine.MachineSpec[E, S]
symbols.doc:
On declares an event transition: [StateMachine.Fire] with event moves an entity
in state from to state to. One event may leave several states, but only one
transition per event and state.

symbols.name: OnEnter
symbols.spelled: func(state S, hook func(context.Context, *E) error) *MachineSpec[E, S]
symbols.canonical: func(state S, hook func(context.Context, *E) error) *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/service/app/statemachine.MachineSpec[E, S]
symbols.doc:
OnEnter adds a hook run when an entity enters state, before it is stored.
Hooks of one state run in declaration order.

An error cancels the transition, and so does a panic — recovered as
[corestm.HookPanicked], with the entity's lock released on the way out. A hook may
change the entity but not its state nor its key ([corestm.HookChangedState],
[corestm.HookChangedKey]), and must not fire its own machine: it runs under the
entity's lock, so the call is refused with [corestm.Reentrant] rather than waiting
for itself.

symbols.spelled: func(hook func(context.Context, ChangeValue[E, S]) error) *MachineSpec[E, S]
symbols.doc:
OnTransition adds a hook run after every stored transition, whoever fired
it — the natural place to publish it. Hooks run in declaration order, once
the entity's lock is released, so a hook may fire the machine again. An
error or a panic is reported through Config.Report; the transition stands
and the next hooks still run.

symbols.name: Problems
symbols.doc:
Problems returns the declaration's mistakes so far, in the order they were
made, each an error carrying a code of this package and log-only fields
naming the event, the state or the function concerned. A missing Initial is
not among them — it is only a mistake once the declaration is complete, and
NewStateMachine reports it as [corestm.InitialMissing].

symbols.name: States
symbols.doc:
States returns every state the declaration names, in the order each was
first mentioned: the initial state, the ends of each transition, the states
that have hooks.

symbols.name: Transitions
symbols.doc: Transitions returns the declared transitions in declaration order.

as soon as guard holds. The guard sees the entity only and is asked each time
the entity is written, never on a clock.

state returns a pointer to the entity's state field: the engine reads the
