it is not. A failed statement is yielded once, as StatementFailed,
and ends the listing.

symbols.name: List
symbols.doc:
List returns every document, in key order — byte order, as Go compares
strings.

symbols.name: Lookup
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, index string, key string) (T, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, index string, key string) (T, error)
symbols.doc:
Lookup returns the document holding key in the unique index named index,
DocumentNotFound when none does, IndexUnknown for an undeclared index and
IndexNotUnique for an index that may hold several: read that one with Find.

symbols.name: OnDelete
symbols.doc:
OnDelete registers fn to be told the key of every document Delete or Trash
removed, on the same terms as OnWrite.

symbols.name: OnWrite
symbols.doc:
OnWrite registers fn to be told the key of every document Put, Insert,
Replace, Update or Restore stored, once the transaction that holds the
write has committed — never for a write that is rolled back — on the
goroutine that committed it, outside every lock. It returns the function
that removes the registration.

symbols.name: Purge
symbols.doc:
Purge empties the trash of the document trashed under key: the trashed
document and every version row of its key go, in one transaction, and a
document written later under the key starts again at version 1. It calls
no hook and asks Held nothing, as Delete does not. DocumentNotTrashed
when no document is trashed under key.

symbols.name: Put
symbols.doc:
Put stores v under its key, creating it or replacing whatever was there.
On a store that keeps versions, it makes one, stamped with nothing.

symbols.name: PutDocument
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string, versions []coredocstore.VersionValue, trashedAt time.Time) error
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string, versions []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.VersionValue, trashedAt time.Time) error
symbols.doc:
PutDocument writes the document key with its versions as they are
given, in one transaction — a savepoint of the caller's when ctx carries
one —, as core/data/docstore.VersionWriterContext says: the document's
row and its index rows unless it is trashed, and a version row for each
version — the trash's row, numbered 0, at trashedAt when it is set. It
calls OnWrite once that transaction commits, for a stored document.
DocumentExists when anything is under key — a document, the trash, or
version rows —, VersionsInvalid, DocumentUndecodable, KeyTooLong or
UniqueKeyTaken for what cannot be written as given, VersionsNotKept on
a store that keeps none; nothing changes on a refusal.

symbols.name: PutStamped
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, v T, stamp coredocstore.StampValue) error
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, v T, stamp github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.StampValue) error
symbols.doc: PutStamped is Put, with what the write says about the version it makes.

symbols.name: Reindex
symbols.doc:
Reindex rebuilds every index row from the stored documents, in one
transaction — a savepoint of the caller's when ctx carries one.

The SQL store keeps its index rows, where the memory and file store rebuild
theirs at every Open. So a change to the declarations — an index added, a
key function or IndexKey changed, an index made unique — files nothing for
the documents already stored until Reindex runs. It drops every row,
including those of an index no longer declared, reads the documents in key
order a page at a time, and files each one's keys again.

Documents that break a unique index refuse the rebuild with INDEX_BROKEN,
naming the index and never the key, and so does a key function that panics;
a document the type no longer fits is DOCUMENT_UNDECODABLE. Nothing changes
then. Run it when no write to the store runs beside it: a write in flight
files its keys under whichever rows it finds.

symbols.name: Replace
symbols.doc:
Replace stores v over the document already under its key: DocumentNotFound
when there is none, so a document deleted meanwhile is never brought back.

symbols.name: ReplaceStamped
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, v T, stamp coredocstore.StampValue) error
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, v T, stamp github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.StampValue) error
symbols.doc:
ReplaceStamped is Replace, with what the write says about the version it
makes.

symbols.name: Restore
symbols.doc:
Restore brings the document trashed under key back exactly as it was —
the same JSON, the same current version — files it again and calls
OnWrite once its transaction commits. DocumentNotTrashed when no
document is trashed under key, UniqueKeyTaken when another document took
one of its unique keys meanwhile, DocumentUndecodable when it no longer
decodes into the store's type; nothing changes on a refusal.

symbols.name: RewriteVersions
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string, fn func(former []coredocstore.VersionValue) ([]coredocstore.VersionValue, error)) error
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string, fn func(former []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.VersionValue) ([]github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.VersionValue, error)) error
symbols.doc:
RewriteVersions rewrites the former versions of the document stored under
key — every version but the current one, which is the document and which
only a write changes — in one transaction, a savepoint of the caller's when
ctx carries one, the document locked as a write locks it. fn receives copies
of them, newest first, and returns those to keep, in the same order, under
the rules of [Store].RewriteVersions: VersionsRewriteRefused otherwise, and
fn's own error returned as it is, nothing changed either way. It calls no
hook: the document did not change.

symbols.name: Tombstones
symbols.doc:
Tombstones returns every document in the trash, in key order: its key and
the instant it was trashed, read in one statement on the transaction ctx
carries. The statement scans the versions table, as List scans the
documents'.

symbols.name: Trash
symbols.doc:
Trash moves the document stored under key to the trash, in one
transaction — a savepoint of the caller's when ctx carries one: its row
and its index rows go, and a version row numbered 0 — no version's
number — holds the document and the instant it was trashed beside its
versions, which stay. It calls OnDelete once that transaction commits.
DocumentNotFound when no document is stored under key, VersionsNotKept
when the store keeps no versions: only a store that keeps versions has a
trash.

symbols.name: Update
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string, fn func(*T) error) (T, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string, fn func(*T) error) (T, error)
symbols.doc:
Update applies fn to a copy of the document stored under key and stores the
result, atomically: the document is locked from the read to the write — its
row on PostgreSQL and MySQL, the database's write lock on SQLite — so no
other write lands between them. An error from fn changes nothing and is
returned for errors.Is to find, and a result whose key is not key is
DocumentKeyChanged. It returns the stored result.

fn runs inside the write's transaction. It may read the store; a read under
a context carrying no transaction runs on the pool, and so needs a second
connection. It must not write the document it updates, which is locked by
the very write that is waiting for fn.

symbols.name: UpdateStamped
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string, stamp coredocstore.StampValue, fn func(*T) error) (T, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string, stamp github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.StampValue, fn func(*T) error) (T, error)
symbols.doc:
UpdateStamped is Update, with what the write says about the version it
makes.

symbols.name: Version
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string, number uint64) (coredocstore.VersionValue, error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string, number uint64) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.VersionValue, error)
symbols.doc:
Version returns the version numbered number of the document stored under
key, VersionNotFound when the document keeps none of that number — never
made, or pruned — and what Versions returns otherwise.

symbols.name: VersionWeight
symbols.doc:
VersionWeight reports what the store keeps beyond its documents, as
core/data/docstore.VersionWeigherContext says: one aggregate statement
over the versions table — its former rows, its trash rows numbered 0,
and the length of the documents they hold —, on the transaction ctx
carries, else on the pool. The database scans the table and sends one
row. VersionsNotKept on a store that keeps none, StatementFailed when
the database does not answer.

symbols.name: Versions
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, key string) (versions []coredocstore.VersionValue, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, key string) (versions []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.VersionValue, err error)
symbols.doc:
Versions returns the versions the store keeps of the document stored under
key, newest first: the current one — the document as it is now — then the
former ones, read in one statement on the transaction ctx carries; a
document in the trash answers the versions it kept, the trashed document
first, in a second one. DocumentNotFound when no document is stored or
trashed under key, VersionsNotKept when the store keeps no versions.

symbols.name: SQLVersionsMigration
symbols.spelled: func(dialect coresql.Dialect, table string, version uint64) (coresql.MigrationValue, error)
symbols.canonical: func(dialect github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.Dialect, table string, version uint64) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.MigrationValue, error)
symbols.doc:
SQLVersionsMigration returns the migration that creates the table a SQL
store named table keeps its versions in on dialect — <table>___vs, one row
per version — as a core/data/sql MigrationValue numbered version, beside the one
[SQLMigration] returns. A store opened with SQLConfig.Versions needs it; one
without never touches it. Its Down drops the table, and every version in it:
run it to turn versions off for good (ADR 0143).

Its one statement does nothing when the table already exists, or is already
gone, as SQLMigration's do.

symbols.name: StatsValue
symbols.spelled: struct{FoldError error; Documents int; Pending int; Folds int; Versions coredocstore.VersionWeightValue}
symbols.canonical: struct{FoldError error; Documents int; Pending int; Folds int; Versions github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.VersionWeightValue}

fields.name: FoldError
fields.doc:
FoldError is the last automatic fold's failure, nil once a fold
succeeds. The write that triggered the fold succeeded either way — its
own entry was already durable — and the entries stay until a fold works.

fields.name: Documents
fields.doc: Documents is how many documents the store holds.

fields.name: Pending
fields.doc:
Pending is how many overlay entries the snapshot does not contain yet:
zero in memory, and after a fold.

fields.name: Folds
fields.doc: Folds is how many folds ran since the store opened, Open's own included.

fields.name: Versions
fields.doc:
Versions is what the store's versions weigh — its former versions, its
trashed documents and their bytes —, a counter every write moves:
zero on a store that keeps none (ADR 0143).

symbols.doc:
StatsValue is what a store can say about itself: how many documents it
holds, how far its overlay has grown, how its folds have gone, and what
its versions weigh.

symbols.name: Store
symbols.doc:
Store is a typed, keyed collection of JSON documents with secondary
indexes. Build one with [Open]. It is safe for concurrent use.

symbols.name: Close
symbols.doc:
Close folds the overlay and closes the store: every later call is
StoreClosed, except Stats and Close, which returns nil. A fold that fails
leaves its entries where they are — the next Open replays them — and is
returned; the store closes either way.

symbols.name: Delete
symbols.doc:
Delete removes the document stored under key, or returns DocumentNotFound.
Its versions go with it: a deletion never reaches the trash, which is
Trash's.

symbols.name: Entries
symbols.doc:
Entries returns up to limit stored documents as JSON, in key order — every
one when limit is not positive — for a caller that shows documents rather
than decoding them. Each JSON is the caller's own copy.

symbols.name: Filter
symbols.doc:
Filter returns the documents keep accepts, in key order. It decodes every
document; an index is the way not to.

symbols.name: Find
symbols.doc:
Find returns the documents filed under key in the index named index, in
store-key order. It reads any index, unique or not, and no document is an
empty slice, not an error.

symbols.name: Fold
symbols.doc:
Fold rewrites the snapshot with every document and removes the overlay
entries it now contains. A write folds by itself when the overlay has grown
enough, and Open and Close fold; Fold is for a caller that wants the
resting state now — before a backup, say. A memory store has nothing to
fold.

symbols.name: Get
symbols.doc: Get returns the document stored under key, or DocumentNotFound.

symbols.name: Insert
symbols.doc: Insert stores v, which must be new: DocumentExists when its key is taken.

symbols.name: InsertStamped
symbols.doc:
InsertStamped is Insert, with what the write says about the version it
makes: version 1, whatever stamp.InPlace says — or, under the key of a
document in the trash, a write over that document.

symbols.name: Keys
symbols.doc:
Keys yields the key of every document the store holds that sorts after
after — every key when after is empty — in key order, and no document.
The keys are taken once, under the read lock, when the range starts:
a write made during the range is not seen by it. What it costs is the
keys' sort, never a document's copy. A closed store yields
StoreClosed once.

symbols.name: List
symbols.doc: List returns every document, in key order.

symbols.name: Lookup
symbols.doc:
Lookup returns the document holding key in the unique index named index,
DocumentNotFound when none does, IndexUnknown for an undeclared index and
IndexNotUnique for an index that may hold several: read that one with Find.

symbols.name: OnDelete
symbols.doc:
OnDelete registers fn to be told the key of every document Delete or Trash
removed, on the same terms as OnWrite.

symbols.name: OnWrite
symbols.doc:
OnWrite registers fn to be told the key of every document Put, Insert,
Replace, Update or Restore stored, once the write is durable, on the
writer's goroutine and outside every lock. It returns the function that
removes the registration. A panic in fn reaches the writer after its write
stood.

symbols.name: Purge
symbols.doc:
Purge empties the trash of the document trashed under key: the trashed
document and every version it kept go, in one durable write, and a
document written later under the key starts again at version 1. It calls
no hook and asks Held nothing, as Delete does not. DocumentNotTrashed
when no document is trashed under key.

symbols.name: Put
symbols.doc:
Put stores v under its key, creating it or replacing whatever was there.
On a store that keeps versions, it makes one, stamped with nothing.

symbols.name: PutDocument
symbols.spelled: func(key string, versions []coredocstore.VersionValue, trashedAt time.Time) error
symbols.canonical: func(key string, versions []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.VersionValue, trashedAt time.Time) error
symbols.doc:
PutDocument writes the document key with its versions as they are
given, in one durable write under the writers' lock, as
core/data/docstore.VersionWriter says: the current version and the
former ones with their numbers, instants and metadata, and — when
trashedAt is set — the document in the trash at that instant. Stored,
it is filed and OnWrite is told; trashed, it is neither. DocumentExists
when anything is under key, VersionsInvalid, DocumentUndecodable or
UniqueKeyTaken for what cannot be written as given, VersionsNotKept on
a store that keeps none; nothing changes on a refusal.

symbols.name: PutStamped
symbols.doc: PutStamped is Put, with what the write says about the version it makes.

symbols.name: Replace
symbols.doc:
Replace stores v over the document already under its key: DocumentNotFound
when there is none, so a document deleted meanwhile is never brought back.

symbols.name: ReplaceStamped
symbols.doc:
ReplaceStamped is Replace, with what the write says about the version it
makes.

symbols.name: Restore
symbols.doc:
Restore brings the document trashed under key back exactly as it was —
the same JSON, the same current version — files it again and calls
OnWrite. DocumentNotTrashed when no document is trashed under key,
UniqueKeyTaken when another document took one of its unique keys
meanwhile, DocumentUndecodable when it no longer decodes into the store's
type; nothing changes on a refusal.

symbols.name: RewriteVersions
symbols.spelled: func(key string, fn func(former []coredocstore.VersionValue) ([]coredocstore.VersionValue, error)) error
symbols.canonical: func(key string, fn func(former []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.VersionValue) ([]github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.VersionValue, error)) error
symbols.doc:
RewriteVersions rewrites the former versions of the document stored under
key — every version but the current one, which is the document and which
only a write changes — in one durable write, under the writers' lock. fn
receives copies of them, newest first, and returns those to keep, in the
same order: it may drop a version, and change the document one holds and
what its writer said, and nothing else — VersionsRewriteRefused for a
version it was not given, out of order, made at another instant or that is
not JSON. An error from fn is returned as it is and changes nothing. It
calls no hook: the document did not change.

It is what an erasure needs: the former versions cleared as the document
is, or dropped. fn runs under the writers' lock, like Update's.

symbols.name: Stats
symbols.doc:
Stats reports what the store holds and where its overlay stands. It answers
after Close too, with the state the store closed in.

symbols.name: Tombstones
symbols.doc:
Tombstones returns every document in the trash, in key order: its key and
the instant it was trashed. It reads every document's versions, as List
reads every document.

symbols.name: Trash
symbols.doc:
Trash moves the document stored under key to the trash, in one durable
write under the writers' lock: it leaves every read and its index keys
are freed, while its versions are kept beside the trashed document and
the instant it was trashed. It calls OnDelete. DocumentNotFound when no
document is stored under key, VersionsNotKept when the store keeps no
versions: only a store that keeps versions has a trash.

symbols.name: Update
symbols.spelled: func(key string, fn func(*T) error) (T, error)
symbols.canonical: func(key string, fn func(*T) error) (T, error)
symbols.doc:
Update applies fn to a copy of the document stored under key and stores the
result, atomically with respect to every other write. An error from fn is
returned as it is and changes nothing, and so does a result whose key is not
key (DocumentKeyChanged). It returns the stored result.

fn runs under the writers' lock: it may read this store, and must not write
to it — the write would wait for the lock fn holds, forever.

symbols.name: UpdateStamped
symbols.spelled: func(key string, stamp coredocstore.StampValue, fn func(*T) error) (T, error)
symbols.canonical: func(key string, stamp github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/docstore.StampValue, fn func(*T) error) (T, error)
symbols.doc:
UpdateStamped is Update, with what the write says about the version it
makes.

symbols.name: Version
symbols.doc:
Version returns the version numbered number of the document stored under
key, VersionNotFound when the document keeps none of that number — never
made, or pruned — and what Versions returns otherwise.

symbols.name: VersionWeight
symbols.doc:
VersionWeight reports what the store keeps beyond its documents — its
former versions, its trashed documents and the bytes of their JSON — as
core/data/docstore.VersionWeigher says. It reads the counter every
write moves, which Stats also reports, and no document.
VersionsNotKept on a store that keeps none, StoreClosed after Close.

symbols.name: Versions
symbols.doc:
Versions returns the versions the store keeps of the document stored under
key, newest first: the current one — the document as it is now — then the
former ones; a document in the trash answers the versions it kept, the
trashed document first. It returns DocumentNotFound when no document is
stored or trashed under key, and VersionsNotKept when the store keeps no
versions.

symbols.name: Consume
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, broker corequeue.Broker, cfg ConsumerConfig) error
symbols.doc:
Consume runs cfg.Handler against broker until ctx is done.

It is the third column of ADR 0053's frontier made concrete: the handler
runs on a goroutine this function owns, not on the publisher's, and it runs
in a different process from the publisher whenever the broker is a durable
one. Publish returned long ago and knows nothing about any of this.

It returns nil when ctx ends — a cancelled consumer is a stopped consumer,
not a failed one — and returns the broker's error when the BROKER fails,
because a queue whose storage has stopped answering is not something a
consumer can poll its way out of. A HANDLER's error is never returned: it
is nacked, retried, and eventually dead-lettered, which is the entire point
of the domain.

Every worker returns before Consume does, so a caller that cancels and
waits knows no handler is still running.

# A stop hands back what it did not do (kitsunium/sdk#474)

When ctx ends, a worker leases nothing more. The message its handler is
running gets [ConsumerConfig.DrainTimeout] to finish before the handler's
context is cancelled; what finishes is acknowledged, and what the stop cut
short is handed back through the broker's [corequeue.Releaser] — receivable
at once, its delivery not counted — as is every message of the batch the
handler never started. A broker without the sibling is nacked instead. Each
of those outcomes is sent past the stop, on ctx without its cancellation,
bounded by [ConsumerConfig.SettleTimeout] on the consumer's clock, so a
caller's stop budget must cover DrainTimeout plus SettleTimeout.

# A handler says when to try again (ADR 0183)

A failure the handler marked with [corequeue.RetryAfter] is handed back
through the broker's [corequeue.DelayedNacker] with the delay it names,
its delivery counted as a nack counts it; a broker without the sibling is
nacked, and the message waits the policy's retry delay instead.
[corequeue.DoNotRetry] wins over it, and a failure a stop cut short is
handed back uncounted, as any other is.

# A handler ends before its lease does

The handler's context is cancelled a margin before the lease it runs under
ends — a tenth of the lease, at most SettleTimeout, read on the consumer's
clock, which must be the broker's — with [corequeue.LeaseExpired] as its
context.Cause: past that instant the broker may hand the message to
another consumer. A message of a batch whose lease is already within that
margin when its turn comes is never started; it is handed back like the
batch a stop interrupts. With [ConsumerConfig.AutoExtend] the lease is
renewed instead, through the broker's [corequeue.LeaseExtender].

A renewal the handler makes itself is not one Consume sees: the bound
stays the lease the handler was handed, and the outcome is reported on
that lease's receipt, which the renewal voided. So a handler that
extends its own lease returns right after — parking its message, as
the mail spool does, which the void receipt's LEASE_EXPIRED leaves
parked — and a handler that must run longer than its lease sets
AutoExtend and does not extend it itself.

symbols.name: ConsumerConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{Handler corequeue.Handler; Clock clock.Timed; PollInterval time.Duration; Parallelism int; BatchSize int; SettleTimeout time.Duration; DrainTimeout time.Duration; AutoExtend bool; HandlerIsIdempotent bool}
symbols.canonical: struct{Handler github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.Handler; Clock github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/clock.Timed; PollInterval time.Duration; Parallelism int; BatchSize int; SettleTimeout time.Duration; DrainTimeout time.Duration; AutoExtend bool; HandlerIsIdempotent bool}

fields.name: Handler
fields.doc: Handler processes one delivery. It must be non-nil.

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock drives the idle wait, the handler's lease bound, the drain, the
bound on each outcome and the lease renewals. Nil means clock.System.

Nothing in this package calls time.Sleep; an idle worker waits through
Waiter.After and a cancelled context wakes it immediately.

A lease's end is the broker's instant and is read on this clock, so it
must be the broker's: a test drives both with one ManualClock. A lease
that already looks ended on this clock the moment it is received —
two clocks that disagree — is not bounded at all, as before the bound
existed, rather than never run.

fields.name: PollInterval
fields.doc:
PollInterval is how long a worker waits after finding the queue empty.
Zero means [DefaultPollInterval]; negative is read as zero.

When the broker is a [corequeue.Waker] — every broker in this package
is — it is an upper bound and not a cadence: a Publish or a Nack in
this process wakes the worker at once, and a retry delay ending or a
lease lapsing wakes it at that instant. What is left for the poll to
find is a publication another process made into a durable queue, so set
it to how late such a message may be noticed — seconds, not
milliseconds, is the usual answer — and an idle consumer then costs
nothing between polls.

fields.name: Parallelism
fields.doc:
Parallelism is how many independent workers run. Each one polls, leases
and processes on its OWN goroutine, which is what makes this the
consumer's goroutine rather than the publisher's.

Non-positive is clamped to 1: one worker is what a caller who did not
think about concurrency wants, it is never wrong, and there is nothing
here for the SDK to invent.

Above 1 there is NO ordering left, in any sense.

fields.name: BatchSize
fields.doc:
BatchSize is how many messages one worker leases per poll. Non-positive
is clamped to 1.

Above 1 a worker processes its batch SEQUENTIALLY, so the extra
messages are held under a lease they are not yet being worked on: a
batch of 50 with a 30-second visibility timeout gives the last message
30 seconds minus the other 49's processing time. Batch for throughput
against a durable broker, where one poll is a directory read; do not
batch to get parallelism, which is what Parallelism is.

A message whose lease has run down to the margin [Consume] keeps
before its turn comes is not started: it is handed back uncounted
and leased again by a later poll — or, with AutoExtend, renewed
before it starts.

fields.name: SettleTimeout
fields.doc:
SettleTimeout bounds each outcome a worker reports once ctx has
ended — an acknowledgement, a nack, a rejection or a release — and
each lease renewal AutoExtend sends. Zero means
[DefaultSettleTimeout]; negative is read as zero.

Every outcome is sent on the consumer's context WITHOUT its
cancellation, so a stop landing between a handler's return and its
acknowledgement does not abandon it (kitsunium/sdk#472) and a batch a
stop interrupts is still handed back. That is what needs a bound: a
medium that stopped answering would otherwise hold the stop forever.
It runs on Clock, from the instant ctx ends — while the consumer
runs an outcome is not timed, and nothing but the worker waits on
it. An outcome the bound cut short is QueueBackendFailed, which a
stopping consumer reads as its stop, not as a failure.

It also caps the margin a handler is stopped by before its lease
ends: a tenth of the lease, at most this.

fields.name: DrainTimeout
fields.doc:
DrainTimeout is how long the message a worker is handling when ctx
ends may still run before its handler's context is cancelled — River's
SoftStopTimeout. Zero cancels it at once, which is what a stop always
did; negative is read as zero.

A handler that finishes inside it is acknowledged; one the drain cut
short is handed back uncounted, through the broker's
[corequeue.Releaser]. No new message is leased once ctx has ended,
and the lease bound still applies: a drain never keeps a handler past
the margin before its lease ends. Measured on Clock. A caller's stop
budget — a lifecycle component's — must cover it plus SettleTimeout.

fields.name: AutoExtend
fields.doc:
AutoExtend renews the lease of the message a handler is running, a
third of the lease after it was granted or last renewed, for as long
as the handler runs — the heartbeat of SQS, JetStream's in-progress
acknowledgement, Temporal's activity heartbeat. A message of a batch
whose lease is a third spent when its turn comes is renewed before
its handler starts. Each renewal is as long as the lease the broker
first granted, and is bounded by SettleTimeout.

It needs the broker's [corequeue.LeaseExtender]; without it, or when
false, the lease is never renewed and the handler is stopped a margin
before it ends. A renewal the broker refuses — the lease lapsed, the
medium failed — cancels the handler's context with that refusal as
its cause: its work is now a duplicate in the making.

A renewal replaces the receipt, and the engine acknowledges with the
newest one. So a handler that extends its own lease — parking its
message, as the mail spool does — must leave AutoExtend false: the
receipt it holds is void after the first renewal.

fields.name: HandlerIsIdempotent
fields.doc:
HandlerIsIdempotent asserts, IN CODE, that Handler is safe to run more
than once for the same message.

It must be true. Its zero value is false and is REFUSED
([corequeue.ConsumerMisconfigured]), and that refusal is the domain's
one piece of deliberate ceremony.

The reason is that this queue delivers AT LEAST ONCE and cannot do
otherwise. A consumer that dies between finishing the work and
acknowledging it has done the work and not said so, and the message
comes back — that is not a bug to be fixed, it is the only honest
behaviour available to a queue whose consumers can die. Exactly-once
delivery does not exist over a transport; what exists is at-least-once
plus an idempotent consumer, and the second half is the caller's.

The SDK cannot check it, so it makes the caller assert it where a
reviewer will see it. It is precisely
resilience.HedgeConfig.Idempotent's instrument, for precisely its
reason, and it has the same useful side effect:
`grep -rn HandlerIsIdempotent` enumerates every place in a codebase
where somebody promised this.

symbols.doc:
ConsumerConfig configures [Consume]: what to run, how many of it, how often
to look, and the one thing about the handler the SDK cannot check for
itself.

Every field except Handler and HandlerIsIdempotent is CLAMPED, so a caller
with no opinion writes two fields and gets a correct consumer. The zero of
each field added since — DrainTimeout, AutoExtend — is what Consume did
before it existed.

symbols.name: DefaultPollInterval
symbols.doc:
DefaultPollInterval is how long an idle worker waits before asking again,
when [ConsumerConfig.PollInterval] is left at zero.

It is a CLAMP and not a refusal (ADR 0031): its zero has one reading — "you
did not think about polling" — and 100 ms is defensible for every queue,
because it bounds idle latency at a tenth of a second while costing one
directory read per worker per tenth of a second. A caller who cares picks
their own.

Every broker in this package is a [corequeue.Waker], so for them it bounds
only what a wake cannot see — a publication made by ANOTHER process into a
durable queue — and a caller that has no such producer can raise it a
hundredfold. It stays at 100 ms because a zero must keep meaning what it
always meant for a broker that cannot wake anyone.

symbols.name: DefaultSettleTimeout
symbols.doc:
DefaultSettleTimeout bounds one acknowledgement, nack, rejection or release
[Consume] sends once its context has ended, and one lease renewal, when
[ConsumerConfig.SettleTimeout] is left at zero.

It is a CLAMP and not a refusal (ADR 0031): its zero has one reading — "you
did not think about how long the medium may take to record an outcome" —
and five seconds is far above what a flush-free rename or one indexed
statement costs while still letting a stop end when the medium has stopped
answering. It is also the most a handler is stopped early by: the margin
kept before a lease ends is a tenth of the lease, at most the
SettleTimeout in force.

symbols.name: FileConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{Clock clock.Clock; Dir string; Policy corequeue.PolicyValue}

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock reads time. It is the narrow half of kernel/clock because this
broker never waits: a lapsed lease is noticed by the next Receive, not
by a timer.

Injecting a ManualClock makes every deadline in a SINGLE-process test
instant. It cannot make a cross-process test instant, and that
asymmetry is not an oversight: a lease deadline is a wall-clock instant
written into a filename precisely so that another process can read it,
and another process does not share this one's fake clock. The
consumer-death test therefore waits on the real clock, and says so.

Nil means clock.System.

fields.name: Dir
fields.doc:
Dir is the queue directory. It is created owner-only when absent, and
refused when it exists and any account outside the owner and group
could replace its entries. Its three state directories are held to the
same rule — created owner-only, checked when somebody else made them —
and refused besides when one is a symlink or not a directory at all.
On Windows "owner-only" is not something a mode can say: a directory
inherits its parent's access control list, and the rule reads that list
instead (dirtrust_windows.go).

Two brokers over one Dir — in one process or in two — are ONE queue.
That is the domain's inter-process claim, and it is the whole reason
the directory is the configuration rather than an implementation
detail.

fields.name: Policy
fields.doc:
Policy is the delivery discipline. Its zero value is refused; see
core/data/queue.PolicyValue.

symbols.doc:
FileConfig configures [NewFile]: which directory holds the queue, which
clock reads its deadlines, and what delivery discipline it enforces.

Its Policy's zero value is refused at construction — see
core/data/queue.PolicyValue — and so is a directory whose entries any account
could replace.

symbols.name: MaxSQLTableLen
symbols.doc:
MaxSQLTableLen is the longest table name [NewSQL] and [SQLMigration] accept,
in bytes: PostgreSQL's identifier limit. The broker derives no table from
it, so the whole limit is the caller's.

symbols.name: MemoryConfig

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock reads time. A memory broker never WAITS — expiry is noticed on
the next Receive — so it asks for the narrow half of kernel/clock and
a test can drive every deadline in this package with a ManualClock and
no sleeping at all.

Nil means clock.System.

fields.name: Policy
fields.doc:
Policy is the delivery discipline. Its zero value is refused; see
core/data/queue.PolicyValue.

symbols.doc:
MemoryConfig configures [NewMemory]: which clock reads its deadlines, and
what delivery discipline it enforces.

Its Policy's zero value is refused at construction through the SAME guard
[NewFile] runs, which is what makes this broker an honest double for that
one.

symbols.name: NewFile
symbols.doc:
NewFile returns a broker whose messages survive the process that published
them.

# Why internal/service/data/vfs, and where it stops

The durable publication of a message is exactly what corevfs.AtomicWriter
promises: a temporary in the same directory, the payload, an fsync of the
FILE, a rename, an fsync of the DIRECTORY — five steps whose failure paths
ADR 0056 tested by injecting a failure at each one and comparing the
destination's hash. Rewriting that here would be eighty lines of subtle
code duplicating something the SDK merged, measured and proved, and the
first thing to rot would be the failure paths, which are the only part that
matters.

It stops at corevfs.WritableFS, which has WriteFile, MkdirAll, Remove and
RemoveAll and NO RENAME. That is not an oversight in vfs and it is not
worked around here: the port is FROZEN (ADR 0039), so adding a fifth method
to carry this domain's state machine would break every downstream
implementation at compile time. The state transitions therefore go through
os.Root directly, which confines them to the queue directory by the same
mechanism vfs itself uses, and the boundary between the two is exactly the
boundary between "publish a whole file" and "move one".

It refuses, at construction rather than at first use: a policy it cannot
honour ([corequeue.QueueMisconfigured]), a directory it cannot use safely
([corequeue.QueueDirectoryUnusable]), and a platform with no atomic replace
or no flushable directory handle — core/proc.UnsupportedPlatform, raised by
internal/service/data/vfs.NewOS and passed through unmodified (ADR 0018).

symbols.name: NewMemory
symbols.doc:
NewMemory returns an in-process broker holding its messages in the heap.

It refuses a policy it cannot honour at CONSTRUCTION rather than at first
use, through the same core/data/queue.PolicyValue.Validate the file broker runs
— which is what makes this an honest double for it.

symbols.name: NewSQL
symbols.doc:
NewSQL returns a broker whose queue is one table of the caller's database,
created by [SQLMigration]. It sends no statement: everything decidable
without a database is decided here.

It refuses, at construction rather than at first use, a policy it cannot
honour (core/data/queue.QueueMisconfigured) and a transactor, dialect or table it
cannot use ([corequeue.SQLQueueMisconfigured]).

symbols.name: SQLConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{Transactor coresql.Transactor; Clock clock.Clock; Table string; Policy corequeue.PolicyValue; Dialect coresql.Dialect; Trail bool}
symbols.canonical: struct{Transactor github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.Transactor; Clock github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/clock.Clock; Table string; Policy github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/queue.PolicyValue; Dialect github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.Dialect; Trail bool}

fields.name: Transactor
fields.doc:
Transactor is the transaction manager of the database the queue lives
in — the one the caller's own transactions are opened with, so a call
made under one of them joins it. It must also be a core/data/sql Joiner and
Deferrer, which the SDK's own transactor is: the first is how a
publication joins the caller's transaction, the second how it wakes a
consumer only once that transaction has committed.

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock stamps every instant the broker writes — a message's visibility,
a lease's deadline, a dead letter's failure — and reads the instant a
lease is judged against. Nil means clock.System.

The instants are the BROKER's, never the database's NOW(): a test
drives every deadline with a ManualClock, as it does the other two
brokers'. Brokers in several processes over one table compare
instants their own clocks wrote, so those clocks must agree to within
the precision a lease needs — as they must for the file broker.

fields.name: Table
fields.doc:
Table names the queue's one table, which [SQLMigration] creates. It is
a lower-case SQL identifier of at most [MaxSQLTableLen] bytes, holds no
three underscores in a row — docstore's derived tables do — and does
not start with "sqlite_".

Two brokers over one database and one Table — in one process or in
twenty — are ONE queue, as two file brokers over one directory are.

fields.name: Policy
fields.doc:
Policy is the delivery discipline. Its zero value is refused; see
core/data/queue.PolicyValue.

fields.name: Dialect
fields.doc:
Dialect is the engine's, and must be the Transactor's own: the SQL the
broker speaks to it.

fields.name: Trail
fields.doc:
Trail makes the broker keep a dead letter's trail
(core/data/queue.DeadLetterValue.Trail) in the table's trail column,
which [SQLMigration] creates and [SQLTrailMigration] adds to a table an
earlier SQLMigration created: run that migration before setting it.
Unset, the broker sends the statements it sent before the column
existed, and a dead letter it buries or reads has no trail.

symbols.doc:
SQLConfig configures [NewSQL]: the database the queue lives in, its table,
which clock stamps its instants, and what delivery discipline it enforces.
Transactor, Dialect and Table are required, and Policy's zero value is
refused as it is for every broker.

symbols.name: SQLMigration
symbols.spelled: func(dialect coresql.Dialect, table string, version uint64) (coresql.MigrationValue, error)
symbols.canonical: func(dialect github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.Dialect, table string, version uint64) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.MigrationValue, error)
symbols.doc:
SQLMigration returns the migration that creates the one table an SQL queue
named table keeps on dialect, as a core/data/sql MigrationValue numbered version,
for the caller's Migrator to run under the caller's version table. Its Down
drops the table, and every message in it — queued, leased and dead.

The SDK numbers nothing: a migration is a value its consumer constructs
(ADR 0055 §D12), and only the consumer knows where the queue's table sits in
its own history. Its one statement does nothing when the table already
exists — or is already gone — so applying it over a table a previous
deployment made changes nothing (ADR 0151). The table it creates has the
trail column SQLConfig.Trail writes; one an earlier release created gets
it from [SQLTrailMigration].

symbols.name: SQLTrailMigration
symbols.spelled: func(dialect coresql.Dialect, table string, version uint64) (coresql.MigrationValue, error)
symbols.canonical: func(dialect github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.Dialect, table string, version uint64) (github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.MigrationValue, error)
symbols.doc:
SQLTrailMigration returns the migration that adds the nullable trail
column, where a broker with SQLConfig.Trail keeps a dead letter's trail,
to the table an SQL queue named table keeps on dialect, as a
core/data/sql MigrationValue numbered version, beside the one
[SQLMigration] returns. The rows already there keep their columns as
they are, and their dead letters read back with no trail.

It does nothing when the table has the column — SQLMigration creates it
with one — or when there is no table, so it may run before or after
SQLMigration and twice over one table. Its Down drops the column, and
every trail in it, when the table has one: unset SQLConfig.Trail before
running it. SQLite drops a column from version 3.35 on.

symbols.name: Config
symbols.spelled: struct{DB *stdsql.DB; Dialect coresql.Dialect; Pool PoolConfig; Clock clock.Timed; CheckTimeout time.Duration}
symbols.canonical: struct{DB *database/sql.DB; Dialect github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.Dialect; Pool github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/service/data/sql.PoolConfig; Clock github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/clock.Timed; CheckTimeout time.Duration}

fields.name: DB
fields.doc:
DB is the caller's pool. REQUIRED — this package never opens one,
because opening one means importing a driver (ADR 0055 §D2).

fields.name: Dialect
fields.doc:
Dialect selects the SQL grammar. REQUIRED and must be a dialect this
SDK can spell; resolve a configuration string through
core/data/sql.ParseDialect, which refuses the engines it cannot support BY
NAME instead of guessing.

fields.name: Pool
fields.doc: Pool is the connection-pool policy, applied to DB at construction.

fields.name: Clock
fields.doc:
Clock is the time source every budget in this package is read from. A
nil Clock falls back to clock.System.

clock.Timed rather than clock.Clock because this package both stamps
(the version table's applied_at) and WAITS (the probe budget, the lock
retry). Reading package time instead would make every budget assertion
a sleep, and a sleep a tolerance, and a tolerance a flake.

fields.name: CheckTimeout
fields.doc:
CheckTimeout is the budget one [core/data/sql.Checker.Check] gets. A
non-positive value clamps to [DefaultCheckTimeout].

symbols.doc:
Config parameterises every constructor in this package: the caller's pool,
the dialect whose grammar the SDK will speak to it, the pool policy applied
at construction, the time source every budget is read from, and the health
probe's budget.

It is passed BY VALUE on purpose. A constructor must not be able to observe
a later mutation of the caller's struct, and the copy happens once per port
rather than once per statement.

symbols.name: DefaultCheckTimeout
symbols.doc:
DefaultCheckTimeout is the liveness-probe budget a non-positive
[Config.CheckTimeout] clamps to. A health check that can hang forever is
not a health check.

symbols.name: DefaultLockRetryInterval
symbols.doc:
DefaultLockRetryInterval is how often a blocked runner retries the
non-blocking lock acquisition. A non-positive
[MigrateConfig.LockRetryInterval] clamps to it.

symbols.name: DefaultLockTimeout
symbols.doc:
DefaultLockTimeout is the migration-lock budget a non-positive
[MigrateConfig.LockTimeout] clamps to.

A migration run that waits forever for another holder is a deployment that
hangs with no output, which is strictly worse than one that fails and says
why. Two minutes is longer than almost every migration and shorter than
every deployment timeout that would otherwise kill the pod first.

symbols.name: DefaultMaxIdle
symbols.doc:
DefaultMaxIdle is the idle-connection ceiling a non-positive
[PoolConfig.MaxIdle] clamps to — the same value database/sql itself uses, so
the clamp changes nothing a caller could have observed.

symbols.name: DefaultMaxLifetime
symbols.doc:
DefaultMaxLifetime is the connection lifetime a non-positive
[PoolConfig.MaxLifetime] clamps to.

database/sql reads 0 as "reuse a connection forever", and a connection that
lives forever survives a failover, a DNS change and a credential rotation —
it keeps talking to a replica that has been demoted, and nothing in the
application ever notices. The exact number matters far less than its being
FINITE, so this is a clamp rather than a refusal (ADR 0031): thirty minutes
is long enough to be invisible on the hot path and short enough that a
topology change is picked up without a restart.

symbols.name: DefaultVersionTable
symbols.doc:
DefaultVersionTable is the table an empty [MigrateConfig.VersionTable]
clamps to. The name matches the de-facto convention of every migration tool
in the ecosystem, so an operator inspecting a database recognises it without
being told.

symbols.name: FileLockSQL
symbols.doc:
FileLockSQL renders the statement that makes a SQLite transaction take the
database file's write lock at once, where BEGIN — which database/sql sends
as SQLite's deferred form — takes none.

It is a DELETE that matches no row. SQLite starts the write transaction a
write statement needs when the statement STARTS, before its WHERE clause is
weighed, so the lock is taken and nothing is changed (ADR 0140). Two
transactions take it: the migration runner's, naming its version table —
the one table it knows exists at that point, since it creates it first in
the same transaction — and the queue's lease, naming its queue's table
before its first read, so the read cannot answer from a snapshot the update
after it would be refused for.

table is interpolated exactly as given — bare, as the runner's validated
version table is, or already quoted, as the queue's is — and must have been
validated at construction, which is the whole defence of an interpolated
identifier.

symbols.name: MigrateConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{Migrations []coresql.MigrationValue; VersionTable string; LockTimeout time.Duration; LockRetryInterval time.Duration}
symbols.canonical: struct{Migrations []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/data/sql.MigrationValue; VersionTable string; LockTimeout time.Duration; LockRetryInterval time.Duration}

fields.name: Migrations
fields.doc:
Migrations is the complete set this binary carries. Order does not
matter — the runner sorts by Version — but every entry must be valid
and no two may share a version.

It is COPIED at construction, so a caller appending to their slice
afterwards cannot change what the runner will apply.

fields.name: VersionTable
fields.doc:
VersionTable names the bookkeeping table. Empty clamps to
[DefaultVersionTable]; anything that is not a bare SQL identifier is
REFUSED, because it is interpolated rather than bound.

fields.name: LockTimeout
fields.doc:
LockTimeout bounds the wait for the advisory lock. Non-positive clamps
to [DefaultLockTimeout].

fields.name: LockRetryInterval
fields.doc:
LockRetryInterval is how often the non-blocking acquisition is retried
while another holder has the lock. Non-positive clamps to
[DefaultLockRetryInterval].

symbols.doc:
MigrateConfig parameterises [NewMigrator].

It carries no directory, no file pattern and no naming convention, and the
SDK ships no example migration tree. Migrations are values the consumer
builds, because the moment the SDK reads a directory it has invented a
convention every consumer must adopt (ADR 0055 §D8).

symbols.name: NewChecker
symbols.doc:
NewChecker returns a bounded liveness probe over cfg.DB.

Like [NewTransactor] it applies cfg.Pool, so a process whose only SQL port
is a health check still gets its pool policy installed.

symbols.name: NewMigrator
symbols.spelled: func(cfg Config, mig MigrateConfig) (runner coresql.Migrator, err error)
symbols.doc:
NewMigrator returns the migration runner for cfg.DB.

Every run is mutually exclusive across processes, and the lock is one its
holder's death releases: the session's advisory lock on PostgreSQL and
MySQL (ADR 0055 §D7), the database file's write lock on SQLite (ADR 0140).
Running unlocked is never offered as a fallback: a runner that silently
drops mutual exclusion is at its most dangerous in exactly the situation it
exists for — two instances of a deployment starting together.

symbols.name: NewTransactor
symbols.doc:
NewTransactor returns the transaction manager for cfg.DB.

It applies cfg.Pool to the caller's *sql.DB. That is a side effect on a
value the caller owns, and it is deliberate: a pool policy that has to be
installed by a second call is a pool policy someone will forget, and the
consequence of forgetting it (unlimited connections, connections that live
forever) lands on the database rather than on this process.

symbols.name: NewWithheld
symbols.doc:
NewWithheld returns cause withheld: reachable by errors.Is and errors.As,
absent from Error().

symbols.name: PoolConfig
symbols.spelled: struct{MaxOpen int; MaxIdle int; MaxLifetime time.Duration; MaxIdleTime time.Duration}
symbols.canonical: struct{MaxOpen int; MaxIdle int; MaxLifetime time.Duration; MaxIdleTime time.Duration}

fields.name: MaxOpen
fields.doc:
MaxOpen is the hard ceiling on open connections. It is REQUIRED and
must be positive.

database/sql reads 0 as UNLIMITED. "As many connections as the
application happens to want" is a decision made by forgetting a line,
and the consequence lands on the database rather than on the process
that forgot — every replica racing to exhaust one server's
max_connections. No value the SDK could invent is defensible either,
because the right one depends on the server's ceiling divided by the
number of replicas, which the SDK cannot see. So this is the REFUSAL
side of ADR 0031.

fields.name: MaxIdle
fields.doc:
MaxIdle is the number of connections kept warm. A non-positive value
clamps to [DefaultMaxIdle]; a value above MaxOpen clamps DOWN to
MaxOpen, because database/sql does that reduction silently and a caller
reading their own configuration back would otherwise be misled.

fields.name: MaxLifetime
fields.doc:
MaxLifetime is how long a connection may be reused. A non-positive
value clamps to [DefaultMaxLifetime]; see that constant for why an
unbounded lifetime is not an option.

fields.name: MaxIdleTime
fields.doc:
MaxIdleTime is how long an unused connection is kept. A non-positive
value is passed through as "no idle deadline", and that is deliberate
rather than an oversight: MaxLifetime is now always finite, so an idle
connection is already retired on a bounded schedule, and a second
timer would only decide how aggressively to shrink a warm pool — a
tuning choice with no dangerous zero.

symbols.doc:
PoolConfig is the connection-pool policy. It is applied to the caller's
*sql.DB at construction, and it is a POLICY rather than a set of hints: a
field whose zero value database/sql would read as a decision nobody made is
either clamped or refused, never passed through (ADR 0031).

symbols.name: Statements
symbols.doc:
Statements returns a [coresql.Step] that runs stmts in order on the
transaction's executor, stopping at the first failure.

This is the smallest helper that is genuinely useful and deliberately not a
file loader. Reading a directory would mean inventing a filename grammar
(`0001_name.up.sql`? `V1__name.sql`?), a statement splitter, and a rule for
what a `;` inside a string literal means — three conventions the SDK would
impose on every consumer and none of them asked for (ADR 0055 §D8).

Each statement is sent as its own Exec rather than as one semicolon-joined
string, because multi-statement execution is a per-driver capability that
several disable by default, and because a failure then names the statement
that failed by its position in the slice.

The text is the caller's own and is never bound: a migration's DDL cannot be
parameterised on any engine. That is exactly why migrations must not be
built from user input, and why this helper takes a variadic of literals
rather than a template.

symbols.name: Withheld
symbols.doc:
Withheld carries a driver's error for errors.Is and errors.As while keeping
its text out of Error().

A driver describes the row a statement touched. PostgreSQL's unique
violation says "Key (doc_key)=(…) already exists" and MySQL's says
"Duplicate entry '…'": a document store's key is routinely an e-mail
address, and a queue's row holds the caller's payload. So a package whose
rows hold a caller's data joins the driver's error through Withheld, beside
a verdict of its own — errors.Join, never errs.Wrap, so the verdict's code
stays the origin (CLAUDE.md rule 6) — and no rendering of the joined error
quotes a row (ADR 0139 §D7, ADR 0151 §D6). The cause stays one errors.As
away for a caller who knows its driver, and what it may log.

Error() says only what names no row: a context's end, in the context's own
words; otherwise the driver error's Go type, with its SQLSTATE or its result
code when a method offers one — a class of failure, never its subject.

The verdict stays each package's own — docstore's STATEMENT_FAILED, queue's
QUEUE_BACKEND_FAILED — since each package's errors are its own; what they
share is only this rendering of somebody else's.

symbols.name: Error
symbols.doc:
Error renders what can be said without the driver's words: a context's end
in its own words, since those hold no data; otherwise the driver error's Go
type, with its SQLSTATE or its result code when a method offers one.

symbols.name: Unwrap
symbols.doc: Unwrap hands errors.Is and errors.As the driver's own error.

symbols.name: FlateCompressor
symbols.doc:
FlateCompressor is the flate (raw DEFLATE) singleton, registered with
core/data/transform at package load. Binding the registration result to a named
var keeps us clear of init().

symbols.name: GzipCompressor
symbols.doc:
GzipCompressor is the gzip singleton, registered with core/data/transform at
package load. Binding the registration result to a named var is idiomatic and
keeps us clear of init().

symbols.name: NewZlibCompressor
symbols.doc:
NewZlibCompressor returns a zlib Compressor encoding at level, which may be
zlib.DefaultCompression, zlib.HuffmanOnly, or any value from zlib.BestSpeed to
zlib.BestCompression. Anything else — including zlib.NoCompression, which the
stdlib accepts but which stores the payload verbatim — is clamped to
zlib.DefaultCompression, so no configuration can hand back a compressor that
silently does not compress (ADR 0031). The result is NOT registered; the
registry entry is the default-level ZlibCompressor singleton.

symbols.name: ZlibCompressor
symbols.doc:
ZlibCompressor is the zlib singleton, registered with core/data/transform at
package load at the stdlib default level. Binding the registration result to a
named var is idiomatic and keeps us clear of init().

symbols.name: NewMem
symbols.doc:
NewMem returns an empty in-memory filesystem containing only its root.

It takes no arguments on purpose. Every knob it could offer — a clock, a
size cap, a starting tree — would be a knob a consumer's test has to set
before it can assert anything, and the value of this type is that a test
double costs one line.

symbols.name: NewOS
symbols.doc:
NewOS opens root as a confined filesystem.

The refusal order is deliberate. The PLATFORM is checked before the path:
on a GOOS without the mechanics this filesystem needs, no directory would
make it work, and reporting "no such directory" for a name that exists would
send the reader looking in the wrong place entirely.

symbols.name: AllowMethods
symbols.doc:
AllowMethods admits only the named HTTP methods. Passing none admits none:
an allowlist that lost its contents must close, not open.

symbols.name: AllowPaths
symbols.doc:
AllowPaths admits only paths matching one of the patterns.

The patterns are supplied UNANCHORED and this constructor anchors them.
Leaving anchoring to the caller is precisely the omission that turns an
allowlist into a sieve — `/v1/profiles` would otherwise be satisfied by
`/anything/v1/profiles/and/more` — and it is invisible in review.

symbols.name: Client
symbols.doc:
Client performs guarded outbound HTTP calls.

Every request it sends — including one forged through the *http.Client that
HTTP returns — passes through a transport that consults the policy first, so
the client's posture cannot be bypassed by forgetting a check at a call site.

symbols.name: Do
symbols.doc:
Do sends req and returns a fully-read response.

It returns a value rather than an *http.Response so the caller cannot leak a
connection by forgetting to close the body, and so the byte count is known —
which is what lets the observation hook report an accurate size. The hook
fires from the body itself, so a caller using the escape hatch is observed on
exactly the same terms.

symbols.name: Get
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, path string, query url.Values) (resp corenet.ResponseValue, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, path string, query net/url.Values) (resp github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.ResponseValue, err error)
symbols.doc:
Get issues a guarded GET against a path relative to the configured base URL.
The query is encoded here so no call site has to remember to escape it.

symbols.name: HTTP
symbols.doc:
HTTP returns the underlying *http.Client.

The policy still applies: it lives in the transport, so a third-party SDK
handed this client cannot escape it. That is precisely why the check was put
there rather than in Do.

symbols.name: DenyPaths
symbols.doc:
DenyPaths refuses paths matching one of the patterns. A deny is final and is
not overridable by an allow pattern, so a narrow exclusion can be carved out
of a broad allow rule without rewriting it into something unreadable.

symbols.name: New
symbols.spelled: func(cfg corenet.ClientConfig, id corenet.IdentityValue, policy corenet.Policy, hook corenet.CallHook) (c *Client, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(cfg github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.ClientConfig, id github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.IdentityValue, policy github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.Policy, hook github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.CallHook) (c *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/service/net/client.Client, err error)
symbols.doc:
New builds a client from cfg, the TLS identity, the policy and the hook.

A nil policy is refused rather than defaulted to "allow everything": an
unguarded egress path wearing the name of a guarded one is worse than none.

symbols.name: Policies
symbols.doc:
Policies requires every policy to allow the request. Composition is by
conjunction so that adding a policy can only ever narrow what is permitted.

symbols.name: Admission
symbols.doc:
Admission is the pre-handshake admission of ADR 0174 D2: a per-address
budget of connections that have not completed their handshake, checked
before any TLS byte is read, with a reserved budget for declared
addresses so a flood from elsewhere never locks them out. It is safe for
concurrent use, and shared by a [StreamGroup] ([PreHandshake]) and by any
transport that runs its own listener.

symbols.name: Admit
symbols.doc:
Admit counts a new connection from remote against its address's budget.
It returns ok false, counted, when the budget is spent: the caller closes
the connection before reading a byte. Otherwise release, idempotent,
gives the slot back once the handshake completes or the connection ends.

symbols.name: Refused
symbols.doc: Refused counts the connections refused before their handshake.

symbols.name: SetReserved
symbols.doc:
SetReserved replaces the reserved addresses. Each is a host or a
host:port, resolved now; one that does not resolve is given no reserved
budget, never an unkeyed one.

symbols.name: AdmissionConfig

fields.name: PerAddress
fields.doc:
PerAddress caps the connections one IPv4 address, or one IPv6 /64, may
hold before their handshake completes. Default 4.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.doc:
Reserved is the budget of the addresses declared with SetReserved.
Default 8.

symbols.doc:
AdmissionConfig parameterises [NewAdmission]. A zero budget is clamped to
its default, never read as "unlimited" (ADR 0031, clamp half).

symbols.name: Adopt
symbols.doc:
Adopt takes over a socket inherited from a supervisor instead of binding one.

Socket activation is what makes a zero-downtime restart possible: the
supervisor holds the bound socket across the exec, so no connection is lost
and no bind races. The name is the one the unit file publishes in
LISTEN_FDNAMES. Repeat the option to adopt several sockets into one group.

A named socket the supervisor did not pass is SocketAdoptFailed, never a
silent fallback to binding: a service that quietly binds its own port has
lost exactly the property activation exists to provide.

symbols.name: BatchSize
symbols.doc:
BatchSize sets how many datagrams one read attempts to collect. One disables
batching explicitly; zero selects the platform default. Where the platform
cannot batch, State reports the degradation rather than hiding it.

symbols.name: GroupOption
symbols.doc: GroupOption configures a StreamGroup.

symbols.name: HandshakeTimeout
symbols.doc:
HandshakeTimeout bounds the TLS negotiation on a group's listeners.

Unset does NOT mean unbounded here, unlike the other three: the handshake is
the phase a peer can stall before any handler exists to notice, so it falls
back to the domain's default rather than to no bound at all.

symbols.name: IdleTimeout
symbols.doc: IdleTimeout bounds how long a connection may sit with no traffic.

symbols.name: Listen
symbols.doc:
Listen adds an address to a group. It is variadic-friendly by repetition:
calling it twice binds two addresses to the same handler, which is how one
service reaches both a TCP port and a Unix socket.

symbols.name: Loop
symbols.doc:
Loop configures a group's loop engine (ADR 0186 §D5): its backend, its loops
and rings, and its per-connection and pressure bounds. It is judged at Start,
once the group's handler is known: a group served by Handle, HandleFunc or
HandleHTTP, or one with no handler, refuses it with LoopOptionUnsupported,
whichever order the declarations came in. No group is served by a loop yet,
so every group refuses it until the loop engine's entry is published.

symbols.name: MaxConns
symbols.doc:
MaxConns caps how many connections the group serves at once.

The budget is per group, not per socket: a group listening on a TCP port and
a Unix socket, or sharded across several listeners, shares one ceiling —
which is what an operator sizing a server actually means. Beyond it a
connection is accepted and closed immediately with ConnLimitReached, because
a refusal the peer can observe beats a timeout it cannot tell from a hang.
Zero means no ceiling.

symbols.name: MaxHeaderBytes
symbols.doc:
MaxHeaderBytes caps how many bytes net/http reads for one request's line and
header fields. A request over the cap is answered 431 Request Header Fields
Too Large and never reaches the handler.

Unset (or non-positive) keeps net/http's own default, 1 MiB
(http.DefaultMaxHeaderBytes) — which was applying silently before this
option existed. net/http reads a small fixed allowance past the cap before
refusing, so the refusal happens a few kilobytes after n, not at the byte.
It has no effect on a group that does not serve HTTP.

symbols.name: MaxPacketSize
symbols.doc:
MaxPacketSize caps the datagram size a group accepts. A larger datagram is
dropped and counted in State, never delivered as a truncated prefix.

symbols.name: New
symbols.doc: New builds a server.

symbols.name: NewAdmission
symbols.doc: NewAdmission returns an admission with no reserved address.

symbols.name: Option
symbols.doc: Option configures a Server.

symbols.name: PacketGroup
symbols.doc:
PacketGroup is a set of datagram sockets sharing one handler, one middleware
chain and one policy. It mirrors StreamGroup deliberately: the whole point of
the domain is that a UDP service is wired the same way a TCP one is.

symbols.name: Handle
symbols.doc: Handle sets the group's handler, replacing any previous one.

symbols.name: HandleFunc
symbols.doc: HandleFunc sets the group's handler from a plain function.

symbols.name: Name
symbols.doc: Name returns the group's name.

symbols.name: Use
symbols.doc: Use appends middlewares, outermost first.

symbols.name: PreHandshake
symbols.doc:
PreHandshake puts the group's accepted connections under a, before any
TLS byte is read (ADR 0174 D2).

symbols.name: ReadBufferSize
symbols.doc: ReadBufferSize sizes the per-connection scratch buffer handed to the handler.

symbols.name: ReadHeaderTimeout
symbols.doc:
ReadHeaderTimeout bounds the HEADER phase of an HTTP request on its own: the
request line and the header fields must arrive within d of the connection
becoming ready for a request, however long the read timeout lets the body
take.

The header phase is the one a slowloris attack stalls — a few bytes a
second, never finishing a line — and it is also the phase a legitimate
client completes in milliseconds, so it deserves a far shorter bound than a
read timeout sized for an upload. Unset (or non-positive) keeps what the
group did before this option existed: the header phase is bounded by the
read timeout. It has no effect on a group that does not serve HTTP.

symbols.name: ReadTimeout
symbols.doc:
ReadTimeout bounds one read from the peer. On an HTTP group it bounds each
read of a request body, refreshed per read, the header phase unless
ReadHeaderTimeout is set, and the wait for the next request unless
IdleTimeout is.

symbols.name: Server
symbols.doc:
Server owns a set of listener groups and their lifecycle.

It is safe for concurrent use. Declaration-time mistakes — a duplicate group
name, an unusable address — are recorded and returned by Start rather than
panicking or forcing an error check on every declaration, which is what keeps
wiring a server down to a handful of readable lines.

symbols.name: Close
symbols.doc:
Close releases every listener and severs every live connection immediately,
without draining.

symbols.name: Group
symbols.doc:
Group declares a listener group and returns it for handler attachment.

It returns the group rather than (group, error) on purpose: a declaration
error is recorded and surfaced by Start, so the common path stays a single
chained expression instead of an error check per line.

symbols.name: PacketGroup
symbols.doc:
PacketGroup declares a datagram listener group and returns it for handler
attachment. It mirrors Group deliberately: the point of the domain is that a
UDP service is declared the same way a TCP one is.

symbols.name: Serve
symbols.doc:
Serve starts the server and blocks until ctx is cancelled, then drains.

It is the one-call entry point: a caller that has nothing else to do on the
main goroutine writes Serve and gets startup, blocking and graceful shutdown
without assembling them.

symbols.name: Shutdown
symbols.doc:
Shutdown stops accepting and waits for in-flight connections to finish,
severing what remains once ctx expires.

symbols.name: Start
symbols.doc:
Start binds every group's listeners and begins accepting.

It returns once every listener is bound, so a caller that gets a nil error
knows the ports are open — which is what makes a test able to dial
immediately, and a supervisor able to report readiness honestly.

symbols.name: State
symbols.doc: State returns a snapshot of the server's lifecycle and listeners.

symbols.name: Shards
symbols.doc:
Shards sets how many listeners to open on each of the group's addresses.

Several listeners on one address is what SO_REUSEPORT buys: the kernel
load-balances incoming connections across them, so N accept loops never
contend on one accept queue. Zero selects one per core; one disables sharding.
Where the platform or the socket family cannot shard, the count collapses to
one and State reports why rather than staying silent.

symbols.name: StreamGroup
symbols.doc:
StreamGroup is a set of listeners sharing one handler, one middleware chain
and one policy. Grouping exists so a server can expose the same handler on a
TCP port and a Unix socket — or two ports with different TLS identities —
without the caller assembling the wiring twice.

symbols.name: Handle
symbols.doc:
Handle sets the group's handler. A group declares one handler, once: a
second declaration on the same group — Handle, HandleFunc or HandleHTTP, in
any order — does not replace the first, and Start returns HandlerAlreadySet
naming the group (ADR 0186 §D1).

symbols.name: HandleFunc
symbols.doc:
HandleFunc sets the group's handler from a plain function. It exists because
the overwhelmingly common case is one function, and making that case require
a named type would be the papercut that decides whether the API feels light.

symbols.name: HandleHTTP
symbols.doc:
HandleHTTP serves an http.Handler over this group's listeners.

The group keeps its own limits, TLS identity and drain; net/http only does
the protocol. That split is ADR 0029 D3: reimplementing HTTP would mean
owning request smuggling defences, HTTP/2 flow control and HPACK to lose,
not gain, throughput.

symbols.name: Name
symbols.doc: Name returns the group's name.

symbols.name: Use
symbols.doc: Use appends middlewares, outermost first.

symbols.name: TLS
symbols.doc:
TLS turns the group's listeners into TLS listeners, or mutual-TLS ones when
the identity requires a client certificate. One option covers both, so the
two cannot drift apart in configuration.

symbols.name: WithDrainTimeout
symbols.doc:
WithDrainTimeout bounds how long Shutdown waits for in-flight connections
before closing them hard.

symbols.name: WriteTimeout
symbols.doc: WriteTimeout bounds one write to the peer.

symbols.name: AppendComment
symbols.doc:
AppendComment appends a comment frame — a line beginning with ':' that
every client ignores — to dst.

It exists for keep-alive: an idle event stream is indistinguishable from a
dead one to a proxy counting idle seconds, and a comment is the only traffic
the format offers that cannot be mistaken for an event.

symbols.name: AppendEvent
symbols.doc:
AppendEvent appends e's wire form to dst and returns the extended slice.

It appends nothing when the frame is invalid: the whole frame is validated
first (corenet.SSEEventValue.Validate), so a stream never emits a partial
one. Appending rather than returning a fresh slice is what lets a stream
reuse one buffer for its whole life.

symbols.name: DefaultKeepAlive
symbols.doc:
DefaultKeepAlive is the comment cadence a stream uses when the caller sets
none. It sits under the idle timeout of every proxy worth naming — nginx and
most cloud load balancers default to 60 s, some CDNs to 30 — so a stream that
has nothing to say still proves it is alive before anything cuts it.

symbols.name: DefaultWriteTimeout
symbols.doc:
DefaultWriteTimeout bounds ONE frame's write. It is not a budget for the
stream, which by nature has none; it is what stops a peer that has stopped
reading from pinning a goroutine and a socket buffer forever.

symbols.name: KeepAlive
symbols.doc:
KeepAlive sets the interval between keep-alive comments.

Zero does NOT mean "never" (ADR 0031): a stream with keep-alive silently
disabled works perfectly on a developer's loopback and dies at one minute
behind a real proxy, which is the worst possible place to learn it. Zero is
clamped to DefaultKeepAlive; a negative interval is refused, because no value
the SDK invented for it would be defensible. To disable it, say so with
[WithoutKeepAlive].

symbols.name: New
symbols.spelled: func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, opts ...Option) (stream *Stream, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(w net/http.ResponseWriter, r *net/http.Request, opts ...github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/service/net/sse.Option) (stream *github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/service/net/sse.Stream, err error)
symbols.doc:
New starts an event stream on w and returns it.

It writes the response headers and flushes them immediately, so the client's
EventSource opens at once rather than at the first event — which on a stream
whose first event may be minutes away is the difference between working and
appearing hung.

It fails when the response cannot be flushed. That is checked before anything
is written, because a stream that cannot flush is not a slow stream: every
frame sits in the transport buffer until the handler returns, and a handler
that never returns delivers nothing at all.

symbols.name: Option
symbols.doc: Option configures a Stream.

symbols.name: Retry
symbols.doc:
Retry sets the reconnection delay the stream advertises in its opening frame.

It is the server's one chance to control how hard clients come back: a fleet
that all reconnect on the browser default of about three seconds is a
thundering herd aimed at a server that has just restarted. Zero sends no
retry field and leaves the client on its own default.

symbols.name: Stream
symbols.doc:
Stream is one open event stream: an HTTP response held open, written one
frame at a time and flushed after each.

It is safe for concurrent use. That is not decoration — the keep-alive runs
on its own goroutine and shares the response writer with the handler, and a
handler that fans events in from several producers is the normal shape.

symbols.name: Close
symbols.doc:
Close ends the stream and joins its goroutines.

A handler should defer it. Returning from the handler also ends the stream —
net/http cancels the request context — but Close makes the moment explicit
and joins the keep-alive rather than leaving it to notice.

symbols.name: Comment
symbols.doc:
Comment writes a comment frame — ignored by every client — and flushes it.

It is what keep-alive is made of, and it is exported because a caller
sometimes needs to prove liveness at a moment of its own choosing: right
after the headers, or after a long computation it knows took too long.

symbols.name: Done
symbols.doc:
Done returns the channel closed when the stream has ended: the client
disconnected, the server began draining, or Close was called.

A streaming handler selects on it. Send refuses once it is closed as well, so
a handler that only ever calls Send in a loop still terminates — but a
handler that watches this can stop between events instead of discovering it
on the next one.

symbols.name: LastEventID
symbols.doc:
LastEventID returns the id the client says it last processed, or "" for a
fresh connection.

The SDK does NOT replay from it, and the shape of the problem is why. A
replay buffer held by the stream would be useless by construction: a
reconnect is a NEW connection and therefore a new stream, so its buffer is
always empty at exactly the moment a resume needs it. A buffer that outlived
the stream would be an application store — it has to know how many events to
keep, how long they stay valid, and whether replaying them is even safe,
which is a question about the events' meaning and not about the transport.
The honest thing is to hand the cursor to the handler and let it resume from
its own log.

symbols.name: Send
symbols.doc:
Send writes one event and flushes it.

The frame is validated before anything is written, so an unrepresentable
event cannot leave half of itself on a stream the peer is already parsing.

symbols.name: WithoutKeepAlive
symbols.doc:
WithoutKeepAlive disables the keep-alive comment entirely.

It exists so that "never" is something a caller writes on purpose rather than
something a zero value does to them. Reach for it when the stream already
carries traffic more often than any intermediary's idle timeout, or when
there is no intermediary at all.

symbols.name: WriteTimeout
symbols.doc:
WriteTimeout bounds how long one frame's write may take.

It is deliberately per-frame. A group's WriteTimeout is an absolute deadline
for the whole response, which for an endless stream means the stream is cut
at that instant; the stream therefore replaces it with this bound, refreshed
on every frame. Zero is clamped to DefaultWriteTimeout, negative is refused.

symbols.name: Config
symbols.spelled: struct{ContentSecurityPolicy string; ReferrerPolicy string; SinglePageApp bool; Immutable func(name string) bool}
symbols.canonical: struct{ContentSecurityPolicy string; ReferrerPolicy string; SinglePageApp bool; Immutable func(name string) bool}

fields.name: ContentSecurityPolicy
fields.doc:
ContentSecurityPolicy is sent on every response. Empty sends
DefaultContentSecurityPolicy; there is no way to send none. A value
holding a control character is refused at construction.

fields.name: ReferrerPolicy
fields.doc:
ReferrerPolicy is sent on every response: one of the eight tokens the
Referrer Policy specification defines, or a comma-separated list of
them. Empty sends DefaultReferrerPolicy. Any other value is refused at
construction, because a browser ignores a token it does not know and falls back
to its own default, which sends the origin to every site.

fields.name: SinglePageApp
fields.doc:
SinglePageApp serves the root's index.html, with 200, for a path that
has no extension and names nothing in the tree. A path with an
extension that names nothing stays a 404, and so does a directory with
no index.html.

fields.name: Immutable
fields.doc:
Immutable reports whether the file at name — slash-separated, relative
to the root, as served: "assets/app-3f2a9c.js" — is content-hashed, so
